1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at 15:43:12 Eastern Daylight Time (19:43:12 UTC), an uncontained engine failure occurred during the cruise phase of flight. The event transpired at an indicated altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 45 nautical miles west-northwest of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. The geographic coordinates of the event location, as recorded by the aircraft's flight data recorder (FDR), were 39.8421° N latitude and 78.2105° W longitude. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger route.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-700, bearing Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) registration number N737AA. The aircraft was owned and operated by Atlas Air, a certificated air carrier conducting commercial passenger transportation services under a Part 121 operating certificate. The aircraft was configured for a maximum of 149 passenger seats, with a standard two-class cabin layout. At the time of the occurrence, the aircraft was carrying 143 passengers and 6 crewmembers.

1.3 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, which governs the operating requirements for domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. The flight plan was filed for a cruise altitude of Flight Level 330 (FL330), with the aircraft maintaining FL325 at the time of the event. The flight was operating under positive air traffic control (ATC) radar coverage, utilizing standard en route navigation procedures. All communications between the flight crew and ATC were recorded and subsequently transcribed for investigative review. The flight was proceeding normally until the sudden onset of the engine anomaly, which prompted immediate crew response and emergency descent procedures.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Experience
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, number 1847293, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The certificate was issued on March 12, 2009, and was current at the time of the accident. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate, issued on January 15, 2018, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded as 12,482 hours, with 3,215 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The captain's most recent line check was completed on February 28, 2018, with satisfactory performance documented across all evaluated parameters.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Experience
The first officer held an ATP certificate, number 2104881, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The certificate was issued on August 22, 2014, and was current at the time of the accident. The first officer possessed a first-class medical certificate, issued on December 10, 2017, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded as 4,891 hours, with 1,942 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer's most recent proficiency check was completed on January 18, 2018, with all required maneuvers and emergency procedures evaluated as satisfactory.

2.3 Training Records and Recent Flight Experience
Both flight crewmembers completed recurrent training in accordance with the operator's FAA-approved training program. The training syllabus included simulator-based emergency procedures, rapid decompression protocols, engine failure during cruise, and crew resource management (CRM) scenarios. Records indicate that both pilots completed a full-motion simulator session on March 5, 2018, which included uncontained engine failure drills, cabin depressurization response, and emergency descent execution. Duty time records for the 72-hour period preceding the event were reviewed and found to be within the limitations prescribed by 14 CFR Part 121.471. Both crewmembers reported adequate rest prior to the flight, and no fatigue-related factors were identified in the preliminary review of duty logs.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Airframe Specifications and History
The airframe was manufactured by The Boeing Company, serial number 32488, and was delivered to the operator on June 14, 2004. At the time of the event, the aircraft had accumulated 48,210 total flight hours and 31,450 total flight cycles. The airframe was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved by the FAA. The aircraft's weight and balance documentation indicated a takeoff weight of 138,450 pounds, with a center of gravity within the approved envelope. The aircraft was equipped with a standard dual-channel autopilot, dual flight management systems (FMS), and a digital flight data acquisition unit (DFDAU) recording 88 parameters at 1-second intervals.

3.2 Engine Specifications and Maintenance
The left engine was a CFM International LEAP engine, model designation LEAP-1B, serial number 88421. The engine was installed on the aircraft on March 10, 2016, following a scheduled shop visit. At the time of the event, the engine had accumulated 14,200 flight hours and 8,900 flight cycles since new. The engine was maintained in accordance with the manufacturer's maintenance planning document (MPD) and the operator's approved maintenance program. The most recent borescope inspection was performed on February 12, 2018, with no anomalies reported. Oil consumption rates were within manufacturer-specified limits, and vibration monitoring data from the engine health monitoring system (EHMS) showed no exceedances in the 30 days preceding the event.

3.3 Applicable Airworthiness Directives and Service Bulletins
A review of the aircraft maintenance records confirmed compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) and service bulletins (SBs) issued by the FAA and the manufacturer. Relevant ADs pertaining to the LEAP engine fan blade retention system, high-pressure compressor casing, and nacelle attachment points were verified as current. The operator's maintenance tracking system indicated that all mandatory inspections, including cyclic and calendar-based requirements, were completed within the prescribed intervals. No deferred maintenance items or minimum equipment list (MEL) deferrals were active for the left engine or associated systems at the time of departure.

3.4 Cabin Pressurization and Window Systems
The aircraft cabin pressurization system was designed to maintain a maximum cabin altitude of 8,000 feet at the aircraft's maximum certified operating altitude. The system utilized dual outflow valves, automatic pressure controllers, and a manual override capability. The passenger windows were constructed of a dual-pane configuration, with an outer structural acrylic pane and an inner scratch-resistant polycarbonate pane, separated by a sealed air gap. The window assembly was certified to withstand differential pressure loads and impact forces in accordance with 14 CFR 25.783. The emergency oxygen system was configured with chemical oxygen generators located above each passenger row, with a deployment threshold set at a cabin altitude of 14,000 feet.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
At the time of the event, the synoptic weather pattern over the northeastern United States was characterized by a high-pressure system centered over the Mid-Atlantic region. Surface analysis indicated clear skies, light winds, and stable atmospheric conditions. No significant frontal boundaries, convective activity, or severe weather advisories were in effect for the flight route. The aircraft was operating in visual meteorological conditions (VMC) at cruise altitude, with no reported turbulence or wind shear.

4.2 METAR/TAF Data and Pilot Reports
Meteorological aerodrome reports (METAR) and terminal aerodrome forecasts (TAF) from stations along the flight path, including KMDT (Harrisburg, PA) and KPHL (Philadelphia, PA), indicated scattered clouds at 12,000 feet, visibility greater than 10 statute miles, temperature 15°C, dew point 4°C, and wind from 240° at 12 knots. Pilot reports (PIREPs) filed within two hours of the event described light chop at FL320, with no reports of icing, thunderstorms, or significant turbulence. The flight crew did not report any adverse weather conditions prior to the engine failure.

4.3 Atmospheric Conditions at Altitude
Atmospheric sounding data from the nearest upper-air observation station indicated a temperature of -48°C at 32,500 feet MSL, with a pressure altitude of 32,480 feet. The tropopause was located at approximately 38,000 feet, with a stable lapse rate below that level. Wind speed at the event altitude was recorded at 45 knots from 260° true. Relative humidity was less than 10%, and no contrail formation or ice crystal precipitation was observed. The atmospheric conditions were consistent with standard cruise environment parameters and did not contribute to the mechanical failure.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The primary wreckage remained airborne following the event, with the aircraft executing an emergency descent and diverting to a nearby airport. Debris from the left engine was recovered from a linear distribution pattern extending approximately 12 nautical miles along the flight path. Ground search teams, coordinated with local law enforcement and FAA personnel, recovered 47 distinct engine components, including fan blade fragments, nacelle panels, and acoustic liner sections. All recovered items were cataloged, photographed, and transported to a secure examination facility. No ground impact damage or secondary fires were reported.

5.2 Engine Examination Findings
The left LEAP engine was removed from the aircraft and subjected to a detailed teardown inspection. Examination revealed an uncontained failure originating in the fan section. The number 14 fan blade exhibited a fatigue crack initiating at the root fillet, propagating through approximately 65% of the cross-sectional area prior to final separation. The blade separated at 15:43:12 UTC, resulting in secondary damage to the fan case, inlet guide vanes, and forward nacelle structure. The fan case containment ring was breached, allowing high-energy debris to exit the engine envelope. Oil and fuel lines routed along the left side of the engine pylon were severed, resulting in localized fluid leakage. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD) or manufacturing defects was identified in the remaining fan blades or disk assembly.

5.3 Fuselage and Cabin Window Damage
High-velocity debris from the engine failure impacted the left fuselage at station 420, approximately 18 inches aft of the leading edge of the left wing. The impact penetrated the outer skin, creating an irregular aperture measuring 14 inches by 9 inches. The debris trajectory intersected the left-side cabin window at row 14, seat A. The outer acrylic pane was completely fractured and displaced inward, while the inner polycarbonate pane sustained multiple radial cracks but remained structurally intact. The breach resulted in rapid cabin decompression, with the cabin altitude rising from 6,200 feet to 18,500 feet within 12 seconds. The emergency oxygen system deployed automatically, and the outflow valves closed as designed.

5.4 Debris Field Analysis
Recovered debris was analyzed for fracture surface characteristics, material composition, and impact energy. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the fan blade root revealed classic fatigue striations, with a final fast-fracture zone exhibiting ductile tearing. The nacelle panels displayed impact deformation consistent with high-velocity, low-angle strikes. Acoustic liner fragments showed localized delamination and thermal discoloration, indicating brief exposure to high-temperature exhaust gases. All debris items were mapped to their respective engine stations, confirming a single-point failure origin with subsequent secondary fragmentation. No evidence of pre-existing corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, or improper assembly was documented.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Atlas Air maintained a comprehensive safety management system (SMS) in accordance with FAA Advisory Circular 120-92B. The operator's maintenance program utilized predictive analytics, engine health monitoring, and cyclic inspection tracking to identify potential anomalies. Emergency response procedures for uncontained engine failures and rapid decompression were documented in the operator's General Operations Manual (GOM) and Flight Crew Training Manual (FCTM). The operator's quality assurance department conducted quarterly audits of maintenance records, training compliance, and operational procedures. All personnel involved in the maintenance and operation of the aircraft were certified and trained in accordance with company and regulatory requirements.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
A review of historical aviation safety databases identified three prior incidents involving uncontained failures in high-bypass turbofan engines operating under similar cruise conditions. In each case, the failure originated in the fan or low-pressure compressor section, with debris penetration of the nacelle and fuselage. The FAA issued safety alerts and service bulletins following those events, mandating enhanced inspection intervals and revised maintenance procedures. The operator had incorporated all relevant industry recommendations into its maintenance program. No systemic fleet-wide anomalies were identified in the operator's LEAP engine population.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Certification Standards
The aircraft and engine were certified in accordance with 14 CFR Part 21, which establishes the certification procedures for products and parts. The airframe met the structural integrity and damage tolerance requirements specified in 14 CFR 25.571 and 25.365. The cabin window assembly was evaluated against 14 CFR 25.783, which prescribes the design, testing, and performance criteria for fuselage doors and windows, including resistance to impact, pressure differentials, and fire. The engine certification basis included 14 CFR Part 33, which governs airworthiness standards for aircraft engines, including uncontained failure containment requirements. The operator's flight operations were conducted under 14 CFR Part 121, with all crew training, maintenance, and dispatch procedures aligned with the regulatory framework.

6.4 Investigative Coordination and Oversight
The investigation was coordinated by the Investigator in Charge (IIC), who established working groups for operations, maintenance, structures, and human performance. The FAA Principal Inspector assigned to the operator participated in the review of maintenance records, training documentation, and operational procedures. All investigative activities were conducted in accordance with NTSB protocols, with evidence preservation, chain-of-custody documentation, and technical analysis performed by accredited specialists. Data from the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, and engine health monitoring system were downloaded, validated, and cross-referenced with maintenance logs and operational records. The factual information contained in this report is derived from physical evidence, recorded data, regulatory documentation, and certified personnel interviews. No determinations regarding probable cause or contributing factors are included in this document.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the technical examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the NTSB Powerplants and Structures Group in support of the investigation into the in-flight uncontained engine failure and subsequent rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines Co, on April 17, 2018. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered engine components, forward fuselage structural damage, cabin window assembly, and the associated flight data recorder (FDR), cockpit voice recorder (CVR), and quick access recorder (QAR) data streams.

The physical examination of recovered hardware was conducted between May 2 and May 18, 2018, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with supplemental non-destructive inspection (NDI) and metallurgical testing performed at the CFM International Engine Services facility in Evendale, Ohio. All dimensional measurements were recorded in inches and millimeters, with conversions provided per ASTM E380. Material testing adhered to applicable AMS, ASTM, and SAE standards. Flight data parameters were decoded using the manufacturer's proprietary software suite and cross-referenced against the aircraft maintenance manual (AMM) and engine shop manual (ESM) baselines.

The examination was coordinated with representatives from Southwest Airlines Co, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), CFM International, and Boeing Commercial Airplanes. All findings documented herein are strictly factual and derived from direct observation, laboratory testing, and recorded data analysis. No operational, maintenance, or certification conclusions are presented in this report.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft was equipped with a CFM LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engine, serial number 789456-LEAP, installed on the left wing pylon station. The LEAP-1B powerplant features a 22-blade composite fan stage with a titanium leading-edge protection strip, a 10-stage high-pressure compressor, a dual-annular combustor, and a 2-stage high-pressure/7-stage low-pressure turbine configuration. The engine is certified under Title 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart H, with airworthiness approval granted per §21.21 and §33.94 for uncontained failure containment requirements. The certification basis for the engine installation and nacelle structure complies with §25.903 and §25.901, mandating that the nacelle and adjacent airframe structures withstand the impact of a single fan blade release without catastrophic failure.

The specific engine unit had accumulated 28,450 flight cycles and 41,200 flight hours at the time of the event. The last scheduled shop visit occurred 14 months prior, during which the fan module underwent borescope inspection, blade tip clearance verification, and vibration balancing per Southwest Airlines Co maintenance planning document (MPD) revision 42. No deferred maintenance items or engine health monitoring (EHM) exceedances were logged in the 90-day period preceding the incident. The engine was operated within the approved flight envelope, with cruise parameters typically maintained at 89.2% N1, 680°C EGT, and 0.35 inches per second (ips) overall vibration.

The forward fuselage structure at the impact zone consists of 2024-T3 aluminum alloy skin panels, 0.063-inch nominal thickness, reinforced with 7075-T6 extruded stringers and formed frames. The affected cabin window assembly, part number 65-43210-12, is a dual-pane acrylic/polycarbonate laminate with a silicone elastomer perimeter seal, designed to withstand a 12.5 PSI differential pressure load per §25.365. The aircraft was cruising at 32,500 feet MSL at a calibrated airspeed of 285 knots when the uncontained failure occurred.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered engine components focused on the No. 13 fan blade, the titanium containment ring, and the forward nacelle acoustic liner. The No. 13 fan blade was recovered in three primary fragments: root section, mid-span body, and tip segment. The fracture surface exhibited a distinct fatigue origin located 12.4 mm from the leading edge, 8.2 mm above the dovetail root interface. Macroscopic examination revealed a semi-elliptical fatigue crack measuring 14.2 mm in length and 3.8 mm in depth, with pronounced beach marks and ratchet lines indicating progressive crack propagation under cyclic loading. The final fracture zone, occupying approximately 35% of the cross-sectional area, displayed ductile dimpling consistent with tensile overload.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) fractography was performed per ASTM E1508. The fatigue initiation site was characterized by intergranular cracking with localized micro-void coalescence. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis confirmed the absence of foreign material, corrosion products, or coating delamination at the origin. The blade's carbon fiber/epoxy composite matrix was evaluated per ASTM D3039 for tensile strength and ASTM D3410 for compressive strength. Coupon testing of adjacent undamaged blade sections yielded a tensile strength of 1,850 MPa and a compressive strength of 1,120 MPa, both within the CFM International material specification envelope (Spec LEAP-CF-004).

The titanium containment ring (P/N 328-000-000-0, S/N 789456-LEAP-CR) exhibited three circumferential tears, each measuring 45 to 62 mm in length, with localized plastic deformation exceeding 18% strain. Impact gouges were observed at 45° and 135° azimuthal positions, with penetration depths of 2.1 mm and 1.8 mm, respectively. Hardness testing per ASTM E18 (Rockwell C scale) yielded values of 34.2 HRC and 33.8 HRC at the impact zones, consistent with Ti-6Al-4V annealed condition. The ring's energy absorption capacity was calculated at 1.18 x 10^6 ft-lbs, exceeding the minimum design requirement of 9.5 x 10^5 ft-lbs per §33.94(a)(2).

Forward fuselage damage was concentrated between fuselage stations 420 and 480, stringers 12 through 16. The primary breach measured 18.4 inches longitudinally by 24.1 inches vertically, with torn skin edges exhibiting 45° shear lips. The adjacent window frame (P/N 65-43210-12) was displaced 1.2 inches aft and 0.8 inches outward, with the perimeter silicone sealant extruded and fractured. The inner acrylic pane was completely separated, while the outer polycarbonate layer remained partially attached to the frame. Structural fasteners in the impact zone showed evidence of tensile overload, with 12 of 18 rivets sheared at the shank.

Non-destructive inspection of the surrounding skin panels utilized phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) per ASTM E2491 and eddy current testing per ASTM E309. No secondary cracking or delamination was detected beyond a 6-inch radius from the primary breach. Material hardness of the 2024-T3 skin panels averaged 128 HB, within the AMS 4037 specification range. Chemical analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed alloy composition within ±0.5% of nominal values.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder parameters were extracted from the solid-state memory module and decoded using the manufacturer's proprietary software (FDR-DEC v4.2.1). The data stream was sampled at 1 Hz for engine parameters and 4 Hz for flight control and cabin pressure parameters. All timestamps are referenced to UTC.

At 14:32:11.4, the FDR recorded a sudden N1 (fan speed) increase from 89.4% to 108.2%, accompanied by an EGT (exhaust gas temperature) spike from 682°C to 864°C. Simultaneously, the engine vibration parameter (VIB) rose from 0.32 ips to 4.18 ips, exceeding the §33.87 continuous operation limit of 1.5 ips. At 14:32:12.1, N1 decayed rapidly to 62.4%, and N2 (core speed) dropped from 94.1% to 71.3%. Oil pressure decreased from 58 PSI to 12 PSI within 1.8 seconds, while oil temperature increased from 98°C to 142°C. The fuel flow parameter indicated a 22% reduction, consistent with the engine control unit (ECU) entering a degraded mode.

Cabin pressure data recorded a differential pressure drop from 8.4 PSI to 0.0 PSI between 14:32:13.2 and 14:32:15.8. The cabin altitude climb rate peaked at 2,840 ft/min, with the cabin altitude reaching 14,200 ft MSL at 14:32:18.0. The outflow valve position parameter indicated a commanded closure at 14:32:12.5, but the actual valve position remained at 68% open, confirming structural breach-induced pressure equalization.

Quick access recorder (QAR) data was cross-referenced with the aircraft's engine health monitoring system. The QAR logged 14 minor vibration exceedances over the preceding 1,200 flight cycles, all below the 1.0 ips threshold. No maintenance action was triggered per the operator's reliability program. The EHM trend analysis indicated a gradual increase in high-cycle fatigue accumulation on the fan module, with a calculated crack growth rate of 0.0042 mm/cycle over the final 8,000 cycles, consistent with Paris' Law parameters for the composite matrix system.

Cockpit voice recorder audio was synchronized with the FDR timeline. At 14:32:11.8, a loud bang was recorded, followed by a 2.4-second period of high-frequency aerodynamic noise. The master caution and engine fire warning aural alerts activated at 14:32:13.0. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent at 14:32:16.2, with the autopilot disengaged and thrust levers retarded to idle. The CVR captured the rapid decompression alarm and subsequent crew coordination, with no abnormal system warnings prior to the event.

Comparison with normal operational parameters confirms that the engine was operating within certified limits prior to the failure. The N1, EGT, and VIB deviations exceeded the §33.87 and §25.903 design envelopes, indicating an uncontained release event. The cabin pressure decay rate of 2,840 ft/min is consistent with a 18x24 inch fuselage breach at 32,500 ft MSL, as modeled by the Boeing rapid decompression simulation tool (RDS v3.1).

5. SUMMARY

The specialist's examination and data analysis yielded the following factual findings:

1. The No. 13 fan blade of the left LEAP-1B engine (S/N 789456-LEAP) experienced a fatigue fracture originating 12.4 mm from the leading edge, with a crack length of 14.2 mm and depth of 3.8 mm. The fracture surface exhibited progressive fatigue propagation followed by tensile overload.

2. Metallurgical and composite material testing confirmed that the blade matrix and titanium leading-edge protection met CFM International material specifications. No evidence of foreign object damage, corrosion, or manufacturing defects was identified at the fatigue origin.

3. The titanium containment ring sustained three circumferential tears and localized plastic deformation, absorbing an estimated 1.18 x 10^6 ft-lbs of impact energy. The ring's performance exceeded the minimum design requirement per §33.94(a)(2).

4. Debris from the uncontained fan blade release penetrated the forward left fuselage skin between stations 420 and 480, creating an 18.4 x 24.1 inch breach. The adjacent cabin window assembly (P/N 65-43210-12) was displaced and partially separated, with the inner acrylic pane completely detached.

5. Flight data recorder parameters recorded a sudden N1 increase to 108.2%, EGT spike to 864°C, and vibration rise to 4.18 ips at 14:32:11.4 UTC, followed by rapid parameter decay and oil pressure loss. Cabin differential pressure dropped from 8.4 PSI to 0.0 PSI within 2.6 seconds, with a cabin altitude climb rate of 2,840 ft/min.

6. Quick access recorder trend data indicated a gradual increase in high-cycle fatigue accumulation over the final 8,000 flight cycles, with a calculated crack growth rate of 0.0042 mm/cycle. No maintenance exceedances or operational anomalies were logged prior to the event.

7. The aircraft was operating at 32,500 ft MSL and 285 knots calibrated airspeed at the time of failure. All recorded parameters and physical damage patterns are consistent with an uncontained fan blade release event, with subsequent fuselage penetration and rapid cabin decompression.

All measurements, test results, and data interpretations documented in this report are based on direct examination, standardized testing procedures, and manufacturer engineering specifications. No operational, maintenance, or certification conclusions are presented herein.

INTERVIEW OF SARAH JENKINS, LEAD FLIGHT ATTENDANT
Date: May 3, 2018
Time: 10:15 AM EST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Interviewer: Investigator M. Davis, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety
Witness: Sarah Jenkins, Lead Flight Attendant, Southwest Airlines Flight 1380

Q: Good morning, Ms. Jenkins. Thank you for coming in today. I’m Investigator Davis with the National Transportation Safety Board. This interview is being recorded for the official record regarding the incident on Southwest Airlines Flight 1380 on April 17th. Do you understand the purpose of this interview and consent to being recorded?
A: Yes, I do. I understand completely. I’m here to help however I can.

Q: Can you start by telling me your position on the flight and your general duties that day?
A: Sure. I was the lead flight attendant—sometimes we call it the purser—on Flight 1380. I was stationed at the forward galley, door 1L. My main responsibilities were coordinating the cabin crew, handling passenger communications, and overseeing the service flow. We were operating under Part 121, obviously, so everything was pretty standard for a domestic turn. We pushed back from LaGuardia around... I want to say 10:45, maybe 10:50 Eastern. The flight was supposed to be about two hours and fifteen minutes to Dallas Love Field.

Q: Walk me through the flight up until the point of the incident. What were you doing, and what did you observe?
A: Okay. So, we climbed out normally. I did my initial cabin check, made sure everyone was buckled, and then I went back to the forward galley to prep the beverage service. We reached our cruising altitude—I think it was thirty-two thousand, five hundred feet. The captain came on the PA, gave the usual altitude announcement, said we’d be cruising for about an hour and a half. It was a pretty quiet flight. Maybe forty-five minutes in, I was just... I was organizing the carts, checking the manifest, that kind of thing.
Then, at approximately... I don’t know, maybe 11:35? 11:36? I heard this... this incredibly loud bang. It wasn’t like a normal turbulence thump. It was sharp, metallic, almost like a cannon going off right outside the left side of the aircraft. The whole plane shuddered. I mean, violently. I was thrown against the forward bulkhead. My coffee cup just... it went everywhere.
Immediately after the bang, there was this roaring sound. Wind. Just a massive, deafening wind noise. And then the cabin pressure dropped. You could feel it in your ears instantly. The oxygen masks deployed. They just dropped from the overhead panels all at once. I remember seeing the yellow masks swinging, and the cabin lights flickered for a second before the emergency lighting kicked in.

Q: What was your first action after the masks deployed?
A: Standard procedure. I grabbed my own mask first, put it on, and then I started moving down the aisle. I was shouting, “Pull the mask, secure your seatbelt, oxygen is flowing!” You know, the drill. But it was... it was chaotic. There was a lot of screaming. People were crying. The air was freezing, and there was this... this mist, like fog, filling the cabin. I could see debris on the floor near the left side, around row 14 or 15. I didn’t know what it was at the time, just... pieces of plastic, maybe insulation.
I got to row 14, and that’s when I saw it. The window on the left side, seat 14A, was completely gone. Just... shattered. There was a passenger in that seat, a woman, and she was... she was partially pulled toward the opening. The wind was just howling through there. I tried to grab her, but the force was too strong. Another passenger, a man in 14B, he was holding onto her, trying to pull her back. I yelled for him to keep holding on, and I grabbed the jumpseat harness strap to brace myself. I was trying to get a better grip, but the turbulence was severe. The plane was banking hard to the left, descending rapidly.

Q: Did you communicate with the flight deck during this time?
A: Yes. I used the interphone. I called the cockpit, but it was... it was hard to hear over the wind noise. I think I got through to the first officer. I told him we had rapid decompression, a missing window, and a passenger trapped. He acknowledged, said they were initiating an emergency descent and diverting to Philadelphia. I remember him saying something about an engine failure, but I couldn’t make out the details. I just told him we were securing the cabin and doing our best.
After that, I focused on the passengers. I moved down the aisle, checking masks, making sure people were breathing. I had to step over some... some loose panels and what looked like engine cowling fragments near the left aisle. I didn’t know it at the time, but later I learned it was from the left engine. The aircraft was shaking pretty badly, but the pilots kept it under control. We leveled off around... I don’t know, maybe ten thousand feet? The wind noise died down a bit, but the cabin was still freezing.

Q: What happened as you approached Philadelphia?
A: The captain came on the PA. His voice was calm, which helped. He said we were diverting to PHL, that we’d be landing shortly, and to follow crew instructions. I started doing a headcount, checking for injuries. There were a few people with minor cuts from flying debris, but the main concern was the passenger at 14A. We had a nurse on board, and she was helping me. We managed to pull the passenger fully into the cabin, but... she wasn’t breathing. We started CPR right there in the aisle. It was... it was really difficult with the oxygen masks on and the turbulence, but we kept going.
We landed hard. I mean, it was a firm touchdown, but the pilots did an amazing job. We taxied to the gate, and emergency vehicles were already there. I helped coordinate the evacuation, but since we were at a gate, we just opened the doors and let the medics and fire crew take over. They took over CPR immediately. I gave them a quick report, then I started accounting for the rest of the passengers and crew.

Q: You mentioned engine debris. Were you aware of the specific engine type or any maintenance history prior to the flight?
A: No, not really. I’m not a mechanic. I just know we fly 737s. I think the left engine was a... a LEAP-1B? I’ve heard the pilots and maintenance talk about them, but honestly, to me it’s just the number one engine. I didn’t notice anything unusual during the pre-flight walkaround or the cabin checks. Everything seemed normal. Southwest Airlines has a really strict maintenance program, and we follow all the Part 121 requirements to the letter. I’ve never had an issue like this in my twelve years with the company.
After the fact, when I was debriefed, they told me it was an uncontained failure. That’s... that’s a term I’d only heard in training. It means the engine basically came apart. The fan blade fractured, and pieces went everywhere. One of them hit the fuselage, took out the window. It’s... it’s hard to wrap your head around.

Q: How would you describe the overall crew response and adherence to emergency procedures?
A: Honestly, everyone did exactly what we were trained to do. The flight attendants in the back, they secured their stations, checked their passengers, and moved forward when it was safe. The pilots handled the aircraft perfectly. We’ve drilled rapid decompression and emergency descents so many times in the simulator and in recurrent training. It’s muscle memory. But... it’s different when it’s real. The noise, the cold, the panic... it’s overwhelming. But we stuck to the checklist. We communicated, we prioritized, we helped each other.
I think the only thing that could’ve been different is... I don’t know. Maybe if the window had been reinforced differently, but that’s not my area. I just know we followed protocol. SWA’s training is solid. We operate under 14 CFR Part 121, so everything is highly regulated, and it shows. The crew knew their roles.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add that we haven’t covered?
A: Just... I want to make sure the family of the passenger at 14A knows we did everything we could. And I want to thank the pilots. They saved a lot of lives that day. I’m still processing it, to be honest. I’ve been to counseling, and I’m back on reserve, but... it stays with you. If you need any more details, I’m happy to provide them. I just hope this helps prevent it from happening again.

A: Thank you. I appreciate it.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND OVERSIGHT REPORT

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
Reference: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-14-08, Amendment 39-19342; NTSB Safety Recommendation A-19-01 through A-19-04; 14 CFR 25.783; 14 CFR Part 121.344.
NTSB Accident Number: DCA18MA088
Date of Occurrence: April 17, 2018
Docket No.: FAA-2018-0412; NTSB Docket No. 2018-0047
Subject Aircraft: Boeing 737-700, Registration N772SW
Operator: Southwest Airlines Co (SWA)
Engine Type: CFM International CFM56-7B (Incident); Comparative Certification Reference: LEAP-1B engine

2. BACKGROUND
This regulatory compliance report addresses the airworthiness and operational oversight framework applicable to the uncontained engine failure event that occurred on April 17, 2018, involving a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines Co. The aircraft was conducting a scheduled passenger service at flight level 325 when the left engine experienced a catastrophic fan blade separation. Resultant high-energy debris penetrated the fuselage structure and compromised a passenger cabin window, precipitating rapid decompression and the subsequent fatality of one occupant.

The regulatory foundation for this investigation and subsequent compliance mandate is established under 14 CFR Part 25, specifically §25.783, which prescribes the structural integrity, retention, and pressure-sealing requirements for fuselage doors and windows. Additionally, 14 CFR Part 121.344 governs the operator’s Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP), while 14 CFR 121.373 mandates continuing analysis and surveillance of maintenance and inspection programs. Prior to this occurrence, the FAA had issued multiple Airworthiness Directives addressing fan blade inspection intervals, non-destructive inspection (NDI) methodologies, and engine health monitoring (EHM) thresholds. However, the existing regulatory architecture did not explicitly require secondary retention mechanisms for cabin windows subjected to high-velocity, uncontained debris trajectories.

Historical safety recommendations issued by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) following prior uncontained engine events highlighted deficiencies in fatigue life modeling and inspection interval harmonization. While the subject aircraft utilized a CFM56-7B series powerplant, the certification standards for modern high-bypass turbofan engines, including the LEAP-1B engine, have since been updated to incorporate enhanced containment ring specifications and revised debris trajectory analysis. These updated standards serve as a regulatory benchmark for evaluating legacy fleet compliance. Furthermore, comparative operational data from Part 121 cargo and passenger operators, including Atlas Air Inc, demonstrates that integrated EHM systems and predictive maintenance algorithms can significantly reduce the probability of undetected high-cycle fatigue propagation.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the operator’s maintenance records, FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) audit findings, and manufacturer service bulletins reveals that SWA maintained baseline compliance with extant ADs governing fan blade eddy-current inspections. However, the investigation identified material deficiencies in the execution and documentation of ultrasonic phased-array inspections, particularly regarding calibration traceability and technician recency requirements under 14 CFR 121.344(a)(2). The Operator’s CAMP did not adequately account for cumulative fatigue damage accumulation beyond the original type certificate assumptions, resulting in an extended inspection interval that permitted sub-critical crack propagation to reach critical failure thresholds.

Regulatory oversight actions initiated by the FAA Certificate Management Office (CMO) included an immediate ramp inspection, a focused audit of the operator’s reliability program, and a mandatory review of all NDI equipment calibration logs. The audit confirmed that while the operator’s Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for window damage were technically compliant with 14 CFR Part 121, Appendix A, they lacked explicit operational restrictions for dispatch following rapid decompression events or structural penetration. This regulatory gap permitted continued operation under conditions that exceeded the original design envelope for secondary pressure sealing.

The analysis further identifies a systemic deficiency in the application of 14 CFR 25.783 to legacy transport category aircraft. The fuselage window retention standard mandates that windows must withstand specified pressure differentials and impact loads, but it does not explicitly require redundant retention hardware or blast-resistant glazing for passenger cabin windows. In contrast, the type certification basis for newer engine platforms, such as the LEAP-1B powerplant, incorporates revised §25.903 engine containment requirements and updated §25.783 window retention criteria that account for higher-energy debris fields. The absence of retroactive application of these enhanced standards to the Boeing 737-700 fleet represents a measurable gap in the regulatory framework.

Additionally, the investigation determined that the operator’s EHM data integration was not fully synchronized with the FAA’s Safety Assurance System (SAS). While Atlas Air Inc has successfully implemented predictive maintenance protocols that correlate vibration signatures with fatigue life models, the subject operator’s CAMP relied predominantly on time-based inspection intervals rather than condition-based monitoring. This discrepancy underscores the need for regulatory modernization to mandate real-time EHM data sharing and algorithmic fatigue tracking for all Part 121 operators.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings detailed herein, the following corrective actions and compliance mandates are hereby established under the authority of 14 CFR Part 21.99 and 14 CFR Part 121.344:

a. Immediate Implementation of Revised NDI Protocols: Southwest Airlines Co shall amend its CAMP to incorporate mandatory ultrasonic phased-array inspections of all fan blades at intervals not exceeding 1,500 flight cycles. All NDI procedures must comply with FAA Advisory Circular 43.13-1B and be subject to quarterly calibration audits by an FAA-designated repair station. Compliance shall be achieved within 90 calendar days of this directive.

b. Window Retention and MMEL Revision: The Operator shall submit a revised MMEL to the FAA Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) within 60 days, incorporating explicit dispatch restrictions for any cabin window exhibiting structural compromise, seal degradation, or impact damage. The revision must align with the enhanced retention standards outlined in 14 CFR 25.783(c) and include mandatory post-decompression structural integrity verification prior to return to service.

c. EHM Integration and Predictive Maintenance Mandate: Within 180 days, SWA shall implement a condition-based maintenance program that integrates real-time engine vibration, exhaust gas temperature (EGT), and oil debris monitoring data into the FAA’s Safety Assurance System. This program shall utilize algorithmic fatigue life modeling consistent with the certification basis applied to the L1B platform. Quarterly compliance reports shall be submitted to the CMO.

d. Regulatory Oversight and Follow-Up Schedule: The FAA CMO shall conduct biannual audits of the operator’s CAMP, NDI documentation, and EHM data integration protocols. The first audit shall occur no later than 120 days following the effective date of this directive. Non-compliance with any provision herein shall result in immediate suspension of the operator’s airworthiness certificate under 14 CFR 121.373(c) and referral to the Office of Chief Counsel for enforcement action.

e. Industry-Wide Applicability: The FAA shall initiate rulemaking proceedings to amend 14 CFR 25.783 to mandate secondary retention mechanisms for all transport category aircraft cabin windows. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 12 months, with a compliance timeline of 36 months for legacy fleets. Operators shall be required to submit retrofit plans within 90 days of NPRM publication.

This directive supersedes all prior guidance regarding fan blade inspection intervals and window retention standards for the affected fleet. All correspondence, compliance documentation, and audit reports shall be filed under Docket No. FAA-2018-0412. Failure to adhere to the prescribed timelines and technical requirements will result in immediate regulatory enforcement action, including but not limited to certificate suspension, civil penalties, and mandatory operational restrictions.
