Southwest Airlines Jet Diverts After Engine Failure Kills Passenger, Triggers Rapid Decompression

Byline: Marcus Thorne, The National Chronicle
Dateline: PHILADELPHIA, Pa. —

A Southwest Airlines passenger jet carrying 149 people made an emergency landing Tuesday afternoon after a catastrophic engine failure tore through the aircraft’s fuselage, shattering a cabin window and killing one passenger. The Boeing 737-700, en route from New York to Dallas, was forced to divert to Philadelphia International Airport following a sudden loss of cabin pressure at 32,500 feet.

The incident began when the aircraft’s left engine suffered an uncontained failure, a rare mechanical event in which internal rotating components fracture and are violently ejected from the engine casing. High-velocity shrapnel pierced the fuselage and struck a passenger window, causing rapid decompression. The sudden pressure differential pulled one passenger partially out of the aircraft before fellow travelers and flight attendants managed to pull her back inside. Despite immediate medical intervention upon landing, the woman was pronounced dead. Several other passengers sustained minor injuries during the steep, rapid descent to lower altitudes where breathable air is available.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of a passenger and are cooperating fully with federal investigators,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson in a statement released Tuesday evening. “Our crew executed emergency procedures flawlessly, and our priority remains supporting the families affected by this tragedy.” The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched a specialized investigative team to Philadelphia to lead the inquiry. “We are examining the engine, the fuselage damage, and the maintenance records,” said NTSB Chairman Robert Sumwalt during a press briefing. “This is a serious incident, and we will leave no stone unturned.” The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it is working alongside the NTSB and has issued an immediate safety alert to operators of similar aircraft.

The aircraft involved is a 13-year-old Boeing 737-700, a narrow-body jet that has served as a backbone of the commercial aviation industry for decades. Southwest Airlines, the largest operator of the 737 family in the United States, has flown this specific model extensively across its domestic network. The jet was equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, a modern powerplant designed for improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions. The flight departed LaGuardia Airport at 10:43 a.m. ET and was scheduled to arrive in Dallas Love Field by 1:30 p.m. ET. Instead, the flight crew declared an emergency, initiated a controlled rapid descent, and touched down in Philadelphia just 13 minutes after the initial mechanical failure.

Aviation safety experts note that uncontained engine failures, while statistically rare, typically stem from metal fatigue or microscopic manufacturing flaws that worsen over thousands of flight cycles. “When a fan blade or turbine disk fractures, the rotational energy can turn debris into projectiles,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor and former FAA consultant. “Modern engines are designed with heavy-duty containment rings, but if a failure occurs outside the expected parameters, the casing can be breached. Investigators will likely focus on the engine’s inspection history and whether recent maintenance adhered to strict ultrasonic testing protocols.”

Survivors described a scene of sudden terror followed by remarkable composure. “There was a loud bang, like a cannon shot, and then the air just vanished,” said passenger David Miller, 42, who was seated three rows behind the damaged window. “Oxygen masks dropped, people were screaming, but the flight attendants kept their voices steady. They told us to brace, and we did.” The deceased passenger, identified by family members as Jennifer Riordan, a 43-year-old mother of two from Albuquerque, New Mexico, was remembered as a devoted community volunteer. “She was the kind of person who always put others first,” her brother said in a statement. “We are heartbroken, but we are so grateful to the passengers and crew who tried to save her.”

Commercial aviation has seen a handful of similar incidents over the past two decades, prompting continuous improvements in aircraft design, inspection standards, and crew training. Federal regulations, including 14 CFR 25.783, mandate rigorous testing for fuselage doors, windows, and structural panels to ensure they can withstand rapid pressure changes and potential debris impacts. The rule requires manufacturers to demonstrate that cabin structures maintain integrity even under extreme stress, a standard that has evolved significantly since the early days of jet travel. Southwest Airlines has maintained a strong safety record, with no fatal accidents in its history prior to this event. However, the aviation industry continues to grapple with the challenge of detecting microscopic cracks in aging engine components before they reach critical failure points.

The NTSB has secured the aircraft and begun a meticulous examination of the damaged engine and fuselage. Investigators are currently downloading the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which will provide crucial insights into the crew’s response and the exact sequence of mechanical failures. Meanwhile, the FAA is reviewing maintenance logs across the fleet to determine if immediate inspections are warranted. Officials in Washington DC are coordinating with engine manufacturers and airline operators to assess whether broader fleet-wide directives are necessary. “We expect preliminary findings within the next 10 days,” Sumwalt said. “But a full investigation will take months. Safety is not a race; it’s a process.” As the investigation unfolds, the aviation community remains focused on understanding how a routine flight turned into a tragedy, and what steps must be taken to ensure it never happens again.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Engineering & Maintenance Safety Division, acting as a technical party to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative hearing regarding the April 17, 2018, uncontained engine failure event. Our organization represents a consortium of commercial operators, maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) providers, and aviation safety engineering professionals. We have been granted party status to provide specialized expertise in propulsion system integrity, structural damage tolerance, non-destructive inspection (NDI) methodologies, and maintenance program optimization.

The scope of this document encompasses a comprehensive technical evaluation of the contributing factors to the fan blade separation, subsequent uncontained failure, and cabin window penetration. We examine metallurgical evidence, maintenance tracking records, inspection interval adequacy, and structural certification margins. Our analysis is grounded in docket materials, peer-reviewed engineering literature, and operational data collected from fleet-wide monitoring programs. We also address the broader regulatory and industry implications, drawing comparative insights from modern propulsion architectures, including the LEAP engine family, and evaluating alignment with current airworthiness and operational oversight frameworks.

We acknowledge the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and the NTSB investigative team for their rigorous coordination of evidence collection, docket management, and transparent dissemination of preliminary findings. This submission is intended to supplement the factual record with engineering analysis, advocate for targeted safety enhancements, and provide actionable recommendations that balance operational feasibility with risk mitigation.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operating at cruise altitude (FL325) experienced a catastrophic left engine failure. Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters indicate a rapid N1 decay, followed by asymmetric thrust, cabin altitude warning, and emergency descent initiation. Cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts confirm crew recognition of abnormal engine indications, immediate execution of the engine failure checklist, and successful diversion to the nearest suitable airport. Tragically, one passenger fatality occurred due to rapid decompression following fuselage and cabin window impact by engine debris.

The NTSB docket contains extensive evidence relevant to this event, including:
- Docket Item ENG-03 through ENG-09: Engine teardown reports, fan blade fracture surface documentation, and metallurgical analysis.
- Docket Item MET-11 through MET-14: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results, fatigue striation measurements, and crack initiation site mapping.
- Docket Item OPS-05: Maintenance program records, cycle accumulation logs, and recent inspection sign-offs.
- Docket Item STR-02: Fuselage and window frame damage assessment, including finite element modeling of impact loads.

The primary failure mode has been identified as a low-cycle fatigue (LCF) crack originating at the fan blade dovetail root, propagating through the airfoil, and culminating in blade liberation. The liberated blade and associated hardware breached the engine containment ring, with secondary debris impacting the forward fuselage and a passenger window. The window assembly failed under combined aerodynamic and impact loading, resulting in explosive decompression.

While the incident aircraft utilized a legacy high-bypass turbofan, the failure mechanics and inspection challenges have direct relevance to contemporary propulsion systems. Modern architectures, such as the CFM LEAP engine, employ advanced composite fan blades, optimized containment rings, and integrated health monitoring. However, the fundamental principles of fatigue crack initiation, NDI probability of detection (POD), and maintenance interval optimization remain universally applicable. Furthermore, the regulatory framework governing airworthiness certification (14 CFR Part 25) and operational maintenance oversight (14 CFR part 135) must be evaluated holistically to ensure consistent safety margins across mixed-fleet operators.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

Our engineering assessment focuses on three interrelated domains: (1) fatigue crack propagation and inspection methodology limitations, (2) debris trajectory and structural impact resistance, and (3) maintenance program optimization and regulatory alignment.

3.1 Fatigue Crack Initiation and NDI Limitations
Metallurgical examination of the fractured fan blade (Docket MET-12) reveals a classic fatigue failure signature. The crack initiated at a subsurface inclusion near the dovetail radius, a region subjected to high cyclic bending stresses during engine start, climb, and cruise power transients. Striation spacing analysis indicates crack growth rates consistent with Paris Law parameters for titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V under variable amplitude loading. The estimated crack propagation timeline suggests the defect was present for approximately 1,200–1,500 flight cycles prior to failure.

The maintenance program relied on eddy current inspection (ECI) at prescribed intervals. However, POD curves for ECI in complex dovetail geometries demonstrate reduced sensitivity to subsurface defects below 0.015 inches in depth. Docket Item NDI-07 confirms that the inspection probe configuration and surface preparation protocols did not fully account for geometric shadowing and oxide layer interference. While the inspection was performed in accordance with the approved maintenance manual, the methodology's inherent limitations allowed a sub-critical crack to remain undetected.

Comparative analysis with next-generation inspection techniques, including phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) and laser ultrasonics, indicates a 30–40% improvement in POD for similar defect morphologies. The LEAP engine family, for example, incorporates integrated blade health monitoring and optimized inspection access ports, reducing reliance on manual NDI in high-stress zones. While retrofitting legacy engines with such systems is not immediately feasible, the data underscores the need for enhanced inspection protocols and interval adjustments based on actual crack growth modeling rather than conservative cycle-based thresholds.

3.2 Debris Trajectory and Structural Impact Resistance
The uncontained failure resulted in multiple debris fragments exiting the engine casing. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and rigid-body trajectory modeling (Docket STR-04) indicate that the primary impactor struck the forward fuselage at an oblique angle, transferring approximately 18,000 ft-lbs of kinetic energy to the window frame assembly. The cabin window, certified under 14 CFR Part 25.365 and 25.571, is designed to withstand bird strike and pressure differential loads, but the certification basis does not explicitly mandate resistance to high-velocity metallic debris from uncontained engine failures.

Finite element analysis of the window frame reveals localized yielding and fastener pull-out under the impact load. The acrylic laminate failed due to combined tensile and shear stresses exceeding the material's dynamic fracture toughness. While the window design complies with existing airworthiness standards, the incident highlights a gap between certification assumptions and real-world uncontained failure scenarios. Industry best practices, as outlined in SAE ARP4761 and AC 25.571-1D, recommend damage tolerance assessments that account for worst-case debris trajectories. Our analysis supports revising guidance to incorporate probabilistic impact modeling and enhanced energy absorption margins for forward cabin windows.

3.3 Maintenance Program Optimization and Regulatory Alignment
The maintenance tracking system for the incident aircraft recorded all required inspections, but cycle accumulation was calculated using standard flight hour/cycle conversion factors that did not fully account for high-stress operational profiles (e.g., frequent short-haul sectors, rapid power transients). Docket Item OPS-08 indicates that the operator's reliability program flagged minor vibration anomalies in the preceding 200 cycles, but these were classified as within acceptable limits per the engine manufacturer's service bulletin.

This underscores a systemic challenge: maintenance programs optimized for average fleet conditions may not adequately address outlier operational stressors. The regulatory framework governing airworthiness (14 CFR Part 25) establishes design and certification requirements, while operational oversight (14 CFR part 135) dictates maintenance execution and recordkeeping. However, data sharing between design authorities, operators, and regulators remains fragmented. Organizations such as Atlas Air Inc. have demonstrated the value of predictive maintenance frameworks that integrate real-time engine health monitoring, digital twin modeling, and machine learning-driven anomaly detection. Implementing similar paradigms across commercial fleets would enable dynamic inspection interval adjustments and proactive component replacement before critical crack thresholds are reached.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the technical evidence, metallurgical data, and operational records reviewed, our position is as follows:

The primary contributing factor to the uncontained engine failure was an undetected low-cycle fatigue crack in the fan blade dovetail, which propagated to critical size due to limitations in the applied NDI methodology and conservative cycle-based inspection intervals. Secondary factors include the inherent geometric constraints of legacy inspection access, operational stress accumulation not fully captured by standard cycle tracking, and cabin window structural margins that, while compliant with 14 CFR Part 25, were not optimized for high-velocity metallic debris impact.

We acknowledge the complexity of balancing inspection feasibility, operational continuity, and safety margins. However, the evidence clearly indicates that current maintenance paradigms require modernization to address subsurface fatigue initiation and dynamic impact scenarios. The Investigator-in-Charge's docket materials provide a robust foundation for regulatory and industry action.

Recommended safety improvements include:
- Revision of NDI protocols to incorporate phased array ultrasonic testing and enhanced surface preparation standards for high-stress engine components.
- Implementation of dynamic inspection interval modeling based on actual operational stress profiles rather than fixed cycle thresholds.
- Development of updated certification guidance for cabin window impact resistance, incorporating probabilistic debris trajectory analysis and enhanced energy absorption design.
- Establishment of a standardized, industry-wide data-sharing platform for engine health monitoring, maintenance anomalies, and fatigue crack growth trends.
- Harmonization of maintenance oversight requirements across 14 CFR Part 25 and 14 CFR part 135 operators to ensure consistent application of predictive maintenance technologies.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the incident and preliminary NTSB findings, our organization and affiliated operators have implemented the following immediate corrective actions:

- Fleet-wide eddy current and ultrasonic inspections of all fan blades in the affected engine family, with enhanced focus on dovetail root regions and subsurface defect detection.
- Issuance of Maintenance Program Bulletin MPB-2018-04, mandating revised inspection intervals and updated NDI probe configurations for high-cycle engines.
- Integration of real-time vibration and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) trend monitoring into reliability programs, with automated alert thresholds for early-stage anomaly detection.
- Crew training enhancements focused on rapid decompression response, emergency descent procedures, and cabin pressure management, aligned with FAA Advisory Circular 120-108.

Proposed future improvements include:

- Deployment of AI-assisted NDI analysis software to standardize defect interpretation and reduce human variability in inspection results.
- Development of digital twin models for high-cycle engine components, enabling predictive maintenance scheduling based on actual stress accumulation rather than conservative cycle estimates.
- Collaboration with OEMs and regulatory authorities to revise 14 CFR Part 25 certification guidance, incorporating updated debris impact modeling and enhanced cabin window structural requirements.
- Establishment of a cross-operator maintenance data consortium, modeled after the predictive maintenance frameworks successfully implemented by Atlas Air Inc., to facilitate real-time sharing of fatigue crack growth data, inspection POD metrics, and operational stress profiles.
- Advocacy for regulatory harmonization between Part 25 design standards and Part 135 operational oversight, ensuring that maintenance program approvals reflect modern predictive analytics and dynamic risk assessment methodologies.

We respectfully submit this analysis to the NTSB investigative team and the Investigator-in-Charge for consideration in the final report and subsequent safety recommendations. The aviation industry has consistently demonstrated its capacity to learn from adverse events and implement engineering-driven solutions. By modernizing inspection methodologies, enhancing structural certification margins, and embracing predictive maintenance technologies, we can significantly reduce the probability of recurrence and further advance the safety of commercial air travel.

TO: All Maintenance Control, Line Maintenance, Engineering, and Quality Assurance Personnel
FROM: Director of Maintenance Quality & Safety / Engineering Compliance Division
DATE: May 14, 2018
SUBJECT: URGENT: Enhanced Inspection Protocols for High-Bypass Turbofan Nacelle & Fuselage Interface Following Uncontained Engine Failure Event
REF: QSA-2018-0417, ENG-ALERT-089, WO-7742-REV3, Prior Memo M-2018-0312

PURPOSE:
This Safety Communication and Process Instruction establishes immediate, mandatory inspection and documentation requirements for all high-bypass turbofan installations and adjacent fuselage structures. The directive is issued to mitigate risk associated with uncontained engine failures, rapid decompression events, and secondary debris impact. All personnel must implement the updated work cards, NDT procedures, and reporting protocols outlined herein effective immediately.

BACKGROUND:
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 experienced an uncontained engine failure during cruise flight at 32,500 feet. High-energy debris from the left engine penetrated the nacelle, struck the forward fuselage, and compromised a passenger cabin window. The event resulted in rapid decompression and one passenger fatality. The incident, widely reported as involving Southwest Airlines (SWA) Flight 1380, has triggered industry-wide scrutiny of fan blade fatigue, containment ring integrity, and window frame load paths.

While the failed powerplant was a CFM56-7B, our managed fleet includes multiple high-bypass architectures, including the newly inducted LEAP-1B engine series. Engineering analysis confirms that debris trajectory, kinetic energy transfer, and secondary impact zones are consistent across modern turbofan designs. Furthermore, our maintenance and operational standards must align with 14 CFR Part 25 airworthiness requirements, specifically addressing structural integrity and emergency egress. Section 25.783 of the Federal Aviation Regulations mandates rigorous testing and inspection of fuselage doors and windows to withstand pressure differentials and impact loads. Although our primary operating certificate falls under 14 CFR Part 135, we voluntarily maintain Part 25-equivalent structural inspection intervals for all transport-category aircraft in our managed fleet.

Cross-industry coordination with major MRO providers, including Atlas Air, has confirmed that accelerated fatigue cracking in fan blade retention systems and adjacent fuselage skin requires enhanced non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols. This bulletin supersedes prior guidance in M-2018-0312 and aligns our internal standards with the latest OEM service bulletins and FAA emergency airworthiness directives.

DETAILS:
The following procedural updates apply to all aircraft equipped with high-bypass turbofan engines. Compliance is mandatory for all scheduled and unscheduled maintenance events.

1. Enhanced Visual & Borescope Inspections:
   - All fan cowl assemblies, thrust reverser cascades, and adjacent fuselage skin panels (Zones 100-300) must undergo detailed visual inspection per updated Work Order WO-8821-INSPECT.
   - Technicians must document any scoring, gouging, or paint delamination exceeding 0.015 inches in depth.
   - Borescope inspection of the fan blade retention ring and forward compressor case is required at every A-check interval. Reference Part Number P/N 737-5000-12A for retention hardware torque values.

2. Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) Requirements:
   - Eddy current and ultrasonic testing must be performed on all window frame doublers and adjacent longerons. Use NDT Procedure NDT-44B-REV2.
   - Any indication of micro-fracturing or stress corrosion cracking must be reported to Engineering within 4 hours of discovery.
   - Replace any window assembly showing deformation or seal compromise. Reference Part Number P/N 737-8000-44B for replacement kits.

3. Structural & Pressure Integrity Verification:
   - All cabin pressure relief valves and outflow actuators must be functionally tested per AMM Chapter 21-30-00.
   - Verify compliance with 14 CFR 25.783 load path requirements for all forward fuselage window installations. Engineering has issued Supplemental Structural Inspection Document (SSID) SSID-2018-05 to address localized stress concentrations.
   - Document all findings in the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS) under defect code ENG-DEBRIS-01.

4. Cross-Fleet Applicability:
   - While this alert was triggered by a narrowbody event, the LEAP-1B powerplant installations on our widebody and next-generation narrowbody aircraft require identical inspection rigor. The containment ring design and debris dispersion patterns are functionally equivalent.
   - Maintenance Control will issue revised routing cards for all aircraft with >15,000 flight cycles.

ACTION REQUIRED:
All responsible departments must execute the following actions by the specified deadlines. Failure to comply will result in immediate grounding of affected aircraft and quality audit escalation.

1. Line Maintenance & Base Maintenance:
   - Complete initial visual and borescope inspections on all active aircraft within 72 hours of this bulletin’s release.
   - Apply updated torque values and NDT procedures to all open work orders. Close out WO-7742-REV3 and transition to WO-8821-INSPECT.
   - Deadline: May 17, 2018, 23:59 UTC.

2. Quality Assurance & Compliance:
   - Conduct random audits on 15% of the fleet to verify inspection documentation, NDT calibration logs, and MTS defect coding.
   - Submit audit findings to the Director of Maintenance Quality by May 30, 2018.
   - Ensure all technicians have signed the acknowledgment form (QA-FORM-2018-0417) and completed the associated e-learning module (MOD-ENG-DEBRIS-01).

3. Engineering & Technical Publications:
   - Revise the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) and Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) to reflect permanent inspection interval reductions.
   - Publish updated SSID-2018-05 and distribute to all MRO partners, including Atlas, for cross-fleet harmonization.
   - Deadline: June 15, 2018.

4. Training & Human Factors:
   - All licensed mechanics and inspectors must complete the updated training bulletin on uncontained failure recognition and rapid decompression response.
   - Training records must be uploaded to the LMS by May 25, 2018.
   - Supervisors will conduct daily toolbox talks focusing on debris impact zones and window frame integrity until further notice.

All maintenance releases must include a specific sign-off block referencing this bulletin. Any deviation requires written approval from the Chief Inspector and Engineering Director. Questions regarding procedure application, part substitutions, or regulatory interpretation should be directed to the Engineering Compliance Desk at ext. 4402 or via the internal maintenance portal.

This document will be retained in the corporate quality archive and is subject to regulatory review. Maintain strict adherence to all referenced work orders, part numbers, and compliance deadlines.

SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), a Boeing 737-700, registered as N772SW and operated by Southwest Airlines (SWA), experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. The aircraft was en route from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Dallas Love Field (DAL) when debris from the left engine penetrated the fuselage and a passenger cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one passenger fatality. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and diverted to Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), where the aircraft landed without further incident. This preliminary document outlines the initial factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and documents procedural determinations made by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in the early stages of the inquiry.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the flight was operating under the provisions of 14 CFR Part 121, which governs domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. Initial data retrieved from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) suggest a sudden loss of thrust and abnormal vibration parameters associated with the left engine prior to the decompression event. The aircraft was equipped with a CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engine, and early examination of recovered engine components points to a potential structural anomaly within the fan section, though definitive metallurgical analysis remains pending.

Witness accounts from surviving passengers and cabin crew members, collected during initial interviews, describe a loud bang followed by immediate cabin depressurization, the deployment of oxygen masks, and visible damage to the left-side fuselage near the wing root. Several individuals reported observing a portion of the engine cowling and other debris passing the cabin windows. The flight crew’s initial radio communications, as captured by air traffic control recordings, indicate a Mayday declaration and a request for an immediate descent to a lower altitude.

Meteorological data obtained from the National Weather Service and onboard weather radar imagery indicate that the aircraft was operating in visual meteorological conditions (VMC) at the time of the event, with no significant convective activity, turbulence, or icing reported along the flight path. Preliminary examination of the airframe reveals a localized breach in the fuselage skin and a fractured cabin window frame on the left side, consistent with high-velocity impact from engine-generated debris. The rapid decompression appears to have been contained to the forward cabin section, and emergency evacuation procedures were not initiated upon landing.

It is important to note that all findings documented herein are preliminary in nature and subject to revision as additional data is recovered, analyzed, and correlated. No conclusions regarding the root cause of the engine failure, maintenance history, or operational factors have been established at this time.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The Lead Investigator (LI) has formally activated the following NTSB investigative groups to address the multidisciplinary nature of this event: Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group has been tasked with collecting, preserving, and analyzing evidence within their respective domains. The investigation is being conducted in accordance with established NTSB protocols and under the authority of 49 U.S.C. § 1131.

Parties to the investigation have been designated in accordance with NTSB regulations. Southwest Airlines has been included as the operator, with technical representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) serving as an advisory party. Additional parties include the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, and the pilot and flight attendant unions. While the operational framework of this flight falls under 14 CFR Part 121, certain maintenance and operational interfaces have been cross-referenced with standards applicable to 14 CFR Part 135 operations to ensure comprehensive regulatory alignment during the review of maintenance tracking and crew duty limitations. Furthermore, maintenance tracking protocols have been cross-referenced with industry standards, including comparative data from operators such as Atlas Air, to evaluate common inspection intervals and component lifecycle management practices. Fuel system safety evaluations will incorporate historical compliance data related to Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88), particularly concerning flammability reduction and ignition source prevention, although no fuel-related anomalies have been identified to date.

Evidence secured to date includes the FDR and CVR, which have been transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for readout and transcription. Recovered engine debris, including fan blade fragments, cowling sections, and fuselage skin panels, have been cataloged and secured at a designated NTSB storage facility. Initial non-destructive testing (NDT) and dimensional inspections are scheduled to commence within the next 72 hours. The aircraft remains parked at a secure ramp area at PHL, pending further structural assessment and evidence recovery.

The Lead Investigator has established a centralized evidence tracking system to maintain chain-of-custody documentation for all physical and digital materials. All investigative activities are being coordinated through daily briefings to ensure data integrity and prevent premature speculation.

NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks will focus on the systematic examination of the recovered engine components, with particular emphasis on the fan disk, containment ring, and associated mounting hardware. Metallurgical and fractographic analyses will be conducted to determine the initiation point and propagation characteristics of any material failures. Concurrently, the Operations group will review maintenance records, engine shop visit history, and airworthiness directives compliance to identify any potential contributing factors.

The Systems and Structures groups will collaborate to evaluate the fuselage damage pattern, window frame integrity, and cabin pressure control system response during the decompression event. Human Performance specialists will continue to conduct structured interviews with the flight crew and cabin personnel, focusing on workload management, emergency procedure execution, and physiological responses to rapid decompression.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated to be released within 30 days, pending the completion of initial recorder readouts and component examinations. Subsequent updates will be issued as significant milestones are reached, including the completion of engine teardown, metallurgical results, and regulatory compliance reviews. All findings will remain strictly preliminary until the final investigative report is published, which will include a comprehensive analysis of all data, safety recommendations, and, if applicable, probable cause determinations.

The NTSB remains committed to a thorough, transparent, and methodical investigation. Stakeholders and the public are advised that early-stage information is subject to change as additional evidence is evaluated and technical analyses progress.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at 15:43:12 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), an in-flight event occurred involving a Boeing 737-700 series airplane. The event transpired during the cruise phase of flight at a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL). The geographic coordinates of the occurrence were approximately 39.812° North latitude and 79.245° West longitude, over rural terrain in southwestern Pennsylvania. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger route. The flight was en route from LaGuardia Airport (LGA), New York, to Dallas Love Field (DAL), Texas.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-7H4, bearing United States registration number N772SW. The airplane was manufactured by The Boeing Company and delivered to the operator in March 2000. The registered operator was Southwest Airlines, a certificated air carrier conducting scheduled domestic passenger operations. The aircraft was configured for 143 passenger seats in a single-class layout, with a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 154,500 pounds. At the time of the event, the aircraft was operating under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, which governs domestic, flag, and supplemental operations.

1.3 Nature of the Flight and Operational Context
The flight was designated as a regularly scheduled revenue passenger service. The flight plan was filed in accordance with standard Part 121 dispatch procedures, utilizing a computerized flight planning system that calculated fuel requirements, alternate airport selections, and en route weather minima. The flight departed LGA at 14:12:05 EDT, climbed to an assigned cruise altitude of 32,500 feet, and proceeded along airway J146. At 15:43:12 EDT, while maintaining a calibrated airspeed of approximately 285 knots and a Mach number of 0.78, the flight crew experienced a sudden, loud acoustic event accompanied by severe airframe vibration. The crew immediately initiated emergency descent procedures, declared a Mayday, and diverted to Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). The aircraft landed at PHL at 16:02:45 EDT without further incident. The event resulted in rapid cabin decompression, structural damage to the left fuselage, and one passenger fatality.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1234567, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain also held a commercial pilot certificate with single-engine land and instrument ratings. Total flight time recorded in the pilot’s logbook was 11,247 hours, of which 8,912 hours were accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The captain held a first-class medical certificate issued on January 15, 2018, with no limitations. The pilot’s most recent line check was completed on February 22, 2018, with satisfactory performance documented across all evaluated maneuvers and emergency procedures.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications
The first officer held an ATP certificate, certificate number 2345678, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The first officer also held a commercial pilot certificate with single-engine land and instrument ratings. Total flight time recorded was 7,634 hours, with 3,189 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer held a first-class medical certificate issued on March 10, 2018, with no limitations. The pilot’s most recent proficiency check was completed on January 18, 2018, with all required tasks evaluated as satisfactory.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crew members completed recurrent training within the preceding 12 calendar months in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121.409 and Part 121.411. Training records indicate that both pilots participated in a full-flight simulator session on November 12, 2017, which included scenarios for rapid decompression, engine failure at cruise altitude, and emergency descent procedures. The training syllabus incorporated crew resource management (CRM) protocols, checklist discipline, and communication with air traffic control during abnormal and emergency conditions. Duty time records for the accident flight indicated that both pilots were within the limits prescribed by 14 CFR Part 117, with a scheduled duty period of 9 hours and 15 minutes. Rest periods prior to the flight met the minimum 10-hour requirement. No fatigue-related factors were documented in the crew’s pre-flight self-assessment or post-incident interviews.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Airframe Specifications and Service History
The airframe, serial number 28421, was manufactured in accordance with the Boeing 737-700 production specifications. At the time of the event, the airplane had accumulated 58,412 total flight hours and 42,108 flight cycles. The airframe was equipped with a standard Boeing 737 Next Generation (NG) avionics suite, including dual flight management computers, autopilot/flight director systems, and a digital flight data recorder (DFDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) compliant with 14 CFR Part 121.343 and Part 121.359. The cabin pressurization system utilized a dual-pack environmental control system with automatic outflow valve regulation. The fuselage structure incorporated aluminum alloy skin panels, stringers, and frames designed to meet the damage tolerance requirements of the applicable airworthiness standards.

3.2 Engine and Propulsion System
The left engine was a CFM International LEAP-1B engine, serial number 88421, installed on the left wing pylon. The powerplant was a high-bypass turbofan rated at 24,500 pounds of thrust. The engine was equipped with a full-authority digital engine control (FADEC) system, dual-channel ignition, and a 22-blade titanium fan assembly. At the time of the event, the engine had accumulated 14,205 flight hours and 10,882 cycles since new. The right engine, a matching LEAP-1B unit, operated normally throughout the flight and was not involved in the event. Engine health monitoring data indicated normal parameters for exhaust gas temperature (EGT), fuel flow, oil pressure, and vibration levels during the climb and initial cruise phases.

3.3 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records were reviewed for compliance with the operator’s approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP). The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check) was completed on August 14, 2017, at 56,100 flight hours. All applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) were documented as complied with, including AD 2016-15-09, which mandated ultrasonic inspection of fan blades for subsurface cracking. The left engine underwent a shop visit on May 3, 2016, during which the fan disk, blades, and containment ring were inspected and returned to service. No deferred maintenance items related to the engine, fuselage, or pressurization system were recorded in the aircraft maintenance logbook for the 30 days preceding the event. The operator’s maintenance tracking system indicated that all scheduled inspections, lubrication tasks, and component replacements were performed within the prescribed intervals.

3.4 Certification and Regulatory Framework
The aircraft was originally type certified under 14 CFR Part 25, which establishes airworthiness standards for transport category airplanes. The certification basis included compliance with 14 CFR 25.783, which addresses fuselage doors, windows, and emergency exits, including requirements for structural integrity and pressure differential containment. The engine was certified under 14 CFR Part 33, with design and testing requirements for uncontained failure containment and debris trajectory analysis. The operator’s maintenance program was approved under 14 CFR Part 121.369 and Part 121.373, with oversight provided by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) through the designated Principal Inspector. The aircraft’s continued airworthiness was maintained in accordance with Part 21, which governs certification procedures for products and parts, including supplemental type certificates and major alterations.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Conditions
On April 17, 2018, a high-pressure system dominated the northeastern United States, resulting in stable atmospheric conditions along the flight route. Upper-level analysis at 300 hPa indicated a light westerly flow at approximately 45 knots, with no significant jet stream disturbances or tropopause folding. The freezing level was reported at 11,500 feet MSL, well below the cruise altitude. No convective activity, frontal boundaries, or significant wind shear were present in the en route airspace.

4.2 Terminal and En Route Weather Data
Automated weather observations from stations along the route were reviewed. At 15:00 EDT, the Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) METAR reported wind 270° at 8 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, clear skies, temperature 12°C, dewpoint 4°C, and altimeter setting 30.12 inches of mercury. The Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) TAF, valid from 12:00 to 18:00 EDT, forecasted VFR conditions with scattered clouds at 8,000 feet, wind 250° at 10 knots, and no significant weather. En route weather radar imagery from the National Weather Service indicated no precipitation, turbulence, or icing conditions between 30,000 and 35,000 feet. The aircraft’s onboard weather radar was not activated during cruise, as no convective returns were detected.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Atmospheric Observations
A review of pilot reports (PIREPs) filed between 14:00 and 16:00 EDT along the J146 airway revealed no reports of moderate or greater turbulence, clear air turbulence (CAT), or structural icing. Multiple aircraft operating at similar altitudes reported smooth ride conditions and standard atmospheric density. The flight crew did not report any meteorological anomalies prior to the event. Post-incident interviews confirmed that visibility was unrestricted, and no weather-related factors contributed to the initiation of the emergency descent or the subsequent diversion.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The primary wreckage remained with the aircraft, which landed intact at PHL. Secondary debris was recovered from a linear distribution pattern extending approximately 12.5 nautical miles along the flight path. Debris recovery operations were coordinated with local law enforcement and FAA field personnel. Recovered items included a fractured fan blade segment, portions of the engine inlet cowl, acoustic insulation panels, and cabin interior components. All recovered items were cataloged, photographed, and transported to a secure examination facility. The debris field exhibited a forward-aft trajectory consistent with high-velocity ejection from the left engine nacelle.

5.2 Fuselage and Cabin Examination
Examination of the left fuselage revealed a localized penetration at the aft edge of the row 14 window frame. The penetration measured approximately 14 inches in length and 6 inches in width, with outward deformation of the surrounding skin panels. The window assembly was completely dislodged, and the adjacent cabin sidewall exhibited tearing and delamination of the composite insulation blanket. The rapid decompression event triggered automatic deployment of the passenger oxygen masks in the affected cabin section. The cabin pressure controller recorded a pressure differential drop from 8.6 psi to 0.2 psi within 4.2 seconds. Structural analysis confirmed that the fuselage frames and stringers adjacent to the penetration remained intact, with no evidence of progressive structural failure. The emergency evacuation slides were not deployed, and the aircraft was taxied to the gate under its own power.

5.3 Engine and Component Analysis
The left LEAP-1B engine was removed from the aircraft and transported to a dedicated teardown facility. Initial inspection revealed a catastrophic failure of the number 13 fan blade, which separated at the dovetail root. The blade fragment penetrated the fan case containment ring, exited the nacelle, and impacted the fuselage. The fan disk exhibited localized scoring and thermal discoloration consistent with high-energy debris impact. The oil system sustained secondary damage, with the scavenge pump housing fractured and the oil filter bypass valve actuated. The FADEC recorded a rapid N1 decay, followed by automatic fuel shutoff and ignition termination. The right engine operated within normal parameters throughout the event. Metallurgical examination of the failed fan blade revealed a fatigue crack originating from a subsurface inclusion, with progressive crack growth consistent with high-cycle fatigue mechanisms. The containment ring exhibited localized deformation but maintained structural integrity in accordance with design specifications.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Southwest Airlines maintains a comprehensive safety management system (SMS) in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121.373 and FAA Advisory Circular 120-92B. The operator’s maintenance program includes predictive analytics for engine health monitoring, with vibration trend analysis and oil debris monitoring utilized to identify potential component degradation. The flight operations manual (FOM) contains detailed procedures for rapid decompression, emergency descent, and engine failure at cruise altitude. Crew training emphasizes checklist discipline, cross-verification of system parameters, and coordinated communication with air traffic control. The operator’s internal safety reporting system documented 14 similar engine-related events over the preceding five years, none of which resulted in uncontained failures or cabin penetration. All reported anomalies were investigated, and corrective actions were implemented through revised inspection intervals and component replacement schedules.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Similar Events
The investigation reviewed historical data on uncontained engine failures in high-bypass turbofan engines. Industry databases indicate that fan blade separation events, while rare, have occurred across multiple engine manufacturers and airframe types. Previous incidents have demonstrated that debris trajectory is influenced by rotational velocity, blade mass, and nacelle geometry. The National Transportation Safety Board has previously investigated similar events, with findings typically focusing on material fatigue, inspection methodology, and containment ring design. The operator’s maintenance tracking system was cross-referenced with manufacturer service bulletins and FAA airworthiness directives to identify any recurring patterns. No systemic deficiencies were identified in the operator’s compliance with established maintenance protocols.

6.3 Regulatory and Advisory Guidance
The aircraft and engine were certified in accordance with 14 CFR Part 25 and Part 33, which establish minimum performance standards for structural integrity, pressurization, and engine containment. Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88) addresses fuel tank system safety and was reviewed for applicability; however, the event did not involve fuel system components. The certification basis for the fuselage window assembly required compliance with 14 CFR 25.783, which mandates that windows and doors withstand specified pressure differentials and impact loads. The engine manufacturer’s design documentation referenced Part 21 for production approval and continued airworthiness requirements. The FAA Principal Inspector responsible for the operator’s oversight conducted routine surveillance audits, with all findings documented and resolved in accordance with established procedures. The investigation team coordinated with NTSB headquarters to ensure standardized examination protocols, data acquisition methodologies, and regulatory compliance verification. All technical data, maintenance records, and examination findings were compiled in accordance with NTSB Group Chairman reporting standards and will be retained for further analysis.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the technical examination, materials analysis, and flight data recorder (FDR) parameter evaluation conducted in support of the aviation accident investigation involving a Boeing 737-700, registration N772SW, which experienced an uncontained engine failure during cruise flight on April 17, 2018. The scope of this examination encompasses the left engine (LEAP engine), recovered fan blade fragments, containment case segments, impacted fuselage skin panels, cabin window assembly, and associated digital flight data. The examination was conducted under the direction of the Lead Investigator, with oversight from the Chief Inspector, and in coordination with the NTSB Materials Laboratory, Washington, D.C., and the engine teardown facility in Cincinnati, Ohio.

The physical examination and materials testing were performed between May 2 and May 18, 2018. Items examined included: (1) the left engine fan rotor assembly (P/N 2145-889, S/N 88421-LEAP), (2) fractured fan blade #13, (3) forward and aft containment ring segments, (4) fuselage skin panels from stations 412 to 438, (5) the No. 14 cabin window frame and glazing assembly, and (6) the solid-state FDR (P/N 980-4700-042, S/N 114882). All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, ASTM International standards, and applicable manufacturer engineering specifications. Maintenance and operational records were reviewed per 14 CFR part 121 requirements, with component tracking and logistics coordination facilitated through Atlas Air (AA) technical support channels. The investigation adhered strictly to factual documentation standards, with no determination of probable cause included herein.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft was equipped with a LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engine, certified under 14 CFR Part 21 for type design approval and integrated into the Boeing 737-700 airframe under supplemental engineering authorization. The LEAP engine features a 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan blade array, a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) fan disk, and a dual-containment case constructed from Inconel 718 and Kevlar-reinforced epoxy composite. The engine is rated for a maximum continuous thrust of 24,500 lbf, with a design fan rotational speed (N1) of 5,180 RPM at sea level static conditions. The certification basis for the airframe and engine installation complies with 14 CFR part 25, specifically addressing structural integrity, pressurization loads, and uncontained engine failure scenarios.

The fuselage structure surrounding the impacted area is manufactured from 2024-T3 Alclad aluminum alloy, with a nominal thickness of 0.063 inches, reinforced by longitudinal stringers (P/N 65-44120-1) and circumferential frames. The cabin window assembly at station 426, frame 14, consists of a three-pane configuration: outer structural acrylic (0.250 in), inner structural acrylic (0.250 in), and a scratch-resistant inner pane (0.125 in), mounted in a 7075-T6 aluminum alloy frame. The pressurization system is designed to maintain a maximum cabin differential pressure (ΔP) of 8.6 PSI at 32,500 ft MSL, in accordance with Section 25.783, which mandates structural resistance to rapid decompression events and retention of window assemblies under dynamic loading.

The specific LEAP engine unit (S/N 88421-LEAP) accumulated 28,450 flight hours and 14,210 flight cycles prior to the event. Maintenance records indicate compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives, service bulletins, and cyclic inspection intervals. The engine was last removed for borescope inspection on February 12, 2018, with no anomalies reported. Operational history was reviewed under 14 CFR part 121.380, confirming adherence to approved maintenance programs and flight operations specifications. The Chief Inspector verified all documentation chains, while the Lead Investigator coordinated cross-disciplinary data correlation between powerplant, structures, and flight data groups.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered fan blade #13 revealed a complete transverse fracture at the mid-span region, approximately 142 mm from the blade root datum. The fracture surface exhibited distinct fatigue initiation features at the trailing edge, with a primary crack length of 18.4 mm and a maximum depth of 4.2 mm. Beach marks were clearly visible under low-magnification stereomicroscopy, indicating progressive crack growth over an estimated 1,200 to 1,500 flight cycles. Ratchet marks at the crack front suggest multiple initiation sites coalescing under high-cycle fatigue loading. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD), corrosion, or manufacturing defects was observed.

Non-destructive examination (NDE) was performed using phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) per ASTM E2491 and eddy current inspection per ASTM E309. The PAUT scan confirmed the absence of subsurface voids or delaminations in the composite blade root, while eddy current mapping identified localized stress concentration at the trailing edge fillet radius (R = 1.2 mm). Fracture surface topography was analyzed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 500x to 5,000x magnification. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the base material composition as Ti-6Al-4V (Grade 5), with aluminum at 6.12 wt%, vanadium at 4.08 wt%, and iron at 0.18 wt%, consistent with AMS 4928 specifications.

The containment ring exhibited a localized breach at the 2 o'clock position, with a tear length of 210 mm and a maximum deformation of 38 mm outward. The Inconel 718 liner showed ductile tearing with microvoid coalescence, characteristic of high-velocity impact loading. Tensile testing of extracted containment coupons per ASTM E8 yielded an ultimate tensile strength of 1,380 MPa and a yield strength of 1,120 MPa, within the manufacturer's specified range of 1,310–1,450 MPa. Fracture toughness testing per ASTM E399 indicated a K_IC value of 112 MPa√m, confirming adequate material resistance to crack propagation under static loading.

Impact energy calculations were derived from debris trajectory reconstruction and finite element modeling (FEM) of the fan blade fragment. The fragment mass was measured at 14.8 kg, with an estimated exit velocity of 1,180 ft/s relative to the engine axis. The kinetic energy at impact was calculated at approximately 4,210 ft-lbs. The fragment penetrated the 2024-T3 Alclad fuselage skin at a 22° angle relative to the longitudinal axis, creating an elliptical breach measuring 185 mm × 92 mm. The surrounding skin exhibited plastic deformation, with strain hardening observed in the 0.5-inch perimeter zone.

The No. 14 cabin window assembly was recovered with the outer structural acrylic pane completely fractured and the inner pane partially delaminated. The 7075-T6 aluminum frame showed localized yielding at the forward mounting lugs, with bolt hole elongation of 0.8 mm. Fastener torque verification per NASM1312-7 indicated that all four primary retention bolts were torqued to 185 ± 10 in-lbs, within specification. The window retention system failed to maintain structural continuity under the combined aerodynamic and decompression loads, consistent with the dynamic pressure differential exceeding the design limit of 12.4 PSI transient load.

Chemical analysis of the fracture surface residues via inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) per ASTM E1473 detected trace amounts of nickel, chromium, and molybdenum, consistent with secondary impact from downstream compressor components. No lubricant or hydraulic fluid contamination was identified. The Chief Inspector reviewed all material test reports, while the Lead Investigator directed correlation of the physical damage patterns with the recorded flight data parameters.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The solid-state FDR recorded 88 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with high-frequency vibration data captured at 64 Hz. Data extraction was performed using the NTSB standard readout protocol, with parameter validation against manufacturer calibration certificates. The timeline reconstruction was synchronized with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and quick access recorder (QAR) data, establishing a precise event sequence.

At 14:22:18.4 UTC, the aircraft was in steady cruise at 32,500 ft MSL, with an indicated airspeed of 284 knots, Mach 0.78, and a cabin differential pressure of 8.6 PSI. The left engine N1 was stable at 94.2%, N2 at 98.1%, and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) at 712°C. At 14:22:19.1, a sudden vibration spike was recorded on the left engine 1X and 2X channels, peaking at 1.8g and 2.4g respectively, exceeding the normal operational threshold of 0.5g. Within 0.8 seconds, N1 decayed to 88.4%, followed by a rapid EGT increase to 890°C, indicating a loss of compressor efficiency and potential turbine overtemperature.

At 14:22:20.3, the cabin altitude parameter began a steep ascent from 6,500 ft to 18,200 ft over a 12-second interval, corresponding to a ΔP drop from 8.6 PSI to 0.2 PSI. The rate of decompression was calculated at 1,050 ft/min, consistent with a large fuselage breach. The outflow valve position parameter indicated full closure at 14:22:20.8, as the pressurization control system attempted to maintain cabin pressure. The aircraft pitch attitude remained within ±2° of the cruise reference, and the autopilot remained engaged until manual disengagement at 14:22:24.1.

Comparison with normal operational parameters per 14 CFR part 121.340 and manufacturer flight manual limitations confirms that the vibration, EGT, and N1 decay rates exceeded all approved envelope boundaries. The engine control unit (ECU) recorded a fault code for "FAN BLADE OVERSPEED/IMBALANCE" at 14:22:19.6, triggering automatic fuel flow reduction to 62% of commanded value. The QAR data corroborated the FDR parameters, with no discrepancies in time synchronization or parameter scaling.

The Lead Investigator directed a parametric sensitivity analysis to evaluate the structural response of the fuselage to the rapid pressure transient. Using the recorded ΔP decay curve and the known breach geometry, the peak dynamic load on the window frame was estimated at 14.8 PSI, exceeding the static design limit of 12.4 PSI by 19.4%. The structural response aligns with the observed plastic deformation and fastener elongation documented in Section 3. The data confirms that the uncontained failure initiated a cascading sequence of aerodynamic, structural, and pressurization system responses, all captured within the 6.2-second primary event window.

5. SUMMARY

The technical examination and data analysis yielded the following factual findings:

1. The left LEAP engine (S/N 88421-LEAP) experienced an uncontained failure initiated by a fatigue fracture of fan blade #13 at the mid-span trailing edge. The fracture surface exhibited progressive crack growth over an estimated 1,200–1,500 cycles, with no evidence of FOD, corrosion, or manufacturing anomalies.

2. The fan blade fragment exited the containment case at an estimated velocity of 1,180 ft/s, carrying approximately 4,210 ft-lbs of kinetic energy. The fragment penetrated the 2024-T3 Alclad fuselage skin at station 426, creating an elliptical breach measuring 185 mm × 92 mm.

3. The No. 14 cabin window assembly failed under the combined aerodynamic and decompression loads, with the outer acrylic pane completely fractured and the 7075-T6 aluminum frame exhibiting localized yielding and bolt hole elongation. The peak dynamic load on the window frame was estimated at 14.8 PSI, exceeding the static design limit of 12.4 PSI.

4. FDR data recorded a rapid N1 decay from 94.2% to 68.1% within 4.2 seconds, accompanied by an EGT spike to 890°C and a cabin altitude climb from 6,500 ft to 18,200 ft over 12 seconds. The cabin differential pressure dropped from 8.6 PSI to 0.2 PSI, consistent with a large fuselage breach.

5. All recovered components and materials met manufacturer specifications and certification requirements under 14 CFR Part 21 and 14 CFR part 25. The structural design complied with Section 25.783 for pressurization and window retention, though the transient dynamic load exceeded the static design envelope.

6. Maintenance and operational records reviewed per 14 CFR part 121 confirmed compliance with all applicable inspection intervals and service bulletins. Component tracking and logistics coordination were facilitated through Atlas Air technical support channels, with documentation verified by the Chief Inspector.

7. The event sequence, as reconstructed from FDR, QAR, and physical evidence, occurred within a 6.2-second primary window, with no recorded system anomalies prior to the initial vibration spike. All data parameters were within calibrated tolerances, and no instrumentation errors were identified.

This report contains factual technical findings only. No determination of probable cause, contributing factors, or safety recommendations is included herein.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER MARCUS THORNE
Date: May 2, 2018
Time: 09:15 CDT
Location: Southwest Airlines Training Facility, Dallas, Texas
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Reynolds, on behalf of the IIC

Q: Good morning, Mr. Thorne. Thank you for making yourself available today. I’m recording this interview for the official record. You understand this is part of the ongoing investigation into the April seventeenth incident?
A: Yes, sir. I do. I’ve already sat down with the company safety team, but I’m ready to go over it again. Whatever helps the board figure out what happened.

Q: Let’s start with your role on the flight. You were the pilot flying, correct?
A: That’s right. I was the first officer, handling the controls for that leg. The captain was pilot monitoring, running the checklists, handling the radios. Standard rotation. We were operating under 14 CFR Part 121, obviously, given it’s a scheduled airline operation. Not like the Part 135 commuter stuff I flew years ago. Different rules, different pace. But the fundamentals… they don’t change.

Q: Walk me through the flight up to the event. What was your altitude, and what were you doing when it happened?
A: We were, uh, level at flight level three-two-five. So thirty-two thousand, five hundred feet. Cruising over central Pennsylvania, I believe. Smooth air. I had the autopilot engaged, just monitoring the FMC, fuel burn, that sort of thing. It was about… oh, ten minutes past the top of descent point. Maybe 10:32 local time? I don’t have the exact minute memorized, but the CVR will have it.
Then—there was this sound. Not a bang, exactly. More like a deep, metallic rip. Like a giant sheet of aluminum tearing. The whole airframe shuddered. Hard. I mean, it wasn’t turbulence. It was a violent, instantaneous jolt. The yoke kicked in my hands. I immediately disengaged the autopilot.

Q: What did you see?
A: I looked left. The number one engine… it was just… well, the cowling was shredded. There was a lot of smoke, maybe some vapor, and the vibration was severe. And then the cabin pressure warning went off. The master caution, the altitude alert. The captain called out “rapid decompression” almost at the same time. I could hear the wind roaring through the cabin. It was deafening. I remember thinking, “We’ve got a hole in the fuselage.” I turned around, just for a second, and I saw… I saw a window was missing. Or blown out. There was a passenger seatbelted in that row, and the oxygen masks had dropped. It was chaotic. I had to focus on the aircraft. I initiated the emergency descent. We pushed the nose down, throttles to idle, speed brakes out. We were trying to get below ten thousand feet as fast as we could. The captain was on the radio declaring Mayday, squawking 7700.

Q: During the descent, were you concerned about structural integrity?
A: Absolutely. I mean, you’re trained for it, but… you don’t expect it. The fuselage took a hit. I was thinking about the certification standards, you know? 14 CFR part 25 has those damage tolerance requirements. The windows are supposed to handle a certain pressure differential, but when debris punches through… it’s a different scenario. I was just praying the remaining structure would hold. We kept the descent rate aggressive but controlled. Didn’t want to overstress the airframe. We were watching the airspeed, the vertical speed, the structural limits. It’s… it’s a lot to process in thirty seconds.

Q: You mentioned the engine. Do you know the specific model?
A: It was a CFM56-7B. I know the maintenance logs, obviously. I’ve heard some folks in the industry talking about the newer LEAP-1B engines on the MAX fleet, but this was definitely the older series. The fan blade failure… it was uncontained. The debris went through the nacelle, hit the fuselage, took out the window. It’s… it’s hard to wrap your head around. You look at the maintenance intervals, the inspections, and you think it’s covered. But metal fatigue… it doesn’t always show up on a borescope.

Q: After landing, what was your immediate interaction with the crew and emergency personnel?
A: We got on the ground at Philadelphia. I think it was around 10:45. We taxied to the gate, shut down the remaining engine, ran the emergency evacuation checklist. The flight attendants did an incredible job. They were calm, professional. I stayed in the cockpit to secure the aircraft, then we deplaned. I didn’t see the full extent of the cabin damage until later, when the investigators let us back on. It was… sobering. The oxygen system had deployed, there was debris everywhere, and the seat row… well, I won’t go into detail. The paramedics were already there. We just stepped back and let them work.

Q: Have you been in contact with the IIC or the team at NTSB headquarters?
A: Yes. The IIC reached out a few days after. We’ve been coordinating on the CVR and FDR data. I’ve also been in touch with the safety department at Southwest Airlines. They’ve been very supportive. I know the NTSB headquarters team is compiling everything, and I’m just trying to be as accurate as possible. Memory can be… fuzzy under stress. I’m relying on my training notes and the flight data. I’ve been reviewing the QRH procedures, the emergency descent profiles, just to make sure I’m not missing anything.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add about the sequence of events or your actions?
A: Just that… we followed the QRH. We followed the emergency procedures. The captain and I have flown together for years. We trusted each other. When that window blew, the priority was getting down, getting the passengers breathing, and getting on the ground. Everything else was secondary. I know the investigation will look at the engine maintenance, the inspection intervals, the metallurgy… and it should. But in the moment, it’s just you, the airplane, and the checklist. I’ve been through simulator training for rapid decompression, but… it’s different when it’s real. The noise, the pressure drop, the smell of ozone and cold air… it sticks with you.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification on any of the technical points.
A: Of course. I’m here to help. Just… let me know if you need me to walk through the descent profile again. I can pull up my notes. I want to make sure the record is accurate.

HEADLINE: Southwest Airlines Flight Suffers Catastrophic Engine Failure, Leaving One Dead After Midair Emergency

BYLINE: By Marcus Thorne, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA —

A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737-700 suffered a catastrophic uncontained engine failure on April 17, 2018, while cruising at 32,500 feet, triggering a rapid cabin decompression that killed one passenger and forced an emergency diversion. The aircraft, en route from New York to Dallas, was safely landed at Philadelphia International Airport after pilots executed a steep, high-speed descent to reach breathable air.

The incident began when a single fan blade inside the jet’s left engine fractured due to metal fatigue. The broken component shattered the engine’s outer casing, sending high-velocity debris tearing into the fuselage. One piece of shrapnel struck a passenger window, blowing it outward and causing explosive decompression. The sudden pressure differential violently pulled loose items and cabin air toward the breach, injuring several passengers and fatally striking one woman seated near the damaged section. Flight crews immediately donned oxygen masks, initiated emergency descent procedures, and guided the aircraft to the nearest suitable runway.

Federal investigators and airline leadership moved swiftly to address the tragedy. “Our hearts are with the family of the passenger we lost, and we are providing full support to everyone who was on board,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson in a statement released Tuesday evening. “We are cooperating completely with federal authorities as they examine every maintenance record and operational detail.” The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched a specialized go-team to the scene. “We are treating this as a top-priority investigation,” said NTSB Chairman Robert Sumwalt during a press briefing. “Preliminary visual evidence indicates a fatigue fracture in an engine fan blade, but we will withhold definitive conclusions until metallurgical testing is complete.” The Federal Aviation Administration, headquartered in Washington DC, issued an immediate airworthiness directive requiring enhanced ultrasonic inspections for similar engine models across the commercial fleet.

The aircraft involved was a 15-year-old Boeing 737-700, a staple of the domestic short-haul market operated by Southwest Airlines. While the carrier flies under Part 121 regulations governing scheduled passenger service, the broader aviation ecosystem—including cargo and charter operators like Atlas Air—relies on overlapping maintenance frameworks to ensure fleet reliability. The engine in question, a CFM International CFM56-7B, differs from next-generation powerplants like the LEAP-1B, but both are certified under 14 CFR Part 25, the federal standard that establishes airworthiness requirements for transport-category aircraft. Investigators are also scrutinizing compliance with 14 CFR 25.783, the regulation that dictates structural integrity standards for fuselage doors and windows during sudden pressure loss.

Aviation safety experts emphasize that uncontained engine failures, though statistically rare, represent one of the most severe threats to commercial flight. “When a rotating component inside a high-bypass turbofan breaks, it essentially becomes a supersonic projectile,” explained Dr. Elena Rostova, an aerospace engineering professor and former FAA consultant. “The containment ring is engineered to catch debris, but extreme fatigue or manufacturing anomalies can allow fragments to breach the casing and strike the airframe.” Rostova noted that cyclic stress from thousands of takeoff and landing cycles can initiate microscopic cracks. “If those aren’t detected during scheduled borescope inspections, they can propagate until the material can no longer withstand operational loads.”

Inside the cabin, passengers described a scene of sudden chaos. “There was a deafening explosion, and then the window just vanished,” said passenger David Chen, who was seated three rows behind the breach. “Oxygen masks dropped instantly, people were screaming, and the plane dropped so fast my ears popped painfully. The flight attendants were incredible—they kept moving through the aisles, telling us to secure our masks and stay seated.” The family of the deceased passenger, a 43-year-old business traveler, released a brief statement through legal counsel. “We are devastated beyond words. She was a devoted mother, a brilliant professional, and a light to everyone who knew her. We ask for privacy as we grieve this unimaginable loss.”

The tragedy echoes historical aviation incidents that reshaped industry safety protocols. In 1988, Aloha Airlines Flight 243 suffered a massive fuselage rupture, prompting sweeping reforms in aging aircraft inspection cycles. More recently, regulators have focused on systemic risk mitigation, including fuel tank safety mandates under SFAR 88, a special federal aviation regulation designed to eliminate ignition sources in aircraft fuel systems. Southwest Airlines has maintained a strong operational safety record over its five-decade history, but this incident highlights the persistent engineering challenges of maintaining high-utilization fleets.

As of Wednesday morning, the NTSB has secured the damaged engine components, the aircraft’s flight data recorder, and the cockpit voice recorder. Investigators are conducting detailed metallurgical analysis on the fractured fan blade and reviewing maintenance logs spanning the past decade. The FAA has mandated that all operators of similar engine models complete enhanced inspections within 30 days. Meanwhile, Southwest Airlines has temporarily grounded a portion of its 737-700 fleet pending regulatory clearance. “We will not return these aircraft to service until we are absolutely certain they meet every safety threshold,” the airline’s chief operating officer stated. The investigation is expected to take several months, with preliminary findings slated for public release in the coming weeks.

1. INTRODUCTION
Southwest Airlines Co. (SWA) submits this technical analysis as the designated operator party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the April 17, 2018, in-flight event. As the operator of the subject Boeing 737-700, SWA’s engineering, maintenance, and flight operations divisions have conducted a comprehensive internal review aligned with the NTSB’s investigative framework. This submission outlines our technical position regarding the uncontained failure of the left LEAP-1B engine, the subsequent structural and cabin environment impacts, and the operational response protocols executed by the flight crew. The scope of this document encompasses metallurgical and fatigue analysis of the failed fan blade, evaluation of non-destructive inspection (NDI) efficacy, assessment of rapid decompression dynamics, and a review of maintenance program compliance. Our objective is to provide the Board with operator-derived data, contextualize the event within established industry safety management systems, and advocate for targeted, evidence-based enhancements to engine health monitoring and cabin structural certification standards.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 UTC, the subject aircraft was operating at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet when the left powerplant experienced a catastrophic, uncontained failure. Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters indicate a rapid decay in N1 and N2 rotational speeds, accompanied by a sharp increase in engine vibration levels preceding the event. Cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts, reviewed under docket reference SWA-OPS-2018-0417, confirm immediate crew recognition of abnormal engine indications, followed by a loud bang, cabin depressurization, and activation of the master caution system. Debris from the failed engine penetrated the left fuselage skin and compromised a passenger window, resulting in rapid decompression and the tragic loss of one occupant.

Maintenance records submitted to the docket (SWA-MNT-REC-0417) confirm that the affected LEAP-1B engine had accumulated 28,412 flight cycles and 41,205 flight hours since new. The most recent borescope inspection, conducted 142 cycles prior to the event, revealed no visible anomalies. Post-event metallurgical examination, coordinated with the OEM and documented in the NTSB materials laboratory report, identified a subsurface fatigue crack originating at the dovetail root of the failed fan blade. The crack propagated through approximately 60% of the blade cross-section before final fracture.

The Lead Investigator’s preliminary findings, as outlined in the hearing briefing package, correctly identify the fatigue initiation site and note the limitations of conventional ultrasonic testing in detecting early-stage subsurface defects in titanium aluminide fan blades. SWA acknowledges these findings and emphasizes that our maintenance program strictly adhered to the approved maintenance planning document (MPD) and all applicable airworthiness directives at the time of the event. Furthermore, while our operations are governed under 14 CFR Part 121, we have benchmarked certain predictive maintenance and safety management protocols against Part 135 commuter and on-demand operator standards, recognizing that the latter’s emphasis on high-frequency, short-cycle operational monitoring offers valuable insights for fleet-wide engine health tracking. Cross-industry data sharing initiatives, including those coordinated with operators such as Atlas Air, have further informed our understanding of how varying duty cycles and environmental stressors influence component degradation trajectories.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS
