3.4 Regulatory and Maintenance Program Alignment
The maintenance program for the subject aircraft was developed in coordination with the FAA Principal Inspector and adheres to the carrier’s approved CAMP. However, the docket reveals that the inspection interval for the affected fan blade series was not dynamically adjusted in response to emerging fleet data. This static approach contrasts with modern safety management system (SMS) principles, which advocate for continuous data integration and predictive analytics. 

The regulatory framework governing engine maintenance and airworthiness directives (ADs) operates within a reactive-to-proactive continuum. While Part 21 establishes the baseline for type design and continued airworthiness, the implementation of fleet-wide inspection modifications often lags behind real-time operational data. The carrier has since implemented enhanced data-sharing protocols with the OEM and regulatory authorities, but the incident demonstrates the need for a more agile, data-driven AD issuance process that incorporates real-world fatigue tracking and NDI efficacy metrics.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the technical evidence, metallurgical analysis, and operational data reviewed, Southwest Airlines concludes that the April 17, 2018, event was initiated by low-cycle fatigue crack propagation in a left engine fan blade, exacerbated by inspection interval limitations and sub-surface crack detectability constraints. The containment system performed within its certified parameters, but debris trajectory and nacelle shielding design permitted fuselage penetration. The cabin window assembly, while compliant with 14 CFR Part 25, exhibited structural vulnerability under direct high-velocity impact, contributing to rapid decompression and occupant ejection.

Our position is that the contributing factors are not attributable to maintenance negligence or procedural failure, but rather to the inherent limitations of time-based inspection intervals, the probabilistic nature of fatigue crack growth, and the current certification thresholds for cabin window impact resistance. The incident underscores the necessity of transitioning from reactive maintenance scheduling to predictive, condition-based monitoring, and highlights the value of integrating advanced materials and structural redundancies into cabin design.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Implementation of advanced NDI techniques, including phased-array ultrasonic testing and thermographic inspection, to improve sub-surface crack detection in titanium fan blades.
- Revision of inspection intervals to incorporate fleet-specific operational stress data and real-time engine health monitoring.
- Enhancement of aft nacelle shielding and debris deflection geometries to mitigate fuselage penetration risks during uncontained failures.
- Adoption of hybrid polycarbonate-acrylic cabin window assemblies with improved impact resistance and crack-arrest properties.
- Development of a regulatory framework that enables dynamic, data-driven AD issuance and maintenance program adjustments, drawing upon the systemic risk mitigation model established by SFAR 88.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

Southwest Airlines has already implemented several immediate and intermediate corrective actions in response to the incident. Within 72 hours of the event, the carrier initiated a fleet-wide inspection campaign targeting all engines of the affected series, utilizing enhanced eddy current and ultrasonic protocols. The FAA Principal Inspector and our engineering team coordinated the rollout, resulting in the identification and replacement of three additional fan blades exhibiting early-stage crack propagation. 

The carrier has also revised its CAMP to incorporate condition-based maintenance triggers, integrating real-time engine vibration and temperature data into the maintenance scheduling algorithm. Crew training programs have been updated to include enhanced rapid decompression response drills, with a focus on passenger restraint verification and emergency oxygen system deployment. Additionally, SWA has established a joint technical working group with the OEM and regulatory authorities to evaluate nacelle shielding modifications and cabin window design enhancements.

Looking forward, Southwest Airlines proposes the following future improvements:
- Deployment of predictive maintenance analytics platforms that utilize machine learning algorithms to forecast fatigue life and optimize inspection intervals.
- Collaboration with certification authorities to develop updated Part 25 guidance for cabin window impact resistance, incorporating hybrid material testing and occupant retention standards.
- Expansion of engine health monitoring systems to include acoustic emission sensors and fiber-optic strain gauges for real-time structural integrity assessment.
- Advocacy for regulatory harmonization that aligns Part 21 continued airworthiness requirements with modern SMS principles, ensuring that maintenance programs evolve in tandem with operational data and technological advancements.

The lessons learned from this event have been integrated into our safety management framework and will inform future engineering, maintenance, and operational decisions. Southwest Airlines remains committed to transparency, continuous improvement, and collaborative safety enhancement with the NTSB, regulatory authorities, and industry partners. We submit this analysis to support the Board’s investigative objectives and to advance the broader goal of preventing similar occurrences in commercial aviation.

TO: All Maintenance Control, Line Maintenance, Heavy Maintenance, Quality Assurance, and Fleet Engineering Personnel
FROM: Director of Maintenance & Quality Assurance / Reliability Engineering Division
DATE: May 14, 2018
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2018-047: Enhanced Fan Blade Retention & Nacelle Latch Verification Protocols
REF: QA-2018-047, WO-737-ENG-8842, SB-CFM-72-0114, NTSB Docket Entry #SWA-1380-0042

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate implementation of revised inspection, torque verification, and documentation procedures for high-bypass turbofan engine fan blade retention systems, forward nacelle latches, and adjacent fuselage window assemblies. The directive is issued to ensure strict compliance with Part 121 operational standards, mitigate risks associated with uncontained engine failures, and standardize maintenance execution across all active fleet types.

BACKGROUND:
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operating under Part 121 (14 CFR Part 121) experienced an uncontained engine failure during cruise flight at 32,500 feet. Debris from the left engine penetrated the nacelle and adjacent fuselage skin, resulting in rapid cabin decompression and one passenger fatality. Preliminary industry analysis indicates fatigue cracking in a fan blade root, compounded by inadequate retention hardware torque verification during prior heavy maintenance checks. While the event occurred on a Southwest Airlines (SWA) aircraft, our internal audit of similar CFM56-7B and transitioning LEAP engine platforms has identified procedural gaps in our current NDT scheduling, latch retention verification, and digital log traceability workflows.

Regulatory frameworks including SFAR 88 (14 CFR Part 121) and Section 25.783 (14 CFR § 25.783) establish baseline design and maintenance expectations for fuel system fault tolerance and fuselage door/window structural integrity. However, operational experience demonstrates that maintenance execution must exceed minimum compliance thresholds to address aging fleet dynamics, environmental stressors, and evolving failure modes. Atlas Air Inc (AAI) recently published a fleet-wide technical advisory highlighting similar torque drift in forward cowl retention systems, reinforcing the need for standardized cross-fleet inspection rigor. This alert aligns our internal practices with industry best practices and prepares our documentation for potential regulatory review.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all maintenance personnel shall adhere to the following revised protocols:

1. Fan Blade Retention & NDT Scheduling
   • All CFM56-7B and LEAP engine (CFM LEAP-1B) installations shall undergo eddy current inspection (ECI) of fan blade dovetail roots at intervals not exceeding 1,500 flight cycles, regardless of OEM-recommended thresholds.
   • Reference Work Order WO-737-ENG-8842, Rev. 3, for updated ECI probe calibration, scan pattern mapping, and data export requirements.
   • Any indication of crack propagation exceeding 0.015 inches shall trigger immediate engine removal, quarantine, and submission to Engineering for metallurgical review.

2. Forward Nacelle Latch & Hinge Verification
   • During all A-checks and above, forward cowl latches (P/N 65-43210-1 through -8) shall be torque-verified using calibrated digital torque wrenches (Model DTW-4500, calibration due within 30 days).
   • Torque values must be recorded in the aircraft technical log and cross-referenced with Maintenance Tracking System (MTS) Entry Code ENG-LATCH-04.
   • The Chief Inspector (Chief Insp.) or designated QA representative must physically witness and sign off on the first three aircraft per base following this directive.

3. Fuselage Window Frame & Seal Integrity
   • In alignment with Section 25.783 structural requirements, all passenger window assemblies shall undergo ultrasonic thickness testing (UTT) of the outer acrylic and aluminum retainer ring during C-checks.
   • Any retainer ring showing corrosion pitting deeper than 0.008 inches or fastener elongation shall be replaced per IPC Chapter 53-40-00.
   • Rapid decompression drill scenarios will be integrated into recurrent cabin crew training, coordinated with Flight Operations and the Safety Management System (SMS) office.

4. Documentation & Traceability
   • All inspection results must be uploaded to the centralized Quality Management System (QMS) within 24 hours of completion.
   • Missing or incomplete torque logs will be classified as Level 2 Nonconformances and routed to the IIC (Investigator in Charge) for root cause analysis and corrective action tracking.
   • Reference internal bulletin QA-2018-031 for updated digital signature protocols, audit trail requirements, and data retention standards.

ACTION REQUIRED:
• Line Maintenance Supervisors: Implement revised inspection checklists by May 21, 2018. Ensure all shift personnel complete the 45-minute e-learning module (Course ID: QA-ENG-2018-047) prior to performing engine or nacelle work.
• Heavy Maintenance Planners: Reschedule all pending C-checks to incorporate UTT of window retainers and forward latch torque verification. Submit revised work packages to Engineering by May 18, 2018.
• Quality Assurance Auditors: Conduct unannounced spot checks on a minimum of 15% of all engine-related work orders through June 30, 2018. Report findings directly to the Chief Inspector.
• Engineering & Reliability: Analyze torque trend data from the past 24 months and issue a fleet-wide reliability report by June 15, 2018. Coordinate with Atlas Air Inc technical representatives to benchmark inspection intervals and share failure mode data.
• All Personnel: Acknowledge receipt of this Quality Alert via the internal compliance portal by May 16, 2018. Failure to comply will result in immediate suspension of maintenance authorization pending retraining.

This directive supersedes all prior guidance regarding fan blade retention and nacelle latch verification. Questions regarding technical execution should be directed to the Fleet Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or the Quality Assurance Duty Manager.

Distribution: Maintenance Control, Line Stations, Heavy Maintenance Bays, Quality Assurance, Engineering, Training Department, SMS Office
Classification: INTERNAL – OPERATIONAL SENSITIVE
Retention: Permanent / NTSB Docket Reference #SWA-1380-0042

1. SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines Co, experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. Initial information indicates that debris from the left engine penetrated the fuselage and compromised a cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one passenger fatality. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and diverted to a nearby airport, where the aircraft landed without further incident. This preliminary report outlines the initial factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and documents procedural determinations made during the early phase of the inquiry. All findings documented herein are subject to revision as additional evidence is collected and analyzed.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information gathered from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads indicates that the left engine experienced a sudden loss of thrust and abnormal vibration signatures approximately 12 minutes prior to the emergency descent. Initial witness accounts from surviving passengers and cabin crew describe a loud bang followed by immediate cabin depressurization, localized structural damage near the left-side window, and the deployment of oxygen masks. Flight crew communications with air traffic control, as captured on preliminary audio transcripts, reflect standard emergency procedures, including a Mayday declaration, rapid descent to a lower altitude, and coordination for an immediate diversion.

Weather conditions at the time of the event, as reported by meteorological data and radar imagery, were characterized by clear skies with minimal turbulence and no significant convective activity along the flight path. Preliminary examination of the aircraft wreckage and recovered debris suggests that the primary damage is concentrated along the left fuselage section, with secondary fragmentation distributed across a wide area. The compromised window frame and adjacent fuselage skin exhibit signs of high-energy impact consistent with uncontained engine debris. Maintenance records for the accident aircraft are currently under review to establish the service history of the affected engine and its associated components. While the accident aircraft is equipped with a CFM56-series turbofan, the investigative team will also reference contemporary certification data and fatigue life methodologies applicable to modern high-bypass engines, including the LEAP-1B, to evaluate broader industry maintenance and inspection paradigms.

Damage assessment remains ongoing. Initial structural evaluations indicate that the rapid decompression did not compromise primary flight control systems, though localized damage to cabin interior components and adjacent wiring harnesses has been documented. The investigation will continue to assess whether any secondary systems were affected by the debris trajectory or pressure differential.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) has formally activated the following investigative groups: Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group has been tasked with collecting, cataloging, and analyzing evidence within their respective disciplines. The parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and relevant labor organizations. All party participation is governed by NTSB procedural guidelines to ensure impartiality and technical rigor.

Evidence secured to date includes the FDR and CVR, which have been transported to the NTSB laboratory for data extraction and transcription. Recovered engine components, including fan blade fragments and casing sections, have been secured and are undergoing preliminary metallurgical and dimensional analysis. The Chief Inspector has coordinated with local law enforcement and airport authorities to establish a secure perimeter around the aircraft and to facilitate the systematic recovery of additional debris. Maintenance logs, crew training records, and operational dispatch documentation have been obtained from Southwest Airlines Co and are currently being cross-referenced with regulatory requirements.

Procedural decisions have been made to expand the regulatory review scope to include compliance assessments under 14 CFR Part 21, specifically focusing on type certification requirements and continued airworthiness directives applicable to the engine model. Additionally, the investigation will examine maintenance tracking and inspection protocols to determine alignment with industry standards, including comparative evaluations of Part 135 maintenance documentation practices where subcontracted services were utilized. Given the nature of the fuselage penetration and rapid decompression, the investigative team will also conduct a targeted review of fuel system integrity and electrical routing in accordance with SFAR 88 guidelines, to rule out any secondary ignition or system degradation risks.

All examinations are being conducted under strict chain-of-custody protocols. Preliminary metallurgical testing has revealed surface anomalies on several recovered fan blade fragments, though the root cause of these anomalies remains undetermined. Further non-destructive testing and fractographic analysis are scheduled to clarify the initiation and propagation characteristics of the observed damage.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks include the completion of FDR and CVR data analysis, continuation of engine component teardown and inspection, and detailed structural mapping of the fuselage damage. The Systems group will conduct a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s pressurization and environmental control systems to evaluate their response to the rapid decompression event. The Human Performance group will proceed with crew interviews and duty-time analysis, while the Survival Factors group will finalize the assessment of emergency evacuation procedures and cabin safety equipment performance.

The IIC will convene a preliminary technical briefing with all party representatives within 30 days to review initial data trends and adjust investigative priorities as necessary. Additional metallurgical and materials testing will be conducted at accredited laboratories, with results expected to be integrated into the investigative record by the end of the second quarter. The Chief Inspector will oversee the continued recovery and cataloging of debris, ensuring that all recovered items are properly documented and preserved for future analysis.

A public hearing is anticipated once the factual record has been sufficiently developed, though no specific date has been established. Interim updates will be issued as significant technical milestones are reached, and all parties will be notified of schedule adjustments in accordance with NTSB procedural directives. It is emphasized that all current observations, data interpretations, and procedural determinations are preliminary in nature and subject to revision as the investigation progresses. No conclusions regarding probable cause or contributing factors will be drawn until the complete factual record has been thoroughly evaluated and peer-reviewed.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 General
On April 17, 2018, at 15:43:12 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) / 19:43:12 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), a Boeing 737-700, registration N737XX, experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight. The accident occurred at approximately 40.1234° North latitude, 75.9876° West longitude, near New Holland, Pennsylvania. The aircraft was operating under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121 as a scheduled passenger flight. At the time of the event, the aircraft was maintaining a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL) with a calibrated airspeed of 285 knots and a Mach number of 0.78. The flight was en route from John F. Kennedy International Airport (KJFK), New York, to Dallas Love Field (KDAL), Texas.

1.2 Flight History
The flight departed KJFK at 14:15:30 EDT / 18:15:30 UTC. The flight crew received a standard dispatch release, including a flight plan, weather briefing, and NOTAM review. The aircraft climbed through 10,000 feet MSL at 14:28:12 EDT, transitioning to standard instrument departure procedures. The aircraft reached its assigned cruise altitude of 32,500 feet MSL at 14:41:05 EDT. The flight proceeded normally until the event. Air traffic control (ATC) radar data and flight data recorder (FDR) parameters indicate a stable cruise profile with no deviations from the filed route or assigned altitude prior to the occurrence. The aircraft was under the control of the Philadelphia Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZNY) at the time of the event.

1.3 Event Sequence
At 15:43:12 EDT, the flight data recorder recorded a sudden loss of N1 (fan speed) and N2 (core speed) parameters on the left engine (Engine No. 1), accompanied by a rapid increase in engine vibration levels exceeding 4.0 inches per second. Simultaneously, the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) captured an audible bang followed by the activation of the master caution and engine fire warning systems. The flight crew immediately initiated the appropriate emergency checklist and declared an emergency with ATC. While preliminary telemetry and acoustic signatures strongly suggest a fan blade liberation as the initiating event, the precise failure origin and subsequent secondary component interactions remain subject to ongoing metallurgical review, and alternative initiation sequences cannot be entirely excluded pending final teardown analysis.

1. INTRODUCTION
This report documents the factual findings of the specialist examination conducted by the NTSB Powerplants and Structures Group regarding the uncontained engine failure event involving a Boeing 737-700, registration N772SW, operated by Southwest Airlines. The examination was conducted under the authority of the Chief Inspector at the NTSB Materials and Engineering Laboratory in Washington, D.C., between May 14 and May 22, 2018. The scope of the examination encompassed the recovered left engine (CFM International LEAP-1B, serial number 784521), associated fan blade debris, the forward fuselage pressure bulkhead, the impacted cabin window assembly, and the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) parameter extraction. All components were received in a secured chain of custody, cataloged under NTSB evidence control numbers ENG-2018-0417-001 through -014. The examination methodology adhered to NTSB investigative protocols, ASTM International standards for metallurgical and composite analysis, and manufacturer engineering specifications. Data extraction and synchronization were performed using ARINC 717 frame decoding software with a 1 Hz baseline resolution, supplemented by high-frequency QAR sampling at 8 Hz for vibration and pressure parameters.

2. BACKGROUND
The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737-700, certified under 14 CFR Part 25, equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines. The left engine, P/N 2000-LEAP-1B-26, S/N 784521, was manufactured in 2015 and accumulated 18,420 flight hours and 11,205 flight cycles at the time of the event. The engine’s certification basis complies with 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart E, and incorporates type design data approved under TC E00001EN. The fan assembly consists of 18 blades, each incorporating a 3D woven carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) airfoil with a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V, AMS 4911) leading edge and trailing edge reinforcement. The fan case incorporates a composite containment ring (P/N 450-882-03) designed to meet 14 CFR Part 25.903(d) uncontained rotor burst requirements, utilizing a hybrid Kevlar/epoxy layup optimized for high-strain-rate energy absorption.

Maintenance records indicate the engine was last removed for a scheduled shop visit on November 12, 2016, and overhauled by Atlas Air Inc. at their MRO facility in Miami, FL. The overhaul included a borescope inspection of all 18 fan blades, eddy current testing of the dovetail roots, and replacement of the fan case acoustic liner. The engine was returned to service on December 3, 2016, with a documented time-since-overhaul of 1,840 hours and 1,102 cycles. The aircraft’s pressurization system and cabin window assemblies are certified in accordance with 14 CFR 25.783, which mandates structural integrity and pressure retention capabilities for fuselage penetrations. The impacted window (station 420, left side, row 14) is a dual-pane acrylic assembly (P/N 65-44210-1) mounted in a 7075-T6 aluminum alloy frame, designed to withstand a differential pressure of 8.6 PSI at maximum operating altitude. The window retention system incorporates four titanium alloy shear pins (P/N 65-44210-3) and a secondary safety latch mechanism.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS
Physical examination of the recovered engine components was conducted in a controlled cleanroom environment. The left engine fan case exhibited a 14.2-inch longitudinal breach at the 10 o’clock position, consistent with high-energy debris ejection. The composite containment ring was fractured circumferentially, with delamination observed across 11 of 16 plies. Ultrasonic C-scan mapping (ASTM E2580) confirmed a delamination area of 18.4 square inches, with fiber pull-out and matrix cracking characteristic of dynamic impact loading exceeding 45,000 ft-lbs of kinetic energy. The acoustic liner exhibited localized ablation and resin charring, with peak thermal exposure estimated at 310°C based on thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) of the phenolic binder.

The primary failure origin was identified on fan blade number 12 (P/N 300-445-01, S/N FB-8842). The blade was recovered in three major fragments. Macroscopic examination revealed a fatigue crack initiation site at the trailing edge fillet radius, approximately 1.8 inches from the dovetail root. The initiation site was located within a 0.004-inch deep machining mark that exceeded the manufacturer’s surface finish specification of 32 μin Ra. Fluorescent penetrant inspection (ASTM E1417) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) confirmed a fatigue crack propagation zone measuring 0.62 inches in length, exhibiting classic beach marks and striations with an average spacing of 0.0008 inches, indicative of high-cycle fatigue under centrifugal loading. The final fracture zone, occupying approximately 35% of the cross-sectional area, displayed ductile dimple rupture consistent with tensile overload at rotational speeds exceeding 5,100 RPM.

Metallurgical analysis of the Ti-6Al-4V leading edge reinforcement was performed per ASTM E8 and ASTM E384. Tensile testing of a representative coupon from the undamaged portion of the blade yielded an ultimate tensile strength of 138 ksi and a yield strength of 124 ksi, within AMS 4911 specifications. Microhardness testing (Vickers, 500g load) averaged 342 HV across the heat-affected zone, indicating no thermal degradation or improper heat treatment. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the alloy composition as 6.1% Al, 4.0% V, balance Ti, with no evidence of foreign object damage (FOD) or corrosion pitting at the crack origin. The CFRP airfoil matrix exhibited no signs of moisture ingress or delamination prior to the failure event, as verified by cross-sectional microscopy and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR).

The fuselage impact zone was examined at station 418.5, left side. The 2024-T3 aluminum skin (0.063-inch thickness) exhibited a 9.4-inch by 4.1-inch irregular penetration. The impacted cabin window assembly was completely dislodged from its mounting frame. The acrylic pane exhibited radial cracking and localized melting at the impact interface, with a maximum temperature exposure estimated at 210°C based on polymer degradation analysis. The window retention clips were sheared at the fastener shanks, with fracture surfaces indicating shear overload at approximately 18,500 lbf. The surrounding fuselage stringers (S-14L and S-15L) exhibited plastic deformation but remained structurally continuous, with no evidence of crack propagation into the pressure bulkhead. Finite element analysis (FEA) of the impact zone, utilizing LS-DYNA explicit dynamics, confirmed that the localized stress concentration exceeded the 7075-T6 yield strength of 73 ksi, resulting in fastener pull-through and frame distortion.

4. DATA ANALYSIS
Flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) data were extracted and synchronized with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) timeline. The aircraft was in cruise flight at 32,500 ft MSL, maintaining 285 KIAS, with an outside air temperature of -48°C. At 14:22:17 UTC, the FDR recorded a sudden N1 vibration (V1A) increase from 0.12 in/s to 4.2 in/s, coinciding with a 120 RPM N1 decay over 1.8 seconds. Engine gas temperature (EGT) rose from 685°C to 892°C within 3.4 seconds, followed by a rapid N2 spool-down to 68% RPM. The engine fuel control unit (FCU) commanded a fuel flow reduction, but the uncontained failure resulted in immediate thrust asymmetry. The FDR recorded a maximum lateral acceleration of 0.38g during the initial decompression event, consistent with asymmetric thrust and localized airflow disruption.

Cabin pressure parameters recorded a differential pressure drop from 8.2 PSI to 3.1 PSI within 4.2 seconds, triggering the cabin altitude warning at 10,000 ft equivalent. The outflow valve commanded full open, and the emergency descent profile was initiated at 14:22:24 UTC. The aircraft descended to 10,000 ft MSL over 6 minutes, with indicated airspeed fluctuating between 240 and 290 KIAS due to aerodynamic drag from the open fuselage breach. The QAR high-frequency sampling captured transient pressure oscillations at 14.2 Hz, corresponding to acoustic resonance within the cabin volume following the window dislodgement. The rapid decompression rate of 1.22 PSI/sec exceeded the design threshold of 0.8 PSI/sec specified in 14 CFR 25.841, but remained within the structural tolerance limits of the fuselage pressure vessel.

Comparison with baseline operational data from the QAR indicates that the N1 vibration trend had remained within the manufacturer’s green band (0.05–0.25 in/s) for the preceding 1,102 cycles. No exceedances of torque limits, EGT margins, or oil pressure parameters were recorded during the final 50 flight hours. The engine’s full authority digital engine control (FADEC) logged a fault code 32-11 (Fan Vibration Exceedance) at 14:22:17.2 UTC, followed by an automatic thrust reduction command. The window retention system performed as designed until the localized impact energy exceeded the 18,500 lbf shear capacity of the mounting hardware. Structural load calculations based on the FDR-derived deceleration profile indicate a peak dynamic pressure of 1,840 psf acting on the forward fuselage, well below the ultimate design load of 2,400 psf for the 737-700 pressure vessel.

5. SUMMARY
The specialist examination of the left engine and associated airframe components yielded the following factual findings:
- The uncontained engine failure originated from a fatigue fracture of fan blade number 12 (P/N 300-445-01, S/N FB-8842), with crack initiation at a trailing edge fillet machining mark exceeding surface finish specifications.
- Fatigue crack propagation measured 0.62 inches, culminating in tensile overload at rotational speeds exceeding 5,100 RPM. Metallurgical testing confirmed Ti-6Al-4V material properties within AMS 4911 limits, with no evidence of thermal degradation, corrosion, or foreign object damage.
- The composite containment ring fractured under dynamic impact loading, resulting in a 14.2-inch breach in the fan case and ejection of high-energy debris. Ultrasonic C-scan mapping confirmed 11-ply delamination consistent with impact energy exceeding 45,000 ft-lbs.
- Debris impact at fuselage station 418.5 penetrated the 2024-T3 aluminum skin and dislodged the left row 14 cabin window assembly. The window retention clips failed in shear at approximately 18,500 lbf, consistent with localized impact energy exceeding design thresholds.
- FDR and QAR data recorded a rapid N1 vibration spike, EGT excursion, and cabin pressure decay from 8.2 PSI to 3.1 PSI within 4.2 seconds. The aircraft maintained structural integrity during the emergency descent, with no propagation of damage into the primary pressure bulkhead.
- The engine’s last overhaul was performed by Atlas Air Inc., with maintenance records indicating compliance with manufacturer inspection intervals. The aircraft and engine certification basis complies with 14 CFR Part 21 and 14 CFR Part 25, including 14 CFR 25.783 requirements for fuselage window structural integrity.
All findings are documented in the accompanying photographic exhibits, metallurgical reports, and data parameter logs maintained by the NTSB Powerplants and Structures Group. The examination was conducted under the supervision of the Chief Inspector, with all procedures adhering to established NTSB investigative protocols and ASTM testing standards.

INTERVIEW OF MARK R. HENDERSON, LEAD MAINTENANCE INSPECTOR
Date: May 14, 2018
Time: 10:15 AM
Location: Southwest Airlines Co. Maintenance Operations Center, Dallas, Texas
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Miller

Q: Please state your full name, current title, and your role relative to the April 17th incident.
A: Mark R. Henderson. I’m a Lead Maintenance Inspector for Southwest Airlines Co. I’ve been with the company for, uh, about fourteen years now. On the seventeenth, I was on shift in Maintenance Control when the flight—Flight 1380, I believe—diverted to Philadelphia. My role was to coordinate the initial technical response, pull the maintenance logs, and then actually go out to the aircraft once it was secured to do the preliminary damage assessment. I also served as the company liaison for the NTSB and FAA teams once they arrived on site.

Q: Walk me through how you first became aware of the event. What was the initial information you received?
A: Yeah, so it was... I want to say around 11:15 Eastern time. We got a call from the flight deck. The captain reported a loud bang, followed by a severe vibration, and then a cabin depressurization. They were declaring an emergency. At first, honestly, we thought maybe a tire blowout or a bird strike, but the altitude was thirty-two thousand, five hundred feet, so that ruled out most of the usual suspects. The crew mentioned the left engine was running rough, and they were shutting it down. I remember thinking, "Okay, uncontained failure is a real possibility here." We immediately started pulling up the maintenance history for that specific airframe and the engine. The ACARS messages started coming in a minute or two later, confirming the shutdown and the rapid descent.

Q: What did you observe when you first inspected the aircraft after it landed?
A: Right. The aircraft touched down in Philly around 11:45, I think. I wasn’t on the ground yet, obviously, but I was on the phone with the local line maintenance team. When I finally got eyes on it—this was later that evening, after the NTSB secured the scene and we got clearance to approach—the damage was... it was pretty severe. The left engine cowling was completely gone. I mean, just shredded. There was a large hole in the fuselage, right around row fourteen, I believe. The window was blown out. You could see the insulation blankets torn, wiring harnesses exposed, and the frame was bent inward. The smell of... well, burnt hydraulic fluid and ozone, mostly. And the debris field on the ground was extensive. We had to cordon off a huge area. It was... it was sobering, honestly.

Q: Can you describe the engine involved and your familiarity with its maintenance requirements?
A: Sure. It was a CFM International LEAP engine. Specifically, the LEAP-1B variant. We’ve been transitioning our fleet to these over the last few years. They’re... they’re incredibly efficient, but they’re also highly stressed components. The fan blades are made of a titanium aluminide alloy, and the containment ring is designed to handle a blade-off event. But in this case, the failure propagated beyond the containment ring. I’ve worked on dozens of these. The maintenance program is pretty rigorous. We follow the manufacturer’s service bulletins to the letter, and we’re constantly tracking cycle counts, vibration trends, borescope results. This particular engine had been through a recent shop visit, I think around... maybe eighteen months prior? I’d have to check the exact records. Actually, no, it was closer to twenty-two months. I’m looking at the logbook now.

Q: How does your maintenance program align with federal regulations, particularly regarding certification and operational standards?
A: Well, we operate strictly under 14 CFR Part 121. That’s the big one for scheduled air carriers. Everything we do—from crew training to maintenance intervals, to how we handle an uncontained failure—is governed by Part 121. It’s a lot more prescriptive than, say, 14 CFR Part 135, which covers charter and commuter ops. We don’t have the flexibility that Part 135 operators might have. Every inspection, every repair, it’s documented, tracked, and audited. And when it comes to the aircraft itself, the original type certification was done under 14 CFR part 25. That’s the airworthiness standards for transport category airplanes. The fuselage, the windows, the emergency depressurization protocols—they’re all designed to meet those part 25 requirements. The engine itself, the LEAP, was certified under 14 CFR Part 21, which covers the certification procedures for products and parts. So, you know, the whole system is layered. We don’t just fix things; we have to prove they meet the original design intent and the ongoing regulatory mandates.

Q: Were there any immediate concerns about the structural integrity of the airframe following the impact?
A: Absolutely. When debris hits the fuselage at cruise speed, you’re looking at potential damage to the pressure bulkheads, the stringers, the skin panels. We had to do a full structural assessment. The NTSB and the FAA were on site, obviously. We used ultrasonic testing, eddy current, the whole nine yards. The window frame was compromised, which is why the rapid decompression happened. But the primary structure held. That’s... that’s a testament to the part 25 design standards, honestly. The aircraft was built to survive a certain level of damage. Still, it was a close call. The crew did an incredible job getting it down. I mean, they managed a single-engine descent, handled the decompression, and landed safely. You don’t train for that every day, but the procedures are there for a reason.

Q: Can you give me a rough timeline of your actions from the initial notification through the end of your shift that day?
A: Let’s see. I got the call at 11:15. By 11:30, I had the maintenance control team pulling the engine logs, the last A-check records, the borescope reports. Around noon, we were coordinating with the FAA and the NTSB. The aircraft landed at 11:45, but it took a while to get it to a remote stand, secure the scene, and get the passengers off. I was on the phone with the Philly station manager, the lead mechanic, the captain’s union rep... it was chaotic. By 2:00 PM, I had a preliminary damage report drafted. I didn’t actually fly out to Philly until the next morning, but I was working straight through until about 8:00 PM that night. Then I came back in early the next day to assist the investigators. I think I logged about sixteen hours that day, give or take.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add regarding the maintenance history or the operational context of this flight?
A: Just that... I mean, we take this stuff seriously. Every time an engine goes through a shop visit, we’re looking for fatigue cracks, blade tip rubs, anything out of tolerance. The LEAP is a great engine, but it’s not immune to material fatigue. We follow the manuals, we follow the ADs, we follow the service bulletins. We operate under Part 121, which means we’re held to the highest standard. But sometimes, despite all the checks, something slips through. Or the failure mode is just... unpredictable. I’ve been in aviation long enough to know that. We’ll learn from this. We always do. And, uh, I want to make sure the record reflects that the crew’s actions were textbook. They followed the emergency checklist, they communicated clearly, and they prioritized passenger safety. That’s what matters.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Henderson. We’ll follow up if we need clarification on the maintenance logs or the structural testing results.
A: Yeah, absolutely. I’ll have the digital records uploaded to the secure portal by end of day. Let me know if you need anything else.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND COMPLIANCE REPORT

DOCKET NO. FAA-2018-0417-NTSB
REFERENCE: NTSB/AAR-19/01 (Adapted)
DATE: April 20, 2018
DISTRIBUTION: Flight Standards Service (AFS), Aircraft Certification Service (AIR), Office of Rulemaking (ARM), Principal Operations Inspectors (POI), Principal Maintenance Inspectors (PMI)

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
Reference: 14 CFR Part 33.94, 14 CFR 25.903, 14 CFR 121.344, and Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-14-09 (Docket No. FAA-2018-0417).
NTSB Accident Number: DCA18MA073
Date of Occurrence: April 17, 2018
Subject: Regulatory Compliance Assessment, Corrective Action Framework, and Oversight Protocol Following Uncontained Engine Failure and Subsequent Rapid Decompression Event Involving a Boeing 737-700 Series Aircraft.

2. BACKGROUND
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700, operating under the provisions of 14 CFR Part 121, experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine during cruise flight at Flight Level 325 (32,500 feet mean sea level). The failure resulted in high-energy debris penetration of the forward fuselage structure, compromise of a passenger cabin window, and subsequent rapid decompression. The event resulted in one fatality and multiple injuries. The powerplant involved was a CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engine, certified under 14 CFR Part 33 and installed pursuant to an approved type certificate amendment. The incident prompted immediate regulatory scrutiny regarding engine containment standards, fuselage structural integrity, and emergency decompression protocols.

The regulatory framework governing this occurrence is anchored in 14 CFR 25.903, which mandates that engines must be designed, installed, and maintained to prevent hazards to the aircraft in the event of failure. Additionally, 14 CFR 25.365 and 14 CFR 25.783 establish requirements for pressurized compartment loads and fuselage door/window structural integrity, respectively. The operator’s maintenance program, as required under 14 CFR 121.344, must incorporate manufacturer service bulletins, Airworthiness Directives, and approved inspection intervals to ensure continued airworthiness.

Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration has issued multiple ADs addressing fan blade fatigue, containment ring degradation, and secondary system vulnerabilities in high-bypass turbofan architectures. Prior to this occurrence, AD 2016-08-12 mandated ultrasonic inspection intervals for fan blade dovetail regions. Furthermore, the regulatory philosophy established under Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88) regarding fuel tank system fault tolerance has been referenced in subsequent rulemaking to address secondary system vulnerabilities following high-energy debris strikes. The FAA’s oversight of Part 121 operators, including entities such as Atlas Air, Inc. (AAI), has emphasized the integration of predictive maintenance analytics, engine health monitoring (EHM) data thresholds, and enhanced non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols to mitigate uncontained failure risks. The certification basis for the subject airframe and powerplant combination requires strict adherence to the approved Maintenance Review Board Report (MRBR) and Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP) documentation.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of the operator’s compliance posture, maintenance records, and regulatory oversight mechanisms reveals several critical findings. The designated NTSB Lead Investigator, in coordination with FAA Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (AFS) personnel, determined that the uncontained failure originated from a fatigue crack propagation in the LEAP-1B fan blade root, which exceeded the certified containment envelope. The debris trajectory subsequently impacted the forward fuselage, compromising the structural continuity of the cabin window frame and initiating rapid decompression.

Compliance Status: The operator’s maintenance program, as documented in the approved CAMP and aligned with 14 CFR 121.344 and 14 CFR 121.369, was found to be nominally compliant with existing regulatory mandates. However, the inspection intervals for fan blade ultrasonic testing were not aligned with the accelerated fatigue degradation rates observed in the subject powerplant fleet. The Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for cabin window integrity and pressurization system redundancy were not fully optimized for post-impact rapid decompression scenarios. Furthermore, supplemental type certificate (STC) modifications for cabin window reinforcement lacked standardized post-installation verification protocols, resulting in inconsistent compliance verification across the fleet.

Regulatory Oversight Actions: The FAA initiated a targeted surveillance campaign under 14 CFR 121.373 and FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 6, Chapter 2, focusing on EHM data analytics and NDT compliance verification. Oversight actions included mandatory reporting of all fan blade vibration anomalies exceeding 0.5 inches per second, as well as a fleet-wide review of containment ring installation procedures per 14 CFR 33.94. The FAA coordinated with the manufacturer to issue an Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) 2018-14-09, mandating immediate visual and eddy-current inspections of all LEAP-1B fan blades within 50 flight cycles. Principal Maintenance Inspectors (PMIs) were directed to conduct unannounced ramp inspections to verify compliance with revised torque specifications and containment ring retention hardware.

Gaps Identified in Regulatory Framework: The investigation highlighted a systemic gap in the integration of secondary system fault tolerance following uncontained engine failures. While 14 CFR 25.903 addresses primary engine containment, it does not explicitly mandate structural redundancy for adjacent fuselage penetrations or cabin window assemblies. Furthermore, the regulatory framework lacks a unified standard for post-debris impact pressurization system isolation, a deficiency previously addressed in fuel system design under SFAR 88 but not extended to cabin environmental control systems. The oversight of STC modifications for cabin window reinforcement has also been fragmented, resulting in inconsistent compliance verification across Part 121 operators. Additionally, the current type certification basis does not require dynamic debris trajectory modeling for high-altitude cruise conditions, limiting the predictive accuracy of containment envelope validation.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
To address the identified deficiencies and ensure continued airworthiness, the following corrective actions and regulatory recommendations are mandated:

Corrective Actions Required:
1. All operators of Boeing 737-700 series aircraft equipped with LEAP-1B engines shall implement an enhanced fan blade inspection protocol, incorporating phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) at intervals not exceeding 1,000 flight cycles, in accordance with 14 CFR 121.344 and 14 CFR 33.15.
2. The manufacturer shall revise the Engine Maintenance Manual (EMM) to include mandatory containment ring torque verification and debris trajectory analysis, ensuring compliance with 14 CFR 25.903 and 14 CFR 33.94.
3. Operators shall update their MMEL and Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) procedures to include explicit rapid decompression isolation protocols, with emphasis on cabin window structural failure mitigation and emergency oxygen system deployment.
4. All STC holders for cabin window reinforcement shall submit revised installation and inspection procedures to the FAA for approval, ensuring alignment with 14 CFR 25.783 and 14 CFR 25.365.

Timeline for Compliance:
- Phase I (Immediate): EAD 2018-14-09 compliance shall be achieved within 30 calendar days of issuance. All affected fan blades shall be removed from service and subjected to laboratory metallurgical analysis.
- Phase II (Short-Term): Implementation of PAUT inspection protocols and EMM revisions shall be completed within 180 days. Operators shall submit compliance verification reports to the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) by the 150-day mark.
- Phase III (Long-Term): Rulemaking action to amend 14 CFR 25.783 and 14 CFR 25.365 shall be initiated within 12 months, incorporating enhanced fuselage penetration resistance standards and post-impact pressurization isolation requirements.

Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule:
The FAA Office of Aviation Safety will conduct quarterly compliance audits of all Part 121 operators utilizing LEAP-1B powerplants. These audits will verify adherence to the revised inspection intervals, EHM data reporting thresholds, and MMEL procedural updates. The NTSB Lead Investigator will participate in biannual technical review panels to assess the efficacy of the corrective actions and evaluate emerging fatigue data. Additionally, a joint FAA-NTSB working group will be established to harmonize engine containment standards with secondary system fault tolerance requirements, drawing upon the regulatory precedents established under SFAR 88. Final compliance certification and regulatory closure will be documented in the Federal Register upon successful completion of all mandated actions, with a target completion date of December 31, 2025.

This report constitutes the official regulatory response to the April 17, 2018, occurrence. All referenced entities, including Atlas Air, Inc., shall ensure full compliance with the directives outlined herein. Failure to adhere to the prescribed timelines and inspection protocols will result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.19 and 14 CFR 121.373. All correspondence regarding this docket shall be directed to the Office of Rulemaking, Docket Management Facility, under the reference number cited above.

HEADLINE: Engine Failure at 32,500 Feet Claims One Life, Forces Emergency Landing

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, Global Aviation Desk
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA —

A commercial Boeing 737-700 made a harrowing emergency landing on Tuesday, April 17, 2018, after a catastrophic engine failure at 32,500 feet shattered a cabin window and triggered rapid decompression, killing one passenger and injuring several others. The aircraft, carrying 144 passengers and five crew members, diverted to the nearest major airport where emergency responders met it on the tarmac.

The incident unfolded mid-flight when the jet’s left engine suffered an uncontained failure—a rare and dangerous event where internal rotating components fracture, breach the engine casing, and are ejected at high velocity. Debris from the explosion struck the fuselage, blowing out a passenger window and causing a sudden, violent drop in cabin pressure. Pilots immediately initiated an emergency descent protocol, dropping thousands of feet in minutes to reach breathable air before safely touching down. One passenger, who was partially pulled toward the breached window by the pressure differential, was extracted by first responders and transported to a nearby hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Several other passengers sustained minor injuries from flying debris and the rapid pressure change.

Federal investigators have launched a comprehensive probe into the tragedy. “Our priority is determining the exact sequence of mechanical events that led to this failure,” said the Chief Inspector at NTSB headquarters in Washington, D.C. “We are treating this as a high-priority investigation and will leave no stone unturned.” The Investigator in Charge, commonly referred to as the IIC, confirmed that the engine’s fan blades, turbine disk, and containment ring are being examined for signs of metal fatigue or manufacturing defects. Meanwhile, a Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson emphasized that the aircraft’s design includes redundant safety systems, but acknowledged the severity of the decompression. “The crew’s swift response undoubtedly saved lives,” the FAA representative stated. “We are working closely with the airline and manufacturers to ensure all similar aircraft are grounded for immediate inspection if necessary.”

The aircraft, a twin-engine narrow-body jet, was operating a scheduled passenger route when the failure occurred. While the flight was managed under a commercial charter framework, industry operations involving similar aircraft often fall under strict regulatory oversight, including 14 CFR Part 135, which governs commuter and on-demand flight operations. The airline, which has partnered with major logistics and charter operators like Atlas Air Inc for fleet management and maintenance support, has temporarily suspended flights using the same engine model pending inspection. The powerplant in question is a high-bypass turbofan, distinct from newer-generation engines like the LEAP-1B, though investigators are reviewing maintenance logs across multiple engine families to identify potential industry-wide vulnerabilities.

Aviation safety experts suggest that uncontained engine failures, while extremely rare, typically stem from microscopic cracks in rotating components that grow over time. “Metal fatigue is a silent threat,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor and former FAA consultant. “Even with rigorous inspection schedules, stress fractures can develop in hard-to-reach areas. The fact that debris penetrated the fuselage indicates the containment ring failed to do its job, which is highly unusual.” Chen noted that modern engines are designed to withstand blade loss, but extreme rotational speeds and material degradation can occasionally overwhelm those safeguards. He cautioned against premature conclusions, noting that investigators must first rule out foreign object damage or improper maintenance procedures.

Survivors described a scene of sudden chaos followed by intense focus. “There was a deafening bang, and then the air just vanished,” said passenger David Lin, who was seated three rows from the damaged window. “Oxygen masks dropped, people were screaming, but the flight attendants were incredibly calm. They told us to brace, and we just held on.” The family of the deceased passenger released a brief statement through their attorney, expressing profound grief and requesting privacy. “She was a beloved mother and colleague who traveled frequently for work,” the statement read. “We are devastated by this sudden loss and trust that investigators will uncover the truth so no other family has to endure this pain.”

The incident echoes a handful of similar tragedies in commercial aviation history, most notably a 2009 event involving a different carrier where an engine failure also resulted in a fatal decompression. However, the overall safety record of the Boeing 737 family remains among the strongest in the industry, with millions of flights completed without incident. Regulatory bodies have continuously updated inspection protocols over the decades, particularly for older engine models, to catch fatigue before it becomes catastrophic. Airlines operating similar aircraft are already conducting enhanced ultrasonic inspections on their fleets, and the FAA is reviewing whether to mandate accelerated maintenance intervals.

As of Wednesday, the National Transportation Safety Board continues to analyze recovered engine components, cockpit voice recordings, and flight data. The IIC confirmed that a preliminary report will be issued within 30 days, though a final determination on the root cause could take up to two years. “We are committed to transparency and safety,” the Chief Inspector reiterated. “Every piece of data we recover brings us closer to preventing this from happening again.”

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Engineering and Maintenance Division of Southwest Airlines Co (SWA), acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative proceedings. Our role in this investigation encompasses the provision of technical expertise regarding airframe-engine integration, maintenance program compliance, non-destructive inspection (NDI) methodologies, and operational response protocols. The scope of this document is to present a comprehensive technical assessment of the uncontained engine failure event, evaluate the contributing maintenance and design factors, and articulate our position on systemic safety improvements. We submit this analysis in support of the Board’s fact-finding mission and to inform the development of actionable safety recommendations.

As we convene in Washington DC for this investigative hearing, it is imperative that our evaluation remains grounded in empirical data, metallurgical evidence, and established engineering principles. The Operator acknowledges the tragic loss of life and recognizes the profound responsibility that accompanies the operation of a high-density commercial fleet. This submission does not seek to assign blame, but rather to isolate the technical and procedural variables that converged on April 17, 2018, and to demonstrate how industry-wide practices can be refined to mitigate recurrence. Our analysis draws upon maintenance logs, flight data recorder (FDR) parameters, cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts, and independent metallurgical examinations, all of which have been cataloged in the official docket.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 aircraft operating under 14 CFR Part 121 air carrier regulations experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine during cruise flight at approximately 32,500 feet. The aircraft was en route on a scheduled passenger service when the flight crew reported a sudden loss of thrust, accompanied by severe airframe vibration and an immediate cabin depressurization event. Debris from the failed engine penetrated the left fuselage skin and compromised a passenger window, resulting in rapid decompression and the tragic fatality of one occupant. The crew executed an emergency descent and diversion, successfully landing the aircraft without further loss of life.

Docket materials, including Maintenance Record Log 2018-04-12 and Engine Health Monitoring (EHM) trend reports, confirm that the affected engine had accumulated approximately 32,000 flight cycles and 45,000 flight hours. The most recent shop visit occurred 18 months prior to the event, during which the fan blade assembly underwent standard eddy current inspection per the approved maintenance program. Post-event metallurgical analysis (Docket Exhibit 14A) identified a low-cycle fatigue (LCF) crack originating at the dovetail root of the number 13 fan blade. The crack propagated through multiple flight cycles until the remaining cross-section could no longer sustain operational centrifugal loads, resulting in blade liberation and subsequent uncontained failure.

The regulatory framework governing this operation is distinct from that of Part 135 on-demand operators, as 14 CFR Part 121 mandates rigorous maintenance tracking, continuous airworthiness monitoring, and structured reliability programs. While the Operator’s maintenance program was fully compliant with all applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) and Service Bulletins (SBs) at the time of the event, the failure highlights inherent limitations in current inspection intervals and NDI sensitivity thresholds for aging high-cycle components. Furthermore, while Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) 88 established comprehensive fuel tank flammability reduction standards, the current incident underscores the necessity of applying similarly rigorous, system-wide risk assessment methodologies to engine containment and cabin structural integrity.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The technical evaluation of this event centers on three interrelated domains: fracture mechanics and material degradation, inspection methodology limitations, and airframe response to uncontained debris. Each domain is examined against industry standards, certification requirements, and operational data.

Fracture Mechanics and Material Degradation
Metallurgical examination of the recovered fan blade fragment (Docket Exhibit 14A) reveals classic LCF crack initiation characteristics, including beach marks and striation patterns consistent with cyclic loading. The crack originated at a subsurface inclusion near the dovetail radius, a region subjected to high tensile stress during engine spool-up and spool-down. Finite element modeling (FEM) conducted by the Operator’s engineering team, cross-referenced with OEM stress analysis, indicates that the local stress concentration factor exceeded the material’s endurance limit after approximately 28,000 cycles. The remaining 4,000 cycles facilitated stable crack propagation until the critical fracture toughness threshold was breached. This progression aligns with established damage tolerance principles but exposes a vulnerability in the current inspection interval, which assumes a slower crack growth rate than observed in this specific operational environment.

Inspection Methodology and NDI Limitations
The approved maintenance program utilized conventional eddy current testing (ECT) for fan blade dovetail inspection. While ECT is highly effective for surface-breaking defects, its sensitivity diminishes for subsurface flaws, particularly in complex geometries with tight radii. Docket Exhibit 19C, which details the pre-event inspection report, confirms that the inspection was performed within tolerance and yielded no rejectable indications. However, post-event phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) on adjacent blades revealed micro-cracking in two additional units that were undetected by ECT. This discrepancy highlights a systemic limitation in current NDI protocols. Industry best practices, as demonstrated in next-generation powerplant maintenance programs such as those developed for the LEAP-1B, incorporate multi-modal inspection techniques, including laser ultrasonics and automated eddy current mapping, to improve subsurface defect detection. The Operator’s analysis indicates that transitioning to advanced NDI methodologies, coupled with reduced inspection intervals for high-cycle engines, would significantly enhance early crack detection.

Airframe Response and Certification Margins
The uncontained failure resulted in high-velocity debris impacting the left fuselage and a passenger window. The aircraft’s structural response was evaluated against 14 CFR part 25 certification requirements, specifically §25.363 (side load on engine and wing attachment structures) and §25.775 (windshields and windows). While the fuselage skin and primary structure maintained load-bearing integrity, the cabin window failed under localized impact loading, initiating rapid decompression. The certification basis for passenger windows assumes bird strike and pressure differential loads, but does not fully account for high-energy metallic debris penetration at cruise altitudes. Comparative analysis with other operators, including Atlas Air, which manages similar airframe-engine configurations in cargo operations, reveals that window reinforcement and secondary containment barriers are not uniformly mandated across the industry. The Operator’s engineering assessment concludes that the current certification framework requires modernization to address the kinetic energy profiles of modern high-bypass turbofan failures.

Operational and Human Factors Considerations
FDR and CVR data (Docket Exhibits 22A and 22B) confirm that the flight crew responded appropriately to the asymmetric thrust, vibration, and decompression alerts. The emergency descent was initiated within 12 seconds of the failure, and cabin pressure management procedures were executed per standard operating procedures. However, the rapid decompression event exposed limitations in passenger oxygen mask deployment timing and cabin crew communication protocols under high-stress, high-noise conditions. While not a primary causal factor, these operational variables warrant integration into future training curricula and aircraft system design.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the comprehensive review of docket materials, metallurgical evidence, and engineering analysis, Southwest Airlines Co concludes that the uncontained engine failure was primarily driven by undetected low-cycle fatigue crack propagation in the fan blade dovetail, exacerbated by the inherent sensitivity limitations of conventional eddy current inspection methodologies. The failure sequence was not attributable to maintenance negligence, improper handling, or operational error, but rather to the convergence of material aging, inspection interval assumptions, and certification design margins that have not been fully updated to reflect modern high-cycle operational profiles.

The Operator acknowledges the complexity of this event. Engine containment, structural response, and cabin integrity are interdependent systems, and isolating a single point of failure oversimplifies the engineering reality. However, the evidence clearly demonstrates that current NDI protocols and inspection intervals are insufficient for detecting subsurface LCF initiation in high-cycle fan blades. Additionally, the cabin window failure reveals a gap between 14 CFR part 25 certification assumptions and real-world uncontained failure dynamics. While the aircraft’s primary structure performed within design limits, the rapid decompression scenario underscores the need for enhanced secondary containment and updated window strength standards.

The Operator’s position is that safety improvements must be proactive, data-driven, and aligned with next-generation maintenance philosophies. We recommend the following:
- Implementation of advanced multi-modal NDI techniques (PAUT, laser ultrasonics) for fan blade dovetail inspections.
- Reduction of inspection intervals for engines exceeding 25,000 flight cycles, with cycle-based rather than time-based scheduling.
- Revision of 14 CFR part 25 window certification standards to include high-energy debris impact testing and mandatory secondary containment barriers.
- Industry-wide data sharing of EHM trends and crack propagation models to refine predictive maintenance algorithms.
- Enhanced crew training modules focused on asymmetric decompression management and rapid cabin pressure stabilization.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In the immediate aftermath of the event, Southwest Airlines Co initiated a comprehensive fleet-wide inspection campaign targeting all CFM56-7B engines operating above 20,000 flight cycles. This campaign, completed within 45 days, involved the removal and shop inspection of 112 fan blade assemblies, with three units identified as having early-stage LCF cracking. All affected blades were replaced, and the inspection results were shared with the FAA and the engine manufacturer to inform ongoing Airworthiness Directive development.

The Operator has also revised its approved maintenance program to incorporate enhanced NDI protocols. Conventional eddy current testing has been supplemented with phased-array ultrasonic scanning for all fan blade dovetail inspections, and inspection intervals have been reduced by 20% for high-cycle engines. Additionally, the Operator has implemented a predictive maintenance analytics platform that integrates EHM data, flight cycle tracking, and environmental stress factors to generate dynamic inspection schedules. This system has already identified two additional engines requiring early shop visits, demonstrating the efficacy of data-driven maintenance optimization.

Looking forward, the Operator proposes several industry-wide improvements. First, we advocate for the development of a standardized high-energy debris impact test protocol under 14 CFR part 25, ensuring that cabin windows and secondary fuselage structures are certified against realistic uncontained failure scenarios. Second, we recommend the establishment of a centralized industry database for LCF crack propagation data, enabling operators, manufacturers, and regulators to collaboratively refine inspection intervals and material specifications. Third, we propose the integration of next-generation maintenance paradigms, such as those being developed for the LEAP-1B powerplant, into legacy fleet management programs. These paradigms emphasize condition-based monitoring, automated defect recognition, and lifecycle material tracking, all of which align with modern safety management system (SMS) principles.

Finally, the Operator has updated its emergency response and cabin crew training programs to address rapid decompression scenarios. New simulation modules focus on asymmetric thrust management, oxygen system deployment verification, and passenger communication under high-noise, low-pressure conditions. These enhancements have been incorporated into recurrent training cycles and are subject to continuous evaluation through line operations safety audits (LOSA).

Southwest Airlines Co remains fully committed to transparency, regulatory cooperation, and the continuous improvement of aviation safety. We submit this analysis with the understanding that the lessons learned from this event must be translated into actionable, industry-wide standards. The Operator stands ready to collaborate with the NTSB, the FAA, OEMs, and fellow operators to implement the recommended safety improvements and ensure that commercial aviation continues to operate at the highest levels of technical and operational integrity.

TO: All Maintenance Control, Line Maintenance, Heavy Maintenance, and Quality Assurance Personnel
FROM: Director of Engineering & Maintenance Programs, Atlas Air
DATE: 15 May 2018
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2018-047: Enhanced Fan Blade Inspection & Containment Protocol Review for High-Bypass Turbofan Fleet
REF: QA-2018-031, WO-7742-LEAP, SB-CFM-72-0114, NTSB Docket Entry 2018-05-12-004

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert is issued to mandate immediate updates to our engine inspection, tracking, and containment verification procedures for all high-bypass turbofan installations, with specific emphasis on the CFM International LEAP engine series. The directive establishes revised inspection intervals, documentation requirements, and engineering review steps to ensure continued compliance with 14 CFR part 121 operational standards and 14 CFR Part 25 airworthiness design criteria.

BACKGROUND:
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 suffered an uncontained engine failure during cruise flight at 32,500 feet. Debris from the left engine struck the fuselage and a cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one fatality. While the subject aircraft operated a different powerplant, the failure mode underscores critical vulnerabilities in fan blade fatigue monitoring, containment ring integrity, and rapid decompression response protocols across all modern high-bypass platforms.

Atlas Air’s engineering review board has completed a preliminary risk assessment of our current maintenance programs. The assessment identified three areas requiring immediate procedural reinforcement:
- Ultrasonic inspection (USI) frequency for fan blade dovetail roots
- Nacelle containment liner wear threshold documentation
- Cross-referencing of engine health monitoring (EHM) data with scheduled heavy maintenance events

Current work orders (WO-7742-LEAP and WO-7743-LEAP) do not reflect the updated fatigue life tracking parameters recommended by the OEM following recent service difficulty reports. Additionally, our internal tracking system (MRO-Track v4.2) lacks mandatory fields for containment ring borescope verification, creating a documentation gap that could impact regulatory audits and compromise our safety management system (SMS) reporting chain.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all maintenance personnel shall implement the following procedural updates:

1. Fan Blade Inspection Intervals
   - Reduce mandatory USI interval for all LEAP engine fan blades from 10,000 flight cycles to 7,500 flight cycles.
   - All blades removed for inspection must be tagged with Form QA-88B and logged in the Engine Component Tracking Database (ECTD) under Module 4.
   - Any blade exhibiting surface pitting, edge wear >0.015”, or dovetail micro-cracking must be quarantined and reported to Engineering within 24 hours.
   - Reference Part Number P/N-LEAP-FB-04A for all replacement blade installations.

2. Containment & Nacelle Verification
   - During all C-checks and engine shop visits, technicians must perform a 360-degree borescope inspection of the fan case containment ring.
   - Document liner thickness at four quadrants (12, 3, 6, and 9 o’clock positions) using calibrated depth gauges. Record values on Work Order Addendum WO-7742-LEAP-REV3.
   - If liner thickness falls below 0.080” at any measurement point, initiate a Nonconformance Report (NCR-2018-089) and suspend engine return-to-service until Engineering disposition is received.

3. EHM Data Integration
   - Maintenance Control must cross-reference EHM vibration trend data (specifically N1 rotor imbalance and bearing temperature spikes) with upcoming scheduled maintenance.
   - Any EHM alert exceeding OEM threshold limits must trigger an unscheduled fan blade inspection, regardless of cycle count.
   - Upload all EHM reports to the central server under directory /FLEET/LEAP/EHM/2018/ prior to aircraft release.

4. Regulatory Compliance Alignment
   - All procedures outlined herein are designed to maintain strict adherence to 14 CFR part 121.373 (maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations) and 14 CFR Part 25.903 (engine installation and containment requirements).
   - Quality Assurance will conduct random spot audits on 15% of all LEAP engine work orders completed between 15 May and 30 June 2018.
   - Discrepancies in documentation, missed inspection steps, or failure to log containment verification will result in immediate work stoppage and mandatory retraining.

ACTION REQUIRED:
The following actions must be completed by the responsible parties within the specified timeframes:

- Maintenance Control (Deadline: 18 May 2018)
  • Update all active work orders in MRO-Track to reflect the revised 7,500-cycle USI interval.
  • Distribute revised WO-7742-LEAP-REV3 and QA-88B forms to all line and base stations.
  • Confirm receipt and implementation via email to Engineering Programs (eng-programs@atlasair.com).

- Line & Base Maintenance Technicians (Deadline: 22 May 2018)
  • Complete mandatory 2-hour training module “LEAP Fan Blade Containment & Inspection Protocols” (Course ID: ENG-LEAP-2018-04).
  • Apply updated inspection checklists to all active engine work packages.
  • Report any legacy documentation gaps to your Shift Supervisor immediately.

- Quality Assurance Department (Deadline: 30 May 2018)
  • Conduct initial compliance audit on 10 randomly selected LEAP engine maintenance records.
  • Submit audit findings and corrective action plan to the Director of Engineering.
  • Update the internal audit schedule to include monthly containment verification reviews.

- Engineering & Reliability (Deadline: 15 June 2018)
  • Finalize integration of EHM alert thresholds into the automated maintenance scheduling system.
  • Publish a follow-up technical bulletin summarizing fleet-wide inspection results and any OEM service bulletin adoptions.
  • Coordinate with regulatory affairs to ensure all procedural changes are reflected in our approved maintenance program (AMP) revision.

Failure to comply with this Quality Alert will be treated as a serious deviation from approved maintenance procedures. All personnel are reminded that uncontained engine events pose a direct threat to flight safety, regulatory standing, and operational continuity. Questions regarding implementation, form revisions, or training access should be directed to the Engineering Programs desk or your assigned Quality Assurance representative.

This document has been reviewed and approved for internal distribution and will be retained in accordance with Atlas Air records retention policy (RET-2015-09). A copy will be forwarded to the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector and entered into the corporate safety management system (SMS) database.

SYNOPSIS

On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines, experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. The aircraft was en route from John F. Kennedy International Airport to Dallas Love Field when debris from the left engine penetrated the fuselage and a passenger cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one passenger fatality. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and diverted to Philadelphia International Airport, where the aircraft landed without further incident. This preliminary document outlines the initial factual data, establishes the investigative framework, and documents procedural decisions made during the early phase of the inquiry. All information contained herein is subject to revision as additional evidence is recovered, analyzed, and correlated.

INITIAL FINDINGS

Preliminary information gathered from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads indicates that the left engine experienced a sudden loss of thrust and abnormal vibration parameters prior to the reported failure event. Initial witness accounts from flight attendants and surviving passengers describe a loud acoustic event followed by rapid cabin depressurization, with oxygen masks deploying automatically. Several occupants reported observing visible damage to the left-side fuselage and a compromised window assembly. Weather data obtained from the National Weather Service and aviation meteorological sources indicate that the aircraft was operating in visual meteorological conditions with minimal turbulence and no significant convective activity at the time of the event.

Preliminary examination of the recovered engine components suggests that the failure originated within the fan section, though the exact failure mode remains undetermined. The National Transportation Safety Board has secured the left engine core, fan blades, and associated nacelle components for further metallurgical and dimensional analysis. It should be noted that while the aircraft is equipped with a CFM56-7B series powerplant, comparative data from the LEAP-1B engine family will be reviewed to assess potential design or maintenance parallels relevant to high-cycle fatigue mechanisms.
