The operator, Southwest Airlines, has provided initial maintenance records, which are currently under review for compliance with 14 CFR Part 121 airworthiness directives and manufacturer service bulletins.

Damage assessment conducted by NTSB structural specialists indicates localized fuselage skin deformation, a fractured window frame, and minor secondary damage to adjacent systems. The rapid decompression event appears to have been contained to the forward left cabin section, with no evidence of structural compromise to primary load-bearing members. All findings documented herein are preliminary, subject to revision as additional data is recovered, analyzed, and correlated. No conclusions regarding the sequence of events or probable cause have been established at this stage.

INVESTIGATION STATUS

The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The following groups have been formally established and are currently conducting field and laboratory examinations: Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group is operating under the direction of the designated Lead Investigator, who is responsible for coordinating inter-group activities, managing evidence chain-of-custody protocols, and ensuring adherence to established investigative procedures.

Parties to the investigation have been formally notified and include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and relevant labor organizations. Representatives from Atlas Air have also been included in the maintenance and powerplant working groups to provide industry-wide operational context and comparative maintenance data. All party representatives have been briefed on their roles, limitations, and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding preliminary data. The investigation is being conducted in accordance with Title 49 of the United States Code and applicable NTSB regulations governing aviation accident inquiries.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data and cockpit voice recorders, which have been successfully downloaded and are undergoing preliminary data validation. The left engine assembly, along with recovered fan debris and nacelle fragments, has been transported to a secure NTSB facility for detailed teardown and non-destructive testing. Maintenance logs, crew training records, and dispatch documentation have been obtained from SWA and are currently being cross-referenced against Title 14 Part 121 operational requirements. Additionally, air traffic control radar data, communications transcripts, and meteorological reports have been archived for timeline reconstruction.

Planned examinations include a comprehensive metallurgical analysis of the fractured fan blade, computational fluid dynamics modeling of the debris trajectory, and a review of the cabin pressure control system response during the decompression event. The IIC has authorized the use of specialized imaging techniques to evaluate internal component degradation and has scheduled a joint review session with manufacturer engineering teams to discuss preliminary failure indicators. All investigative activities are being documented in accordance with standard NTSB protocols, and any deviations from established procedures will be formally recorded and justified.

NEXT STEPS

The immediate focus of the investigation will center on the completion of the powerplant teardown, the validation of flight recorder data, and the reconstruction of the aircraft’s final approach and landing sequence. Additional interviews with flight crew members, maintenance personnel, and air traffic controllers are scheduled to commence within the next ten business days. The Operations and Human Performance groups will collaborate to evaluate crew resource management, emergency checklist adherence, and decision-making processes during the rapid decompression and diversion phases.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated to be released within 30 days, pending the completion of initial laboratory analyses and the consolidation of group findings. Subsequent updates will be issued as significant technical milestones are achieved, including the completion of metallurgical testing, the finalization of maintenance record reviews, and the integration of air traffic control data into the event timeline. The Lead Investigator will continue to coordinate with all participating parties to ensure transparent, methodical, and scientifically rigorous examination of all available evidence.

It is emphasized that all information contained in this document is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation progresses. The National Transportation Safety Board will not issue any determinations regarding probable cause or contributing factors until all relevant data has been thoroughly analyzed, peer-reviewed, and formally approved by the Board. Further procedural directives, including public hearing schedules and final report publication timelines, will be communicated through official NTSB channels as the inquiry advances.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at 15:43:12 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), an in-flight uncontained engine failure occurred aboard a Boeing 737-700 during the cruise phase of flight. The event transpired at an indicated altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 40.1423° North latitude and 079.8712° West longitude, over rural terrain in western Pennsylvania. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger route. Following the failure, the flight crew initiated an emergency descent, declared a Mayday with Cleveland Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC), and subsequently diverted to Philadelphia International Airport (KPHL), where the aircraft landed without further incident at 16:12:45 EDT.

1.2 Aircraft Type, Registration, and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-700, bearing United States registration N737AA. The aircraft was operated by Atlas Air under a scheduled passenger service agreement. The operator maintained the aircraft under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The aircraft was configured for 143 passenger seats and operated in a standard commercial airline livery. All required airworthiness certificates, registration documents, and operating specifications were current and valid at the time of the occurrence.

1.3 Nature of the Flight
The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, specifically as a scheduled domestic passenger operation. The flight departed from Chicago O'Hare International Airport (KORD) at 14:15:00 EDT, with a planned destination of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (KATL). The flight plan called for a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet, a true airspeed of approximately 445 knots, and a Mach number of 0.78. The flight was operating in the en route phase when the uncontained engine failure occurred. The event resulted in rapid cabin decompression, structural damage to the left fuselage, and one passenger fatality.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Pilot Qualifications, Certificates, and Ratings
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating. The captain also held a commercial pilot certificate with instrument and multiengine ratings, and a flight instructor certificate. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on January 12, 2018, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 14,250 hours, with 3,100 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer held an ATP certificate, airplane multiengine land, with a Boeing 737 type rating, and a first-class medical certificate issued on February 28, 2018. Total flight time for the first officer was 4,800 hours, with 1,200 hours in type. Both pilots met all certification requirements outlined in 14 CFR Part 61.

2.2 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Records indicate that both flight crew members completed their most recent recurrent training and proficiency checks within the preceding 60 days. The captain's last line check was conducted on February 14, 2018, and the first officer's was conducted on March 22, 2018. Both evaluations were documented as satisfactory. Training records confirm that the crew completed simulator-based emergency procedure training covering rapid decompression, engine failure at cruise altitude, emergency descent profiles, and single-engine approach and landing procedures. All training was conducted in accordance with the operator's FAA-approved training program and 14 CFR 121.401 through 121.417.

2.3 Duty and Rest Compliance
The flight crew's duty period commenced at 09:30:00 EDT on April 17, 2018, following a scheduled rest period of 12 hours and 15 minutes. The total flight duty period (FDP) at the time of the event was 6 hours and 13 minutes, well within the limits prescribed by 14 CFR 117.15. Both pilots reported adequate rest prior to duty commencement. No fatigue-related factors were identified in the crew's scheduling records, and the operator's fatigue risk management system (FRMS) data indicated compliance with all applicable rest requirements.

2.4 Medical and Fitness for Duty
Both pilots were medically cleared for flight operations. Pre-flight health declarations were completed without incident. Post-accident toxicology testing, conducted in accordance with 14 CFR 121.458, returned negative results for all tested substances, including alcohol, controlled substances, and prescription medications. The crew's physiological status was documented as normal, with no reported symptoms of hypoxia or decompression sickness prior to the event.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Aircraft Make/Model, Serial Number, and Total Time
The aircraft was a Boeing 737-700, manufacturer serial number 32456, manufactured in 2008. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 42,150 total flight hours and 28,400 flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a standard commercial avionics suite, including dual flight management computers (FMCs), autopilot/flight director systems, and a digital flight data recorder (DFDR) compliant with 14 CFR 121.344. The airframe had undergone a C-check inspection 1,200 flight hours prior to the event, with all structural and system inspections documented as satisfactory.

3.2 Maintenance History and Applicable Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program approved by the FAA and administered by Atlas Air. Maintenance records indicate compliance with all applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs), including AD 2017-15-09, which mandated enhanced inspection intervals for high-cycle engine components. The left engine, a CFM International LEAP-1B, serial number 88421, was installed on the airframe in 2016. At the time of the event, the powerplant had accumulated 18,200 flight hours and 11,500 cycles since new. The most recent borescope inspection was performed 480 flight hours prior, with no anomalies documented. All maintenance actions were recorded in accordance with 14 CFR 121.373 and 121.363.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The aircraft's environmental control system (ECS) and pressurization system were functioning normally prior to the event. The cabin altitude warning system was calibrated to activate at 10,000 feet cabin altitude. The left fuselage skin at row 14 was constructed of 2024-T3 aluminum alloy, with a thickness of 0.050 inches. The cabin window assembly consisted of a three-pane configuration: an outer structural pane, a middle pressure pane, and an inner scratch pane. The window frame was secured to the fuselage structure via titanium fasteners. The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were operational, with data retrieval confirming continuous recording up to the time of engine shutdown.

3.4 Maintenance Program and Quality Assurance
The operator's maintenance program incorporated a reliability monitoring system that tracked component failure rates, unscheduled removals, and in-flight shutdowns. The program was audited annually by the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI). Quality assurance records indicate that all scheduled inspections, component overhauls, and service bulletin implementations were completed within prescribed intervals. The maintenance control center (MCC) maintained 24-hour oversight of the fleet, with technical dispatch support available for all operations. No deferred maintenance items were recorded for the aircraft at the time of departure.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Weather Conditions at the Time of the Accident
At the time of the event, meteorological conditions along the flight path were characterized by visual meteorological conditions (VMC). The atmosphere was stable, with no convective activity, turbulence, or significant cloud cover reported. The standard atmosphere model applied, with a temperature of -42°C and a dew point of -48°C at cruise altitude. Wind direction was 240° true at 12 knots, with a vertical wind shear component of less than 5 knots per 1,000 feet. Visibility exceeded 10 statute miles throughout the en route segment.

4.2 METAR/TAF Data and Pilot Reports
The nearest aviation weather reporting station, Pittsburgh International Airport (KPIT), issued a METAR at 15:53 EDT indicating clear skies, wind 230° at 10 knots, temperature 18°C, dew point 8°C, and altimeter setting 30.12 inches of mercury. The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) for KPHL, valid from 12:00 to 18:00 EDT, forecasted scattered clouds at 8,000 feet, visibility greater than 6 statute miles, and no significant weather. Pilot reports (PIREPs) filed within 100 nautical miles of the accident location indicated smooth air, no icing, and no turbulence. No SIGMETs or AIRMETs were active for the region.

4.3 Meteorological Relevance to the Event
Meteorological data confirm that atmospheric conditions did not contribute to the uncontained engine failure. The absence of convective activity, severe turbulence, or volcanic ash eliminates weather-related ingestion or structural stress as causal factors. The standard temperature and pressure profile at 32,500 feet MSL were within normal operational parameters for the aircraft and engine. The flight crew's decision to initiate an emergency descent was executed in clear, stable atmospheric conditions, with no meteorological impediments to aircraft control or navigation.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Impact Marks
The aircraft sustained no ground impact and was recovered intact at KPHL. Debris from the uncontained engine failure was distributed along a 120-nautical-mile flight track, with primary fragments recovered in rural Pennsylvania and Ohio. The debris field consisted of engine casing segments, fan blade fragments, and acoustic insulation material. No ground impact craters or secondary damage to structures were documented. The aircraft's flight path remained controlled throughout the event, with no deviation from the intended emergency descent corridor.

5.2 Component Examination Findings
Examination of the left engine revealed an uncontained failure originating from the fan section. The fan blade at station 13 separated at the dovetail root, resulting in a high-energy release of debris. The engine casing exhibited a breach at the 9 o'clock position, measuring approximately 18 inches in length and 12 inches in width. Metallurgical analysis of the fractured fan blade revealed fatigue crack initiation at the root fillet, with progressive crack propagation consistent with high-cycle fatigue. The fracture surface exhibited beach marks and striations, indicating a long-term degradation process. The engine's containment ring was compromised, allowing debris to exit the nacelle.

5.3 Fuselage and Cabin Window Damage
Debris trajectory analysis confirmed that a high-velocity fragment penetrated the left fuselage at row 14, striking the cabin window assembly. The outer structural pane was completely fractured, and the middle pressure pane was displaced inward. The window frame exhibited plastic deformation, with fastener holes elongated by approximately 0.08 inches. The penetration resulted in rapid cabin decompression, with cabin altitude rising from 6,500 feet to 28,000 feet within 12 seconds. The inner scratch pane remained intact but was displaced by the pressure differential. Structural damage was limited to the fuselage skin, adjacent stringers, and window frame. No damage to primary flight control systems or hydraulic lines was identified.

5.4 Component Analysis and Regulatory Compliance
The engine components were examined in accordance with 14 CFR 33.15 and 33.27, which govern engine design and containment requirements. The fan blade material, a titanium alloy, met all specified mechanical properties at the time of manufacture. However, the fatigue crack initiation site indicated a localized stress concentration that exceeded design thresholds under cyclic loading. The engine manufacturer's service life limits were within published parameters, but the failure mode suggests a need for enhanced inspection protocols. The cabin window assembly complied with 14 CFR 25.365 and 25.773, with the pressure pane designed to withstand a 100 psi differential. The rapid decompression event was consistent with a sudden loss of cabin pressure, triggering the automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Relevant Organizational Policies
Atlas Air maintained a comprehensive safety management system (SMS) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.373 and FAA Advisory Circular 120-92. The operator's maintenance program incorporated predictive analytics, component tracking, and reliability monitoring to identify potential failure modes before they manifested. Training programs emphasized emergency response, rapid decompression procedures, and single-engine operations. The operator's quality assurance department conducted quarterly audits of maintenance facilities, with all findings documented and corrective actions implemented within prescribed timeframes. The organization's safety reporting system allowed for anonymous submission of maintenance and operational concerns, with all reports reviewed by the safety review board.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
Historical data indicate that uncontained engine failures in high-bypass turbofan engines have occurred at a rate of approximately 0.0001 per 1,000 flight hours. Previous incidents involving similar engine models have resulted in casing breaches, fuselage penetration, and rapid decompression. The FAA has issued multiple service bulletins and airworthiness directives addressing fan blade inspection intervals, ultrasonic testing protocols, and containment ring reinforcement. The manufacturer has implemented enhanced borescope inspection criteria and revised maintenance schedules to mitigate fatigue-related failures. The NTSB has investigated several similar events, with findings consistently pointing to high-cycle fatigue, material degradation, or manufacturing anomalies as primary contributors.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The investigation referenced multiple regulatory provisions, including 14 CFR 121.310 (emergency equipment), 14 CFR 121.311 (seat belts and shoulder harnesses), 14 CFR 121.313 (cabin pressure and ventilation), and 14 CFR 121.373 (maintenance requirements). The operator's compliance with 14 CFR 121.363 (maintenance program) was verified through audit records and maintenance logs. FAA Advisory Circular 120-92B provided guidance on safety management systems, while AC 120-100 addressed fatigue risk management. The Investigator in Charge (IIC) coordinated with FAA principal inspectors, engine manufacturer representatives, and metallurgical specialists to ensure all regulatory and technical standards were applied consistently. The IIC oversaw the factual examination, data collection, and component analysis, ensuring adherence to NTSB investigative protocols.

6.4 Recorder Data and Timeline Reconstruction
Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters indicate that at 15:43:12 EDT, the left engine N1 parameter decreased from 88.5% to 0% within 1.2 seconds. The right engine N1 remained stable at 89.1%. Cabin altitude increased from 6,500 feet to 28,000 feet over a 12-second interval, triggering the automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent at 15:43:18 EDT, reducing altitude to 10,000 feet MSL within 4 minutes. Cockpit voice recorder (CVR) data confirm that the crew followed standard emergency procedures, including donning oxygen masks, declaring Mayday, and executing the emergency descent checklist. The timeline reconstruction aligns with the physical evidence, confirming that the uncontained engine failure was the initiating event, with subsequent rapid decompression and structural damage occurring as a direct result. All data were preserved, downloaded, and analyzed in accordance with NTSB standard operating procedures.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the technical examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Powerplants, Structures, and Flight Data Recorder groups in support of the investigation into the uncontained engine failure event involving a Boeing 737-700 aircraft. The scope of this examination encompasses the physical and metallurgical evaluation of recovered engine components, structural assessment of the impacted fuselage and cabin window assembly, and the decoding and analysis of flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) parameters. The examination was authorized by the Investigator-in-Charge and conducted under NTSB Group Chairman directives.

Items examined included the left engine (CFM International LEAP-1B, serial number 8842-LEAP-1B, part number 200-991-001), recovered fan blade fragments, containment ring segments, forward fuselage skin panels (stations 410 through 450), the impacted cabin window assembly (row 14, left side), and the solid-state flight data recorder (Honeywell SSFDR, part number 060-0800-00, serial number 1145-882). The physical examinations were conducted between May 2 and May 18, 2018, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the Powerplants Group facility in Fort Worth, Texas. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, with continuous photographic documentation, chain-of-custody logging, and cross-referenced maintenance records provided by Southwest Airlines and contracted maintenance provider Atlas Air Inc.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737-700, certified under 14 CFR Part 25, and operated by Southwest Airlines under a Part 121 air carrier certificate. The left engine is a CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan, featuring a 22-blade 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan stage, a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) mid-span shroud, and an Inconel 718 fan containment ring. The engine is type-certificated under 14 CFR Part 33, with airframe integration and structural compliance evaluated against 14 CFR Part 25 requirements. Specifically, the fuselage and cabin window assembly design basis references 14 CFR 25.783, which establishes requirements for fuselage doors, windows, and emergency exits, including structural integrity under rapid decompression and debris impact scenarios.

The LEAP-1B engine (S/N 8842) accumulated 18,422 total time since new (TTSN) and 14,881 total cycles since new (TCSN) at the time of the event. The most recent shop visit occurred on November 12, 2016, during which the fan blade set was inspected, balanced, and reinstalled per CFM International Service Bulletin LEAP-1B-72-0042. Maintenance documentation, including component tracking logs and non-destructive inspection (NDI) records, was maintained in accordance with 14 CFR Part 135 operational tracking standards for commercial air carrier component life-limiting parts, as cross-referenced during the records review phase. The engine was operated within approved flight envelope parameters, with no recorded exceedances or maintenance deferrals in the 1,200 flight hours preceding the event.

The forward fuselage structure consists of aluminum alloy 2024-T3 skin panels, chemically milled to a nominal thickness of 0.063 inches, with longitudinal stringers (7075-T6) and circumferential frames (2024-T3) providing primary load paths. The cabin window assembly comprises a dual-pane acrylic/polycarbonate laminate (part number 65-42110-1) with a silicone elastomer seal, designed to withstand a maximum differential pressure of 8.6 PSI at 40,000 feet MSL. The certification basis for the window and surrounding structure required compliance with 14 CFR 25.783 and 14 CFR 25.365 (pressurized compartment loads), with impact resistance validated through ballistic testing per SAE ARP 5412.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered fan blade fragments revealed a complete separation of blade #13 at the root attachment. Macroscopic inspection of the fracture surface identified a fatigue initiation site located at the leading edge root fillet, approximately 0.18 inches from the blade platform interface. The initiation zone exhibited a smooth, oxidized appearance with distinct beach marks radiating outward, indicative of progressive crack propagation under cyclic loading. The fatigue crack propagated through approximately 85% of the cross-sectional area before transitioning to a final fast-fracture zone, which accounted for the remaining 15% of the fracture surface. The fast-fracture region displayed a characteristic chevron pattern oriented toward the trailing edge, consistent with tensile overload at high rotational speed.

Non-destructive inspection of the remaining fan blade set was performed using fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) per AMS 2644, Type 1, Method A, and eddy current testing per ASTM E309. No additional surface-breaking cracks or subsurface anomalies were detected in the remaining 21 blades. The containment ring exhibited three circumferential tears, with localized plastic deformation measuring up to 0.42 inches in radial displacement. The ring material, Inconel 718 (AMS 5662), was sectioned for metallurgical analysis. Hardness testing yielded an average of 38 HRC, within the specified range of 36-42 HRC. Tensile testing per ASTM E8 confirmed ultimate tensile strength of 185 ksi and yield strength of 155 ksi, consistent with as-manufactured specifications.

Metallurgical examination of the fan blade root was conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The material composition matched Ti-6Al-4V (AMS 4928), with aluminum at 6.12 wt%, vanadium at 4.08 wt%, and balance titanium. Microstructural analysis revealed a bimodal alpha-beta grain structure with an average alpha grain size of 8.2 micrometers. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD), corrosion, or manufacturing defects was observed at the initiation site. Fatigue crack growth rate testing per ASTM E647, conducted on representative Ti-6Al-4V coupons, yielded a Paris law exponent of 3.1 and a threshold stress intensity factor (ΔKth) of 4.8 MPa√m. Based on the measured crack length and operational load spectrum, the fatigue crack initiated approximately 1,200 flight cycles prior to the event.

Structural examination of the impacted fuselage section revealed a primary impact crater at station 432, buttock line 18.5, with a maximum diameter of 14.2 inches. The aluminum 2024-T3 skin exhibited localized tearing, with three radial cracks extending 6.8, 9.1, and 11.4 inches from the impact center. The underlying frame (STA 430) sustained plastic deformation of 0.31 inches, with no evidence of complete structural failure. The cabin window assembly (row 14, left side) was completely dislodged from its mounting frame. The outer acrylic pane exhibited radial cracking and delamination, while the inner polycarbonate layer showed localized melting and thermal degradation consistent with high-velocity debris impact and adiabatic heating. The silicone seal was fractured circumferentially, with residual adhesive transfer indicating rapid pressure differential loading.

Photographic documentation of all examined components is referenced in NTSB-ENG-001 through 045 and NTSB-STR-010 through 022. All measurements were recorded using calibrated digital calipers (±0.001 in), laser profilometry, and coordinate measuring machine (CMM) systems. Material samples were preserved in accordance with NTSB evidence handling protocols and archived for future reference.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) media were recovered intact and downloaded using a Honeywell FDR/CVR readout system compliant with ARINC 717 and ARINC 767 standards. The FDR recorded 256-word frames at a 4 Hz sampling rate for engine parameters, with 1 Hz sampling for cabin pressure and altitude. Data decoding was performed using manufacturer-specific parameter mapping tables, with all values cross-verified against the aircraft's quick access recorder (QAR) data stream.

The FDR data indicates that at 14:22:15 UTC, the aircraft was in steady-state cruise at 32,500 feet MSL, 412 knots indicated airspeed (KIAS), Mach 0.78, with a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet and a differential pressure of 8.2 PSI. Engine parameters were nominal: N1 (fan speed) at 94.1%, N2 (core speed) at 94.3%, exhaust gas temperature (EGT) at 712°C, and N1 vibration at 0.4 inches per second (IPS). At 14:22:17 UTC, a sudden N1 vibration spike to 12.4 IPS was recorded, followed immediately by an N1 overspeed to 108.2% and a rapid decay to 42.1% within 1.8 seconds. Concurrently, N2 decreased from 94.3% to 61.8%, and EGT exceeded the redline limit, peaking at 968°C (limit: 925°C). The engine fuel control unit (ECU) commanded automatic fuel shutoff at 14:22:19 UTC, as indicated by the fuel flow parameter dropping to 0.0 lb/hr.

Cabin pressure parameters recorded a rapid decompression event beginning at 14:22:18 UTC. The cabin altitude rate of climb reached +4,200 feet per minute, with cabin altitude increasing from 8,000 feet to 28,500 feet within 14 seconds. Differential pressure dropped from 8.2 PSI to 0.3 PSI, triggering the cabin altitude warning horn and master caution illumination. The aircraft's pressurization system attempted to compensate, but the outflow valve reached full open position (100%) at 14:22:20 UTC, confirming a large structural breach. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent at 14:22:21 UTC, with vertical speed reaching -4,800 feet per minute and airspeed increasing to 445 KIAS during the descent phase.

The CVR audio track captured a loud bang at 14:22:17 UTC, followed by crew communication referencing "engine failure," "decompression," and "emergency descent." The audio spectrum analysis revealed a broadband acoustic transient peaking at 142 dB SPL, consistent with an uncontained engine failure and subsequent fuselage impact. The timeline reconstruction aligns with the physical evidence: fatigue crack propagation culminated in blade separation at cruise power, resulting in uncontained debris ejection, containment ring breach, and fuselage penetration.

Comparison with normal operational parameters confirms that all recorded values exceeded design limits. Normal N1 vibration during cruise is maintained below 0.8 IPS, with EGT typically ranging between 680°C and 740°C. The cabin pressure decay rate under normal conditions is less than 500 feet per minute. The recorded parameters indicate a catastrophic loss of engine integrity and rapid structural decompression, with no evidence of pre-existing system anomalies or control input deviations prior to the event.

5. SUMMARY

The technical examination and data analysis yielded the following factual findings:

- The left engine (LEAP-1B, S/N 8842) experienced an uncontained failure initiated by fatigue crack propagation in fan blade #13. The crack originated at the leading edge root fillet and propagated over approximately 1,200 flight cycles before final fracture at cruise power.
- Metallurgical analysis confirmed the fan blade material as Ti-6Al-4V (AMS 4928) with a bimodal alpha-beta microstructure. No foreign object damage, corrosion, or manufacturing defects were identified at the initiation site.
- The Inconel 718 containment ring sustained three circumferential tears and localized plastic deformation, indicating energy absorption beyond design limits. Material properties remained within certified specifications.
- Debris impact compromised the forward fuselage skin at station 432, buttock line 18.5, resulting in a 14.2-inch diameter penetration. The underlying frame sustained plastic deformation but maintained structural continuity.
- The impacted cabin window assembly (row 14, left side) was dislodged from its mounting frame. The acrylic/polycarbonate laminate exhibited radial cracking, delamination, and thermal degradation consistent with high-velocity debris impact.
- FDR data recorded an N1 overspeed to 108.2%, EGT exceedance to 968°C, and N1 vibration spike to 12.4 IPS at 14:22:17 UTC. Cabin differential pressure dropped from 8.2 PSI to 0.3 PSI within 14 seconds, with cabin altitude climbing to 28,500 feet.
- The aircraft was operating at 32,500 feet MSL, 412 KIAS, Mach 0.78, with all pre-event parameters within normal operational envelopes. The emergency descent was initiated at 14:22:21 UTC following automatic engine fuel shutoff and cabin pressure warning activation.
- All findings are consistent with an uncontained engine failure resulting in rapid decompression and structural damage to the forward fuselage and cabin window assembly.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER MARCUS T. LIN
Date: April 24, 2018
Time: 10:15 AM EST
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Philadelphia, PA
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Aviation Safety Board
Witness: Marcus T. Lin, First Officer, Flight 1380

Q: Good morning, Mr. Lin. Thank you for coming in. This interview is being recorded for the official NTSB investigation into the April 17, 2018, in-flight event. Please state your full name, your position, and your role aboard the aircraft on the day of the incident.

A: Marcus Thomas Lin. I’m a First Officer, currently flying the Boeing 737-700 for the airline. On the seventeenth, I was the pilot flying for that leg. Actually, I was the SIC, but the captain had me on the controls for the cruise portion. So, yeah, I was the one with my hands on the yoke when it happened.

Q: Walk me through the flight from departure up to the moment of the event. What was the operational environment like?

A: We pushed back around 09:28, I think. Maybe 09:30. It was a pretty standard morning departure. Weather was clear, light winds, nothing out of the ordinary. We climbed out, handed off to Center, and leveled off at... I want to say 32,500 feet. Yeah, that sounds right. The autopilot was engaged, both engines were running smooth, fuel flow was nominal. I was doing my routine cross-checks, monitoring the FMC, just... you know, standard cruise monitoring. The cabin was quiet. I remember thinking it was going to be a routine day.

Q: Describe the initial event. What did you see, hear, and feel?

A: It was... it was sudden. There was a bang. Not a pop, not a thud. It was a sharp, metallic crack, like a cannon going off right outside the left window. The whole airframe shuddered. I felt it through the seat, through my feet on the rudder pedals. The yoke actually jumped in my hands. Then immediately, the master caution lit up, and the left engine parameters just... went wild. EGT spiked, N1 dropped, then it started vibrating so hard the whole left side of the cockpit was shaking. I looked out the left window and... the cowling was gone. Just torn away. I could see the fan case, and there was debris trailing. It was... it was a lot to process in a second.

Q: What were your immediate actions following the event?

A: I took control. The captain immediately started the emergency descent checklist. I pushed the nose down, set the thrust levers to idle on the left engine, and we started descending. The cabin pressure warning came on almost instantly. The air got cold, really fast. You could see the condensation fogging up the overhead panels. And the noise... it was like a vacuum, but louder. A constant, tearing roar. I donned my oxygen mask, the captain did the same. We declared Mayday, gave our position, requested immediate descent to 10,000. I was focused on keeping the wings level, managing the airspeed, and trying to keep the vibration from getting worse.

Q: You mentioned the left engine. Do you recall the specific engine model or any recent maintenance history?

A: The logbook listed it as a CFM... wait, actually, I think it was a LEAP-1B. I know that’s not the standard fit for the -700, but we were part of a limited retrofit program, or maybe I’m mixing it up with the MAX fleet. Honestly, in the moment, I wasn’t thinking about the model number. I was just trying to keep the aircraft stable. But I do remember the maintenance release mentioned a recent fan blade inspection. The chief mechanic had signed off on it. I’m not an engineer, but I know the manuals. The LEAP-1B has different blade retention specs, and if there’s a fatigue crack... well, you get an uncontained failure. That’s what it looked like.

Q: How does your understanding of airworthiness regulations factor into your assessment of what happened?

A: I’ve got a background in quality assurance before I moved to the line, so I’m familiar with the regulatory framework. We operate under 14 CFR Part 121, obviously, which dictates our maintenance programs, crew training, and operational limits. But the engine itself, the certification, that falls under Part 21. If there was a manufacturing defect or a design flaw in the containment ring, that’s a Part 21 issue. And then there’s the fuel system side of things. I remember reading about SFAR 88 compliance for the fuel tank wiring and ignition sources. We’d had a recent audit on that, actually. The wiring harnesses near the pylon were inspected, but... I don’t know. Maybe the debris took out a line, or maybe it was purely mechanical. I’m speculating, though. I’m just a pilot.

Q: You mentioned Atlas Air Inc earlier in your preliminary notes. Can you clarify that reference?

A: Oh, right. Yeah. I was thinking about a similar incident a few years back. Atlas Air Inc had a cargo 747 with an uncontained engine failure, and they completely overhauled their inspection intervals after that. Our maintenance department actually modeled some of our cyclic checks on their revised protocols. I was just... I don’t know, my brain was making connections. It’s not directly related to this flight, but it’s in the back of your mind when you hear a bang like that. You think about containment, you think about what other operators have gone through.

Q: Let’s establish a timeline as best you can. When did the event occur, and how long did the emergency descent take?

A: I’d say the bang happened at... I want to say 10:11, maybe 10:12 local. The CVR will have the exact second, but it felt like 10:11:45. We started the descent immediately. It took about four minutes to get down to 10,000 feet. Maybe a little longer, I’m not sure. The whole thing from the initial failure to touchdown was... I’d say under ten minutes. We diverted to Philadelphia, declared emergency, got vectors. The approach was rough because of the asymmetric thrust, but the aircraft handled it. We landed around 10:22. It felt like an hour, but it was quick.

Q: What did you observe regarding the cabin and passengers during and after the descent?

A: We got the lead flight attendant on the interphone. She was... she was trying to stay calm, but you could hear the wind. She reported a window was compromised. Actually, it was shattered. There was a passenger partially pulled out of the opening. The crew was trying to pull her back in, but the pressure differential was still there. It was... it was chaotic. I could hear the wind tearing through the cabin, the oxygen masks deployed, people crying. I was focused on flying, but I knew what was happening back there. Once we leveled off and the pressure equalized, the roar died down. The crew managed to secure the passenger, but... she didn’t make it. I don’t know the details. I just know we did everything we could.

Q: After landing, what was your immediate focus?

A: Securing the aircraft. We ran the shutdown checklist, isolated the left engine, cut off fuel, pulled the fire handles. The smell in the cockpit was... ozone, burning oil, and that sharp metallic scent. You don’t forget that. We taxied to the gate, shut down the APU, and waited for emergency services. The captain handled the comms with the tower and the company. I just sat there, breathing, trying to process it. The maintenance team came out, they saw the damage. The left side of the fuselage was pitted, the window frame was torn, the engine was... well, it was gone. Just a mess.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add that we haven’t covered?

A: Just that... the aircraft performed exactly as it was designed to. The structure held. The emergency procedures worked. The crew did their jobs. I don’t know if it was a fatigue crack, a manufacturing defect, or an inspection gap. I hope the investigation finds it. I know Part 21 and 14 CFR Part 121 are strict for a reason. If there’s a gap, it’ll be closed. I just... I hope the family gets answers. And I hope the rest of the fleet is safe. That’s all I can say, really.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Lin. We’ll follow up if we need clarification. You’re free to go.

A: Thank you. I appreciate it.

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
   - Regulatory Reference: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Compliance Directive and Safety Recommendation Response; Docket No. FAA-2018-0452; NTSB Safety Recommendations A-19-012 through A-19-015
   - NTSB Accident Number: DCA18MA088
   - Date of Occurrence: April 17, 2018
   - Applicable Regulatory Framework: 14 CFR Part 21, 14 CFR Part 121, 14 CFR Part 25, 14 CFR Part 43
   - Subject: Uncontained Engine Failure, Fuselage Penetration, and Cabin Pressurization System Integrity; Operator Maintenance Program Compliance and Airworthiness Directives

2. BACKGROUND
   On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 aircraft experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine during cruise flight at Flight Level 325 (32,500 feet). High-energy debris penetrated the engine nacelle, impacted the forward fuselage structure, and compromised a passenger cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one fatality. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) initiated a major investigation under docket DCA18MA088, subsequently issuing multiple safety recommendations addressing engine containment ring design, fuselage structural integrity, and operator maintenance protocols.

   This regulatory response addresses the broader applicability of the incident findings to the commercial aviation sector, with specific emphasis on operators conducting scheduled air carrier operations under 14 CFR Part 121. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has evaluated the airworthiness implications for high-bypass turbofan propulsion systems, including the CFM International LEAP engine family, which shares design philosophies, material specifications, and certification baselines with the affected powerplant. Pursuant to 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart D, the FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) has reviewed the type certificate (TC) and supplemental type certificate (STC) data to ensure continued compliance with airworthiness standards.

   Historically, the regulatory framework governing engine containment and cabin pressurization has evolved through iterative rulemaking. 14 CFR § 25.903(d) mandates that engine installations must be designed to prevent hazardous effects on the aircraft structure or systems in the event of an uncontained failure. Additionally, 14 CFR § 121.344 requires air carriers to establish and maintain an approved maintenance program that ensures continued airworthiness. Prior to the 2018 occurrence, Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-09-05 and subsequent amendments addressed ultrasonic inspection intervals for fan blades and containment ring integrity. The NTSB’s post-accident recommendations highlighted deficiencies in the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for cabin window damage and the adequacy of non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols for high-cycle fatigue components.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
   A comprehensive compliance audit of affected air carriers, including Atlas Air, Inc. (hereinafter “AA” or “the Operator”), reveals varying degrees of adherence to the regulatory mandates established under 14 CFR Part 121 and Part 21. The Operator’s maintenance program, as approved under § 121.373, incorporates manufacturer-recommended service bulletins and FAA-issued ADs. However, the FAA’s oversight review identified procedural gaps in the implementation of enhanced inspection regimes for engine fan disk assemblies and fuselage window frame stress concentrations.

   Under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart J, the FAA holds type certificate holders accountable for continued airworthiness reporting. The analysis indicates that while the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) complied with mandatory service difficulty reporting (SDR) requirements per § 21.3, the dissemination of critical fatigue life data to operators was delayed, resulting in inconsistent application of life-limited part (LLP) tracking protocols. Furthermore, the integration of the LEAP engine into mixed-fleet operations necessitated supplemental type certificate (STC) modifications that introduced additional structural load paths not fully accounted for in the original MMEL. The FAA’s Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) and Principal Operations Inspector (POI) teams documented instances where operators relied on legacy MMEL provisions that did not adequately address rapid decompression scenarios involving compromised cabin glazing.

   Regulatory oversight actions taken by the FAA include the issuance of Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) 118, which temporarily mandated enhanced NDT intervals for high-bypass turbofan engines operating above 30,000 feet. The FAA also initiated a targeted surveillance program under 14 CFR § 121.373(a)(2) to verify compliance with revised maintenance planning documents (MPDs). Despite these interventions, the analysis reveals a systemic gap in the regulatory framework: the absence of a unified, real-time data-sharing mechanism between OEMs, operators, and the FAA for tracking in-service degradation of critical containment structures. The current AD process, while robust, operates on a reactive timeline that may not align with the accelerated fatigue accumulation observed in modern high-cycle engine operations.

   Additionally, the Operator’s compliance with 14 CFR § 121.344(b) regarding the establishment of a reliability program was found to be technically adequate but operationally deficient in predictive analytics. The FAA’s review of AA’s maintenance tracking system indicated that while historical failure rates were monitored, the integration of flight data monitoring (FDM) parameters with engine health monitoring (EHM) systems was not fully leveraged to anticipate uncontained failure precursors. This deficiency underscores the need for regulatory modernization to mandate predictive maintenance integration under Part 121.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
   In response to the identified compliance gaps and to ensure continued airworthiness across the commercial fleet, the FAA hereby issues the following mandatory actions and regulatory recommendations:

   1. Enhanced Inspection Mandate: All operators conducting scheduled air carrier operations under 14 CFR Part 121 shall implement revised ultrasonic and eddy current inspection protocols for engine fan blades, containment rings, and fuselage window frame assemblies. Compliance shall be achieved within 180 days of the effective date of this directive, in accordance with 14 CFR § 43.13 and § 121.373. Operators must submit revised maintenance program supplements to their respective Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) for approval.

   2. MMEL Revision and Operational Limitations: The FAA’s Flight Standards Service (AFS) shall coordinate with the Aircraft Evaluation Group (AEG) to revise the Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) for affected aircraft types. The revised MMEL shall explicitly prohibit dispatch with any cabin window exhibiting structural compromise, regardless of pressurization system redundancy. Operators, including Atlas Air, must incorporate these limitations into their approved MMEL within 90 days.

   3. Predictive Maintenance Integration: Pursuant to 14 CFR § 121.344(c), all Part 121 operators shall integrate real-time engine health monitoring (EHM) and flight data monitoring (FDM) analytics into their reliability programs. The FAA will issue Advisory Circular (AC) 120-XX to provide implementation guidance. Full compliance is required within 24 months, with quarterly progress reports submitted to the Principal Maintenance Inspector.

   4. Type Certificate Holder Reporting Requirements: Under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart J, all type certificate and supplemental type certificate holders shall establish a mandatory 72-hour reporting protocol for any in-service event involving uncontained engine debris, fuselage penetration, or rapid decompression. This requirement supersedes previous SDR timelines and shall be enforced through FAA Order 8110.4C.

   5. Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule: The FAA will conduct targeted surveillance audits of all affected operators within 12 months of this directive’s publication. Audits will verify compliance with enhanced inspection intervals, MMEL revisions, and predictive maintenance integration. Non-compliance will result in enforcement action under 14 CFR § 13.19, including potential suspension of operating certificates. A comprehensive regulatory review will be completed by the FAA’s Office of Aviation Safety (AVS) within 36 months to assess the efficacy of these measures and determine the necessity of permanent rulemaking under 14 CFR Part 21 and Part 121.

   This directive is issued under the authority of the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, in accordance with 49 U.S.C. § 44701 and 14 CFR Chapter I. All affected entities shall acknowledge receipt and initiate compliance planning within 30 calendar days. Failure to comply may result in administrative or enforcement proceedings as authorized by law.

HEADLINE: Southwest Flight Makes Emergency Landing After Engine Failure Claims One Passenger

BYLINE: By Elena Rostova, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA —

A Southwest Airlines passenger jet bound for Dallas made a harrowing emergency landing in Philadelphia on Tuesday after a catastrophic engine failure tore through the aircraft’s fuselage, shattering a cabin window and killing one passenger. The Boeing 737-700, carrying 144 passengers and five crew members, was cruising at 32,500 feet when the left engine disintegrated, triggering a rapid loss of cabin pressure.

Investigators say a fan blade inside the engine fractured during flight, sending high-velocity metal debris into the aircraft’s body. The impact breached the cabin wall and blew out a window, causing explosive decompression that partially pulled a passenger toward the opening. Flight attendants and fellow travelers managed to pull the woman back inside, but she later succumbed to her injuries. The pilot executed a steep, rapid descent to a lower altitude where breathable air is more abundant, ultimately landing safely at Philadelphia International Airport.

“We are devastated by the loss of a passenger and are cooperating fully with federal investigators,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson in a statement released Tuesday evening. “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family, and we are providing support to all passengers and crew on board.” The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched a specialized response team to Philadelphia to lead the probe. “The preliminary evidence points to an uncontained engine failure, meaning the engine casing could not contain the broken components,” said NTSB Chairman Robert Sumwalt during a press briefing. “We will examine maintenance records, the fractured fan blade, and the aircraft’s flight data recorder to determine the root cause.” The Federal Aviation Administration also issued an emergency directive, grounding similar aircraft for immediate inspections. “Safety is our highest priority,” an FAA representative said. “We are working closely with the manufacturer and the airline to ensure all affected engines meet strict operational standards.”

The aircraft, a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines, was flying from LaGuardia Airport in New York to Dallas Love Field. Southwest, the largest domestic carrier in the United States, operates an all-Boeing 737 fleet. The specific engine model involved in the incident is the CFM International LEAP-1B, a high-bypass turbofan known for its fuel efficiency and quiet operation. The aircraft was operating under 14 CFR part 121, the federal regulation that governs scheduled commercial airline operations in the United States, which mandates rigorous maintenance schedules, pilot training protocols, and strict airworthiness standards.

Aviation safety experts note that uncontained engine failures are rare but not unprecedented. “When a fan blade fails, it can act like a shrapnel grenade,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor at Purdue University. “Modern engines are designed with containment rings to catch debris, but extreme metal fatigue or manufacturing defects can sometimes overcome those safeguards.” Chen cautioned that while material fatigue is a leading suspect, investigators must rule out improper maintenance, foreign object damage, or operational stress before drawing conclusions. “The NTSB will look at the fracture surface under a microscope to see if there were pre-existing cracks,” he added.

Survivors described a scene of sudden chaos followed by remarkable calm. “There was a loud bang, and then the cabin filled with fog,” said passenger David Martinez, 42, who was seated three rows behind the damaged window. “People were screaming, oxygen masks dropped, and the plane started dropping fast. But the crew was incredible. They kept telling us to breathe and stay seated.” The airline has not yet publicly released the name of the deceased passenger, pending family notification, but confirmed that medical personnel met the aircraft upon landing. “We are heartbroken,” said a family friend who asked not to be named. “She was a mother of two, traveling for work. We just want answers and to know she didn’t suffer.”

Commercial aviation has seen a dramatic decline in fatal accidents over the past two decades, thanks to improved engine design, stricter oversight, and advanced pilot training. However, engine-related incidents have occasionally made headlines. In 2016, a Southwest Airlines flight experienced a similar, though non-fatal, engine failure that forced an emergency landing in Pensacola, Florida. That incident also involved a fractured fan blade and led to industry-wide inspections. Southwest has maintained a strong safety record, with no fatal accidents in its history prior to Tuesday’s tragedy. The carrier’s fleet undergoes regular inspections mandated by federal regulators, and the airline has consistently ranked among the top U.S. carriers for operational reliability.

The NTSB investigation is expected to take 12 to 18 months, with preliminary findings likely within weeks. Investigators have recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, both of which are being analyzed in Washington, D.C. The fractured engine components have been transported to a specialized laboratory for metallurgical testing. Meanwhile, the FAA has ordered immediate ultrasonic inspections of all LEAP-1B engines with similar flight cycles, and Southwest has temporarily grounded a portion of its fleet to comply with Part 121 regulations. “We will not rush to conclusions,” Sumwalt emphasized. “Every piece of data will be scrutinized to ensure this never happens again.” Passengers from the flight have been rebooked or provided with ground transportation, and the airline has established a dedicated hotline for families and travelers seeking information.

1. INTRODUCTION
Southwest Airlines Co. submits this technical analysis in support of the ongoing NTSB investigative hearing regarding the April 17, 2018, in-flight uncontained engine failure. As the operator of the affected aircraft, Lead Investigator has participated as a designated party to the investigation, providing comprehensive maintenance records, operational telemetry, and subject-matter expertise in fleet engineering, propulsion reliability, and maintenance program management. This submission is authored by our Lead Fleet Engineering and Maintenance Reliability Division, representing the carrier’s technical position on the contributing factors, inspection methodologies, and operational protocols relevant to the event. The scope of this document encompasses a detailed review of the maintenance history, non-destructive inspection (NDI) limitations, engine health monitoring data, and the operational response during the decompression event. Our objective is to provide the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and the Board with a transparent, evidence-based assessment that aligns with industry safety management principles while advocating for targeted, data-driven improvements to prevent recurrence.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 UTC, the subject Boeing 737-700 was operating at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet when an uncontained failure occurred in the left engine. The aircraft was equipped with a CFM International LEAP engine, specifically the LEAP-1B variant, which had accumulated 32,115 flight cycles and 41,208 flight hours at the time of the event. Debris from the failed fan blade assembly penetrated the left-side fuselage, resulting in the loss of a cabin window, rapid decompression, and the tragic fatality of one passenger. The flight crew executed emergency descent procedures, declared a Mayday, and successfully diverted to the nearest suitable airport.

The factual record, as documented in Docket Items 04-A through 09-C, confirms that the aircraft’s maintenance program was fully compliant with all applicable FAA Airworthiness Directives, OEM service bulletins, and Southwest Airlines Co. approved maintenance schedules. The most recent borescope inspection of the affected engine was conducted 1,842 flight cycles prior to the event, with no anomalies reported. Vibration monitoring data extracted from the Quick Access Recorder (QAR) and Engine Health Monitoring (EHM) system, referenced in Exhibit SWA-12, indicates a gradual but statistically insignificant increase in N1 vibration levels over the preceding 300 cycles, remaining well within the manufacturer’s operational envelope. The Chief Inspector’s post-event teardown report, submitted as Docket Item 11-F, identified a fatigue crack originating at the trailing edge of the fan blade root, propagating through the airfoil and culminating in a high-energy release. Metallurgical analysis confirmed the presence of a subsurface inclusion that served as the crack initiation site, a condition not readily detectable through conventional eddy current or visual inspection techniques.

The IIC’s preliminary findings, presented during the Washington, D.C. public hearing, have appropriately highlighted the intersection of material science, inspection technology, and operational risk management. Southwest Airlines Co. acknowledges the complexity of this event and recognizes that while our maintenance and operational protocols met all regulatory requirements, the incident underscores the need for enhanced predictive capabilities and refined inspection thresholds for high-cycle fatigue management in next-generation turbofan architectures.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS
The uncontained failure of the LEAP engine must be evaluated through a multidisciplinary lens encompassing materials engineering, non-destructive evaluation (NDE) limitations, and real-time operational monitoring. The primary technical finding centers on the fatigue crack initiation mechanism within the titanium alloy fan blade. As detailed in the metallurgical report (Docket Item 11-F), the crack originated from a microstructural anomaly located approximately 1.2 mm beneath the blade surface. This subsurface defect, consistent with a localized alpha-case formation during the forging process, acted as a stress concentrator under cyclic loading. The LEAP-1B’s advanced aerodynamic design and higher bypass ratio inherently subject the fan blades to increased centrifugal and aerodynamic loads, accelerating fatigue propagation once a critical threshold is breached.

Current industry-standard NDI protocols, including fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) and conventional eddy current testing, are optimized for surface-breaking defects. However, as demonstrated by the fracture mechanics modeling in Exhibit SWA-18, the probability of detection (POD) for subsurface inclusions below 1.5 mm depth drops below 60% using standard field-deployable equipment. This limitation is not unique to Southwest Airlines Co. but represents a systemic challenge across operators utilizing high-cycle, high-bypass turbofans. The maintenance interval of 1,842 cycles between borescope inspections was established in accordance with OEM recommendations and FAA-approved reliability programs. While this interval is statistically sound for surface defect detection, it does not account for the accelerated subsurface crack growth rates observed in this specific blade lot.

Operational telemetry further supports this assessment. The EHM data, cross-referenced with the QAR vibration traces, shows a 0.08 ips increase in broadband N1 vibration over the final 150 cycles. While this trend remained within the 0.15 ips alert threshold, retrospective analysis using advanced spectral decomposition reveals a subtle shift in the 1X and 2X harmonic signatures, indicative of early-stage mass imbalance. Had predictive algorithms been applied to this dataset, the anomaly could have been flagged for targeted inspection. However, at the time of the event, the carrier’s maintenance decision support system relied on threshold-based alerts rather than trend-based prognostics, a limitation shared across much of the commercial aviation sector.

From a human factors and operational perspective, the flight crew’s response to the rapid decompression was exemplary. The CVR transcript (Docket Item 07-D) confirms immediate recognition of the event, prompt donning of oxygen masks, and execution of the emergency descent checklist within 12 seconds. The cabin pressure differential dropped from 8.2 psi to ambient in approximately 4.3 seconds, consistent with a 14-inch fuselage breach. The structural integrity of the remaining cabin windows and the fuselage skin performed as designed, with no secondary failures observed. This underscores the robustness of the 737-700’s damage tolerance design, while simultaneously highlighting the critical importance of rapid crew response in mitigating passenger exposure to hypoxia and decompression trauma.

Industry best practices, as outlined in the FAA’s Aging Aircraft Safety Program and the IATA Engine Reliability Working Group guidelines, emphasize a shift from reactive to predictive maintenance paradigms. The integration of phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT), digital twin modeling, and machine learning-driven vibration analytics represents the next evolution in engine health management. Southwest Airlines Co. has already initiated pilot programs in these areas, but the April 2018 event demonstrates the urgency of accelerating their fleet-wide deployment.

4. CONCLUSIONS
Based on the comprehensive review of maintenance records, metallurgical findings, operational telemetry, and industry standards, Southwest Airlines Co. concludes that the uncontained engine failure was primarily driven by a subsurface fatigue crack initiation in the LEAP-1B fan blade, which propagated undetected due to the inherent limitations of conventional NDI methodologies. While the carrier’s maintenance program was fully compliant with all regulatory and OEM requirements, the incident reveals a critical gap in the detection of deep-seated material anomalies under high-cycle operational conditions. The contributing factors are multifaceted: (1) the presence of a microstructural inclusion that served as a crack nucleation site, (2) the reduced probability of detection for subsurface defects using standard field inspection techniques, (3) the reliance on threshold-based rather than predictive vibration monitoring, and (4) the accelerated fatigue growth rates associated with the LEAP engine’s advanced aerodynamic loading profile.

Southwest Airlines Co. maintains that no single procedural failure or maintenance oversight precipitated this event. Rather, it represents a convergence of material science limitations, inspection technology constraints, and the natural evolution of high-cycle fatigue in next-generation propulsion systems. The carrier’s position is that safety improvements must focus on enhancing early detection capabilities, refining inspection intervals based on actual fleet data rather than conservative OEM baselines, and integrating advanced prognostic health management into routine maintenance workflows. Furthermore, the successful crew response validates the effectiveness of current emergency training protocols, though the tragic fatality underscores the need for continued emphasis on passenger safety briefings and rapid decompression mitigation strategies.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS
In the immediate aftermath of the April 17, 2018, event, Southwest Airlines Co. implemented a series of corrective actions in coordination with the OEM, the FAA, and the IIC. Within 72 hours, the carrier initiated a fleet-wide borescope inspection campaign targeting all LEAP-1B engines exceeding 25,000 flight cycles. This campaign, documented in Maintenance Directive SWA-MD-2018-04, resulted in the identification and removal of three additional fan blades exhibiting early-stage fatigue indicators, none of which had reached critical propagation thresholds. Concurrently, the carrier revised its Engine Condition Monitoring (ECM) program to incorporate advanced spectral analysis of N1 and N2 vibration data, lowering the alert threshold from 0.15 ips to 0.10 ips and implementing automated trend tracking for harmonic shifts.

The Chief Inspector’s office, in collaboration with Southwest Airlines Co. engineering, has also mandated the adoption of enhanced borescope imaging protocols, including high-definition video capture and AI-assisted defect recognition software, to improve the consistency and accuracy of field inspections. Training modules for maintenance technicians have been updated to emphasize subsurface defect recognition, with a focus on interpreting subtle acoustic emission signatures and correlating them with EHM data.

Looking forward, Southwest Airlines Co. proposes several industry-wide improvements to enhance propulsion system safety. First, we recommend the development and certification of portable phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) equipment for line maintenance use, enabling reliable detection of subsurface inclusions without requiring engine removal. Second, we advocate for the establishment of a centralized, anonymized engine health data repository, allowing operators, manufacturers, and regulators to share real-time fatigue progression metrics and refine predictive maintenance algorithms. Third, we support the FAA’s ongoing review of inspection interval methodologies, urging a transition from fixed-cycle schedules to condition-based maintenance frameworks that dynamically adjust inspection frequency based on actual operational stress profiles.

Finally, Southwest Airlines Co. remains committed to advancing cabin safety through enhanced passenger education and rapid decompression response training. We have partnered with the FAA and industry stakeholders to develop updated safety demonstration protocols that emphasize the critical importance of immediate oxygen mask deployment and proper seatbelt retention during sudden pressure loss events.

The April 2018 incident serves as a sobering reminder of the relentless pursuit of safety required in commercial aviation. Southwest Airlines Co. will continue to collaborate with the NTSB, the IIC, and the broader aviation community to implement data-driven, technologically advanced solutions that mitigate risk, enhance detection capabilities, and ensure the continued safety of passengers and crew. We respectfully submit this analysis for the Board’s consideration and stand ready to provide additional technical data or expert testimony as required.

TO: Fleet Engineering, Maintenance Control, Quality Assurance, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Training & Standards Division
FROM: VP of Engineering & Maintenance / Chief Safety Officer, Southwest Airlines Co
DATE: 20 April 2018
SUBJECT: URGENT: Enhanced Fan Blade & Forward Fuselage Containment Inspection Protocols
REF: QA-2018-0417, SWA-ENG-DIR-089, NTSB Docket Entry #SWA-1380-004

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate implementation of revised inspection, documentation, and reporting procedures for all CFM56-7B powered aircraft in the active fleet. The directive establishes interim containment verification standards, aligns maintenance practices with current airworthiness baselines, and ensures rapid identification of fatigue-related anomalies pending final investigation findings.

BACKGROUND:
On 17 April 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operating at 32,500 feet experienced an uncontained left engine failure. High-energy debris penetrated the forward fuselage, compromised a passenger window, and resulted in rapid decompression and one fatality. Preliminary telemetry and recovered component analysis indicate a fatigue-initiated fracture in a fan blade, with subsequent secondary damage to the containment ring, nacelle structure, and adjacent fuselage skin. While the investigation remains under the authority of the NTSB IIC, Southwest Airlines Co is implementing proactive engineering controls to mitigate recurrence risk across the fleet.

Current certification standards under 14 CFR Part 21 require that engine installations demonstrate adequate containment and that failure modes will not result in hazardous conditions to the aircraft. Additionally, 14 CFR 25.783 governs fuselage door and window structural integrity under pressurization, impact loading, and rapid decompression scenarios. This alert bridges operational maintenance practices with those regulatory baselines, ensuring our inspection intervals and NDT thresholds reflect worst-case debris trajectories. Engineering is also cross-referencing this event data against LEAP-1B containment ring certification packages to validate design margins and window frame reinforcement protocols prior to next-generation fleet entry into service.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all scheduled and unscheduled maintenance events involving engine removal, fan case inspection, or forward fuselage structural checks shall adhere to the following revised parameters:

1. Fan Blade Dovetail & Root Inspection
   • All CFM56-7B engines exceeding 15,000 cycles since new (CSN) or 5,000 cycles since last shop visit (CSLSV) require Level II fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) of all 24 fan blade dovetails.
   • Execute per Work Order WO-ENG-737-4412, Rev. 3. Document all indications per NDT-STD-088.
   • Any blade showing linear indications >0.015”, branching cracks, or surface pitting at the root fillet must be quarantined and reported to Engineering within 2 hours.

2. Containment Ring & Nacelle Structure Verification
   • Perform borescope inspection of the aft fan case and containment ring for scoring, gouging, delamination, or fastener back-out.
   • Reference Part Number P/N 328A1100-501 for containment ring replacement criteria. Any ring exhibiting >0.030” material loss or visible fiber exposure requires immediate removal.
   • If impact damage is suspected, initiate Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-10-01 assessment and notify Fleet Engineering before returning the aircraft to service.

3. Forward Fuselage & Window Frame Assessment
   • All aircraft with >20,000 flight hours require ultrasonic thickness testing (UTT) of the forward fuselage skin panels adjacent to the engine pylon (Stations 340–420).
   • Inspect window frame retainers, load-bearing doublers, and sealant channels for stress cracking, fastener elongation, or sealant degradation per SWA-AMM-53-22-00.
   • Replace any window assembly showing deformation, crazing, or compromised load path integrity. Do not apply temporary patches without Engineering disposition.

4. Documentation & Traceability
   • All inspections must be logged in the Maintenance Tracking System (MTS) under Event Code ENG-CONTAIN-01.
   • Attach high-resolution borescope imagery, NDT reports, and technician sign-offs to the aircraft technical log.
   • Retain all removed components in the Quarantine Bay (Hangar 4, Bay 12) pending Engineering disposition. Tag with Form QA-4412-REV and include cycle count, flight hours, and last inspection date.

ACTION REQUIRED:
• Line Maintenance Supervisors: Ensure all active aircraft are pulled for inspection within 72 hours of this alert. Prioritize aircraft with >15,000 CSN, recent heavy turbulence reports, or prior fan blade vibration events.
• Quality Assurance: Audit 100% of completed inspections against WO-ENG-737-4412, Rev. 3. Submit compliance report to Engineering by 27 April 2018. Flag any deviations for immediate corrective action.
• Training & Standards Division: Issue mandatory 2-hour recurrent module “Uncontained Engine Failure: Debris Trajectory & Containment Verification” to all A&P/IA personnel. Completion required by 01 May 2018. Update CBT platform with revised NDT acceptance criteria.
• Fleet Engineering: Coordinate with OEM technical representatives and the IIC liaison to update inspection thresholds as investigation data is released. Publish interim service bulletin draft by 30 April 2018.
• Procurement & Logistics: Expedite delivery of replacement fan blades (P/N 328A1100-501 series) and containment ring kits. Maintain 14-day forward stock at DAL, MDW, and DEN hubs.

Non-compliance with this directive will result in immediate grounding of the affected aircraft and escalation to the Director of Maintenance. All personnel are reminded that containment verification is a critical airworthiness function. Report any anomalies, tooling deficiencies, or procedural conflicts directly to the Engineering Duty Manager via the 24/7 Maintenance Control hotline.

This document is classified as INTERNAL – SAFETY CRITICAL. Distribution is restricted to authorized maintenance, engineering, and quality personnel. Retain in accordance with Record Retention Policy RR-2015-09.

SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines (SWA) experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. The event resulted in rapid cabin decompression, structural damage to the airframe, and one passenger fatality. The aircraft subsequently executed an emergency descent and landed safely at FAA. This preliminary procedural document outlines initial factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and documents early-stage directives. All information contained herein is subject to revision as additional evidence is collected, analyzed, and validated. No conclusions regarding the sequence of events or contributing factors have been reached.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information indicates that the flight was en route when the flight crew reported a sudden loss of thrust, abnormal vibrations, and a loud acoustic event originating from the left engine. Initial witness accounts from surviving passengers and cabin crew members describe rapid depressurization, automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks, and visible damage to the left-side fuselage. Radar telemetry and initial flight data recorder (FDR) parameters suggest a rapid degradation in engine performance metrics consistent with an uncontained failure event. Weather conditions at the time of the incident, as reported by meteorological services and corroborated by pilot reports, were characterized by clear skies, light winds, and no significant convective activity along the flight path.

Preliminary examination of the recovered airframe sections revealed a breach in the left fuselage skin and a fractured cabin window frame. Debris impact patterns suggest that high-energy fragments from the left powerplant, identified in maintenance records as a LEAP-1B engine, penetrated the nacelle and adjacent fuselage structure. The operator’s maintenance logs, currently under review, indicate that the engine had accumulated approximately 32,000 flight cycles since its last major overhaul. It should be emphasized that these observations are preliminary and do not constitute a determination of mechanical failure mode, material defect, or maintenance deficiency.

Additionally, initial review of operational documentation suggests that certain maintenance and inspection protocols were conducted under the regulatory framework of 14 CFR part 135, though the primary operator holds a 14 CFR part 121 certificate. This regulatory overlap is currently being evaluated to determine its relevance to the maintenance history and operational oversight of the aircraft. The Chief Inspector (CI) has directed that all maintenance records, crew training files, and airworthiness directives compliance documentation be secured and cross-referenced with manufacturer service bulletins. All regulatory interpretations remain preliminary and subject to further legal and technical review.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The following groups have been formally established and are currently conducting field and laboratory examinations: Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group is operating under the direction of a designated group chair and is adhering to standard NTSB investigative protocols.

Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, Southwest Airlines, and relevant labor organizations.
