All party representatives have been briefed on the preliminary scope and are required to submit factual reports within established timeframes. The Lead Investigator (LI) has emphasized that party participation is strictly limited to the provision of technical expertise and factual data; no party shall engage in speculative analysis or public commentary regarding the event.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data recorder (FDR), cockpit voice recorder (CVR), recovered engine fragments, damaged fuselage panels, and the fractured cabin window assembly. These items have been cataloged, photographed, and transported to NTSB headquarters for detailed forensic analysis. Additional examinations planned include metallurgical testing of the recovered fan blade fragments, non-destructive evaluation of the remaining engine components, and a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s structural repair history. The Chief Inspector has authorized the establishment of a dedicated evidence control room to maintain chain-of-custody documentation and ensure secure storage of all physical and digital materials.

Coordination with external entities is ongoing. Preliminary discussions have been initiated with Atlas Air Inc (AAI) regarding potential maintenance support contracts and historical data sharing, though their direct involvement in this specific airframe’s maintenance history remains under verification. All communications with external contractors and third-party service providers will be documented and routed through the designated investigative channels to preserve the integrity of the inquiry.

NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities for the immediate future include the complete readout and analysis of the FDR and CVR data, which is expected to be completed within 14 days. The Powerplants group will conduct a teardown and dimensional inspection of the recovered engine components, with metallurgical and fractographic analyses scheduled to follow. The Structures group will perform a detailed mapping of the debris impact zones and assess the structural integrity of the remaining airframe. Human Performance specialists will conduct confidential interviews with the flight crew, cabin crew, and selected passengers to establish a timeline of events and evaluate crew resource management during the emergency descent.

The Lead Investigator will convene a preliminary status conference within 30 days to review group progress, address data discrepancies, and adjust investigative priorities as necessary. A public hearing is not anticipated at this stage; however, a factual update will be issued to the public and relevant stakeholders upon completion of the initial data collection phase. All findings, technical reports, and procedural decisions will be compiled into a comprehensive docket for internal review.

It is imperative to reiterate that this document represents an early-stage procedural summary. All observations, data interpretations, and investigative directives are preliminary and subject to change as additional evidence is recovered, analyzed, and validated. No conclusions regarding the sequence of events, contributing factors, or probable cause have been reached. The investigation will proceed in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with all factual determinations subject to peer review and final approval by the Board. Further updates will be disseminated through official channels as the inquiry progresses.

GROUP CHAIRMAN’S FACTUAL REPORT
AVIATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION
NTSB DOCKET NO. DCA18MA088

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), an uncontained engine failure occurred during the cruise phase of flight. The event transpired at a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 42 nautical miles west-northwest of Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Pennsylvania. The geographic coordinates of the event were recorded as 39°58.2′ N, 075°42.1′ W. The aircraft subsequently initiated an emergency descent and diverted to PHL, where it landed without further incident at 16:02 EDT.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-7H4, bearing United States registration number N772SW. The aircraft was operated by Southwest Airlines under a scheduled passenger service. The flight was designated as Southwest Airlines Flight 1380, operating from LaGuardia Airport (LGA), New York, to Dallas Love Field (DAL), Texas. The aircraft was configured for 143 passenger seats and was equipped with two underwing-mounted turbofan engines.

1.3 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, governing domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. The flight plan was filed under instrument flight rules (IFR) and was cleared for a direct routing at flight level 320 prior to the event. The aircraft was operating in a controlled airspace environment under the jurisdiction of the New York Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZNY). All operational parameters, including dispatch release, weight and balance calculations, and fuel planning, were documented in accordance with the operator’s approved operations specifications and 14 CFR Part 121 requirements.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Records
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, type-rated in the Boeing 737 series, with an unrestricted first-class medical certificate issued on January 12, 2018. The captain’s total flight time was recorded as 11,450 hours, with 8,920 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737. Recent flight experience included 142 hours within the preceding 90 days and 48 hours within the preceding 30 days. The captain’s training records indicated successful completion of the most recent recurrent proficiency check on February 22, 2018, which included simulator-based emergency procedures, rapid decompression drills, and engine failure scenarios. All training was conducted in accordance with the operator’s FAA-approved training program and 14 CFR § 121.433.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Records
The first officer held an ATP certificate, type-rated in the Boeing 737 series, with a first-class medical certificate issued on March 5, 2018. Total flight time was documented as 3,210 hours, with 1,840 hours in the Boeing 737. Recent experience included 118 hours in the preceding 90 days and 36 hours in the preceding 30 days. The first officer’s most recent line-oriented flight training (LOFT) and proficiency evaluation were completed on January 18, 2018. Records confirmed compliance with all regulatory currency requirements, including instrument approaches, holding procedures, and abnormal/emergency checklist execution.

2.3 Duty/Rest and Training Compliance
Review of crew scheduling records, duty logs, and rest period documentation confirmed that both flight crew members were within the duty time limitations prescribed by 14 CFR § 121.470 and § 121.471. The captain reported 10 hours of uninterrupted rest prior to reporting for duty, while the first officer reported 11.5 hours. No fatigue-related factors were documented in the pre-flight briefing or post-accident interviews. The Lead Investigator coordinated the review of crew records, training syllabi, and scheduling databases to verify regulatory compliance and operational readiness. All documentation was cross-referenced with the operator’s internal tracking systems and FAA oversight records.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications and Airframe Data
The aircraft was manufactured by The Boeing Company, bearing manufacturer serial number 28748. The airframe accumulated a total of 56,842 flight hours and 31,204 flight cycles at the time of the event. The aircraft was certified under 14 CFR Part 21, with a standard airworthiness certificate issued on August 14, 2001. The airframe configuration included a blended winglet modification, a Class D cargo compartment, and a standard passenger cabin layout. Structural integrity documentation, including corrosion prevention and control program (CPCP) records, indicated compliance with all manufacturer service bulletins and operator maintenance program requirements.

3.2 Engine and Propulsion Systems
The aircraft was equipped with two CFM International LEAP engine models, serial numbers 784412 (left) and 784415 (right). The left engine, which experienced the uncontained failure, had accumulated 28,110 flight hours and 18,442 cycles since new. The right engine had accumulated 27,980 flight hours and 18,310 cycles. Both engines were maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP). Engine health monitoring (EHM) data, including exhaust gas temperature (EGT) margins, vibration levels, and oil consumption trends, were reviewed for the preceding 500 flight cycles. No exceedances or maintenance write-ups were recorded for the left engine in the 30 days preceding the event.

3.3 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records were examined for compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) and service bulletins. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check) was completed on November 12, 2017, at 55,910 airframe hours. The left engine underwent a borescope inspection on March 3, 2018, which revealed no anomalies in the fan, compressor, or turbine sections. All ADs related to engine mounting, nacelle structure, and fuel system components were verified as current. The operator’s maintenance tracking system confirmed that all scheduled inspections, lubrication tasks, and component replacements were performed within prescribed intervals.

3.4 Systems and Instrumentation
The aircraft was equipped with a digital flight data recorder (DFDR) and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which were recovered and secured for analysis. The pressurization system operated normally until the event, with cabin altitude maintained at approximately 6,500 feet prior to decompression. The emergency oxygen system was configured for automatic deployment at a cabin altitude of 14,000 feet. Electrical, hydraulic, and flight control systems were documented as fully operational during pre-flight checks. The aircraft’s quick access recorder (QAR) data was downloaded and archived for parameter correlation with DFDR data.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 En Route Atmospheric Conditions
At the time of the event, the aircraft was cruising at flight level 320 in a stable atmospheric environment. Upper-air sounding data from the nearest National Weather Service (NWS) rawinsonde station indicated a temperature of -48°C, a dewpoint of -52°C, and a wind direction of 270° true at 45 knots. No significant turbulence, icing, or convective activity was reported along the flight path. The tropopause was located at approximately 38,000 feet MSL, with a stable lapse rate above 25,000 feet.

4.2 Terminal Weather Observations and Forecasts
The aviation routine weather report (METAR) for Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) at 15:53 EDT recorded wind 280° at 12 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, scattered clouds at 4,500 feet, broken at 8,000 feet, temperature 14°C, dewpoint 6°C, and altimeter setting 30.12 inches of mercury. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for PHL, valid from 12:00 to 18:00 EDT, predicted similar conditions with no significant weather changes. Departure airport (LGA) METAR at 14:53 EDT indicated wind 260° at 10 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, few clouds at 3,000 feet, temperature 13°C, and altimeter 30.10 inches of mercury.

4.3 Pilot Reports and ATC Communications
No pilot reports (PIREPs) of turbulence, wind shear, or volcanic ash were filed along the route of flight. Air traffic control (ATC) communications were reviewed from the time of departure through the emergency descent. The flight crew reported normal cruise parameters until 15:43:12 EDT, when a loud bang was reported, followed by a request for an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. ATC cleared the aircraft immediately and provided vectors to PHL. No meteorological anomalies were cited by the flight crew or ATC personnel during the event sequence.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Debris Field
The uncontained engine failure resulted in the ejection of multiple high-energy components from the left engine nacelle. Debris was recovered from a linear distribution pattern extending approximately 1.2 nautical miles along the flight path. Primary debris included a fractured fan blade segment, portions of the inlet cowl, and fragments of the acoustic liner. Secondary debris, including insulation blankets, wiring harness segments, and nacelle fasteners, was located within a 0.5-nautical-mile radius of the primary impact zone. All recovered components were cataloged, photographed, and transported to a secure examination facility.

5.2 Engine and Nacelle Examination
Examination of the left engine revealed a fatigue fracture originating at the root of the number 13 fan blade. The fracture surface exhibited characteristic beach marks and a final overload zone consistent with high-cycle fatigue. The containment ring, designed to retain fan blade fragments, was breached at the 10 o’clock position. The inlet cowl was separated aft of the thrust reverser cascade, and the fan case exhibited localized deformation and gouging. The right engine remained intact and showed no evidence of foreign object damage (FOD) or structural compromise. All engine parameters recorded by the DFDR indicated a rapid loss of thrust, followed by automatic fuel shutoff and engine fire warning activation.

5.3 Fuselage and Cabin Structural Damage
High-velocity debris penetrated the left fuselage skin at station 420, frame 18, resulting in a 14-inch by 8-inch breach. The impact compromised the adjacent cabin window, causing rapid decompression. Structural examination revealed localized buckling of the stringers and skin panels surrounding the breach. The window frame exhibited plastic deformation and fastener shear. No evidence of pre-existing corrosion, fatigue cracking, or manufacturing defects was identified in the surrounding airframe structure. The fuselage breach was consistent with a single-point high-energy impact event.

5.4 Emergency Systems and Occupant Impact
The rapid decompression triggered automatic deployment of the passenger oxygen masks. Cabin pressure dropped from 6,500 feet to approximately 22,000 feet equivalent altitude within 12 seconds. The emergency descent was initiated at 15:43:18 EDT, with the aircraft reaching 10,000 feet at 15:46:42 EDT. One passenger fatality was documented, with injuries consistent with blunt force trauma and hypoxia. Medical examiner reports confirmed the cause of death as traumatic injury secondary to cabin decompression and debris impact. All other occupants sustained minor injuries or no injuries. The cabin crew executed emergency procedures in accordance with the operator’s training manual, including securing the cabin, administering first aid, and coordinating with the flight deck.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Southwest Airlines maintains a comprehensive safety management system (SMS) and maintenance program approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The operator’s policies require mandatory reporting of all abnormal engine events, immediate grounding of affected aircraft, and coordination with the manufacturer for technical support. Maintenance personnel are trained in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L, and are required to complete recurrent training on engine inspection techniques, non-destructive testing (NDT), and component tracking. The operator’s flight operations manual (FOM) and quick reference handbook (QRH) contain specific procedures for uncontained engine failures, rapid decompression, and emergency descents. All procedures were reviewed and found to be current and compliant with regulatory standards.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Service Experience
The investigation group reviewed historical data on uncontained engine failures in commercial turbofan engines. Previous incidents involving similar engine architectures have documented fatigue cracking in fan blade roots, often associated with manufacturing anomalies, operational stress cycles, or environmental exposure. Service bulletins and airworthiness directives issued by the manufacturer and regulatory authorities have addressed inspection intervals, borescope techniques, and blade replacement criteria. The operator’s internal safety database was queried for similar events, revealing three prior reports of fan blade anomalies over the preceding five years, all of which were resolved through scheduled maintenance and component replacement. No systemic fleet-wide deficiencies were identified.

6.3 Regulatory Framework and Certification Standards
The aircraft and engine were certified in accordance with 14 CFR Part 25, which establishes airworthiness standards for transport category airplanes. Section 25.903 addresses engine installation and requires demonstration of containment capability for uncontained failures. Section 25.365 addresses pressurized cabin loads and structural integrity under rapid decompression scenarios. The engine certification process, governed by 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart E, requires rigorous testing, including blade-out containment tests, vibration analysis, and fatigue life validation. Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) 88, which addresses fuel tank ignition prevention, was referenced during the post-accident inspection of fuel system wiring and bonding to ensure no secondary ignition hazards were introduced by the debris impact. All regulatory requirements were verified as met at the time of certification and throughout the aircraft’s operational life.

6.4 Data Analysis and Laboratory Support
Flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder data were extracted, decoded, and analyzed at NTSB headquarters. The DFDR provided 88 parameters, including engine pressure ratio (EPR), N1/N2 rotational speeds, fuel flow, cabin altitude, and control surface positions. The CVR captured 120 minutes of audio, including crew communications, aural warnings, and ambient sounds. Metallurgical examination of the fractured fan blade was conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and fractography. The analysis confirmed a fatigue initiation site with no evidence of corrosion, overheating, or foreign object damage. All laboratory results, maintenance records, and operational data were compiled into a centralized database for group review. The Lead Investigator coordinated the synthesis of findings across the powerplant, structures, human performance, and operations groups to ensure factual accuracy and regulatory compliance. No probable cause determinations or safety recommendations are included in this factual report.

1. INTRODUCTION
This Specialist’s Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis of the powerplant, associated structural components, and recorded flight parameters related to the uncontained engine failure event involving a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines, on April 17, 2018. The scope of this examination encompasses the recovered engine debris, the left engine fan case, the impacted forward fuselage section, and the associated flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) data streams. The examination was conducted under the direction of the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and at the Southwest Airlines maintenance facility in Dallas, Texas, between March 15 and April 10, 2018. Items examined included the fractured fan blade assembly (Part Number 328A1000-001, Serial Number 88421), the titanium fan containment ring, the forward fuselage skin panel (Station 420 to 460), the No. 14 cabin window frame, and the complete FDR/CVR data stream. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, with test procedures calibrated to ASTM and SAE standards.

2. BACKGROUND
The subject aircraft was equipped with a CFM International LEAP-1B engine, a two-spool, high-bypass turbofan featuring a 3D-woven carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) fan blade array, a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) fan case, and a full-authority digital engine control (FADEC) system. The engine was certified under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart E, and met the airworthiness requirements of 14 CFR Part 33, including Section 33.94 for uncontained engine failure containment. The aircraft operated under 14 CFR Part 121 scheduled passenger service, with maintenance and airworthiness directives administered by the assigned Principal Inspector. Compliance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) was documented in the operator’s fuel tank ignition prevention program, which included periodic inspections of engine pylon wiring harnesses, bonding strap continuity verification, and ignition source mitigation protocols.

The specific LEAP-1B engine (Serial Number 77492) had accumulated 28,412 flight hours and 14,883 flight cycles at the time of the event. The most recent heavy maintenance visit occurred on November 12, 2017, during which the fan blade root dovetail interfaces were inspected using fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) per ASTM E1417. No anomalies were recorded. The engine’s operational history, as maintained in the operator’s reliability tracking system, indicated normal vibration trends, with average cruise N1 vibration levels remaining below 0.4 inches per second (ips) over the preceding 1,200 cycles. The certification basis for the engine installation required compliance with 14 CFR Part 21.21 for type design approval and 14 CFR Part 121.363 for continued airworthiness maintenance programs. The fan blade design incorporated a titanium alloy leading edge protector and a CFRP airfoil bonded to a metallic root platform, with a design ultimate load factor of 1.5 times the maximum operational centrifugal force at 105% N1. The manufacturer’s engineering data specified a maximum allowable stress intensity factor range (ΔK) of 22 MPa√m for the titanium dovetail under cyclic loading conditions.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS
The physical examination of the recovered fan blade fragment (designated as Blade 14) revealed a complete separation at the root-to-airfoil transition zone. The fracture surface exhibited distinct fatigue crack propagation features, with a primary initiation site located at the trailing edge of the titanium dovetail insert, approximately 12.4 mm from the blade root datum. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis confirmed the presence of fatigue striations with an average spacing of 0.85 μm, corresponding to a crack growth rate (da/dN) of approximately 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ mm/cycle under the applied cyclic loading spectrum. The crack propagated through the titanium alloy substrate before transitioning into the CFRP composite matrix, where delamination and fiber pull-out were observed. Fracture mechanics modeling utilizing the Paris-Erdogan equation (da/dN = C(ΔK)^m) yielded a fatigue life estimate of 14,200 cycles from initiation to final fracture, consistent with the engine’s accumulated cycle count.

Chemical composition analysis via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the titanium insert met AMS 4928 specifications, with aluminum content at 6.12 wt%, vanadium at 4.08 wt%, and iron at 0.18 wt%. Hardness testing (Rockwell C scale) yielded an average value of 34.2 HRC, consistent with the specified heat treatment condition. The CFRP airfoil exhibited no evidence of manufacturing defects, void content, or foreign object damage (FOD). However, microscopic examination of the trailing edge revealed localized fretting damage at the interface between the titanium insert and the composite layup, with oxide debris accumulation indicating prolonged cyclic micro-movement. The fretting zone measured 4.1 mm in length and 0.8 mm in depth, with surface roughness (Ra) values of 1.2 μm.

The fan containment ring (Part Number 328A2000-005) displayed a 142 mm longitudinal breach at the 3 o’clock position, with gouge depths ranging from 3.2 mm to 8.7 mm. The titanium case exhibited localized plastic deformation and adiabatic shear bands, consistent with high-velocity impact from the liberated blade fragment. Metallurgical cross-sections of the impact zone revealed dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement, with microhardness values increasing from 310 HV to 485 HV in the deformed region. The containment ring’s structural integrity was evaluated against 14 CFR 33.94 requirements, which mandate that the casing must contain all blade fragments at maximum rotational speed. The observed breach exceeded the design containment threshold, indicating an uncontained failure mode.

The impacted fuselage section (Boeing 737-700, Station 435) exhibited a 210 mm × 180 mm penetration through the aluminum alloy skin (2024-T3, per AMS 4037). The window frame (No. 14, left side) was completely severed, with the acrylic window panel ejected from the airframe. Fracture mechanics analysis of the window frame revealed ductile tearing with a final fracture zone exhibiting 45° shear lips, consistent with rapid pressure differential loading. The cabin pressure relief valve was found in the open position, with the diaphragm ruptured at a differential pressure of 8.9 PSI, exceeding the nominal 8.6 PSI relief setting.

Non-destructive testing (NDT) of the remaining fan blades (Blades 1–13 and 15–22) was performed using eddy current inspection per ASTM E309 and ultrasonic phased array testing per ASTM E2491. Calibration was verified using reference standards per ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4. No additional cracks or material degradation were identified. The FADEC unit was downloaded and analyzed, revealing no fault codes or software anomalies prior to the event. All test procedures and measurements were documented in NTSB Engineering Report ENG-2018-0417, with photographic evidence cataloged under references NTSB-ENG-001 through NTSB-ENG-015.

4. DATA ANALYSIS
The flight data recorder (FDR) captured 88 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with high-frequency vibration data recorded at 64 Hz. The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) provided synchronized audio and warning annunciations. Data analysis was performed using NTSB-standardized decoding software, with parameters cross-referenced against the aircraft’s quick access recorder (QAR) data for validation. Parameter resolution was verified against ARINC 717 and ARINC 767 standards, with time synchronization accuracy within ±0.05 seconds.

At 14:32:15 UTC, the aircraft was in cruise flight at 32,500 ft MSL, with an indicated airspeed of 284 knots, Mach 0.78, and an outside air temperature of -48°C. The left engine N1 was stable at 92.4%, N2 at 98.1%, and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) at 732°C. At 14:32:17.3 UTC, a sudden N1 decay was recorded, dropping from 92.4% to 68.1% within 0.8 seconds. Concurrently, the left engine vibration parameter (VIB) spiked from 0.32 ips to 4.2 ips, exceeding the 1.5 ips caution threshold. The EGT increased to 890°C within 1.2 seconds, followed by a rapid fuel flow (FF) reduction from 4,820 lbs/hr to 2,150 lbs/hr as the FADEC initiated automatic thrust rollback. The N2 parameter exhibited a transient overshoot to 101.3% before stabilizing at 84.7%, consistent with compressor aerodynamic instability following blade liberation.

The cabin altitude parameter began rising at 14:32:18.1 UTC, with a rate of climb of 2,840 ft/min, indicating rapid decompression. The cabin pressure differential dropped from 8.4 PSI to 1.2 PSI within 4.5 seconds. The aircraft’s autopilot disengaged at 14:32:19.0 UTC, and the crew initiated an emergency descent. The FDR recorded a maximum descent rate of 6,200 ft/min, with airspeed increasing to 342 knots before speed brake deployment. The right engine remained within normal operational parameters throughout the event, with N1, N2, and EGT values tracking within ±1.5% of baseline cruise values.

Comparison with normal operational data from the operator’s fleet database (n=142 LEAP-1B engines) indicates that the observed N1 decay rate of 30.3%/sec and vibration spike of 3.88 ips exceed the 99.9th percentile of recorded anomalies. The EGT rise of 158°C in 1.2 seconds is consistent with an uncontained blade release and subsequent compressor stall. The cabin decompression rate of 2,840 ft/min aligns with a 210 mm fuselage breach at 32,500 ft MSL, as modeled using the Bernoulli equation for compressible flow through an orifice. The QAR data corroborated the FDR timeline, with no discrepancies in parameter synchronization. The CVR captured the master warning chime, “ENGINE FIRE” and “CABIN ALTITUDE” aural alerts, and crew coordination for the emergency descent. Structural load path analysis of the forward fuselage indicated that the impact energy was partially absorbed by the stringer and frame network, with localized stress concentrations reaching 42 ksi at the window frame attachment points, exceeding the 2024-T3 yield strength of 39 ksi.

5. SUMMARY
The examination of the recovered LEAP-1B engine components, fuselage structure, and flight data recorder parameters yielded the following technical findings:
- The left engine fan blade (Blade 14) experienced a fatigue-initiated fracture at the titanium dovetail-to-CFRP interface, with crack propagation originating at the trailing edge.
- Metallurgical analysis confirmed the titanium insert met AMS 4928 specifications, with localized fretting damage and oxide accumulation at the composite-metallic interface.
- The fan containment ring sustained a 142 mm longitudinal breach, with impact-induced adiabatic shear bands and localized plastic deformation exceeding design containment thresholds.
- The fuselage skin (2024-T3 aluminum alloy) and No. 14 cabin window frame were penetrated by liberated debris, resulting in a 210 mm × 180 mm structural breach.
- The cabin pressure relief valve activated at 8.9 PSI differential, with the cabin altitude rising at 2,840 ft/min, consistent with rapid decompression dynamics.
- FDR data recorded a 0.8-second N1 decay from 92.4% to 68.1%, a vibration spike to 4.2 ips, and an EGT increase to 890°C, followed by automatic FADEC thrust rollback.
- The remaining fan blades exhibited no additional material degradation or structural anomalies per ASTM E309 and ASTM E2491 inspection criteria.
- All recorded parameters were within the operational envelope of the aircraft’s certification basis under 14 CFR Part 21 and 14 CFR Part 121, with maintenance compliance documented per the operator’s approved program and Principal Inspector oversight.
- The data timeline, structural damage measurements, and material analysis results are consistent with an uncontained engine failure sequence at cruise altitude.

This report contains factual findings derived from physical examination, materials testing, and flight data analysis. No conclusions regarding probable cause or operational recommendations are presented herein. All referenced measurements, test procedures, and engineering standards are documented in the supporting NTSB technical appendices.

INTERVIEW OF MARK T. HENDERSON, SOUTHWEST AIRLINES SENIOR MAINTENANCE INSPECTOR
Date: April 19, 2018
Time: 14:30 EST
Location: Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Gate Operations Office, Terminal B
Interviewer: J. Miller, NTSB Investigator-in-Charge
Witness: Mark T. Henderson, Southwest Airlines Senior Maintenance Inspector (Deadhead Passenger)

Q: Mr. Henderson, thank you for making yourself available on such short notice. For the record, could you please state your full name, your current title, and your relationship to the aircraft involved in the April 17th event?

A: Yeah, sure. Mark Thomas Henderson. I’m a Senior Maintenance Inspector with Southwest Airlines. I’ve been with the company for, uh, about twenty-two years now, mostly working out of our Baltimore heavy maintenance base. On the seventeenth, I was actually deadheading on Flight 1380. I was scheduled to report to a structural repair team in Baltimore, so I was riding in the cabin as a non-revenue passenger. Seat 14A, left side, just forward of the wing.

Q: Can you walk me through the pre-flight and initial climb? Did you notice anything unusual before the event occurred?

A: Not really. I mean, it was a pretty standard morning. Boarding was on time, pushback was around 10:30, maybe 10:35 local time. I remember the engines spooling up normally. No weird vibrations, no unusual smells, no abnormal EGT indications on the overhead panel—I was just casually watching out of habit. We climbed out of LaGuardia, and I was… I had my laptop open, reviewing some work orders for a different tail number. We leveled off at, I think it was flight level three-two-five. Thirty-two thousand, five hundred feet. Everything was smooth. The cabin was quiet, just the usual white noise. I’d say we were in cruise for maybe forty, forty-five minutes before it happened.

Q: Describe what happened next. What did you see, hear, or feel?

A: Okay. It was… I’d say about 10:42, maybe 10:43 Eastern. I was looking at a maintenance log on my screen when I heard this… this massive bang. Not like a tire blowout or a door slam. It was deeper. Like a cannon shot, honestly. Right outside my window. The whole airframe shuddered. I mean, violently. My coffee cup just… it jumped off the tray table and hit the floor. Then, immediately after, there was this loud rushing sound. Wind. And the cabin pressure just dropped. My ears popped hard, and I felt that sudden, sharp cold. I looked out the window and—uh—there was a hole. A jagged opening where the window used to be. I could see the sky, and there was… there was a passenger in the row ahead, 13A, partially pulled toward the opening. It was chaotic. People were screaming, oxygen masks dropped, the whole thing. I unbuckled, moved toward the aisle, but the flight attendants were already moving. They were shouting, “Heads down, stay down!” I remember the smell of ozone and… and something metallic. Like burnt wiring and hydraulic fluid.

Q: How did the flight crew handle the emergency descent and subsequent landing?

A: The pilots did exactly what they’re trained to do. We banked hard to the right, I think, to get away from the left side and reduce the pressure differential on the damaged fuselage. The descent was steep. I could feel the G-forces pushing me into the seatbelt. We were losing altitude fast. I’d say we were down to maybe ten thousand feet in under five minutes. The captain came on the PA, voice was calm but firm, said we were diverting to Philadelphia. The landing was… rough, but controlled. We touched down around 11:15, maybe 11:18. Brakes were hot, I could smell them through the floor. We taxied to the gate, emergency vehicles were already there.

Q: Once on the ground, did you conduct or observe any initial inspections?

A: Yeah. As soon as the aircraft was secured, the passengers were deplaned, and the fire department gave the all-clear, I coordinated with the local Southwest maintenance team. I put on my high-vis and went out to the left side. The damage was… extensive. The engine cowling was completely gone. Fan blades were missing, fractured. The nacelle was shredded. Debris had impacted the fuselage right around the forward cabin windows. I could see the structural tear. It was a classic uncontained failure. I started documenting the damage, taking photos, noting the serial numbers on the remaining hardware, and checking for secondary damage along the wing root and empennage.

Q: In your experience, how does this type of failure relate to current certification and maintenance standards?

A: Well, it’s… it’s a tough one. The aircraft is a 737-700, so it’s certified under 14 CFR Part 25. The structural integrity requirements are strict, but an uncontained engine failure is one of those worst-case scenarios they design for. Specifically, 14 CFR 25.783 deals with fuselage doors and pressure boundaries, and the window frame… it held, mostly, but the debris impact compromised the seal. The rapid decompression was exactly what the regulation anticipates, but the localized damage was severe. We’ve been running these CFM56-7B engines for years. I know people talk about the newer LEAP-1B units on the MAX series, but the inspection intervals and fatigue monitoring are different. The LEAP-1B has different blade retention designs, but the fundamental physics of a fan blade separation… it’s still a high-energy event. You can’t completely eliminate the risk, you just manage it.

Q: Were there any specific maintenance directives or fuel system evaluations that came to mind during your initial assessment?

A: Yeah, actually. When I was checking the wing root area for secondary damage, I was thinking about SFAR 88. You know, the fuel tank system fault tolerance evaluation. Even though this was an engine event, debris can travel aft, and we had to make sure there was no compromise to the fuel lines or the center tank. We ran a full leak check. No issues, but it’s protocol. And, uh, I know Southwest operates under Part 121, but I was also thinking about how Part 135 operators handle similar emergency procedures. The response times, the maintenance release criteria… it’s all interconnected. We had to coordinate with Atlas Air’s MRO team for some of the heavy structural NDT work, since they have the specialized equipment for composite and aluminum fatigue analysis. They’re usually cargo, but their engineering division has the right tooling for this kind of impact mapping.

Q: You mentioned the window frame held. Can you elaborate on the failure sequence as you observed it?

A: Right. So, the outer pane shattered. The middle pane… it cracked but didn’t fully fail. The inner pane held. That’s the design. But the debris impact… it wasn’t just pressure. It was kinetic. A piece of the fan blade or the containment ring came through. It struck the fuselage skin, then the window frame. The rapid decompression pulled the passenger toward the opening. I mean, it was… it was tragic. The flight attendants did everything they could. They tried to pull her back, but the pressure differential was too strong. Once we descended below ten thousand, the pressure equalized, and they were able to secure her. But… she didn’t make it.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add regarding the maintenance history or your observations?

A: Just that… I’ve inspected hundreds of these engines. The vibration monitoring, the borescope inspections, the oil analysis… it’s all there. But fatigue cracks can hide. Especially in the dovetail area. We follow the ADs, we follow the service bulletins. But sometimes… sometimes the metal just gives out. I hope the investigation looks at the full lifecycle. Not just the last inspection, but the whole history. Southwest has a solid program, but this… this is a reminder that we’re always learning.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Henderson. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.

A: Yeah, of course. I’m here. Just… let me know if you need the photos or the maintenance logs I pulled. I’ll send them over.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND COMPLIANCE DIVISION
MEMORANDUM

DATE: November 14, 2023
TO: Chief Inspector, Aircraft Certification Service (AIR-100)
FROM: Director, Flight Standards Service (AFS-1)
SUBJECT: REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE IMPLEMENTATION FOLLOWING UNCONTAINED ENGINE FAILURE EVENT
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA18MA071; Docket No. FAA-2018-0417; 14 CFR Parts 25, 121, and 135

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This memorandum constitutes the formal regulatory response and compliance assessment regarding the uncontained engine failure event that occurred on April 17, 2018, involving a Boeing 737-700, registered N772SW, operated by Southwest Airlines. The event is formally cataloged under National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Accident Number DCA18MA071. This document addresses compliance with applicable airworthiness directives, certification standards under 14 CFR Part 25, and operational maintenance requirements under 14 CFR Part 121 and 14 CFR Part 135. Reference is made to NTSB Safety Recommendations A-18-012 through A-18-015, and the subsequent issuance of Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2018-09-09. The scope of this review encompasses type certificate holder obligations, operator maintenance program adherence, and the regulatory oversight framework governing high-bypass turbofan engine containment and cabin pressurization integrity.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory framework governing transport category aircraft airworthiness is established under 14 CFR Part 25, specifically § 25.903 (Engines) and § 25.783 (Fuselage doors and windows), which mandate that engine components must be contained under foreseeable failure conditions and that cabin windows must withstand rapid decompression events without catastrophic structural compromise. The subject aircraft, certified under Type Certificate No. A16WE, operates under the continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) requirements of 14 CFR § 121.368. 

Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued multiple airworthiness directives addressing fan blade fatigue and containment ring integrity for the CFM International CFM56-7B engine family. However, the April 17, 2018, incident revealed latent inspection interval deficiencies and non-destructive testing (NDT) protocol limitations. Concurrently, the certification basis for next-generation high-bypass turbofan engines, including the LEAP-1B, has been evaluated under amended § 25.903(d) to ensure enhanced debris trajectory modeling and improved acoustic liner retention standards. 

Regulatory oversight extends to operators conducting commercial air transportation under 14 CFR Part 121, as well as charter and cargo operations governed by 14 CFR Part 135. While Southwest Airlines operates under Part 121, comparative analysis of maintenance program equivalency with Part 135 operators, such as Atlas Air, has been conducted to identify systemic gaps in engine health monitoring (EHM) data utilization and minimum equipment list (MMEL) deferral practices. Prior safety recommendations, including NTSB A-14-008, emphasized the necessity of harmonizing ultrasonic inspection intervals with actual fleet utilization rates, a directive that remains partially unimplemented across the affected operator base.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive audit of Southwest Airlines’ maintenance records, engineering orders, and FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) oversight documentation reveals partial compliance with the post-incident airworthiness directives. The operator’s CAMP was found to have incorporated the revised fan blade inspection intervals mandated by AD 2018-09-09; however, discrepancies were identified in the execution of phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) on in-service engines exceeding 30,000 flight cycles. The Chief Inspector’s field review confirmed that while the operator’s reliability program captured elevated vibration trends, the threshold for mandatory engine removal did not align with the updated risk-based maintenance criteria established under § 121.373.

Regulatory oversight actions included the issuance of a Letter of Investigation (LOI) to the operator’s Director of Maintenance, followed by a targeted ramp inspection program focusing on engine cowl fastener torque verification and window plug retention hardware. The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) determined that the original type certification basis for the 737-700 cabin window assembly, while compliant with § 25.783 at the time of issuance, did not account for secondary debris impact trajectories at cruise altitudes exceeding 30,000 feet. This gap necessitates a supplemental type certificate (STC) evaluation for reinforced window retention frames and revised MMEL provisions governing in-flight window damage deferrals.

Furthermore, the regulatory framework governing engine containment standards under 14 CFR Part 25 exhibits a structural deficiency in harmonizing certification requirements across engine families. The LEAP-1B, while not installed on the subject aircraft, shares common design philosophies regarding composite fan blade architecture and containment ring metallurgy. Cross-referencing failure mode analyses indicates that current § 25.903 compliance testing methodologies do not adequately simulate high-cycle fatigue propagation in titanium aluminide components. Comparative oversight of Part 135 operators, including Atlas Air, demonstrates that charter and cargo fleets operating under § 135.421 maintenance programs exhibit higher compliance rates with manufacturer service bulletins due to centralized engineering oversight, whereas Part 121 operators frequently defer critical inspections under MMEL provisions without adequate risk mitigation.

The Chief Inspector’s final determination concludes that the regulatory oversight framework requires enhanced integration of real-time EHM telemetry, mandatory third-party NDT validation, and revised airworthiness directive compliance tracking. The current reliance on operator self-reporting and periodic FAA surveillance is insufficient to address latent manufacturing defects and accelerated fatigue mechanisms in high-utilization turbofan engines.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings detailed herein, the following corrective actions and regulatory mandates are hereby established:

a. MANDATORY INSPECTION PROTOCOL REVISION: Southwest Airlines shall implement a revised engine inspection program within 90 days of this memorandum’s issuance, incorporating mandatory PAUT and eddy current testing at intervals not exceeding 15,000 flight cycles or 36 months, whichever occurs first. Compliance shall be documented in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.368(a)(2) and submitted to the assigned PMI for approval.

b. CABIN WINDOW STRUCTURAL REINFORCEMENT: The operator shall initiate a fleet-wide retrofit program for reinforced cabin window retention assemblies, utilizing FAA-approved STC data. All modifications must be completed within 24 months, with interim operational restrictions prohibiting flight above 30,000 feet for aircraft exhibiting window plug micro-fractures or seal degradation. MMEL Item 52-01 shall be amended to reflect zero-deferral status for structural window damage.

c. ENHANCED EHM INTEGRATION AND REPORTING: All operators subject to this directive shall integrate real-time engine health monitoring telemetry into their CAMP, with automated alert thresholds aligned with § 121.373 reliability program requirements. Data shall be transmitted to the FAA’s Aviation Safety Information Analysis and Sharing (ASIAS) system within 24 hours of exceedance events.

d. REGULATORY FRAMEWORK HARMONIZATION: The FAA shall initiate rulemaking under Docket No. FAA-2023-0891 to amend 14 CFR § 25.903(d), incorporating enhanced debris trajectory modeling and cross-family certification standards applicable to both legacy CFM56 and next-generation LEAP-1B engine architectures. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 180 days.

e. OVERSIGHT AND COMPLIANCE VERIFICATION: The Chief Inspector shall conduct biannual compliance audits of all affected operators, with particular emphasis on Part 121 and Part 135 maintenance program equivalency. Atlas Air and comparable operators shall be subject to parallel review to ensure uniform application of engine containment and cabin pressurization standards. Non-compliance shall result in immediate suspension of operating certificates pursuant to 14 CFR § 119.57.

This memorandum constitutes a binding regulatory directive. All referenced entities shall acknowledge receipt and submit a formal compliance plan to the Office of Aviation Safety within 30 calendar days. Failure to adhere to the prescribed timelines will result in enforcement action under 14 CFR Part 13 and 14 CFR § 121.373.
