HEADLINE: Southwest Flight Diverts After Engine Failure Claims One Life; Probe Underway

BYLINE: By Elena Rostova, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA —

A Southwest Airlines passenger jet bound for Dallas made an emergency landing in Philadelphia on Tuesday after a catastrophic engine failure tore through the aircraft’s fuselage, shattering a cabin window and killing one passenger. The Boeing 737-700, carrying 144 passengers and five crew members, was cruising at 32,500 feet when the left engine suffered an uncontained failure, triggering a rapid loss of cabin pressure and forcing pilots to execute a steep emergency descent.

The incident unfolded shortly after 11:30 a.m. EDT when a fractured fan blade from the aircraft’s left engine broke free, sending high-velocity debris into the wing and fuselage. The impact breached a passenger window, causing explosive decompression that partially pulled a woman from her seat. Flight attendants and fellow passengers managed to pull her back inside, but she later succumbed to her injuries. The crew successfully diverted the aircraft to Philadelphia International Airport, where emergency responders met the plane on the tarmac.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of a passenger and are cooperating fully with federal investigators,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson in a statement released Tuesday evening. “Our pilots and crew followed established emergency procedures, and we are providing all necessary support to the affected families.” Federal regulators and safety investigators have mobilized to the scene. The National Transportation Safety Board’s Lead Investigator confirmed that the probe will focus on the engine’s maintenance history and the structural integrity of the cowling. “The priority right now is securing the wreckage, interviewing the flight crew, and understanding the sequence of events that led to this uncontained failure,” the Lead Investigator said during a press briefing. “We are treating this with the utmost urgency.”

The aircraft, a 17-year-old Boeing 737-700, was operating Flight 1380 from New York’s LaGuardia Airport to Dallas Love Field. Southwest Airlines, the nation’s largest domestic carrier by passenger volume, operates an all-Boeing 737 fleet. The 737-700 variant, introduced in the late 1990s, is a workhorse of the airline’s short- to medium-haul network. The flight was equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B engines, a newer generation turbofan designed for improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions. The LEAP-1B powerplant has been widely adopted across the industry, though this particular aircraft had been retrofitted with the engine model during a recent maintenance cycle.

Aviation safety experts note that uncontained engine failures, while rare, typically stem from metal fatigue in rotating components. “When a fan blade fractures, it can act like a projectile,” explained Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor at a major research university. “The engine casing is designed to contain debris, but extreme stress or undetected micro-fractures can compromise that containment.” Investigators are examining whether maintenance protocols aligned with federal certification standards. The probe will scrutinize compliance with 14 CFR Part 21, which governs the design and certification of aircraft and engine components, as well as fuel system safety directives outlined in SFAR 88, a special federal aviation regulation designed to prevent ignition sources in fuel tanks. While the carrier operates under stricter commercial airline rules, investigators often cross-reference maintenance practices with standards applied to smaller operators under 14 CFR Part 135 to ensure comprehensive oversight across the aviation sector.

Survivors described a scene of sudden chaos followed by remarkable calm. “There was a loud bang, and then the window just blew out,” said passenger David Lin, 42, who was seated three rows behind the breach. “Oxygen masks dropped, and people were screaming, but the flight attendants were incredibly professional. They kept telling us to breathe and stay seated.” The deceased passenger, identified by family members as Jennifer Riordan, a 43-year-old mother of two from Albuquerque, New Mexico, was remembered as a devoted community volunteer. “She was the kind of person who always put others first,” her brother said in a brief statement. “We are heartbroken, but we are grateful to the crew and the passengers who tried to help her.”

Engine failures resulting in fatalities are exceptionally rare in modern commercial aviation. The last comparable incident involving a U.S. carrier occurred in 2016, when a Southwest Airlines 737-700 experienced a similar uncontained engine failure over the Gulf of Mexico, though that flight landed safely without injuries. The Federal Aviation Administration has mandated enhanced inspection protocols for older 737 engines following past incidents, requiring ultrasonic testing of fan blades at specific flight-hour intervals. Southwest Airlines has maintained a strong safety record over its five-decade history, though the carrier has faced scrutiny in recent years over maintenance scheduling and fleet aging.

The NTSB has dispatched a team of specialists to Philadelphia to examine the recovered engine components, review cockpit voice and flight data recorders, and analyze maintenance logs. The investigation is expected to take 12 to 18 months, with preliminary findings likely within weeks. Federal regulators in Washington, D.C., have already issued an emergency airworthiness directive requiring immediate inspections of similar engine models across the industry. “We will not rest until we understand exactly what happened and ensure it never happens again,” the Lead Investigator emphasized. “Safety is a continuous process, and this tragedy will drive meaningful improvements.” As the aviation community mourns, passengers and industry leaders alike are calling for renewed focus on aging aircraft maintenance and transparent safety reporting.

1. INTRODUCTION
This submission is presented by the Engineering, Maintenance, and Flight Operations Safety Division of Southwest Airlines, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative proceeding. Our role encompasses the technical evaluation of maintenance programs, airworthiness compliance, propulsion system performance, and operational safety management systems relevant to the April 17, 2018, event. The scope of this document is to provide an expert engineering and operational analysis of the uncontained engine failure, the subsequent fuselage and cabin window damage, and the rapid decompression sequence. We will address the factual record, evaluate the technical performance of the propulsion system and airframe structures, and present our position on contributing factors and recommended safety enhancements. This analysis is submitted in support of the Investigator-in-Charge’s ongoing review and for formal consideration during the forthcoming public hearing in Washington DC. Southwest Airlines remains fully committed to transparency, regulatory collaboration, and the continuous advancement of aviation safety through evidence-based engineering and proactive risk management.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines was conducting a scheduled revenue flight at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet when an uncontained failure occurred in the left engine, a CFM International LEAP-1B powerplant. The failure resulted in the release of high-energy debris that penetrated the left fuselage skin and compromised a passenger cabin window, initiating a rapid decompression event. Tragically, one passenger sustained fatal injuries. The flight crew executed an emergency descent and diversion in accordance with established procedures, ultimately landing safely at the nearest suitable airport.

The factual record, as documented in the NTSB docket (Exhibits 1-A through 4-C), includes the complete flight data recorder (FDR) parameters, maintenance logs, and post-incident structural assessments. Initial telemetry from the aircraft’s primary avionics bus indicated a peak cabin pressure differential of 8.6 psi at the moment of structural breach, while the independent environmental control system (ECS) transducer array logged a maximum of 8.9 psi — a discrepancy consistent with the known variance between high-frequency digital sampling and analog pressure transduction methodologies.

TO: All Maintenance Technicians, Quality Assurance Inspectors, Engineering Support Staff, Line Maintenance Supervisors
FROM: Director of Maintenance Quality & Airworthiness, MRO Division
DATE: May 02, 2018
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2018-0417: Enhanced Fan Blade & Cowling Retention Inspection Protocols Following Uncontained Engine Failure Event
REF: QA-2018-0417, WO-ENG-737-REV04, AMM 72-00-00, SB-737-72-1189

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate implementation of enhanced inspection, documentation, and release-to-service procedures for high-bypass turbofan engine fan blade retention systems, inlet cowl attachment points, and adjacent forward fuselage/window assemblies. The directive is issued to align our maintenance practices with updated industry safety recommendations and to mitigate secondary impact risks following the April 17, 2018, uncontained engine failure event.

BACKGROUND:
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine during cruise at 32,500 feet. Debris penetration resulted in rapid cabin decompression, structural damage to the fuselage, and a cabin window failure, resulting in one fatality. The NTSB Investigator-in-Charge has released preliminary findings indicating fatigue cracking in a fan blade root, compounded by potential inspection interval gaps and secondary containment vulnerabilities.

While our current fleet operates under mixed engine configurations, the failure mode underscores critical vulnerabilities in containment architecture and post-impact structural integrity. Our organization’s compliance posture must reflect the rigorous standards established under 14 CFR Part 21 for production quality and type certification, as well as 14 CFR Part 25 for transport category airworthiness and damage tolerance. Additionally, lessons from this event intersect with fuel system safety protocols previously emphasized under Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88), particularly regarding debris-induced ignition risks, fuel line routing, and post-impact tank integrity. As we prepare for upcoming LEAP-1B engine integration across our narrowbody transition program, we are proactively standardizing inspection rigor across all high-bypass platforms to ensure consistent airworthiness standards.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all scheduled and unscheduled maintenance involving engine fan sections, inlet cowls, and forward fuselage panels must adhere to the following revised protocols:

1. Enhanced NDT Requirements:
   - Perform eddy current inspection (ECI) on all CFM56-7B and LEAP-1B fan blade dovetail roots per AMM 72-21-00, Task 201.
   - Utilize phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) on cowl attachment lugs and hinge brackets. Reference internal procedure QA-NDT-088.
   - Any indication exceeding 0.015” depth or showing branching characteristics requires immediate blade/cowl removal and quarantine under Tag Q-2018-0417.

2. Torque & Hardware Verification:
   - Verify all cowl retention fasteners against torque values specified in WO-ENG-737-REV04, Table 4.
   - Replace any fastener showing galling, elongation, or missing witness marks. Use P/N 934-112-004 or approved equivalent.
   - Document torque verification in the aircraft technical log and upload to the digital maintenance tracking system (DMTS) under Work Order Category: ENG-RETENTION.

3. Fuselage & Window Assembly Inspection:
   - Conduct detailed visual and borescope inspection of forward fuselage skin panels (Stations 240–320) for micro-fractures, fastener hole elongation, or paint stress cracking.
   - Inspect cabin window retainers and sealant integrity per SB-737-53-0442. Pay particular attention to the aft lower quadrant of each window frame.
   - Any window assembly showing deformation, sealant delamination, or retainer clip fatigue must be replaced prior to next flight.

4. Documentation & Traceability:
   - All inspections must be signed off by a certified Airframe & Powerplant (A&P) technician and countersigned by the assigned Chief Inspector.
   - Attach high-resolution photographs of all inspected zones to the DMTS record.
   - Maintain a centralized log of all findings under QA-2018-0417 for trend analysis and regulatory reporting.

5. Cross-Fleet Alignment:
   - While this alert originates from a 737-700 event, the inspection parameters apply to all high-bypass turbofan installations in our maintenance program, including aircraft operated under contract for Atlas Air Inc.
   - Engineering has issued a temporary deviation waiver (TD-2018-052) for aircraft currently in heavy maintenance, provided enhanced inspection steps are completed before release to service.

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Line Maintenance Supervisors: Distribute this alert to all shift personnel by 0800 local on May 04, 2018. Conduct a 15-minute safety stand-down to review inspection changes and verify tooling availability.
- Quality Assurance Inspectors: Audit 100% of engine fan/cowl work orders completed between April 10 and May 10, 2018. Flag any non-compliant records for immediate corrective action and submit findings to the QA Manager.
- NDT Technicians: Complete updated calibration and procedure familiarization for ECI/PAUT equipment by May 07, 2018. Submit training completion certificates to the Training Department.
- Chief Inspectors: Assume final release authority for all aircraft undergoing fan blade or cowl retention work. No aircraft may be returned to service without dual sign-off and photographic documentation uploaded to DMTS.
- Engineering Support: Monitor inspection data trends and submit a preliminary compliance report to the Director of Maintenance by May 15, 2018. Coordinate with OEM technical representatives for any service bulletin updates and Part 25 damage tolerance revisions.

Failure to comply with these directives will result in immediate work stoppage, mandatory retraining, and potential disciplinary action per Company Policy HR-MAINT-09. All personnel are reminded that our primary obligation is to maintain airworthiness standards that exceed minimum regulatory thresholds.

Questions regarding procedure interpretation, tooling requirements, or documentation protocols should be directed to the Quality Assurance Help Desk (Ext. 4410) or the Engineering Support Desk (Ext. 4425).

SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines Co. experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. The event occurred approximately 75 nautical miles west of the departure airport, resulting in rapid cabin decompression, structural damage to the left fuselage, and one passenger fatality. This preliminary report outlines the initial factual data, establishes the investigative framework, and documents procedural determinations made during the early phase of the inquiry.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the flight crew reported a loud acoustic event followed by severe airframe vibration and a rapid loss of cabin pressure. Initial witness accounts from surviving passengers and cabin crew suggest that debris penetrated the left-side fuselage, compromising a window assembly and causing localized depressurization. The flight crew initiated an emergency descent and successfully diverted to the nearest suitable airport, where the aircraft landed without further incident. Weather conditions at the time of the event, as derived from preliminary meteorological data and pilot reports, were characterized by clear skies, light winds, and no significant convective activity along the route of flight.

Preliminary examination of the recovered airframe and powerplant components suggests that the left engine experienced a catastrophic structural failure. Initial visual inspection of the recovered fan cowl fragments and engine core components indicates that a portion of the rotating assembly separated, resulting in secondary impact damage to the adjacent fuselage skin and window frame. The National Transportation Safety Board has secured the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which have been downloaded and are undergoing preliminary data validation. Maintenance records for the aircraft and the affected powerplant are currently being compiled and reviewed. It should be noted that these observations are strictly preliminary and subject to revision as additional evidence is collected and analyzed.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The Lead Investigator has formally activated the following investigative groups: Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group has been tasked with collecting, preserving, and analyzing evidence within their respective disciplines. Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, Southwest Airlines Co., and the flight crew union. Additionally, technical advisors from Atlas Air have been invited to participate in a limited capacity to provide expertise regarding certain maintenance and operational procedures relevant to the fleet type.

All recovered debris has been cataloged, photographed, and secured at a designated NTSB facility. A detailed metallurgical and dimensional examination of the failed engine components is scheduled to commence upon completion of the initial documentation phase. The investigation will evaluate compliance with applicable airworthiness standards, including but not limited to 14 CFR Part 21, which governs certification procedures for products and parts, and 14 CFR 25.783, pertaining to fuselage door and window structural integrity under pressurization loads. Furthermore, the investigation will review historical maintenance practices and fuel system safety directives, with particular attention to the requirements outlined in SFAR 88, to determine whether any systemic factors may have contributed to the event.

The designated IIC has established a procedural framework to ensure the integrity of the investigative process. All group chairpersons have been instructed to maintain strict chain-of-custody protocols and to refrain from public speculation regarding the sequence of events. Preliminary data sharing with parties is being conducted under controlled conditions to preserve the independence of the investigation. At this stage, no definitive conclusions have been reached, and all findings remain subject to change as the inquiry progresses.

NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks include the completion of the metallurgical analysis of the fractured engine components, a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s maintenance history, and the reconstruction of the flight path using radar and FDR data. The Systems and Structures groups will conduct a detailed assessment of the fuselage damage, focusing on the failure mode of the compromised window assembly and the propagation of impact damage. The Human Performance group will continue to evaluate crew resource management, emergency checklist execution, and physiological factors associated with rapid decompression.

Additional interviews with maintenance personnel, dispatchers, and air traffic control staff are scheduled to be conducted in the near term. The investigation team will also coordinate with the engine manufacturer to review service bulletins, airworthiness directives, and fleet-wide inspection data relevant to the LEAP engine series. All analytical work will be cross-referenced against established certification standards and operational guidelines to identify any potential deviations or contributing factors.

The NTSB will issue subsequent updates as significant milestones are reached and as additional factual information becomes available. A public hearing may be convened at a later date to examine the technical evidence in detail, pending the completion of the laboratory analyses and group reports. Until the investigation is formally concluded, all preliminary observations should be considered provisional. The Board remains committed to a thorough, methodical, and transparent examination of the available evidence to support future safety recommendations.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at 1543:12 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), an uncontained engine failure occurred aboard a Boeing 737-700 during en route cruise flight. The event transpired at approximately 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL), over a geographic position of 39°42'11"N, 078°14'33"W, approximately 18 nautical miles west-southwest of the New River Valley Regional Airport (KBCB), Christiansburg, Virginia. The flight was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger route from LaGuardia Airport (KLGA), New York, to Dallas Love Field (KDAL), Texas. Following the failure, the flight crew initiated an emergency descent and diverted to Philadelphia International Airport (KPHL), Pennsylvania, where the aircraft landed without further incident at 1618:45 EDT.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-700, manufacturer serial number 32484, registered as N772SW. The aircraft was owned and operated by Southwest Airlines (SWA), a certificated air carrier conducting operations under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121. The aircraft was configured for 143 passenger seats and was equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines. The left engine, serial number 728491, was the subject of the uncontained failure. The right engine, serial number 728492, operated normally throughout the flight.

1.3 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted as a scheduled domestic passenger service in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart U. The flight crew operated under standard operating procedures (SOPs) established by the operator and approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The flight was cleared to cruise at flight level 320 (FL320) by air traffic control (ATC) at 1512:00 EDT. At 1543:12 EDT, the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) captured a sudden loss of left engine parameters, accompanied by a rapid cabin pressure differential increase. The flight crew declared an emergency, executed the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) engine failure and rapid decompression checklists, and initiated an emergency descent to 10,000 feet MSL. The aircraft was subsequently vectored to KPHL for an uneventful landing.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Experience
The captain, age 56, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1847293, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain also held a first-class medical certificate, issued on January 12, 2018, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 11,482 hours, with 8,912 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain completed the most recent line check on February 14, 2018, and was found to meet all proficiency standards. The captain's duty period on the day of the accident began at 0915:00 EDT, with a scheduled report time of 1030:00 EDT.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Experience
The first officer, age 43, held an ATP certificate, certificate number 2194857, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The first officer held a first-class medical certificate, issued on March 5, 2018, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 6,214 hours, with 3,891 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer completed the most recent recurrent training and proficiency check on January 22, 2018. The first officer's duty period began at 0915:00 EDT, with a scheduled report time of 1030:00 EDT.

2.3 Training Records and Recent Flight Experience
Both flight crew members completed the operator's mandated 12-month recurrent training cycle, which included simulator-based emergency procedures, rapid decompression scenarios, and uncontained engine failure drills. Training records indicate that both pilots successfully completed the most recent simulator session on March 18, 2018, with satisfactory performance in all evaluated maneuvers. The operator's training program complies with 14 CFR 121.409 and 14 CFR 121.411. Review of the crew's flight logs for the 90 days preceding the accident revealed 142 flight hours, 89 landings, and 112 takeoffs, all within normal operational parameters. No discrepancies, training deficiencies, or medical limitations were documented in either crew member's personnel file.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Airframe and Engine Specifications
The airframe was manufactured by The Boeing Company in 2003 and delivered to the operator on May 14, 2003. At the time of the accident, the aircraft had accumulated 56,842 total flight hours and 31,204 total flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a dual-channel digital flight control system, a dual-pack environmental control system (ECS), and a standard cabin pressurization system compliant with 14 CFR 25.841. The left engine, a CFM International LEAP-1B, was installed on the aircraft on November 3, 2016. The engine had accumulated 18,412 flight hours and 11,089 flight cycles since new. The engine was equipped with a full-authority digital engine control (FADEC) system, a dual-channel vibration monitoring system, and a standard oil system with magnetic chip detectors.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.369. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (D-check) was completed on August 12, 2017, at 54,112 flight hours. The left engine underwent a performance restoration shop visit on September 28, 2017, at 16,890 flight hours. All applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) were documented as complied with in the aircraft maintenance logbook. Notably, AD 2016-18-09, pertaining to high-pressure turbine (HPT) blade inspection intervals, was complied with on October 14, 2017. AD 2017-22-11, addressing fuel system wiring harness routing, was complied with on November 30, 2017. The operator's maintenance tracking system indicated no deferred maintenance items or open work orders related to the left engine or cabin pressurization system at the time of the accident.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The cabin pressurization system utilized two outflow valves, a cabin pressure controller, and dual safety relief valves. The system was designed to maintain a maximum cabin altitude of 8,000 feet at a cruise altitude of 41,000 feet, per 14 CFR 25.841(a). The left engine's fan cowl, thrust reverser, and nacelle were constructed of aluminum alloy and composite materials. The engine's fan blade retention system utilized a dovetail slot design with a titanium alloy fan disk. The aircraft's emergency oxygen system consisted of chemical oxygen generators located above each passenger seat row, with a deployment threshold of 14,000 feet cabin altitude. The flight data acquisition unit (FDAU) and quick access recorder (QAR) were functioning normally and recorded all relevant parameters at 1-second intervals.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
At the time of the accident, a high-pressure system was centered over the Mid-Atlantic region, resulting in stable atmospheric conditions. Surface observations indicated clear skies, light winds from the northwest at 8 knots, and a temperature of 18°C. The tropopause was located at approximately 38,000 feet MSL. No convective activity, turbulence, or icing conditions were reported along the flight path. The National Weather Service (NWS) Aviation Weather Center issued no significant meteorological information (SIGMETs) or convective SIGMETs for the region during the flight's en route phase.

4.2 METAR/TAF Data and Pilot Reports
The nearest METAR reporting station, KBCB, recorded the following conditions at 1553 EDT: wind 310° at 7 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, sky clear, temperature 17°C, dew point 4°C, altimeter 30.12 inHg. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KPHL, valid from 1200 to 1800 EDT, forecasted wind 280° at 10 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, and scattered clouds at 5,000 feet. Pilot reports (PIREPs) along the route indicated smooth air, no turbulence, and standard temperature deviations of +1°C at FL320. No reports of volcanic ash, sand, or foreign object debris (FOD) were documented in the ATC or operator communication logs.

4.3 Atmospheric Conditions at Altitude
At 32,500 feet MSL, the standard atmospheric temperature was -48.5°C. The actual temperature recorded by the aircraft's total air temperature (TAT) probe was -47.2°C. The pressure altitude was 32,480 feet, with a static pressure of 26.8 kPa. The wind at cruise altitude was from 290° at 42 knots, with a temperature deviation of +1.3°C from the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA). The aircraft's true airspeed (TAS) was 448 knots, with a ground speed of 482 knots. The atmospheric conditions were within normal operational limits and did not contribute to the engine failure or subsequent decompression event.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The primary wreckage remained intact and landed under controlled conditions at KPHL. Secondary debris from the uncontained engine failure was recovered from a 12-square-mile area spanning portions of Lancaster and Berks Counties, Pennsylvania. Debris recovery teams documented 47 distinct fragments, including fan blade segments, cowl panel sections, and engine mount hardware. The largest recovered fragment, a 14.2-pound section of the left fan cowl, was located at 40°11'08"N, 076°02'44"W. All recovered debris was cataloged, photographed, and transported to the NTSB headquarters in Washington, D.C., for metallurgical and dimensional analysis. No ground casualties or property damage were reported.

5.2 Fuselage and Cabin Window Examination
Post-flight inspection revealed a 14-inch by 18-inch breach in the left fuselage skin, located at station 420, stringer 12, directly aft of the left engine pylon. The breach exhibited outward deformation consistent with high-velocity internal pressure release. The adjacent cabin window, designated as row 14, window A, was completely dislodged from its frame. The window frame exhibited plastic deformation and fastener shear, indicating a sudden pressure differential exceeding 8.5 psi. The cabin interior showed evidence of rapid decompression, including deployed passenger oxygen masks, displaced overhead bin latches, and minor interior panel separation. The fuselage structure surrounding the breach was examined for fatigue cracking, corrosion, and manufacturing defects. No pre-existing structural anomalies were identified.

5.3 Engine Component Examination Findings
The left engine was removed from the aircraft and transported to a certified engine test facility for teardown and inspection. Examination revealed a fatigue crack originating at the root of the number 13 fan blade, propagating through the dovetail attachment region. The crack exhibited beach marks consistent with high-cycle fatigue, with an estimated initiation point at approximately 14,200 flight cycles. The fan disk exhibited no evidence of overspeed or thermal distress. The high-pressure compressor, combustor, and turbine sections were intact and showed normal wear patterns. The oil system contained no abnormal metallic debris, and the magnetic chip detectors were clean. The FADEC recorded a sudden N1 vibration spike to 4.8 inches per second, followed by a rapid decay in N1, N2, and EGT parameters. The engine's containment ring, designed to meet 14 CFR 33.94 requirements, was breached by the fan blade fragment, resulting in the uncontained release.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Southwest Airlines maintains a comprehensive safety management system (SMS) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.373 and FAA Advisory Circular 120-92B. The operator's engine health monitoring (EHM) program utilizes real-time data streaming from the aircraft's ACARS system to track vibration trends, oil consumption, and performance degradation. At the time of the accident, the EHM system had not generated any maintenance alerts for the left engine. The operator's cabin crew training program includes rapid decompression response, emergency oxygen deployment, and passenger management procedures. The flight crew's adherence to the QRH and standard callouts was documented in the CVR transcript and FDR data. The operator's maintenance control center (MCC) was notified of the event at 1545:30 EDT and coordinated with ATC and ground services for the diversion.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
A review of the National Transportation Safety Board's accident database and the FAA's Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) system identified three prior uncontained engine failure events involving Boeing 737 series aircraft equipped with LEAP-1B engines between 2015 and 2017. In each case, the failures were attributed to high-cycle fatigue in the fan blade root region, with no prior EHM alerts. The manufacturer issued a service bulletin (SB) in 2016 recommending enhanced ultrasonic inspection intervals for fan blades exceeding 10,000 cycles. The operator incorporated the SB into its maintenance program on January 15, 2017. Additionally, a 2014 incident involving a different engine model resulted in a similar cabin window failure and rapid decompression, prompting the FAA to issue a special airworthiness information bulletin (SAIB) regarding window frame reinforcement and inspection criteria.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The aircraft and engine were certified under 14 CFR Part 25 and 14 CFR Part 33, respectively. The uncontained engine failure event was evaluated against 14 CFR 33.94, which requires engine containment to prevent hazardous debris release. The cabin pressurization system was evaluated against 14 CFR 25.841, which mandates rapid decompression survivability and emergency oxygen deployment. The fuel system wiring and tank ignition prevention measures were reviewed for compliance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88), which addresses fuel tank flammability reduction and wiring integrity. The operator's maintenance program was audited for compliance with 14 CFR 121.369 and 14 CFR 43.13. All documentation, including maintenance logs, training records, and EHM data, was secured and archived at the NTSB headquarters for further analysis. The investigation remains ongoing, with additional metallurgical testing, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling, and regulatory compliance reviews scheduled for completion in subsequent phases.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the technical examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the NTSB Powerplants and Structures Group in support of the investigation into the in-flight uncontained engine failure and subsequent rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737-700, registration N772SW, operated by Southwest Airlines (SWA). The examination was initiated under the authority of the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and coordinated with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the engine manufacturer.

The scope of this examination encompassed the left engine (CFM International CFM56-7B26, serial number 683042), recovered fan blade fragments, the forward fuselage skin panel (station 420 to 480, left side), the No. 14 cabin window assembly, the engine inlet cowl, and the associated flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) parameters. Physical examinations were conducted between April 20 and April 26, 2018, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the engine teardown facility in Cincinnati, Ohio. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) guidelines, ASTM E140 standard practices for hardness testing, and SAE ARP 4102 for fracture surface documentation.

The primary objectives of this specialist examination were to: (1) characterize the failure mode and crack propagation history of the fractured fan blade; (2) quantify the structural response of the fuselage skin and window frame to high-velocity debris impact; (3) correlate physical damage with recorded flight parameters; and (4) document material properties and manufacturing characteristics relative to applicable certification and maintenance standards. All findings presented herein are strictly factual and derived from direct observation, laboratory testing, and recorded data analysis.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft was equipped with two CFM56-7B26 high-bypass turbofan engines, each rated at 26,300 lbf of thrust. The left engine had accumulated 30,115 flight hours and 21,485 flight cycles at the time of the event. The engine was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program compliant with 14 CFR part 121, with the most recent borescope inspection performed 1,240 cycles prior to the occurrence. The fan blade assembly consisted of 24 titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V, AMS 4911) wide-chord blades, each secured via a dovetail root interface to the titanium fan disk. The engine nacelle incorporated a Kevlar-reinforced composite containment ring designed to retain blade fragments in accordance with 14 CFR 33.94.

The certification basis for the airframe and engine installation was established under Part 21, with specific structural integrity requirements governed by 14 CFR 25.783 for fuselage doors, windows, and emergency exits. The cabin window assembly at station 460, left side, was a dual-pane acrylic configuration with an outer structural pane (0.250 inches thick) and an inner scratch pane (0.125 inches thick), mounted in an aluminum alloy (7075-T6) frame. The design pressure differential limit for the 737-700 fuselage is 8.6 PSI at maximum operating altitude.

For comparative design context, the investigation reviewed fatigue life methodologies and containment architectures utilized in the CFM LEAP-1B powerplant, which employs a 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan blade and a titanium containment ring. While the LEAP-1B was not installed on the subject aircraft, its certification data under Title 14 CFR Part 21 provided a baseline for evaluating crack initiation thresholds, damage tolerance analysis, and inspection interval optimization. Maintenance records indicated that the subject engine had undergone a performance restoration at an Atlas Air Worldwide Holdings MRO facility in 2014, where fan blade tip clearances were reset to 0.045 inches and vibration trim balancing was performed to 0.15 inches per second (ips).

The operational history of the specific unit showed no recorded exceedances of N1 vibration limits, EGT margins, or oil consumption thresholds. The engine was operated within the approved flight envelope, with cruise parameters typically maintained at 32,000 to 35,000 ft MSL, Mach 0.74 to 0.78, and N1 rotation speeds of 88% to 92%.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered fan blade fragments revealed a complete separation of the No. 13 fan blade at the dovetail root. The fracture surface exhibited distinct fatigue crack initiation at the forward fillet radius, approximately 0.12 inches below the blade platform. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 500x magnification identified a primary crack origin measuring 0.008 inches in depth, characterized by intergranular cracking and localized fretting damage. The fatigue propagation zone extended 0.85 inches circumferentially along the dovetail flank, displaying classic beach marks with an average striation spacing of 0.0004 inches per cycle. The final fast fracture region occupied approximately 35% of the cross-sectional area, exhibiting ductile dimple rupture consistent with overload failure at rotational speeds exceeding 3,200 RPM.

Hardness testing per ASTM E18 yielded an average Rockwell C value of 34.2 HRC across the blade root, within the manufacturer's specified range of 32.0 to 36.0 HRC. Chemical analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed Ti-6Al-4V composition (6.12% Al, 4.08% V, 0.18% Fe, 0.12% O, balance Ti), compliant with AMS 4911. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD), corrosion, or manufacturing defects was identified in the parent material. However, metallographic cross-sectioning revealed localized microstructural deformation at the crack initiation site, with grain elongation and slip band formation indicative of high-cycle fatigue (HCF) under resonant vibratory loading.

The engine inlet cowl exhibited a 14.2-inch longitudinal tear at station 445, left side, with outward deformation of 1.8 inches. The Kevlar containment ring showed localized delamination and fiber breakage over a 22-degree arc, confirming that the blade fragment exceeded the designed containment energy threshold of 1,250 ft-lbs. Debris trajectory analysis, based on impact crater morphology and paint transfer patterns, indicated a primary fragment ejection angle of 18 degrees aft and 12 degrees outboard relative to the engine centerline.

Fuselage skin examination revealed a 9.4-inch by 3.1-inch penetration at station 462, left side, with inward buckling of the surrounding 0.050-inch 2024-T3 aluminum skin. The No. 14 cabin window outer pane was completely dislodged, with the aluminum mounting frame exhibiting plastic deformation of 0.42 inches and fastener shear failure at three of four attachment points. The inner scratch pane remained intact but displayed radial cracking originating from the lower-left quadrant. Pressure differential calculations, derived from cabin altitude decay rates and structural deformation, indicated a peak transient load of 11.3 PSI during the decompression event, exceeding the static design limit by 31%.

All examinations were conducted under the direct oversight of the Chief Inspector, who verified chain-of-custody documentation, calibrated measurement equipment, and adherence to ISO/IEC 17025 laboratory standards. Photographic documentation (NTSB Photo Log 2018-04-20 through 2018-04-26) includes macro and micro fracture surface imaging, dimensional mapping of impact zones, and material sampling locations.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters were extracted from the solid-state memory unit and decoded using standard ARINC 717 protocols. The data stream was sampled at 1 Hz for engine parameters and 4 Hz for flight control and cabin pressure variables. Time synchronization with the CVR was achieved using the 1000 Hz cockpit area microphone tone and UTC timecode alignment.

At 14:43:22.4 UTC, the FDR recorded a sudden N1 vibration increase from 0.18 ips to 4.2 ips, exceeding the 1.0 ips caution threshold. Simultaneously, the left engine N1 speed decayed from 89.4% to 76.1% within 1.8 seconds, while N2 remained stable at 94.2%. Exhaust gas temperature (EGT) on the left engine rose by 42°C above baseline, indicating disrupted airflow and compressor stall onset. The right engine parameters remained nominal, with N1 at 88.9% and EGT within ±3°C of the predicted cruise value.

Cabin pressure data indicated a differential pressure of 8.4 PSI at 14:43:24.1 UTC, consistent with cruise at 32,500 ft MSL. At 14:43:25.8 UTC, the cabin altitude parameter transitioned from 6,800 ft to 18,200 ft within 0.9 seconds, corresponding to a pressure decay rate of 1.2 PSI/sec. The rapid decompression event triggered the cabin altitude warning horn and automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks at 14:43:26.5 UTC. The aircraft initiated an emergency descent, reaching 10,000 ft MSL at 14:48:12 UTC, with a maximum descent rate of 4,800 ft/min and indicated airspeed of 310 knots.

Comparison with normal operational parameters revealed that the N1 vibration spike preceded the structural failure by approximately 1.2 seconds, consistent with the time required for a fatigue-cracked blade to reach critical stress intensity factor (K_IC) under centrifugal loading. The recorded EGT spread of 42°C exceeded the manufacturer's maximum allowable limit of 25°C, confirming asymmetric combustion and airflow disruption. The cabin pressure decay rate of 1.2 PSI/sec was 24 times greater than the nominal leakage rate of 0.05 PSI/sec, validating the complete loss of the outer window pane and fuselage skin penetration.

The CVR captured a sharp acoustic transient at 14:43:23.1 UTC, followed by crew communication referencing "engine failure," "decompression," and "emergency descent." The audio spectrum analysis showed a broadband frequency spike between 800 Hz and 2,400 Hz, consistent with high-velocity debris impact and aerodynamic noise from the open fuselage breach.

Data correlation with maintenance records confirmed that the last fan blade eddy current inspection was performed 1,240 cycles prior, with no anomalies reported. The inspection interval was compliant with the engine manufacturer's service bulletin and 14 CFR part 121 maintenance requirements. However, the fatigue crack propagation rate (da/dN) calculated from the striation spacing and stress intensity factor (ΔK = 18.4 ksi√in) indicated that the crack would have reached critical length within 800 to 1,000 cycles under normal cruise loading conditions.

5. SUMMARY

The technical examination and data analysis yielded the following factual findings:

1. The left engine experienced an uncontained failure due to the complete separation of the No. 13 fan blade at the dovetail root. The failure originated from a high-cycle fatigue crack that initiated at the forward fillet radius and propagated 0.85 inches circumferentially before reaching critical stress intensity.

2. Metallurgical analysis confirmed the blade material met Ti-6Al-4V specifications (AMS 4911) with no evidence of manufacturing defects, corrosion, or foreign object damage. The fatigue crack initiation site exhibited localized fretting and intergranular cracking consistent with resonant vibratory loading.

3. The ejected blade fragment exceeded the designed containment energy threshold of the Kevlar-reinforced ring, resulting in a 14.2-inch tear in the inlet cowl and outward deformation of 1.8 inches. Debris trajectory analysis indicated an ejection angle of 18 degrees aft and 12 degrees outboard.

4. The fuselage skin at station 462 sustained a 9.4-inch by 3.1-inch penetration, with inward buckling of the 0.050-inch 2024-T3 aluminum panel. The No. 14 cabin window outer pane was dislodged, and the aluminum mounting frame exhibited 0.42 inches of plastic deformation and fastener shear failure.

5. FDR data recorded an N1 vibration increase from 0.18 ips to 4.2 ips, followed by a 13.3% N1 speed decay and a 42°C EGT rise within 1.8 seconds. Cabin pressure differential dropped from 8.4 PSI to near ambient within 0.9 seconds, corresponding to a decay rate of 1.2 PSI/sec.

6. The aircraft initiated an emergency descent from 32,500 ft MSL to 10,000 ft MSL, with a maximum descent rate of 4,800 ft/min and indicated airspeed of 310 knots. The rapid decompression event triggered automatic oxygen mask deployment and cabin altitude warnings.

7. Maintenance records indicated compliance with 14 CFR part 121 inspection intervals, with the last fan blade eddy current inspection performed 1,240 cycles prior. Fatigue crack growth calculations suggest the crack would have reached critical length within 800 to 1,000 cycles under normal cruise loading conditions.

All findings are based on direct physical examination, laboratory testing, and recorded flight data analysis. No operational or maintenance exceedances were identified in the available records. The structural response of the fuselage and window assembly to high-velocity debris impact was consistent with the design parameters established under 14 CFR 25.783 and Part 21 certification requirements.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, SENIOR MAINTENANCE CONTROLLER
Date: May 2, 2018
Time: 10:15 AM EDT
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Ashburn, Virginia
Interviewer: Investigator J. Reynolds, NTSB
Subject: April 17, 2018, Boeing 737-700 Uncontained Engine Failure

[Recorder starts]

Q: Mr. Thorne, thank you for coming in today. For the record, please state your full name, your current position, and your role relative to the April 17th incident.

A: Marcus Thorne. I’m a Senior Maintenance Controller with Atlas Air. I was… I was on shift in the Maintenance Control Center that morning, so I was the primary technical liaison for the flight. I was monitoring the aircraft’s health data in real-time, and once the crew declared the emergency, I became their direct line to engineering and dispatch.

Q: Walk me through what you observed from the moment the event began. Try to be as specific as you can with times and sequence.

A: Okay. Let me pull up my shift log… right. It was approximately 10:43 AM Eastern. The aircraft was at cruise, thirty-six thousand feet, I believe. We had the standard ACARS telemetry streaming to our secondary monitors. Everything was nominal until… until it wasn’t. We got a sudden, sharp spike in EGT on the number one engine, followed almost instantly by a high-vibration alert. Then the data just… it fragmented. Not a total loss, but the parameters started oscillating wildly. I remember thinking it was a faulty sensor at first, maybe a wiring harness issue, but then the VHF radio keyed up. The captain’s voice came through, and it was… strained. He said, “We’ve got a loud bang, left side, rapid decompression, we’re descending.” I could hear the wind noise in the background, just this… this roaring, tearing sound. It was hard to make out the exact words, but the urgency was clear.

Q: What was your immediate response, and how did the communications progress?

A: I immediately acknowledged, asked for their intentions, and started pulling up the maintenance logs. They were already turning toward the nearest suitable, which was… Philadelphia, I think. Or wait, no, it was PHL. Right. I told them to secure the engine, run the QRH checklist. They were doing it, but the cabin pressure was dropping fast. I could hear the oxygen masks deploying over the open mic. There was… there was a lot of background commotion. Shouting, but controlled. The first officer was reading off the checklist, but his voice was shaking a little. I stayed on the line, feeding them any data I could pull from the telemetry. We lost the left engine parameters completely after about… maybe two minutes. The right engine was holding steady. I was watching the altitude tape drop. They were descending at a steep rate, probably around six thousand feet per minute.

Q: You mentioned the left engine. Can you confirm the powerplant type installed on that airframe?

A: Yeah. It was a CFM LEAP-1B. Or, well, the full designation is the CFM International LEAP-1B. We’d had it on wing for about… I want to say four thousand cycles. It’s a newer design, high bypass, but we’d seen some minor oil consumption trends in the fleet. Nothing that would’ve grounded it, obviously. But after the failure, when we got the preliminary teardown reports, it was clear we had an uncontained event. The fan blade… it separated. Took out the cowl, sent shrapnel through the fuselage.

Q: The debris struck a cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and a fatality. Were you aware of the structural damage as it was happening?

A: Not in real-time, no. We didn’t have cabin pressure sensors that granular. But when the crew reported the window was… compromised, I knew we were looking at a serious breach. The decompression would’ve been violent. I’ve read the reports since, obviously. The window frame failed, the panel blew out. It’s… it’s a lot to process. The regulations, 14 CFR Part 25, they have specific requirements for rapid decompression and window integrity. I mean, Part 25.251 and the subsequent sections on structural loads. The design is supposed to contain that kind of failure, or at least mitigate it. But when you get a high-energy fragment from an uncontained engine… it’s a different ballgame. The certification standards account for bird strikes, hail, maybe a tire burst, but a fan blade fragment at cruise Mach… it’s extreme.

Q: Let’s go back to the timeline. Approximately how long from the initial alert to landing?

A: From the first ACARS alert to wheels down… I’d say about… twelve, maybe thirteen minutes. The descent was steep. They were at thirty-two-five, dropped to ten thousand, then down to the pattern. I was tracking their altitude and speed on the secondary display. The crew handled it… professionally. I mean, under those conditions, with the noise, the decompression, the… the loss of a passenger… it’s remarkable they got it on the ground safely.

Q: Did you have any direct communication with the cabin crew or passengers?

A: No, just the flight deck. The interphone was… well, it was open to the cockpit, but the cabin was chaotic. I could hear the flight attendants giving commands, “Heads down, stay down,” that sort of thing. But the wind noise was overwhelming. After they landed, the radio went quiet for a bit. Then the captain came back on, voice completely flat, just said, “We’re on the ground. Emergency services are rolling. We have a medical emergency in the cabin.” That’s when I knew it was… it was bad. I handed off to the emergency response team and started compiling the maintenance data for the NTSB and the FAA.

Q: In your professional opinion, what factors contributed to the severity of the fuselage damage?

A: It’s… it’s hard to say definitively without the metallurgy reports, but the trajectory of the debris is key. The LEAP-1B, like most modern high-bypass engines, has a lot of rotational energy. When that blade let go, it didn’t just fall out. It was ejected at a high angle, probably struck the inlet cowl, fragmented further, and then… it punched through the fuselage skin. The window frame is reinforced, obviously, but the impact point was right at the edge of the pane. The rapid decompression that followed… it’s a chain reaction. The pressure differential at thirty-two thousand feet is massive. Once that seal broke, the air rushed out, and the… the forces on the surrounding structure were extreme. I’ve reviewed the Part 25 compliance docs for that window assembly. It meets the static and fatigue requirements, but dynamic impact from engine debris… that’s outside the standard certification envelope.

Q: Were there any prior maintenance actions or service bulletins related to this engine or airframe that you were aware of?

A: Yeah, there were a couple. We’d complied with the latest CFM service letters regarding fan blade inspections. Ultrasonic testing, eddy current… the usual. Nothing came back as a reject. The engine had been on wing since… late 2016, I think. We’d done a borescope inspection maybe six months prior. Clean. So, it’s… it’s frustrating. You follow the manuals, you track the cycles, you do the checks, and then something like this happens. It’s a reminder that… well, that metal fatigue doesn’t always show up on a schedule.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record?

A: Just… I want to make sure the crew gets the credit they deserve. They were flying a damaged aircraft, dealing with a decompression, trying to keep the passengers calm, and they still executed a textbook emergency descent and landing. And… I don’t know. It’s heavy. We lost someone. A passenger. I keep thinking about the window, the noise, the… the suddenness of it. From a maintenance standpoint, we’ll review everything. The LEAP-1B teardown, the ACARS data, the Part 25 structural margins. But at the end of the day, it’s about making sure it doesn’t happen again. That’s… that’s all I’ve got.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification on the telemetry logs.

A: Yeah, of course. I’ll have the raw data files sent over by end of day.
