1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
- Reference: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-14-05, Amendment 39-19342; NTSB Safety Recommendation A-19-012 through A-19-015
- Docket No.: FAA-2018-0412; NTSB Accident No. DCA18MA071
- Date of Incident: April 17, 2018
- Subject Aircraft/Engine: Boeing 737-700 series, equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines
- Regulatory Framework: 14 CFR Part 21, 14 CFR Part 135, 14 CFR Part 25

2. BACKGROUND
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 aircraft operating under commercial passenger service experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine during cruise flight at Flight Level 325 (32,500 feet mean sea level). High-energy debris ejected from the engine nacelle penetrated the forward fuselage and compromised a passenger cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and the subsequent fatality of one occupant. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) initiated a major accident investigation under docket DCA18MA071, with preliminary findings indicating fatigue cracking in the fan blade retention system of the CFM International LEAP-1B powerplant.

The regulatory oversight of this incident intersects multiple statutory frameworks governing aircraft certification, continued airworthiness, and commercial operations. Under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart D, the Federal Aviation Administration establishes certification procedures for products and parts, including the issuance, amendment, and maintenance of type certificates (TC) and supplemental type certificates (STC). The LEAP-1B engine, certified under TC E00017EN, is subject to ongoing airworthiness directives and service bulletin compliance mandates. Concurrently, operators conducting commercial passenger transport under 14 CFR Part 135 must adhere to stringent maintenance, inspection, and operational requirements as delineated in Subpart E and Subpart J.

Historically, uncontained engine failures have prompted iterative regulatory responses, including the issuance of AD 2016-11-08 and subsequent revisions addressing high-cycle fatigue in turbofan fan blades. The NTSB, in its preliminary report, identified systemic gaps in the integration of manufacturer service information into operator maintenance programs, particularly for Part 135 certificate holders transitioning to higher-utilization fleet operations. Furthermore, the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions under 14 CFR 135.179 and 14 CFR 121.344 were scrutinized for their applicability to rapid decompression scenarios involving structural penetration. The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (AFS) have since coordinated a comprehensive review of the regulatory interface between Part 21 design approval holders and Part 135 operators to ensure continued airworthiness standards are uniformly enforced across the national airspace system.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive audit of Atlas Air Inc. (hereinafter “the Operator” or “AAI”) maintenance records, engineering directives, and compliance documentation reveals partial adherence to the applicable airworthiness mandates. While the Operator maintains a valid Part 135 operating certificate and has implemented the majority of mandatory service bulletins issued by the type certificate holder, discrepancies were identified in the tracking and execution of repetitive inspection intervals for high-cycle engine components. Specifically, the Operator’s reliability program, as required under 14 CFR 135.415, did not adequately correlate engine cycle accumulation data with the manufacturer’s recommended non-destructive testing (NDT) thresholds for the LEAP-1B fan blade retention system.

Regulatory oversight actions initiated by the FAA’s Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) and Principal Operations Inspector (POI) included a targeted ramp inspection, a review of the Operator’s Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP), and a formal audit of engineering change management procedures. The audit confirmed that while the Operator’s CAMP complies with 14 CFR 135.423, the integration of supplemental type certificate modifications related to cabin pressurization monitoring systems lacked synchronized compliance tracking. This administrative gap delayed the implementation of enhanced decompression warning protocols, which are critical for mitigating rapid decompression events.

Furthermore, the regulatory framework governing Part 135 operators exhibits structural limitations when applied to high-density, high-cycle commercial operations. Unlike Part 121 carriers, which are subject to mandatory reliability programs and enhanced structural inspection programs (ESIP) under 14 CFR 121.370, Part 135 operators are not uniformly required to implement equivalent fatigue monitoring regimes. The NTSB’s investigation highlighted that the current MMEL framework, as authorized under 14 CFR 135.179, does not explicitly address operational restrictions following uncontained engine debris penetration, thereby creating ambiguity in dispatch authority post-incident. Additionally, the interface between Part 21 design approval holders and Part 135 operators lacks a standardized mechanism for real-time dissemination of critical airworthiness data, resulting in delayed compliance with emergent ADs.

The FAA’s analysis concludes that while Atlas Air Inc. has demonstrated good-faith compliance with baseline regulatory requirements, systemic deficiencies in predictive maintenance analytics, STC integration tracking, and MMEL applicability for structural penetration events necessitate regulatory intervention. The absence of a harmonized fatigue monitoring standard across Part 135 and Part 121 operations represents a material gap in the continued airworthiness framework, particularly for aircraft operating at high altitudes with pressurized cabin configurations.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings detailed herein, the following corrective actions and regulatory recommendations are mandated to ensure compliance with 14 CFR Part 21, 14 CFR Part 135, and applicable airworthiness directives:

1. Enhanced Fatigue Monitoring and Inspection Regime: Atlas Air Inc. shall implement a mandatory high-cycle fatigue tracking program for all LEAP-1B powerplants within its fleet. This program must incorporate ultrasonic and eddy-current NDT inspections at intervals not exceeding 15,000 flight cycles, in accordance with the manufacturer’s latest service bulletin and 14 CFR 135.411. Compliance documentation shall be submitted to the FAA’s Principal Maintenance Inspector within 90 calendar days of this directive.

2. STC and MMEL Integration Audit: The Operator shall conduct a comprehensive audit of all supplemental type certificate modifications affecting cabin pressurization, structural integrity, and emergency decompression systems. The audit must verify that all STC installations are cross-referenced with the approved MMEL and that dispatch limitations are explicitly defined for post-penetration scenarios. A corrective action plan addressing any identified discrepancies shall be filed with the FAA within 60 calendar days.

3. Regulatory Harmonization and Part 135 Structural Inspection Mandate: The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (AFS) shall initiate a rulemaking action to amend 14 CFR Part 135, Subpart J, to require mandatory structural inspection programs for high-cycle commercial operations. This rulemaking shall align Part 135 fatigue monitoring requirements with the standards established under 14 CFR 121.370 and 14 CFR 25.783, ensuring uniform airworthiness oversight across commercial passenger transport categories. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published within 180 calendar days.

4. Real-Time Airworthiness Data Dissemination Protocol: The FAA shall establish a mandatory electronic reporting interface between Part 21 design approval holders and Part 135 operators to facilitate immediate transmission of critical service bulletins, AD compliance deadlines, and reliability data. This system shall be integrated into the existing Aviation Safety Information Analysis and Sharing (ASIAS) framework, with full operational capability required within 12 months.

5. Follow-Up Inspection and Compliance Verification: The FAA’s Principal Maintenance Inspector shall conduct a phased compliance verification audit at 90, 180, and 365 calendar days following the issuance of this directive. Each audit shall include a review of maintenance tracking logs, NDT inspection reports, STC compliance matrices, and MMEL dispatch records. Non-compliance with any mandated action shall result in immediate suspension of the affected aircraft’s airworthiness certificate and potential enforcement action under 14 CFR 13.19.

This regulatory response is issued in accordance with the FAA’s statutory authority under Title 49 of the United States Code, Subtitle VII, and the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative mandate under 49 U.S.C. § 1131. All referenced entities, including Atlas Air Inc., CFM International, and the Federal Aviation Administration, shall coordinate through established regulatory channels to ensure the continued airworthiness of the national airspace system. Compliance with the timelines and procedural requirements outlined herein is mandatory and subject to ongoing FAA oversight.

HEADLINE: Passenger Dies After Engine Failure Forces Emergency Landing on Cross-Country Flight

BYLINE: Marcus Thorne, Global Aviation Desk
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA —

A commercial flight carrying 149 people was forced into a steep emergency descent on Tuesday after a catastrophic engine failure at 32,500 feet, leaving one passenger dead and several others injured. The Boeing 737-700, en route from New York to Dallas, suffered an uncontained engine failure that sent high-velocity debris tearing through the fuselage and shattering a cabin window, triggering rapid decompression.

The incident unfolded shortly after 11:00 a.m. ET as the aircraft cruised over central Pennsylvania. A fractured fan blade in the left engine broke apart, sending metal fragments outward in what investigators call an uncontained failure—a rare event where engine components breach the protective titanium casing designed to contain them. The debris punctured the aircraft’s skin and blew out a passenger window, causing a sudden, violent drop in cabin pressure. Pilots immediately initiated an emergency descent, diverting to Philadelphia International Airport where the plane landed safely within 15 minutes. Emergency crews met the aircraft on the tarmac, and paramedics rushed aboard to treat passengers suffering from hypoxia, a condition caused by oxygen deprivation at high altitudes, and minor trauma.

“We are treating this as a major aviation accident,” said National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Chair Jennifer Homendy in a press briefing Tuesday evening. “Our investigators are already on site, and we will leave no stone unturned in determining the root cause.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an emergency airworthiness directive, grounding all aircraft with the same engine model pending ultrasonic inspections. “Safety is our absolute priority,” said an FAA spokesperson. “We are working closely with the manufacturer and operators to ensure every affected aircraft is thoroughly examined before returning to service.” A representative for the operating carrier confirmed the fatality and expressed condolences. “Our hearts are with the family of the passenger who lost their life, and with everyone on board who endured a terrifying experience,” said Atlas Air spokesperson David Chen. “We are fully cooperating with federal investigators and providing all necessary maintenance records.”

The aircraft, a 15-year-old Boeing 737-700, was being operated under a wet-lease agreement by Atlas Air, a major cargo and passenger charter provider. The flight was part of a scheduled commercial route, though AAI typically focuses on freight and military transport. The engines in question are CFM International models, but investigators are also reviewing broader certification standards that apply to modern high-bypass turbofans, including the newer LEAP-1B powerplant used on next-generation narrow-body jets. Maintenance protocols for these engines fall under strict Federal Aviation Regulations, specifically Part 21, which governs the certification of aircraft, engines, and propellers. Compliance with 14 CFR Part 21 ensures that components meet rigorous fatigue and stress testing before entering commercial service.

Aviation safety experts suggest metal fatigue is the most likely culprit. “Uncontained failures are exceptionally rare, but when they occur, they almost always trace back to microscopic cracks in the fan blades that grow over thousands of flight cycles,” said Dr. Marcus Lin, an aerospace engineering professor at MIT. “The cyclic stress of takeoff, cruise, and landing creates a harsh environment. If a blade isn’t caught during routine inspections, it can eventually fracture.” Lin cautioned against jumping to conclusions, noting that investigators will need to examine the recovered engine components, maintenance logs, and flight data recorder information before confirming a cause. “We’re looking at everything from manufacturing defects to maintenance intervals,” he added.

Inside the cabin, passengers described a scene of sudden chaos. “There was a deafening bang, and then the air just got sucked out,” said passenger Sarah Jenkins, 34, who was seated three rows from the damaged window. “Oxygen masks dropped, people were screaming, and the plane dropped so fast my stomach was in my throat. The flight attendants were incredible—they kept telling us to breathe and stay calm.” The deceased passenger, identified by family members as Jennifer Riordan, a 43-year-old mother of two from Albuquerque, was pulled partially through the broken window by the force of the decompression. Fellow passengers managed to pull her back into the cabin, but she was unresponsive. CPR was administered, but she was pronounced dead after the aircraft landed. “She was the most vibrant person I’ve ever known,” said her husband, Michael Riordan, speaking to reporters outside a local hospital. “We’re just devastated. We want to know why this happened and how it can be prevented.”

While commercial aviation remains one of the safest modes of transportation, uncontained engine failures have occurred before. In 2016, a similar incident involving a Boeing 737-700 resulted in an emergency landing in Pensacola, Florida, though no fatalities occurred. The 2018 event marks the first passenger death in U.S. commercial aviation since 2009. The NTSB has historically recommended more frequent ultrasonic inspections of engine fan blades following past incidents, and airlines have largely complied. The industry’s safety record remains strong, with fatal accidents occurring at a rate of less than one per several million departures.

The NTSB has secured the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, both of which are being transported to Washington, D.C., for analysis. Investigators are also cataloging debris recovered from the crash site and the aircraft’s exterior. The FAA’s emergency directive remains in effect, with airlines expected to complete initial inspections within 48 hours. “This is a developing situation,” Homendy said. “We will provide updates as our technical teams complete their preliminary findings. Our focus right now is on the families, the passengers, and ensuring the traveling public can fly with confidence.”

1. INTRODUCTION

Southwest Airlines Co. submits this technical analysis as the designated operator party to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative hearing regarding the April 17, 2018, in-flight uncontained engine failure. This document is prepared by the Operator’s Chief Engineer, Propulsion Systems & Airworthiness, in coordination with our Maintenance Reliability Directorate and Human Factors Engineering team. The submission outlines our technical position on the contributing factors to the event, evaluates the engineering and operational data recovered during the investigation, and presents evidence-based recommendations for systemic safety improvements.

The scope of this analysis encompasses three primary domains: (1) propulsion system fatigue mechanics and non-destructive inspection (NDI) efficacy, (2) airframe structural response to high-energy debris impact and rapid decompression dynamics, and (3) regulatory and maintenance program alignment under current airworthiness frameworks. Southwest Airlines Co. acknowledges the complexity of uncontained failure events, which inherently involve stochastic material degradation, inspection interval trade-offs, and multi-system interaction under extreme flight conditions. Our position is grounded in metallurgical evidence, flight data recorder (FDR) parameters, maintenance program records, and comparative industry data. We respectfully submit this analysis to assist the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) and the Board in developing a comprehensive understanding of the event and in formulating actionable safety recommendations.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On April 17, 2018, at approximately 10:43 local time, the subject Boeing 737-700 was operating in cruise flight at 32,500 feet when the left engine experienced an uncontained failure. Debris from the fan section penetrated the engine nacelle, impacted the forward fuselage, and breached a passenger cabin window. The resulting rapid decompression led to one passenger fatality and multiple injuries. The flight crew executed emergency descent and diversion procedures, landing safely at the nearest suitable airport.

Relevant docket materials reviewed in preparation of this submission include:
- Docket Item 3.1.4: Engine teardown and metallurgical examination report
- Docket Item 4.2.1: FDR and CVR data transcripts, including N1 vibration, EGT, and cabin pressure decay rates
- Docket Item 5.3.2: Maintenance program records, last scheduled ultrasonic inspection logs, and borescope imagery
- Docket Item 6.1.0: NDI procedure validation studies and OEM service bulletin compliance tracking

The subject engine, a CFM56-7B series high-bypass turbofan, had accumulated approximately 32,000 flight cycles and 41,000 flight hours at the time of failure. Maintenance records confirm compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) and manufacturer service bulletins (SBs) in effect at the time. The last scheduled fan blade ultrasonic inspection was performed 1,200 cycles prior to the event, within the approved interval. Metallurgical analysis identified a low-cycle fatigue (LCF) crack originating at the fan blade dovetail root, with evidence of progressive crack growth and final overload fracture.

While the failed unit belongs to the CFM56 family, the investigation’s broader implications for high-bypass turbofan maintenance, inspection sensitivity, and containment design extend to next-generation platforms, including the LEAP-1B engine architecture. The Operator recognizes that fatigue initiation mechanisms, NDI threshold limitations, and debris trajectory modeling are cross-cutting challenges that require harmonized industry responses. Furthermore, the event occurred under 14 CFR Part 121 operational parameters, which govern scheduled passenger carriers. The maintenance and training frameworks established under Part 121 differ in scope and frequency from those under 14 CFR part 135, particularly regarding predictive maintenance integration and advanced NDI deployment. This regulatory distinction is relevant when evaluating industry-wide safety recommendations.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The uncontained failure resulted from a confluence of material fatigue progression, inspection interval limitations, and localized structural vulnerability. Our technical assessment is organized into three analytical domains.

3.1 Propulsion Fatigue Mechanics and NDI Efficacy
Metallurgical examination (Docket Item 3.1.4) confirms that the initiating crack propagated from a subsurface inclusion at the fan blade dovetail radius. The crack growth rate followed a classic Paris Law trajectory, with accelerated propagation occurring after approximately 28,000 cycles. The final fracture surface exhibits characteristic beach marks transitioning to a ductile overload zone, consistent with high-stress rotational loading at cruise RPM.

The approved NDI protocol at the time relied on conventional ultrasonic testing (UT) and eddy current surface scanning. While these methods are effective for detecting surface-breaking cracks and volumetric flaws above 0.030 inches, they exhibit reduced sensitivity to early-stage subsurface LCF initiation, particularly in complex dovetail geometries where acoustic coupling and probe access are constrained. Our internal reliability modeling, cross-referenced with OEM fatigue test data, indicates that the crack likely reached detectable thresholds only within the final 800–1,000 cycles prior to failure. This aligns with the 1,200-cycle inspection interval, which was established based on historical fleet data and conservative safety margins.

However, the event demonstrates that traditional interval-based inspections may not adequately capture stochastic crack initiation in high-cycle engines. Advanced phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) and automated eddy current arrays offer improved signal-to-noise ratios and volumetric coverage. Comparative data from the LEAP-1B engine family, which incorporates composite fan blades and redesigned containment architectures, shows that next-generation inspection paradigms are shifting toward condition-based monitoring rather than fixed-cycle thresholds. The Operator advocates for accelerated adoption of these technologies across legacy platforms.

3.2 Airframe Structural Response and Decompression Dynamics
FDR data (Docket Item 4.2.1) indicates a cabin pressure decay rate exceeding 1,200 feet per minute within the first 15 seconds post-impact. The debris trajectory analysis confirms that a single fan blade fragment penetrated the forward fuselage skin and impacted the passenger window at an oblique angle. The window assembly, certified under Section 25.783, is designed to withstand specified pressure differentials and localized impact loads. However, the certification basis for §25.783 primarily addresses uniform pressure loading and standardized projectile tests, not the combined effects of high-velocity metallic debris, localized stress concentration, and rapid decompression-induced structural flexure.

Our structural engineering team conducted finite element analysis (FEA) using the recovered debris mass, impact velocity, and window laminate configuration. The simulation indicates that the polycarbonate inner pane experienced localized delamination and edge stress concentrations that exceeded the design limit load. While the window met original type certification requirements under 14 CFR Part 21, the event highlights a gap between historical ballistic testing parameters and real-world uncontained failure scenarios. The Operator recommends revising impact testing protocols to incorporate multi-axis debris trajectories and dynamic pressure decay modeling.

3.3 Regulatory and Maintenance Program Alignment
Southwest Airlines Co. maintains a Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP) fully compliant with 14 CFR Part 121 requirements. The program integrates OEM service bulletins, FAA ADs, and internal reliability tracking. However, the investigation reveals that maintenance program optimization often lags behind emerging fatigue data and NDI technological advancements. The regulatory framework under Part 121 provides robust oversight, but the transition from reactive to predictive maintenance requires updated guidance on data-driven inspection intervals, real-time engine health monitoring (EHM) integration, and standardized NDI validation metrics.

For context, operators in the 14 CFR part 135 category, including regional and charter carriers, often operate with different maintenance scheduling constraints and fleet utilization profiles. While the regulatory distinction is operationally justified, the underlying engineering principles of fatigue management and NDI sensitivity are universal. Cross-category data sharing and harmonized inspection standards would enhance industry-wide safety. The Operator notes that organizations such as Atlas Air have successfully implemented advanced EHM and predictive maintenance algorithms across mixed fleets, demonstrating the feasibility of scalable, data-driven maintenance optimization.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the engineering data, metallurgical findings, and operational records reviewed, Southwest Airlines Co. concludes the following:

1. The primary contributing factor to the uncontained engine failure was undetected low-cycle fatigue crack propagation in the fan blade dovetail, initiated at a subsurface material inclusion and accelerated by high-cycle operational loading.
2. The approved NDI inspection interval and methodology, while compliant with existing regulatory and OEM standards, lacked the sensitivity to detect early-stage subsurface crack initiation within the final 1,000 cycles prior to failure.
3. The cabin window assembly met original certification requirements under Section 25.783 and 14 CFR Part 21, but the combined effects of high-velocity debris impact, localized stress concentration, and rapid decompression exceeded the design envelope for passenger window retention.
4. The maintenance program operated in full compliance with 14 CFR Part 121 requirements; however, the event underscores the need for industry-wide adoption of predictive maintenance technologies, advanced NDI validation, and dynamic impact testing protocols.

The Operator’s position is that the event was not the result of maintenance negligence or regulatory non-compliance, but rather a manifestation of inherent limitations in legacy inspection paradigms and historical certification testing parameters. The complexity of fatigue crack growth, combined with the stochastic nature of debris trajectory and decompression dynamics, necessitates a shift toward condition-based monitoring, enhanced NDI sensitivity, and updated structural impact standards.

We recommend the following safety improvements:
- Mandate phased-array ultrasonic testing and automated eddy current scanning for high-cycle fan blades, with reduced inspection intervals based on real-time fatigue modeling.
- Revise Section 25.783 testing requirements to include multi-axis debris impact scenarios, dynamic pressure decay simulation, and edge-stress concentration analysis.
- Establish an industry-wide data-sharing framework for EHM and NDI results, enabling predictive maintenance algorithms to be calibrated across engine families, including legacy CFM56 platforms and next-generation architectures like the LEAP-1B.
- Develop standardized training curricula for maintenance personnel on advanced NDI interpretation, fatigue mechanics, and human factors in defect recognition.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

Southwest Airlines Co. has implemented immediate and sustained corrective actions in response to the event, in coordination with the IIC, the FAA, and the engine manufacturer.

5.1 Actions Already Taken
- Fleet-Wide Inspection Campaign: Within 72 hours of the event, the Operator initiated a mandatory ultrasonic and borescope inspection of all fan blades across the 737-700/800 fleet. Over 1,200 engines were inspected, with three blades identified for early removal based on crack indications below the previous rejection threshold.
- Maintenance Program Revision: The CAMP was updated to incorporate reduced inspection intervals for high-cycle engines, enhanced NDI documentation requirements, and mandatory PAUT deployment for all fan blade dovetail inspections.
- Crew Training Enhancement: Rapid decompression and emergency descent procedures were revised to include scenario-based training on asymmetric cabin pressure loss, debris impact awareness, and passenger management during high-stress events.
- EHM Integration: Real-time engine health monitoring parameters, including N1 vibration harmonics, EGT spread, and oil debris detection, were integrated into the Operator’s predictive maintenance dashboard. Threshold alerts now trigger immediate maintenance review rather than deferred troubleshooting.
- Regulatory Coordination: The Operator submitted a formal petition to the FAA for an updated AD mandating advanced NDI protocols and revised inspection intervals, supported by metallurgical and reliability data.

5.2 Proposed Future Improvements
- AI-Assisted NDI Analysis: The Operator is piloting machine learning algorithms to analyze ultrasonic and eddy current scan data, reducing human interpretation variability and improving early crack detection rates. Initial validation shows a 35% improvement in subsurface flaw identification.
- Dynamic Window Impact Testing: In collaboration with airframe manufacturers and certification authorities, the Operator proposes a joint research initiative to develop updated ballistic testing standards that reflect real-world uncontained failure dynamics, including oblique impact angles and rapid decompression loading.
- Cross-Operator Data Harmonization: The Operator advocates for an industry-wide maintenance data repository, enabling operators under 14 CFR Part 121 and 14 CFR part 135 to share fatigue progression models, NDI results, and EHM trends. This initiative would accelerate predictive maintenance adoption and reduce redundant testing.
- Certification Framework Review: The Operator recommends that the FAA and EASA review 14 CFR Part 21 certification requirements for high-bypass turbofan containment and cabin window retention, incorporating lessons learned from this event and aligning standards with modern materials and operational profiles.
- Human Factors Integration: Maintenance training programs will be updated to include cognitive load management, fatigue recognition, and standardized defect reporting protocols. The Operator will partner with academic institutions to develop evidence-based training modules that address the intersection of engineering complexity and human performance.

Southwest Airlines Co. remains fully committed to the highest standards of aviation safety, regulatory compliance, and continuous improvement. We appreciate the thorough and collaborative efforts of the IIC, the NTSB, and all participating parties in this investigation. The Operator stands ready to support the Board’s final report and to implement any additional safety recommendations that emerge from this proceeding. Through engineering rigor, data-driven maintenance, and industry-wide cooperation, we can mitigate the risk of future uncontained failures and enhance the safety of commercial aviation for all passengers and crew.

TO: All Maintenance Engineering Personnel, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Fleet Reliability Group, Technical Training Division
FROM: J. R. Vance, Director of Maintenance & Quality Assurance, Southwest Airlines

SUBJECT: QA-2018-0417: Uncontained Engine Failure Response & Enhanced Fan Blade Inspection Protocol
REF: SWA-ENG-737-089, FAA AD 2018-09-05, Internal Memo SWA-QA-2018-0312, NTSB Docket Entry (Pending)

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert is issued to mandate immediate implementation of enhanced fan blade inspection procedures, revise maintenance tracking parameters, and align all 737 fleet operations with updated fatigue monitoring requirements following the April 17, 2018, in-flight event. All personnel must comply with the directives outlined herein to ensure continued airworthiness and regulatory compliance under 14 CFR Part 121.

BACKGROUND:
On 17 April 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operating under our certificate experienced an uncontained engine failure during cruise at FL325 (32,500 feet). High-energy debris from the left engine penetrated the fuselage and compromised a passenger cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one fatality. Preliminary metallurgical review indicates a fatigue-initiated fracture in a fan blade root, consistent with high-cycle fatigue progression. While the affected powerplant is a legacy CFM56-7B, the failure mode underscores critical vulnerabilities in rotating component lifecycle management that directly impact our entire narrowbody fleet, including the incoming LEAP engine integration program.

The Federal Aviation Administration has initiated emergency rulemaking, and our Principal Inspector (PI) has directed immediate fleet-wide verification of maintenance records and inspection compliance. This alert supersedes prior guidance in SWA-ENG-737-089 and establishes interim protocols pending OEM service bulletin issuance. All actions must be documented per 14 CFR Part 121.380 and reported through the Safety Management System (SMS) portal.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, the following technical and procedural updates apply to all 737-700/800/MAX aircraft under our maintenance program:

1. Enhanced Fan Blade Inspection (EFBI) Protocol
   • All fan blades must undergo Level 3 ultrasonic testing (UT) and eddy current inspection (ECI) at intervals not exceeding 1,500 flight cycles or 12 months, whichever occurs first.
   • Reference Work Order WO-ENG-2018-0417-A for step-by-step NDT procedures.
   • Part numbers subject to mandatory inspection: P/N 1234-5678 (CFM56-7B) and P/N 9876-5432 (LEAP-1B). Cross-reference with the Component Tracking Database (CTD) for cycle counts.
   • Any blade exhibiting surface pitting, root radius anomalies, or coating delamination must be quarantined and tagged with QA-RED-001. Do not return to service.

2. Fuselage & Window Frame Post-Event Verification
   • Conduct detailed visual and borescope inspection of all forward fuselage panels (Stations 100–300) and window retainers.
   • Use SWA-STRUCT-CHK-044 checklist. Document findings in the Aircraft Maintenance Log (AML) with reference code “QA-2018-0417-FUS”.
   • Replace any window assembly showing stress cracking, seal degradation, or fastener elongation per IPC Chapter 56-10.

3. Regulatory & Documentation Compliance
   • All maintenance actions must satisfy 14 CFR Part 121.373 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations) and 121.380 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alteration Programs).
   • Log all inspections in the Reliability Tracking System (RTS) under Event Code “UNCONTAINED-0417”.
   • Retain NDT reports, work order sign-offs, and material disposition records for a minimum of 10 years per FAA Advisory Circular 120-78A.

4. Fleet Transition & LEAP Engine Integration
   • The LEAP engine shares similar high-bypass architecture and fatigue monitoring requirements. All incoming LEAP-1B units must undergo baseline UT/ECI prior to installation.
   • Update the Engine Health Monitoring (EHM) software to v4.2.1 to capture real-time vibration and temperature anomalies.
   • Coordinate with OEM technical representatives for service bulletin alignment. Reference SWA-LEAP-INT-009 for integration checklists.

ACTION REQUIRED:
The following actions are mandatory and time-critical:

1. Immediate Fleet Grounding for Inspection (Deadline: 24 April 2018, 2359Z)
   • Line Maintenance Supervisors must pull all aircraft exceeding 1,200 cycles since last fan blade inspection.
   • Complete EFBI per WO-ENG-2018-0417-A. Submit completion reports to QA via the RTS portal.
   • Responsible: Base Maintenance Managers, Line Supervisors.

2. Training & Competency Verification (Deadline: 30 April 2018)
   • All NDT technicians and engine mechanics must complete the updated “High-Cycle Fatigue Detection & Uncontained Failure Response” module (Course ID: SWA-TRN-ENG-2018-04).
   • Training Division will issue digital badges upon successful assessment. No technician may sign off on fan blade inspections without current certification.
   • Responsible: Technical Training Division, QA Compliance Auditors.

3. Record Audit & PI Coordination (Deadline: 02 May 2018)
   • Maintenance Records Group will conduct a 100% audit of all engine maintenance logs from 01 January 2017 to present.
   • Prepare summary report for review by the Principal Inspector during the scheduled compliance meeting on 03 May 2018.
   • Ensure all discrepancies are resolved and documented per 14 CFR Part 121.380(c).
   • Responsible: Records Management, Quality Assurance Auditors.

4. Ongoing Monitoring & Reporting
   • Fleet Reliability will issue weekly trend reports on fan blade anomalies, EHM alerts, and inspection findings.
   • Any suspected fatigue-related defect must be reported to the Safety Action Group (SAG) within 2 hours of discovery.
   • Responsible: Fleet Reliability Engineers, Station Managers.

Non-compliance with this Quality Alert will result in immediate suspension of maintenance privileges and referral to the FAA under 14 CFR Part 121.373. All personnel are reminded that our primary obligation is the safe operation of our fleet and the protection of passengers and crew.

Direct technical questions to the Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or email QA-Engineering@swa.com. Training scheduling inquiries should be routed to the LMS portal.
