1. SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines Co, experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. The event resulted in rapid cabin decompression, localized structural damage to the airframe, and one passenger fatality. The aircraft subsequently diverted and landed safely at Philadelphia International Airport, Pennsylvania. This preliminary report outlines the initial factual data, establishes the investigative framework, and documents early procedural determinations. All information contained herein is subject to revision as the investigation progresses.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the flight was operating under instrument flight rules with a scheduled route from LaGuardia Airport, New York, to Dallas Love Field, Texas. Initial data recovered from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) suggest a sudden loss of thrust and associated vibration originating from the left engine at approximately 15:43 EDT. Crew communications captured on the CVR indicate an immediate recognition of an engine anomaly, followed by the execution of emergency descent and decompression checklists.

Initial witness accounts from surviving passengers and cabin crew members describe a loud acoustic event, followed by rapid depressurization and the deployment of passenger oxygen masks. Several individuals reported observing damage to the left-side fuselage and a compromised cabin window. Medical personnel attending to passengers post-landing confirmed one fatality, with several others sustaining minor injuries consistent with rapid decompression and turbulence.

Meteorological data obtained from the National Weather Service and onboard weather radar imagery indicate that the aircraft was operating in clear air conditions at the time of the event. No significant convective activity, turbulence reports, or icing conditions were documented along the flight path. Preliminary examination of the airframe revealed localized damage to the left engine nacelle, fan cowl, and adjacent fuselage skin. A single cabin window on the left side was breached, with surrounding structural members exhibiting deformation consistent with high-velocity debris impact. The right engine and remaining airframe systems appear to have sustained minimal to no damage. All findings remain preliminary and are subject to further technical analysis.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The Investigator in Charge (IIC) has formally established the investigative framework in accordance with National Transportation Safety Board protocols. The following investigative groups have been activated: Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group is tasked with collecting, preserving, and analyzing relevant data within their respective disciplines. The IIC has coordinated with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the aircraft manufacturer to ensure appropriate technical support and regulatory oversight.

Parties to the investigation include representatives from Southwest Airlines, the engine manufacturer, the airframe manufacturer, and the FAA. Additionally, technical advisors from Atlas Air, Inc. have been consulted regarding maintenance record-keeping practices and fleet-wide component tracking methodologies, given their operational experience with similar powerplant configurations. The Chief Inspector has been assigned to oversee the chain of custody for all recovered debris and to ensure compliance with evidence handling procedures. All parties have been briefed on the scope of the investigation and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding preliminary data.

Evidence secured to date includes the FDR and CVR, which have been transported to the NTSB laboratory for readout and transcription. Recovered engine components, including fan blades, containment ring fragments, and nacelle debris, have been cataloged and secured at a designated examination facility. Preliminary metallurgical and fractographic examinations are scheduled to commence within the next 72 hours. The investigation will evaluate compliance with 14 CFR Part 25 airworthiness standards, specifically focusing on engine containment requirements, cabin pressurization system integrity, and emergency descent procedures. The IIC has directed that all group chairpersons submit daily status reports to ensure coordinated progress and to identify any emerging safety concerns that may warrant immediate attention.

4. NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks will focus on comprehensive data analysis, component testing, and operational review. The Powerplants group will conduct a detailed teardown and inspection of the failed engine, with particular attention to the LEAP-1B turbofan architecture and associated maintenance history. Metallurgical analysis will be performed to determine the initiation and propagation characteristics of any observed fractures. The Systems group will evaluate the performance of the cabin pressurization and oxygen distribution systems during the decompression event, while the Structures group will complete a full-scale damage mapping of the affected fuselage section.

The Operations and Human Performance groups will conduct structured interviews with the flight crew, cabin crew, and maintenance personnel to reconstruct the sequence of events and assess procedural adherence. All interview transcripts will be cross-referenced with FDR/CVR data to establish a preliminary timeline. The IIC has authorized the deployment of additional NTSB specialists to assist with advanced non-destructive testing and computational modeling of debris trajectories.

A public hearing is not anticipated at this stage; however, a factual update will be issued within 30 days, pending the completion of initial laboratory examinations and data readouts. All findings, conclusions, and safety recommendations will be developed through a collaborative, evidence-based process and will be subject to rigorous peer review prior to publication. The investigation remains in its preliminary phase, and no determination regarding probable cause or contributing factors has been made. The NTSB will continue to provide updates as additional information becomes available and as the investigative scope is refined.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), an uncontained engine failure occurred during the cruise phase of flight. The event transpired at a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL), approximately 45 nautical miles west-southwest of Harrisburg International Airport (MDT), Pennsylvania. The geographic coordinates of the event were recorded as 40°08'12"N, 77°22'45"W. The aircraft was en route from LaGuardia Airport (LGA), New York, to Dallas Love Field (DAL), Texas.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-7H4, bearing registration number N772SW. The airframe was manufactured by The Boeing Company and operated by Southwest Airlines (SWA). The aircraft was configured for a maximum seating capacity of 143 passengers and was equipped with two high-bypass turbofan engines. At the time of the occurrence, the aircraft was under the operational control of Southwest Airlines, with flight operations conducted under the carrier's approved operations specifications.

1.3 Nature of the Flight
The flight was conducted as a scheduled domestic passenger service in accordance with 14 CFR part 121. The flight plan was filed under instrument flight rules (IFR) and was cleared for cruise at flight level 320. The flight was operating under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) § 121.1, which governs domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. All operational, maintenance, and crew duty parameters were required to comply with the regulatory framework established for Part 121 air carriers.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Experience
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1234567, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on January 12, 2018, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 11,240 hours, with 4,890 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The captain completed a recurrent proficiency check on February 14, 2018, and a line-oriented flight training (LOFT) session on March 5, 2018. All training records were current and compliant with 14 CFR § 121.433 and § 121.434.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Experience
The first officer held an ATP certificate, certificate number 2345678, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. A first-class medical certificate was issued on December 8, 2017, with no restrictions. Total flight time was documented at 6,120 hours, with 2,340 hours in the Boeing 737. The first officer successfully completed a recurrent simulator evaluation on January 22, 2018, and a line check on February 28, 2018. Training documentation indicated full compliance with Part 121 recurrent training requirements.

2.3 Cabin Crew and Training Records
The flight was staffed with four flight attendants, all holding valid FAA certificates and current emergency procedure qualifications. Each cabin crew member had completed Southwest Airlines' annual recurrent training program, which included rapid decompression drills, emergency oxygen deployment, and passenger evacuation procedures. Training records were maintained in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.417 and were verified as current at the time of the flight.

2.4 Duty Time and Rest Compliance
Flight and duty time records were reviewed for the 30-day period preceding the accident. The captain and first officer were within the limits prescribed by 14 CFR § 121.470 and § 121.471. The crew reported for duty at 11:15 EDT, with a scheduled block-out time of 13:30 EDT. The total duty period at the time of the event was 4 hours and 28 minutes, well within the 14-hour maximum duty period for a two-pilot crew. Rest periods prior to the duty day met the minimum 10-hour requirement.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 Airframe Specifications and History
The Boeing 737-7H4, serial number 28768, was delivered to the operator on May 14, 2001. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 56,842 total flight hours and 38,912 total flight cycles. The aircraft was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The last heavy maintenance visit (D-check equivalent) was completed on November 12, 2017, at 55,100 flight hours.

3.2 Engine Configuration and Maintenance
The aircraft was equipped with two CFM LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines. The left engine, serial number 88421, was installed on the aircraft on August 3, 2016, and had accumulated 18,450 flight hours and 12,890 flight cycles at the time of the failure. The right engine, serial number 88422, had accumulated 17,920 flight hours and 12,410 cycles. Maintenance records indicated that the left engine underwent a performance restoration shop visit on June 15, 2017, at 14,200 hours. All scheduled inspections, including borescope examinations and vibration monitoring, were documented as completed within prescribed intervals.

3.3 Applicable Airworthiness Directives
A review of the aircraft maintenance logs and FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) tracking system confirmed compliance with all applicable ADs. Relevant directives included AD 2016-18-05, which mandated enhanced inspection protocols for high-pressure turbine components, and AD 2017-22-11, which required ultrasonic testing of fan blade dovetails. The operator's maintenance control center verified that all compliance actions were documented and signed off by authorized inspectors. No outstanding ADs or deferred maintenance items were recorded for the left engine or associated nacelle components.

3.4 Relevant Systems and Components
The aircraft pressurization system was configured to maintain a cabin altitude of 6,500 feet at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet, resulting in a differential pressure of approximately 8.3 psi. The emergency oxygen system consisted of chemical oxygen generators located above each passenger seat row, with a continuous flow duration of 12 minutes. The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were installed in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.343 and § 121.344. Both recorders were recovered intact and forwarded to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction and analysis.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 En Route Conditions
At the time of the event, the aircraft was operating in clear air at flight level 320. Upper air data from the National Weather Service indicated a stable atmospheric profile with no convective activity, turbulence, or icing conditions reported along the route. The ambient temperature at 32,500 feet was -48°C, with a dew point depression exceeding 20°C. Wind direction was from 270° true at 45 knots, with a temperature deviation of -2°C from the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA).

4.2 Surface Observations and Forecasts
Surface weather observations from nearby reporting stations were reviewed. The 15:53 EDT METAR for Harrisburg International Airport (KMDT) reported: KMDT 171553Z 28008KT 10SM CLR 18/02 A3012. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for the region indicated continued visual meteorological conditions (VMC) with no significant weather expected through 20:00 EDT. Visibility was unrestricted, and cloud cover was absent below 12,000 feet MSL.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Upper Air Data
A review of the Aviation Weather Center's pilot report (PIREP) database for the 14:00 to 16:00 EDT timeframe revealed no reports of turbulence, wind shear, or volcanic ash along the flight path. Upper air sounding data from the nearest radiosonde launch site confirmed a dry, stable airmass with a tropopause height of 38,000 feet. No meteorological factors were identified that would have contributed to or exacerbated the engine failure or subsequent decompression event.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
Following the uncontained failure, debris from the left engine was recovered across a 12-nautical-mile corridor extending from the event coordinates to the emergency landing site at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). Primary debris included a fractured fan blade segment, portions of the inlet cowl, acoustic liner fragments, and nacelle fairing panels. All recovered components were cataloged, photographed, and secured for metallurgical examination. The distribution pattern was consistent with high-velocity forward and lateral ejection from the engine core.

5.2 Fuselage and Cabin Damage Assessment
Examination of the airframe revealed a 14-inch by 18-inch puncture in the left fuselage skin, located at station 420, stringer 12. The breach was situated directly aft of the left engine pylon and aligned with the trajectory of the ejected fan blade segment. The adjacent passenger window, designated as row 14, window A, was completely dislodged from its frame. The window frame exhibited plastic deformation and fastener shear consistent with rapid pressure differential loading. Interior cabin damage was localized to the immediate vicinity of the breach, with overhead bin deformation, seat track displacement, and oxygen mask deployment observed.

5.3 Engine Component Examination
The left engine was removed from the aircraft and transported to a secure examination facility. Visual inspection of the fan rotor assembly revealed a complete fracture of one fan blade at the dovetail root. The fracture surface exhibited classic fatigue crack propagation features, including beach marks and a final fast-fracture zone. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis confirmed the presence of a subsurface inclusion at the crack initiation site. The containment ring exhibited localized deformation and penetration marks, indicating that the blade segment exceeded the designed containment capability. The right engine was inspected and found to be undamaged, with all parameters within normal operating limits.

5.4 Debris Trajectory and Containment Analysis
Engineering analysis of the debris field and impact marks on the fuselage was conducted using three-dimensional coordinate mapping and ballistic trajectory modeling. The data indicated that the fractured fan blade segment exited the engine casing at an estimated velocity of 1,250 feet per second, striking the fuselage at an angle of 32° relative to the longitudinal axis. The impact energy exceeded the structural design limits of the cabin window assembly, resulting in immediate loss of cabin pressure. The rapid decompression event was characterized by a pressure drop from 8.3 psi differential to ambient conditions within 1.8 seconds, as recorded by the FDR cabin pressure transducer.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Maintenance and Operational Policies
Southwest Airlines maintains a comprehensive maintenance program governed by FAA-approved procedures and internal quality assurance protocols. The operator's engineering department utilizes predictive maintenance analytics, including engine health monitoring (EHM) and vibration trend analysis, to schedule component removals. Maintenance records indicate that the left engine was monitored through the operator's centralized maintenance tracking system, with no exceedances or fault codes logged in the 30 days preceding the event. Atlas Air (AAI) was contracted to provide heavy maintenance support and component overhaul services for the operator's fleet. Documentation from Atlas Air confirmed that the engine's last shop visit included compliance with all manufacturer service bulletins and FAA-mandated inspection intervals.

6.2 Historical Precedents and Similar Events
A review of NTSB and FAA databases identified three prior uncontained engine failure events involving high-bypass turbofan engines in commercial service between 2010 and 2017. Each event involved fatigue-related fan blade fractures, with subsequent investigations resulting in revised inspection intervals and enhanced non-destructive testing (NDT) requirements. The FAA issued Safety Alert for Operators (SAFO) 18004 in response to the current event, mandating accelerated ultrasonic inspections of fan blade dovetails across affected engine models. Historical data indicates that uncontained failures represent less than 0.001% of total engine flight hours, with containment ring design standards governed by 14 CFR § 33.94.

6.3 Regulatory Framework and Inspector Findings
The investigation was conducted in accordance with the NTSB's Group Chairman's Factual Report procedures and FAA oversight guidelines. The Chief Inspector assigned to the maintenance group reviewed all applicable maintenance logs, work orders, and compliance documentation. The Chief Inspector's preliminary findings confirmed that all maintenance actions were performed by FAA-certified repair stations and signed off by authorized inspectors in compliance with 14 CFR § 121.373 and § 121.375. The regulatory framework governing engine airworthiness, maintenance tracking, and operational safety was fully adhered to by the operator. No deviations from approved procedures, training deficiencies, or regulatory non-compliance were identified in the preliminary review of maintenance and operational records. All factual data, including FDR parameters, CVR transcripts, and metallurgical reports, have been compiled and archived for further analysis by the NTSB investigative team.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the powerplant, materials, and flight data recorder (FDR) examinations conducted in support of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the uncontained engine failure event involving a Boeing 737-700, registration N772SW, on April 17, 2018. The examination was performed under the authority of the NTSB Powerplants and Materials Groups, with coordination from the Structures and Flight Data Recorder Groups. The primary scope of this report encompasses the physical and metallurgical evaluation of the left engine assembly, recovered fan blade fragments, containment ring, inlet cowl, and associated airframe impact zones, alongside the decoding, validation, and parameter analysis of the aircraft's FDR, Quick Access Recorder (QAR), and Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) data.

The physical examination of the engine components and recovered debris was conducted between May 2 and May 18, 2018, at the NTSB headquarters facility in Washington, D.C., and at the manufacturer's materials testing laboratory in Evendale, Ohio, with the final metallurgical assessment finalized prior to the preliminary FDR data synchronization phase. FDR and QAR data extraction, synchronization, and parameter mapping were completed at the Board headquarters between May 3 and May 10, 2018. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) guidelines, ASTM International standards, and applicable Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) Aerospace Material Specifications (AMS). This report presents factual observations, measured data, and analytical results derived from the examination. No conclusions regarding probable cause are included herein.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft was equipped with a CFM International LEAP-1B26 high-bypass turbofan engine, serial number 884217, part number 2000M12-001, installed on the left wing pylon. The LEAP-1B engine is a two-spool, axial-flow turbofan featuring a 18-blade fan stage constructed from 3D-woven carbon fiber composite material with a titanium alloy leading edge protection strip. The fan blades are retained in a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) disk via a dovetail root configuration. The engine core incorporates a 10-stage high-pressure compressor, annular combustor, and 2-stage high-pressure turbine, with a 4-stage low-pressure turbine driving the fan. The engine is controlled by a dual-channel Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC) system, compliant with RTCA DO-178C Level A software assurance standards.

The engine was type certified under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart B, with a certification basis that includes §21.21 (Type certification), §25.903 (Engines), and §33.94 (Engine containment). The containment system design incorporates an Inconel 718 nickel-based superalloy fan case ring, engineered to retain fan blade fragments under high-energy release conditions per §33.94(a) and (b). The aircraft was operated under a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 air carrier certificate, with maintenance tracking and inspection intervals established per the manufacturer's Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) and MSG-3 reliability-centered maintenance framework. The operator's engineering department referenced comparative fleet data from Atlas Air Worldwide Holdings (AAWW) to validate inspection thresholds for composite fan blade trailing edge fatigue monitoring, as documented in AAWW Engineering Bulletin 2017-04-112.

At the time of the event, the subject engine had accumulated 18,450.3 flight hours and 12,890 flight cycles. The last scheduled shop visit occurred on November 14, 2017, at 17,920 hours, during which a borescope inspection of the fan stage, high-pressure compressor, and turbine sections was performed per the engine manufacturer's Service Bulletin (SB) 72-0045. No anomalies were recorded. The engine's fuel system and associated wiring were evaluated for compliance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88), which mandates fuel tank system fault tolerance evaluation and ignition source prevention. All SFAR 88-mandated inspections, including fuel pump wiring harness integrity checks and bonding strap resistance measurements (<0.005 ohms), were documented as compliant in the aircraft maintenance logbook. The engine's operational history indicated no prior uncommanded shutdowns, surge events, or vibration exceedances exceeding 1.5 inches per second (ips) root mean square (RMS).

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The left engine was received at the NTSB headquarters facility with the inlet cowl detached, fan case breached, and multiple fan blade fragments recovered from the accident site. The engine was secured to a heavy-duty inspection cradle, and all external components were cataloged per NTSB evidence tracking protocol. A total of 14 fan blade fragments were recovered, with fragment #13 (outboard section, trailing edge) identified as the primary failure origin. The remaining 17 fan blades were visually inspected and subjected to non-destructive testing (NDT) per ASTM E1444 (magnetic particle) and ASTM E2373 (ultrasonic phased array). No additional cracks, delaminations, or impact damage were detected on the remaining blades.

Fractographic analysis of the primary failure fragment was conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 15 kV accelerating voltage. The fracture surface exhibited a distinct fatigue initiation site located 12.4 mm from the trailing edge, approximately 85% span from the root. The initiation zone measured 0.8 mm in width and displayed characteristic beach marks and fatigue striations. Striation spacing was measured at 0.0021 to 0.0048 mm per cycle, indicating progressive high-cycle fatigue propagation. The final fast fracture zone occupied approximately 38% of the cross-sectional area and exhibited ductile dimple rupture morphology consistent with overload failure at high rotational speed. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the base material composition as Ti-6Al-4V ELI (Extra Low Interstitial), with aluminum at 6.12 wt%, vanadium at 4.08 wt%, and interstitial elements (O, C, N, H) within AMS 4911 limits. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD), corrosion, or manufacturing inclusions was observed.

Hardness testing was performed on the fracture surface and adjacent parent material using a Rockwell C scale indenter. Average hardness measured 34.2 HRC, consistent with the specified 32-36 HRC range for solution-treated and aged Ti-6Al-4V. Microstructural evaluation per ASTM E112 revealed an equiaxed alpha-beta grain structure with an average grain size of 8.2 μm, indicating no abnormal thermal exposure or microstructural degradation. Tensile coupon testing of adjacent material (ASTM E8/E8M) yielded an ultimate tensile strength of 1,085 MPa and a yield strength of 965 MPa, both within the manufacturer's material specification envelope.

The fan containment ring (P/N 2000M45-003, Inconel 718) exhibited localized plastic deformation and a 42 mm by 18 mm penetration at the 10 o'clock position. The penetration path aligned with the trajectory of the outboard fragment of blade #13. The ring's residual thickness at the impact zone measured 3.1 mm, compared to the nominal 6.5 mm design thickness. Despite the breach, the containment ring maintained structural continuity, and no secondary fragmentation occurred. The inlet cowl (P/N 65-45210-1) displayed a 1.2 m longitudinal tear with composite delamination and aluminum honeycomb core crushing. Impact debris mapping indicated a primary strike at fuselage station 420, waterline 185, resulting in a 0.65 m by 0.45 m breach in the forward cabin window frame. The window assembly (P/N 65-45215-3) exhibited radial cracking and complete loss of structural integrity, with the outer acrylic ply fully separated.

All physical measurements, fracture surface imaging, and NDT results were documented in NTSB photographic series ENG-2018-04-17-001 through ENG-2018-04-17-045. Dimensional verification of the fan blade dovetail root was performed using coordinate measuring machine (CMM) techniques, confirming root clearance within ±0.025 mm of design specifications. No evidence of fretting, galling, or improper assembly torque was identified.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) and QAR data were extracted from the aircraft's solid-state memory modules using a certified data retrieval system compliant with ARINC 717 and ARINC 767 standards. The FDR recorded 88 parameters at a 1 Hz sampling rate, while the QAR provided high-resolution engine and airframe data at 8 Hz. Data synchronization was achieved via GPS timecode alignment, with a maximum temporal offset of ±0.12 seconds. Parameter decoding followed the aircraft manufacturer's Flight Data Acquisition Unit (FDAU) mapping tables and was cross-validated against the engine manufacturer's FADEC data bus protocol.

The timeline reconstruction indicates the following sequence:
- 14:22:09 UTC: Engine vibration (VIB) parameter for the left engine increased from a baseline of 0.32 ips to 1.8 ips. QAR spectral analysis revealed a dominant 1xN1 harmonic at 1,840 RPM, indicating a developing mass imbalance.
- 14:22:11 UTC: N1 (fan speed) rapidly increased to 108.5% (exceeding the 104% redline limit), while N2 (core speed) decayed from 92.1% to 78.4%. Exhaust gas temperature (EGT) rose from 682°C to 728°C within 1.2 seconds. Fuel flow (FF) remained stable at 2,840 kg/hr, indicating no fuel control system malfunction.
- 14:22:13 UTC: Engine vibration exceeded 4.2 ips, triggering the EICAS "ENG 1 VIB" caution. FADEC initiated automatic thrust reduction, but the N1 decay rate was insufficient to arrest the imbalance.
- 14:22:14 UTC: Cabin differential pressure (ΔP) dropped from 8.6 PSI to 2.1 PSI within 0.8 seconds. Cabin altitude rate of climb registered 2,840 ft/min. The rapid decompression event coincided with the structural failure of the forward cabin window.
- 14:22:16 UTC: Autothrottle disengaged. Thrust lever position moved to idle. N1 stabilized at 42.3%, N2 at 38.1%. EGT peaked at 745°C before declining.
- 14:22:18 UTC: Crew initiated emergency descent. Aircraft altitude decreased from 32,500 ft MSL to 10,000 ft MSL over 4 minutes 12 seconds.

CVR audio analysis confirmed a sharp acoustic transient at 14:22:11 UTC, followed by crew statements referencing a "loud bang," "engine fire warning," and "rapid decompression." The audio waveform exhibited a broadband frequency spike peaking at 142 dB SPL, consistent with an uncontained high-energy release.

Comparison with normal operational parameters confirms the event deviated significantly from baseline cruise conditions. At FL325, standard cruise N1 for the LEAP-1B26 is 89.2% ±1.5%, with EGT at 680°C ±15°C and vibration <0.5 ips. The observed N1 overshoot, EGT excursion, and vibration spike are characteristic of a sudden fan blade mass imbalance and aerodynamic disruption. The FADEC's automatic response followed programmed logic per the engine control software specification, but the rate of structural failure exceeded the system's corrective bandwidth.

Decompression dynamics were modeled using the aircraft's pressurization system parameters. The cabin pressure controller (CPC) attempted to maintain ΔP at 8.6 PSI, but the window breach created an effective orifice area of 0.28 m². The resulting mass flow rate of 14.2 kg/s of cabin air exceeded the outflow valve's maximum capacity, resulting in the observed rapid altitude climb. The FDR recorded a cabin altitude of 18,500 ft MSL at 14:22:19 UTC, consistent with the aircraft's emergency descent profile.

All data parameters were validated against manufacturer engineering limits, with no evidence of sensor drift, data corruption, or recording anomalies. The QAR high-resolution vibration spectrum provided critical insight into the pre-failure imbalance progression, confirming a 1xN1 harmonic growth rate of 0.45 ips/second over the 2.1 seconds preceding structural release.

5. SUMMARY

The examination of the left engine assembly, recovered fan blade fragments, and associated airframe components, combined with the analysis of FDR, QAR, and CVR data, yielded the following factual findings:

1. The uncontained engine failure originated from a fatigue crack in the trailing edge of fan blade #13 (P/N 2000M12-001, S/N 884217). The crack initiated approximately 12.4 mm from the trailing edge and propagated over an estimated 2,100 flight cycles, as determined by striation spacing analysis and fatigue life modeling.

2. Metallurgical evaluation confirmed the fan blade material (Ti-6Al-4V ELI) met all AMS 4911 chemical, mechanical, and microstructural specifications. No manufacturing defects, foreign object damage, corrosion, or thermal degradation were identified.

3. The final fracture occurred at 32,500 ft MSL during cruise flight, resulting in the release of the outboard blade section. The released fragment penetrated the Inconel 718 containment ring, creating a 42 mm by 18 mm breach. The containment ring maintained structural continuity and prevented secondary fragmentation, consistent with §33.94 design requirements.

4. Debris impact at fuselage station 420, waterline 185, compromised the forward cabin window assembly, resulting in rapid decompression. The cabin differential pressure dropped from 8.6 PSI to 2.1 PSI within 0.8 seconds, with a cabin altitude climb rate of 2,840 ft/min.

5. FDR and QAR data recorded a rapid N1 increase to 108.5%, N2 decay to 78.4%, EGT rise to 728°C, and engine vibration exceeding 4.2 ips. The 1xN1 harmonic growth rate of 0.45 ips/second preceded the structural release by 2.1 seconds. The FADEC responded per programmed logic, but the rate of failure exceeded corrective capability.

6. All maintenance records, inspection logs, and compliance documentation for the engine and airframe were reviewed. The engine was maintained in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121 requirements, with SFAR 88 fuel system evaluations and Part 21 certification documentation verified as current. Comparative engineering data from Atlas Air Worldwide Holdings (AAWW) confirmed that the observed fatigue progression aligns with known high-cycle fatigue mechanisms for composite-titanium hybrid fan blades under sustained cruise loading.

7. No evidence of improper assembly, maintenance error, operational exceedance, or system malfunction was identified. The failure mode is consistent with progressive high-cycle fatigue leading to sudden structural release under normal cruise conditions.

All measurements, test results, and data parameters documented in this report are factual observations derived from standardized examination procedures and validated data decoding methodologies.

INTERVIEW OF MARK R. HENDERSON, SENIOR MAINTENANCE COORDINATOR, SOUTHWEST AIRLINES
Date: April 24, 2018
Time: 10:15 AM CDT
Location: Southwest Airlines Maintenance Control Center, Dallas, Texas
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Vance, Powerplants Group

Q: Mr. Henderson, thank you for making time today. This interview is being recorded for the official record of the NTSB investigation into the April 17, 2018, event involving a Boeing 737-700. Please state your full name, title, and your role on the day of the incident.

A: Mark R. Henderson. I’m a Senior Maintenance Coordinator here at the MCC. On the seventeenth, I was working the day shift, covering the eastern and central route banks. So when Flight 1380... uh, the 737-700 out of LaGuardia, I was the primary maintenance point of contact. Basically, if the flight deck had a mechanical issue, it came to my console first.

Q: Walk me through what happened from your perspective, starting from when you first became aware of the situation.

A: Right. It was... let me pull up my shift log. About 10:30 AM Eastern, so 9:30 our time. I was monitoring the ACARS feed and the flight tracking board. The aircraft was in cruise, level at 32,500 feet. Everything was nominal. Then, out of nowhere, a priority message popped up. It wasn’t a standard maintenance squawk. It was coded, but the keywords were clear: rapid decompression, left engine failure, diverting to Philadelphia. I remember my stomach just... dropped. I immediately pulled up the aircraft’s tail number, N772SW, and started scrolling through the recent maintenance history. I was on the satphone with the captain within, I don’t know, maybe two minutes. He sounded... calm, but you could hear it in the background. Wind noise, the master caution, the usual. He said they’d had a loud bang, the aircraft yawed hard left, autopilot kicked off, and they were manually flying it down.

Q: Did he describe the nature of the failure or any specific system indications?

A: He mentioned the number one engine parameters had gone erratic, then flatlined. EGT spiked, then dropped. N1 and N2 were fluctuating. He said it sounded like a... like a cannon shot, he actually used those words. Then the cabin pressure warning came on almost immediately. I just told him to run the emergency checklist, declare an emergency, and that we’d have emergency services staged at PHL. I didn’t want to distract him. At that point, it’s all about getting them on the ground. I was already pulling the QAR data stream and the engine health monitoring reports.

Q: What was your role after the aircraft landed?

A: I stayed on the line with the flight deck until they were clear of the aircraft and the cabin was secure. Then I coordinated with the station manager in Philly, got our line maintenance team rolling out to the ramp, and started compiling everything for our internal safety office and, obviously, for the FAA and the NTSB. I was on a call with our FAA Principal Inspector, David Chen, around 1:00 PM. He wanted a preliminary rundown. I gave him the basics: uncontained failure, debris penetration, rapid decompression. He asked if we’d seen any similar trends in the fleet. I told him no, not on this model. We’ve had... well, we’ve had minor vibration issues, a few minor oil leaks, but nothing like this.

Q: Let’s talk about the engine itself. Were there any recent maintenance actions or inspections that might be relevant to this failure?

A: Yeah, that’s... that’s where it gets complicated. The left engine was a CFM56-7B. It had been through several hundred cycles since its last borescope inspection. We follow the manufacturer’s recommendations strictly, obviously, and we’re audited on it. But you know, with the -7B, the fan blade retention system is... it’s robust, but fatigue can be tricky. We were actually in the middle of a fleet-wide review of our inspection intervals. There was some internal discussion about whether to adopt newer ultrasonic inspection protocols, similar to what’s being rolled out for the LEAP-1B engines on the MAX program. I mean, the LEAP-1B is a completely different architecture, different composite materials, different certification basis, but the inspection philosophy was being cross-referenced. We hadn’t implemented it yet. It was still under engineering evaluation.

Q: You mentioned the LEAP-1B. Can you clarify how that relates to your maintenance program and this investigation?

A: Sure. It’s more of a... a procedural comparison, really. When we were reviewing our maintenance program, we looked at how the FAA was handling 14 CFR Part 21 compliance for the newer engine types. Part 21 covers certification procedures for products and parts, and there was a lot of internal debate about whether our current inspection intervals for the -7B were still aligned with the latest airworthiness data and fatigue models. We were working with our engineering group to see if we needed to adjust our program to account for newer crack propagation data. But again, this was all pre-incident. We hadn’t changed anything. The engine was within all service limits, all ADs were complied with. It was... it was by the book.

Q: Did you personally inspect the aircraft after it arrived in Philadelphia?

A: Not immediately. I was tied up in MCC, but I flew out to Philly the next morning. When I got to the hangar... man, it was... it was sobering. The left engine cowling was gone. Just shredded. The fan case had a massive breach, maybe... I don’t know, two feet across. Debris had gone through the fuselage, right around row 14. The window was completely blown out. You could see the insulation, the wiring harnesses, the structural frames... it was a mess. The smell of... I don’t know, ozone, burnt oil, maybe hydraulic fluid. It was heavy in the air. I walked the perimeter with the NTSB team. We were careful not to disturb anything. I remember pointing out the exact location of the debris field on the ramp. It was mostly concentrated forward of the wing, near the leading edge.

Q: What was your assessment of the maintenance records at that point?

A: I pulled the full engine log. Everything was... by the book. The last shop visit was about eighteen months prior. The fan blades had been inspected, the retention rings checked, the dovetail slots measured. No discrepancies. But when you look at the fracture surface later... and I’m not a metallurgist, I’ll be clear about that... but the investigators showed me the photos. It was a fatigue crack. Started at the root, propagated over time. It’s... it’s one of those things where the inspection interval might have been just a little too long. Or maybe the crack grew faster than predicted. I don’t know. That’s for the materials lab.

Q: Were there any communications with the Principal Inspector regarding the investigation’s scope or fleet actions?

A: Yeah, David Chen was on site by day two. We had a daily briefing. He was coordinating with the NTSB on the airworthiness directives. He asked if we had any other engines in the fleet with similar cycle counts or maintenance histories. I ran the query. We had three others within five hundred cycles of the failed engine. We grounded them for immediate borescope inspections. It was a precaution, obviously. The Principal Inspector was pushing for a fleet-wide review, and we were fully cooperative. We’ve always had a good relationship with the FAA. They’re not... they’re not out to get us. They’re trying to figure out what happened so it doesn’t happen again.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record regarding the incident or your observations?

A: Just... I want to be clear. We take this seriously. Every single day. The crew did exactly what they were trained to do. The maintenance program was compliant. But when something like this happens, you have to look at everything. The design, the inspections, the operational environment. I know the NTSB is going to dig into the certification basis, the Part 21 stuff, the fatigue models. I hope they find what they need. And I hope... I hope the family of the passenger gets some answers. It’s... it’s heavy. We’re all just trying to make sure it doesn’t happen again.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Henderson. That concludes this portion of the interview.

A: Yeah. Thank you.

MEMORANDUM

DATE: November 14, 2023
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service & Flight Standards Service
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-19-XX AND COMPLIANCE ASSESSMENT REGARDING UNCONTAINED ENGINE FAILURE
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA18MA088; Date of Occurrence: April 17, 2018; Docket No. FAA-2023-0842; NPRM 23-ANE-14

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This document constitutes the formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-19-XX, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the uncontained engine failure event involving a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines Co., on April 17, 2018. The referenced occurrence transpired during cruise flight at Flight Level 325 (32,500 feet MSL), resulting in fuselage penetration, rapid decompression, and one fatality. This memorandum addresses compliance obligations under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart D, pertaining to changes to type certificates, and evaluates the applicability of existing airworthiness directives (ADs) and maintenance program requirements. The regulatory framework herein references Docket No. FAA-2023-0842 and aligns with the statutory authority vested in the Administrator under Title 49, United States Code, Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory oversight of turbine engine airworthiness and fuselage structural integrity is governed by a comprehensive framework established under 14 CFR Part 21, which prescribes certification procedures for products, parts, and appliances. Specifically, 14 CFR 21.99 mandates that any change to a type certificate (TC) or supplemental type certificate (STC) must be evaluated for its impact on continued airworthiness, noise, fuel venting, and exhaust emissions. The subject aircraft, certified under TC A16WE, incorporates design features subject to 14 CFR 25.783 (Fuselage doors and windows) and 14 CFR 25.903 (Engines), which establish minimum performance standards for containment, structural resilience, and cabin pressurization integrity.

Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued multiple ADs addressing uncontained engine failures, including AD 2018-12-05, which mandated ultrasonic inspections of fan blades and containment ring integrity. The regulatory environment was further shaped by Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88), which, while primarily directed at fuel tank system safety, established a foundational precedent for mandatory design review, risk assessment protocols, and fleet-wide corrective action mandates that have since been extrapolated to high-energy rotating machinery and cabin pressurization systems.

Prior to the April 17, 2018 occurrence, the FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (AFS) maintained oversight through the Continued Operational Safety (COS) program. The operator, Southwest Airlines Co., maintained an FAA-approved maintenance program under 14 CFR Part 121.344, which incorporated manufacturer-recommended service bulletins and inspection intervals. However, the integration of next-generation propulsion systems, specifically the CFM International LEAP engine family, introduced novel material fatigue characteristics and acoustic emission profiles that were not fully captured under legacy inspection paradigms. Correspondence originating from Washington, D.C. regulatory headquarters has consistently emphasized the necessity of harmonizing type design certification with operational maintenance data to mitigate latent failure modes.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of operator records, maintenance logs, and manufacturer service documentation indicates that Southwest Airlines Co. was in substantial compliance with the minimum requirements of 14 CFR 121.344 and the applicable Airworthiness Limitations Section (ALS) at the time of the event. The operator’s reliability program, as mandated by 14 CFR 121.373, had not generated statistically significant precursor data that would have triggered an accelerated inspection cycle for the affected fan blade assembly.

Regulatory oversight actions taken by the FAA included the immediate issuance of an Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) within 72 hours of the occurrence, mandating repetitive eddy current inspections of all affected LEAP engine fan blades and containment shroud segments. Furthermore, the FAA initiated a Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) review under 14 CFR 21.99 to evaluate whether the original certification basis adequately addressed high-cycle fatigue propagation in advanced composite and titanium aluminide components.

Despite these actions, the investigation identified critical gaps in the regulatory framework. First, the current certification standards under 14 CFR 25.903 do not explicitly require probabilistic risk assessments for debris trajectory modeling in the event of uncontained failures at cruise altitudes. Second, the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions for cabin window integrity, as referenced in 14 CFR 121.628, lack explicit guidance for rapid decompression scenarios involving ballistic impact from engine debris. Third, the transition from legacy CFM56 architectures to the LEAP engine platform introduced a discrepancy between the original type certification basis and the operational maintenance intervals, creating a regulatory lag in fatigue monitoring protocols.

The FAA acknowledges that while Southwest Airlines Co. adhered to prescribed maintenance schedules, the underlying airworthiness directives did not mandate the implementation of advanced non-destructive testing (NDT) methodologies, such as phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT), which could have detected sub-surface crack initiation prior to catastrophic failure. The regulatory oversight framework must therefore evolve to incorporate predictive maintenance analytics and real-time engine health monitoring (EHM) data as a condition of continued airworthiness.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified deficiencies and in accordance with NTSB Safety Recommendation A-19-XX, the FAA hereby mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Mandatory Inspection Protocol: All operators of aircraft equipped with the LEAP engine family shall implement a revised inspection regime requiring phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) of all fan blades and containment ring segments at intervals not to exceed 1,500 flight cycles. This requirement shall be codified under a new Airworthiness Directive, Docket No. FAA-2023-0842, with an effective date of 30 days from publication in the Federal Register.

b. Type Certificate Amendment: The Aircraft Certification Service shall initiate a rulemaking action under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart D, to amend the certification basis for high-bypass turbofan engines. The amendment shall require manufacturers to submit probabilistic debris trajectory analyses and demonstrate compliance with enhanced containment standards under 14 CFR 25.903(c). Compliance shall be required within 180 days for all new type certificate applications and within 36 months for existing production certificates.

c. Maintenance Program Revision: Southwest Airlines Co., and all Part 121 operators utilizing the affected propulsion systems, shall revise their FAA-approved maintenance programs to incorporate real-time engine health monitoring (EHM) data analytics. The revised program must be submitted to the Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) for approval within 90 days. The program shall include mandatory reporting of any vibration anomalies exceeding 0.5 inches per second (IPS) sustained for more than 10 seconds.

d. Cabin Pressurization and Window Integrity Review: The FAA shall convene a joint industry-regulatory working group to evaluate the applicability of 14 CFR 25.783 to ballistic impact scenarios. The working group shall issue a revised MMEL supplement addressing rapid decompression protocols, including mandatory crew training on emergency descent procedures and passenger oxygen system deployment. The final rulemaking shall be published within 24 months.

e. Follow-Up Inspection and Review Schedule: The FAA’s Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) shall conduct targeted surveillance audits of operator compliance with the revised inspection protocols at 6-month intervals for a period of 36 months. The Aircraft Certification Service shall publish a biannual safety bulletin summarizing inspection findings, failure rates, and regulatory adjustments. All compliance documentation shall be maintained in accordance with 14 CFR 121.380 and made available for FAA review upon request.

The Federal Aviation Administration remains committed to the highest standards of aviation safety and will continue to collaborate with the National Transportation Safety Board, aircraft manufacturers, and air carriers to ensure that regulatory frameworks evolve in tandem with technological advancements. This memorandum shall serve as the official record of compliance actions and shall be incorporated into the administrative docket referenced herein.

HEADLINE: Passenger Dies After Engine Failure Forces Emergency Landing on Boeing 737

BYLINE: By Marcus Thorne, Global Aviation News
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA, Pa. —

A passenger died and several others were injured Tuesday after a Boeing 737-700 operated by Atlas Air suffered a catastrophic engine failure at cruising altitude, forcing the flight crew to execute an emergency descent and divert to a nearby airport. The incident occurred on April 17, 2018, as the aircraft traveled at 32,500 feet, leaving federal investigators scrambling to determine the cause of the uncontained mechanical breakdown.

According to preliminary reports, debris from the aircraft’s left engine tore through the fuselage and shattered a cabin window, triggering rapid decompression. The sudden loss of cabin pressure caused oxygen masks to deploy and sent loose objects flying through the aisle. Pilots immediately initiated an emergency descent, dropping thousands of feet in minutes to reach breathable air before safely landing at Philadelphia International Airport. Emergency medical personnel met the aircraft on the tarmac, where one passenger was pronounced dead and multiple others were transported to local hospitals with non-life-threatening injuries.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of life and extend our heartfelt condolences to the family and friends of the victim,” said an Atlas Air spokesperson in a statement released Tuesday evening. “Our crew followed all emergency protocols, and we are cooperating fully with federal investigators.” The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatched a specialized response team to the scene within hours. “This is a serious incident, and we are treating it with the highest priority,” said NTSB Chairman Robert Sumwalt during a press briefing. “Our investigators are already examining the engine debris, reviewing cockpit voice recordings, and interviewing the flight crew.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed it is working alongside the NTSB to review maintenance logs and operational data. “Safety remains our top priority,” an FAA representative stated. “We will issue any necessary directives as soon as the preliminary findings are available.”

The aircraft, a twin-engine Boeing 737-700, was operating a scheduled passenger route from Washington, D.C., to a West Coast destination when the failure occurred. The 737-700 is a widely used narrow-body jet known for its reliability and fuel efficiency, with thousands of units in service worldwide. The carrier, primarily recognized for its global cargo operations, has increasingly expanded into passenger charter and wet-lease services in recent years. The flight carried 143 passengers and five crew members.

Aviation experts note that an uncontained engine failure—where internal components break apart and breach the engine casing—is rare but not unheard of. “Modern turbofan engines are designed with containment rings to catch debris, but extreme metal fatigue or manufacturing defects can sometimes overcome those safeguards,” explained Dr. Elena Rostova, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Michigan. “The investigation will likely focus on the fan blades and the low-pressure turbine section.” While the aircraft’s specific powerplant is under scrutiny, industry analysts are also examining the broader maintenance practices surrounding the LEAP engine family, which shares similar design philosophies and inspection protocols with older turbofan models. “Understanding how stress fractures develop in high-cycle engines is critical,” Rostova added. “We’ll need to see the metallurgical analysis before drawing any conclusions.”

Survivors described a terrifying sequence of events. “There was a loud bang, like a cannon going off, and then the window just blew out,” said passenger Marcus Chen, 34, who was seated three rows from the damaged section. “The wind was howling, and people were screaming. The flight attendants were incredibly calm, telling us to put on our masks and brace. I’ve never been so scared in my life.” The family of the deceased passenger, identified as Jennifer Martinez, 43, of suburban Maryland, released a brief statement through their attorney. “We are heartbroken and struggling to comprehend this sudden tragedy. We ask for privacy as we grieve and thank the medical staff and first responders who did everything they could.”

The incident echoes a handful of similar aviation emergencies over the past two decades, most notably a 2009 Air France flight that experienced an uncontained engine failure over the Atlantic, and a 2016 Southwest Airlines incident that resulted in a similar window breach and passenger fatality. Despite these high-profile cases, commercial aviation remains one of the safest modes of transportation. The FAA reports that turbine engine failures occur at a rate of less than one per million flight hours, and modern aircraft are rigorously tested to withstand such events. “Every incident, no matter how rare, leads to improvements in inspection protocols and engine design,” said aviation safety analyst David Park. “The industry learns from these tragedies to make flying even safer.”

The NTSB has secured the aircraft and is currently cataloging debris from the runway and surrounding area. Investigators are downloading data from the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which will provide a second-by-second account of the crew’s response and the engine’s performance leading up to the failure. The operator has temporarily grounded its fleet of 737-700s pending a mandatory inspection of all left-engine fan blades. “We expect the preliminary report within 30 days, but a full investigation into the root cause could take up to a year,” Sumwalt noted. “Our focus right now is on the facts, the families, and ensuring this never happens again.”

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the engineering and maintenance safety division of Southwest Airlines (SWA), acting in its capacity as the aircraft operator and responsible party for the maintenance, operational control, and safety management of the subject fleet. As the designated party representative to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative hearing, this document outlines the Carrier’s technical position regarding the uncontained engine failure, subsequent fuselage and cabin window damage, rapid decompression event, and resulting fatality that occurred on April 17, 2018. The scope of this analysis encompasses metallurgical and structural failure mechanisms, non-destructive inspection (NDI) efficacy, debris trajectory and containment performance, cabin pressure decay dynamics, and the alignment of maintenance programs with applicable regulatory frameworks. 

Southwest Airlines acknowledges the profound tragedy of this event and reaffirms its unwavering commitment to aviation safety, continuous improvement, and transparent collaboration with the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). This submission synthesizes operational data, maintenance records, engineering teardown reports, and flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) analyses to establish a fact-based technical position. While the investigation has identified material fatigue as the primary initiating mechanism, this document further examines systemic factors, inspection probability of detection (POD) limitations, and the broader implications for fleet-wide maintenance optimization. The Carrier’s position is grounded in rigorous engineering analysis, compliance with established airworthiness and operational standards, and a proactive safety management system (SMS) that prioritizes data-driven risk mitigation.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On April 17, 2018, the subject Boeing 737-700 was operating at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet when the left engine experienced an uncontained failure. FDR parameters indicate a rapid decay in N1 and N2 rotor speeds, accompanied by a sharp increase in engine vibration and a subsequent loss of thrust. Debris from the failed fan assembly penetrated the engine nacelle, impacted the left fuselage, and breached a passenger cabin window. The resulting rapid decompression triggered immediate cabin pressure decay, as documented in the aircraft’s pressurization system logs (Docket Item 08-C, Exhibit SWA-PRESS-02). The flight crew executed an emergency descent, diverted to the nearest suitable airport, and successfully landed the aircraft. Tragically, one passenger sustained fatal injuries due to partial ejection through the compromised window opening.

Maintenance records reviewed by the NTSB and the Carrier’s engineering team confirm that the subject engine had accumulated approximately 32,000 flight cycles and 48,000 flight hours at the time of the event. The most recent scheduled engine shop visit occurred 18 months prior, during which standard ultrasonic inspection (UT) procedures were performed on all fan blades in accordance with the OEM service bulletin and the Carrier’s FAA-approved maintenance program. Metallurgical analysis of the recovered fan blade fragment (Docket Item 14-A, NTSB/MA-18/01) revealed a fatigue crack originating from a subsurface inclusion, with crack propagation consistent with high-cycle fatigue (HCF) mechanisms. The fracture surface exhibited characteristic beach marks and a final fast-fracture zone, indicating progressive degradation over an extended operational period.

The Carrier’s maintenance tracking system, aligned with 14 CFR Part 121 operating requirements, documented all scheduled inspections, component replacements, and engine health monitoring (EHM) alerts. No anomalous vibration trends or oil debris warnings were recorded in the 90 days preceding the event. The aircraft’s structural integrity, including the fuselage skin and window frame, was maintained per the approved structural repair manual and corrosion prevention program. The investigation’s factual record, as compiled in the NTSB docket, confirms that the Carrier’s operational and maintenance practices were fully compliant with applicable regulatory mandates and OEM service directives at the time of the occurrence.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The uncontained engine failure in this event is fundamentally attributable to high-cycle fatigue crack initiation and propagation within a titanium alloy fan blade. Engineering teardown and fractographic analysis (Docket Item 14-A) demonstrate that the crack originated from a metallurgical inclusion located approximately 1.2 mm below the blade surface. Subsurface inclusions, while within OEM material acceptance criteria, can act as stress concentrators under cyclic loading. The fatigue crack propagated over an estimated 12,000 to 15,000 cycles before reaching critical length, at which point the remaining cross-section could no longer sustain operational centrifugal and aerodynamic loads.

A critical factor in this failure sequence is the probability of detection (POD) associated with conventional ultrasonic inspection techniques. Standard phased-array UT methods, while highly effective for surface and near-surface defects, exhibit reduced sensitivity to subsurface anomalies oriented parallel to the acoustic beam. The Carrier’s maintenance program utilized OEM-recommended inspection intervals and scan patterns, which were validated during initial certification and subsequent service experience. However, the stochastic nature of fatigue crack growth, combined with the geometric complexity of modern fan blade airfoils, introduces inherent limitations in NDI coverage. Statistical POD curves for the inspection protocol in use indicate a 90% detection probability for cracks exceeding 0.040 inches in depth, with a 95% confidence interval. The initiating flaw in this case fell below this threshold during the most recent inspection, rendering it undetectable under standard procedures.

Debris containment and structural response were evaluated against 14 CFR Part 25 airworthiness standards, specifically § 25.362 (engine failure) and § 25.775 (windshields and windows). The engine nacelle and fan case are designed to contain blade fragments under defined energy thresholds. In this event, the high-energy trajectory of the detached blade segment exceeded the localized containment capacity of the aft fan case, resulting in nacelle penetration. The debris subsequently impacted the fuselage skin and window assembly. The cabin window, certified under Part 25 requirements for bird strike and pressure differential loads, was not designed to withstand direct high-velocity metallic impact. The resulting breach initiated rapid decompression, with cabin pressure decaying from 8,000 feet equivalent to ambient altitude in approximately 12 seconds, as recorded in the aircraft’s environmental control system (ECS) data logs (Docket Item 08-C).

The Carrier’s maintenance program operates within the framework of 14 CFR Part 121, which mandates continuous airworthiness, reliability monitoring, and corrective action protocols. Engine health monitoring data, including vibration spectra, exhaust gas temperature (EGT) margins, and oil consumption trends, were continuously analyzed. No predictive indicators of impending blade failure were present, consistent with the sudden nature of fatigue-driven uncontained failures. The Carrier’s SMS incorporates fault tree analysis and failure mode effects criticality analysis (FMECA) to prioritize maintenance interventions. While the program aligns with industry best practices, this event highlights the need for enhanced subsurface inspection capabilities and predictive analytics integration.

It is also instructive to consider the methodological legacy of Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88), which established a systematic approach to fuel tank system fault tolerance evaluation. Although SFAR No. 88 was promulgated specifically for ignition prevention in fuel systems, its structured risk assessment framework—emphasizing latent failure identification, inspection interval optimization, and redundancy validation—has been widely adapted across maintenance program development. The Carrier has applied similar fault tolerance principles to engine and airframe critical systems, utilizing reliability-centered maintenance (RCM) methodologies to balance inspection frequency, operational availability, and safety margins. This event underscores the value of extending such systematic risk evaluation to high-cycle fatigue domains, particularly where subsurface defect detection remains a technical challenge.

Looking forward, the Carrier’s fleet modernization strategy includes the integration of the LEAP engine series, which incorporates advanced composite fan blades, improved material homogeneity, and embedded health monitoring sensors. The CFM LEAP architecture features enhanced blade root geometry, optimized stress distribution, and real-time vibration analytics that significantly improve early anomaly detection. While the subject aircraft utilized CFM56-7B powerplants, the operational lessons from this event directly inform the Carrier’s transition protocols for the LEAP-1B and next-generation LEAP series. Enhanced inspection intervals, predictive maintenance algorithms, and OEM collaboration on subsurface NDI validation are being integrated into the Carrier’s engineering standards to mitigate similar failure modes across the fleet.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on comprehensive engineering analysis, maintenance record review, and docket evidence, Southwest Airlines concludes that the primary contributing factor to the April 17, 2018 event was high-cycle fatigue crack initiation and propagation within a titanium fan blade, originating from a subsurface metallurgical inclusion. The failure mechanism was stochastic in nature, with crack growth occurring below the detection threshold of conventional ultrasonic inspection protocols. The Carrier’s maintenance program was fully compliant with 14 CFR Part 121 operational requirements, OEM service directives, and FAA-approved inspection intervals. The engine’s uncontained failure, while exceeding localized containment design parameters, occurred within the recognized operational envelope of transport category aircraft.

Secondary contributing factors include the inherent limitations of current NDI technologies in detecting subsurface flaws oriented parallel to acoustic beams, the certification basis of cabin windows which prioritizes pressure differential and bird strike resistance over high-velocity metallic impact, and the rapid decompression dynamics that followed the fuselage breach. The Carrier’s position is that while regulatory compliance was maintained, industry-wide advancements in inspection technology, predictive analytics, and structural resilience standards are necessary to further reduce the probability of similar events.

Southwest Airlines recommends the following safety improvements: (1) development and validation of advanced subsurface NDI techniques, including guided wave ultrasonics and thermographic inspection, for high-cycle fatigue-prone components; (2) integration of machine learning-driven predictive maintenance models utilizing continuous EHM data to identify subtle degradation trends; (3) revision of inspection intervals based on fleet-wide fatigue life modeling and operational stress profiling; and (4) evaluation of enhanced cabin window debris resistance standards under 14 CFR Part 25, potentially incorporating multi-layer laminated designs or impact-resistant interlayers. These recommendations align with the Carrier’s commitment to proactive risk mitigation and continuous safety enhancement.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In the immediate aftermath of the event, Southwest Airlines implemented a comprehensive corrective action plan in coordination with the FAA, the engine OEM, and industry safety working groups. The Carrier issued an immediate fleet-wide inspection directive, mandating enhanced ultrasonic scanning of all fan blades on the affected engine model, with particular emphasis on high-cycle airframes. Inspection intervals were temporarily reduced by 30% pending completion of a fleet-wide reliability review. All maintenance personnel received updated training on advanced NDI techniques, crack morphology recognition, and documentation protocols. The Carrier also revised its engine health monitoring thresholds to capture subtle vibration anomalies that may precede fatigue-driven failures.

Operational procedures were updated to reinforce crew training for rapid decompression scenarios, including enhanced emergency descent protocols, oxygen mask deployment verification, and passenger management during sudden cabin pressure loss. The Carrier’s SMS was augmented with a dedicated fatigue risk management module, incorporating data analytics from flight operations, maintenance records, and environmental stress factors. Southwest Airlines has also participated in industry task forces focused on uncontained engine failure mitigation, sharing operational data and inspection findings to support broader safety improvements.

Proposed future improvements include the phased implementation of AI-driven predictive maintenance platforms that correlate EHM data, flight cycle profiles, and metallurgical aging models to forecast component degradation. The Carrier is evaluating the integration of digital twin technology for engine health simulation, enabling virtual stress testing and inspection optimization. Additionally, Southwest Airlines is advocating for updated Part 25 certification guidance regarding cabin window impact resistance, proposing standardized testing protocols for high-velocity debris scenarios. The Carrier will continue to collaborate with the FAA, OEMs, and the NTSB to refine maintenance program requirements, enhance NDI validation standards, and promote industry-wide adoption of advanced inspection technologies.

Southwest Airlines remains steadfast in its commitment to aviation safety, regulatory compliance, and continuous operational improvement. The lessons derived from this event have been systematically integrated into the Carrier’s engineering practices, maintenance protocols, and safety management framework. Through proactive risk assessment, technological advancement, and collaborative industry engagement, the Carrier is positioned to further enhance fleet reliability and passenger safety in the years ahead.

**PURPOSE**
This Quality Alert is issued to mandate immediate inspection, documentation, and compliance actions across the Southwest Airlines Co fleet following the April 17, 2018, uncontained engine failure event. The directive establishes mandatory work card revisions, ultrasonic inspection protocols, and reporting requirements to ensure continued airworthiness and strict adherence to 14 CFR Part 121 maintenance and operational standards. All personnel must implement these directives prior to the next scheduled heavy check or within 72 hours of receipt, whichever occurs first.

**BACKGROUND**
On April 17, 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operating under our certificate experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine during cruise flight at approximately 32,500 feet. High-energy debris penetrated the engine cowl, impacted the forward fuselage, and compromised a passenger cabin window. The resulting rapid decompression led to one fatality and multiple injuries. Preliminary metallurgical and operational data indicate a fatigue crack propagation in a fan blade root, consistent with high-cycle fatigue mechanisms previously observed in early-production LEAP engine variants.

The National Transportation Safety Board has opened a major investigation (NTSB Docket DCA18MA058). Our internal Quality Assurance team is coordinating directly with the assigned Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) to preserve maintenance records, engine health monitoring (EHM) data, and component traceability logs. This event underscores critical vulnerabilities in our current inspection intervals and highlights the necessity of enhanced non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols for rotating assemblies. Compliance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations) and Subpart M (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations for Part 121 Operators) remains non-negotiable. All maintenance actions must be documented in accordance with our approved Maintenance Program Manual (MPM) and OEM service bulletins.

**DETAILS**
Effective immediately, the following technical and procedural directives apply to all CFM LEAP-1B powerplants installed on our 737-700/800/MAX fleet:

1. **Mandatory Fan Blade Inspection**
   - All fan blades (P/N 328A1000-XX series) must undergo phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) at the root and dovetail interface.
   - Utilize Work Order WO-88412 (Rev. 3) and reference OEM SB LEAP-1B-72-0014 for acceptance/rejection criteria.
   - Any blade exhibiting crack indications exceeding 0.015 inches or showing secondary fatigue striations must be quarantined and tagged per QA-PROC-009.

2. **Cowl & Fuselage Damage Assessment**
   - Conduct detailed visual and borescope inspections of the left and right engine cowlings, focusing on the forward fan cowl and thrust reverser halves.
   - Inspect fuselage stations 400–600 for micro-fractures, fastener elongation, or skin deformation. Reference Structural Repair Manual (SRM) Chapter 53-10-00.
   - Document all findings using Form QA-INS-2018-04 and upload to the centralized maintenance tracking system (MxTrack v4.2) within 4 hours of completion.

3. **Engine Health Monitoring (EHM) Data Review**
   - Extract and archive the last 500 flight cycles of EHM data for all LEAP engine units.
   - Cross-reference vibration trends, exhaust gas temperature (EGT) margins, and oil consumption rates against baseline parameters.
   - Flag any unit exceeding 1.5 standard deviations from fleet average for immediate removal and teardown inspection.

4. **Regulatory & Documentation Compliance**
   - All maintenance actions must comply with 14 CFR Part 121.373 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations) and 121.375 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations: Records).
   - Ensure all logbook entries, work cards, and NDT reports are signed by appropriately rated technicians and countersigned by a Quality Assurance Inspector.
   - Retain all physical evidence, removed components, and inspection media for a minimum of 10 years or until released by the Investigator-in-Charge.

5. **Training & Competency Verification**
   - All NDT Level II and III personnel must complete refresher training on PAUT techniques for titanium fan blades (Course ID: NDT-LEAP-2018-01).
   - Line maintenance crews must review updated troubleshooting flowcharts for uncontained failure indicators (Ref: SWA-TRN-737-ENG-088).

**ACTION REQUIRED**
The following actions are mandatory and time-critical. Failure to comply will result in immediate grounding of affected aircraft and disciplinary review per company policy.

1. **Station Managers & Maintenance Control (Deadline: April 25, 2018, 1800Z)**
   - Acknowledge receipt of QA-2018-042 via the MxTrack compliance portal.
   - Assign dedicated inspection teams to all aircraft with LEAP engine units exceeding 15,000 flight cycles.
   - Submit preliminary fleet status report to Engineering Support by EOD April 25.

2. **Quality Assurance Auditors (Deadline: April 27, 2018, 1200Z)**
   - Conduct spot audits on 100% of completed WO-88412 work orders.
   - Verify calibration status of all PAUT equipment (Ref: CAL-LOG-2018-Q2).
   - Report non-compliant findings directly to the Director of Maintenance & Engineering.

3. **Engineering & Reliability Department (Deadline: May 1, 2018)**
   - Analyze aggregated EHM and inspection data to determine revised inspection intervals.
   - Draft supplemental service bulletin for FAA review and potential incorporation into the approved maintenance program.
   - Coordinate with the NTSB Investigator-in-Charge to provide requested maintenance logs, component traceability records, and technician training files.

4. **Training & Standards Division (Deadline: May 5, 2018)**
   - Deploy updated training modules to all maintenance bases.
   - Verify 100% completion rate for NDT refresher courses and engine failure recognition training.
   - Issue competency certificates and update personnel qualification records in the HRIS system.

All personnel are reminded that safety and regulatory compliance are the foundation of our operations. This Quality Alert supersedes all prior inspection directives for LEAP engine fan assemblies. Direct technical questions to the Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 4400) or Quality Assurance Compliance (Ext. 4415). Do not deviate from approved procedures without written authorization from the Chief Inspector.
