1. SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, Southwest Airlines Co. Flight 1380, a Boeing 737-700, registered N772SW, experienced an uncontained engine failure while en route from New York, New York, to Dallas, Texas. The aircraft was in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet when the event occurred, resulting in rapid decompression, an emergency diversion to Philadelphia International Airport, and one passenger fatality. This preliminary procedural document summarizes initial factual information, establishes the investigative scope, and outlines the administrative actions undertaken by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) as of the date of issuance. All information contained herein is preliminary and subject to revision as additional data is collected, analyzed, and verified.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary data retrieved from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) indicate that the left engine experienced a sudden loss of thrust and abnormal vibration parameters prior to the flight crew’s initiation of an emergency descent. Initial telemetry suggests a rapid pressure differential across the cabin, consistent with a structural breach. Crew communications captured on the CVR reflect immediate recognition of the decompression event and prompt execution of emergency checklists. Passenger and crew witness statements, collected during the initial response phase, describe a loud acoustic event originating from the left side of the aircraft, followed by a sudden rush of air and visible damage to the cabin interior. Several occupants reported observing a compromised window panel in the forward left cabin section, with associated debris scattered across adjacent seating rows.

Meteorological data obtained from the National Weather Service and onboard weather radar imagery indicate that the aircraft was operating in visual meteorological conditions at the time of the event, with no significant convective activity or turbulence reported along the flight path. Preliminary examination of the recovered airframe components reveals localized damage to the left engine nacelle, fan cowl, and adjacent fuselage skin. The breach in the cabin window appears to have been caused by high-velocity debris impact, though the exact trajectory, mass, and origin of the impacting material remain under evaluation. Initial structural assessments suggest that the primary load-bearing elements of the fuselage remained intact, and the aircraft’s pressurization system responded in accordance with design parameters for rapid decompression scenarios. All findings documented in this section are preliminary in nature and subject to change as additional evidence is processed and correlated.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
In accordance with established NTSB protocols, the following investigative groups have been activated to coordinate the collection and analysis of evidence: Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group is operating under the direction of an assigned investigator-in-charge, with technical specialists deployed to the accident site and the aircraft recovery facility. The investigation is being centrally coordinated from NTSB headquarters, where data management, recorder readouts, and interagency communications are being maintained.

Parties to the investigation have been formally designated in accordance with 49 CFR Part 831. Southwest Airlines Co. has been included as a party representative, alongside the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft manufacturer, and the engine manufacturer. Additional technical advisors from relevant industry organizations have been invited to participate under strict confidentiality and procedural guidelines. All party representatives have been briefed on the preliminary scope of the inquiry and the requirement to maintain the integrity of the investigative process.

Evidence secured to date includes the complete airframe, both flight recorders, maintenance logs, crew training records, and recovered engine components. The left engine, identified as a CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan, has been transported to a secure examination facility for detailed teardown and metallurgical analysis. Initial visual inspection of the recovered fan blades and containment ring suggests localized fracture propagation, though definitive failure mechanisms cannot be established at this stage. The investigation will also evaluate compliance with applicable airworthiness standards, including 14 CFR 25.783, which addresses fuselage door and window structural requirements under pressurization and impact loading conditions. All examinations will be conducted using standardized forensic methodologies, with findings documented and peer-reviewed prior to inclusion in subsequent reports.

4. NEXT STEPS
The investigative teams will proceed with a systematic evaluation of all recovered components, with priority given to the powerplant teardown, flight recorder data correlation, and structural integrity testing. Additional witness interviews will be conducted to supplement initial statements, and maintenance history will be cross-referenced with manufacturer service bulletins and airworthiness directives. The Systems group will analyze the aircraft’s pressurization and environmental control system logs to determine the sequence of events following the decompression. The Human Performance group will continue to review crew training records, duty time limitations, and physiological factors associated with rapid decompression at cruise altitude.

A comprehensive metallurgical and non-destructive examination of the LEAP-1B engine components is scheduled to commence within the next ten business days. Concurrently, the Structures group will perform finite element modeling and stress analysis on the damaged fuselage section to assess load distribution and failure thresholds. All data will be integrated into a centralized investigative database, with periodic technical reviews conducted by senior NTSB staff to ensure analytical consistency.

This document represents an early-stage procedural summary and does not constitute a determination of probable cause or contributing factors. All preliminary observations are subject to change as additional evidence is processed and analyzed. The NTSB will issue a subsequent factual update within thirty days, pending the completion of initial component examinations and recorder data validation. Further public briefings will be scheduled as warranted by investigative milestones, and all findings will be published in accordance with established Board reporting protocols. The investigation remains active, and all personnel are directed to adhere to standard evidence handling and information security procedures until the final report is issued.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date and Time
On April 17, 2018, at 1543:12 Eastern Daylight Time (1943:12 Coordinated Universal Time), the accident sequence initiated during en route cruise flight. The event was recorded by the aircraft's flight data recorder and corroborated by air traffic control radar telemetry. The timeline of subsequent emergency procedures, communications, and landing was documented through cockpit voice recorder transcripts, ACARS data link messages, and ATC facility logs.

1.2 Location
The uncontained engine failure occurred at geographic coordinates 39.85° North latitude, 76.12° West longitude, approximately 75 nautical miles west-southwest of Philadelphia International Airport (KPHL), Pennsylvania. The aircraft was operating on airway J146 at a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet. The subsequent emergency descent and diversion were conducted within controlled airspace under the jurisdiction of the Washington Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZDC).

1.3 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-7H4, United States registration N772SW, serial number 28421. The aircraft was owned and operated by Southwest Airlines Co, a certificated air carrier conducting scheduled domestic passenger service. The operator's principal base of operations was located in Dallas, Texas. The aircraft was configured for a maximum of 143 passenger seats and operated under a standard commercial livery.

1.4 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, as a scheduled revenue passenger service from LaGuardia Airport (KLGA), New York, to Dallas Love Field (KDAL), Texas. The flight plan was filed in accordance with 14 CFR 121.601, and the aircraft was dispatched under 14 CFR 121.639. All operational parameters, including weight and balance, fuel load, and alternate airport selection, were within approved limits at the time of departure.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1234567, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The pilot possessed a first-class medical certificate, issued December 12, 2017, with no limitations. Total aeronautical experience was recorded at 11,420 flight hours, of which 8,240 hours were accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The captain served as pilot-in-command for the accident flight and was seated in the left cockpit position.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The first officer held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 2345678, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. A first-class medical certificate was issued October 5, 2017, with no limitations. Total aeronautical experience was recorded at 7,615 flight hours, with 3,120 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer served as second-in-command and was seated in the right cockpit position.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crew members completed recurrent training and proficiency checks within the preceding 12 calendar months, in compliance with 14 CFR 121.433 and 14 CFR 121.439. Training records maintained by Southwest Airlines Co indicated satisfactory performance in all required maneuvers, including engine failure during cruise, rapid decompression, emergency descent, and single-engine approach and landing. Simulator sessions were conducted in a Level D full-flight simulator certified under 14 CFR Part 60. No training deficiencies or remedial actions were documented in either pilot's personnel file.

2.4 Duty Time and Rest Periods
The flight crew reported for duty at 1315 EDT on April 17, 2018. The accident occurred 2 hours and 28 minutes into the duty period. Both pilots were in compliance with 14 CFR 117 rest requirements, having obtained 10.5 hours of uninterrupted rest in a suitable accommodation prior to reporting. Fatigue risk management system (FRMS) data indicated no cumulative duty time violations or circadian disruption factors.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The Boeing 737-7H4 was manufactured in 2000 and delivered to the operator on March 15, 2000. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 56,842 total flight hours and 32,118 flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a standard avionics suite, including dual flight management computers, weather radar, and TCAS II. The airframe was maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.369.

3.2 Engine Configuration and History
The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines. The left engine, manufacturer serial number 789456, had accumulated 18,214 flight hours and 12,408 cycles since new. The right engine, serial number 789457, had accumulated 16,902 flight hours and 11,814 cycles. The left engine was installed on the accident airframe on March 12, 2017, following a scheduled shop visit. Engine health monitoring (EHM) data indicated normal vibration levels, oil consumption rates, and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) margins throughout the preceding 1,200 flight hours.

3.3 Maintenance Records and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance logs were reviewed for compliance with all applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) and service bulletins. The most recent heavy maintenance inspection (C-check) was completed on February 14, 2018, with no deferred items related to the propulsion or pressurization systems. AD 2016-08-09, requiring enhanced ultrasonic inspection of fan blades at specified intervals, was complied with on January 22, 2018. The inspection report documented acceptable blade geometry and no detectable anomalies. All maintenance actions were recorded in the operator's electronic maintenance tracking system and signed off by FAA-certificated airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanics.

3.4 Cabin Pressurization and Window Systems
The cabin pressurization system utilized a dual outflow valve configuration modulated by the cabin pressure controller (CPC). The system was designed to maintain a maximum cabin differential pressure of 8.6 psi. The passenger windows at row 14 consisted of a three-pane assembly: an outer structural acrylic pane, a middle structural polycarbonate pane, and an inner scratch-resistant pane. The window frame was secured to the fuselage skin via a series of fasteners torqued to manufacturer specifications. The assembly was certified under FAA Type Certificate Data Sheet A16WE and complied with 14 CFR 25.773 (Pilot compartment view) and 14 CFR 25.841 (Pressurization systems).

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Conditions
At the time of the event, a high-pressure ridge dominated the northeastern United States, resulting in stable atmospheric stratification and minimal vertical motion. No significant frontal boundaries, convective systems, or jet stream disturbances were present along the flight corridor. Surface pressure gradients were weak, and atmospheric stability indices indicated a low probability of turbulence or wind shear.

4.2 METAR and TAF Data
The nearest aviation weather reporting station, Harrisburg International Airport (KMDT), issued a METAR at 1953 UTC indicating wind 270° at 12 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, clear skies, temperature 18°C, dew point 4°C, and altimeter setting 30.12 inHg. The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) for Philadelphia International Airport (KPHL), valid from 1800 UTC to 1800 UTC the following day, forecasted visual meteorological conditions (VMC) with scattered clouds at 25,000 feet and no significant weather phenomena.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and Radar Data
A review of the National Weather Service Aviation Weather Center database revealed no pilot weather reports (PIREPs) of moderate or greater turbulence, icing, or volcanic ash along the route segment between New York and Pennsylvania. NEXRAD composite radar imagery from the 1943 UTC scan showed no precipitation echoes, convective cells, or anomalous returns within a 100-nautical-mile radius of the aircraft's position.

4.4 Atmospheric Conditions at Altitude
At the cruise altitude of 32,500 feet, the standard atmosphere temperature was approximately -48°C. Upper-air sounding data from the 1800 UTC launch at Wallops Island, Virginia, indicated a westerly wind flow at 45 knots with negligible vertical wind shear. The tropopause was located at approximately 38,000 feet, and the aircraft remained well within the tropospheric layer. No significant clear-air turbulence (CAT) was forecasted or reported in the vicinity.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
The aircraft remained under positive aerodynamic control throughout the event and executed a successful emergency landing at Philadelphia International Airport at 2012 UTC. No in-flight structural breakup or loss of control occurred. Primary damage was localized to the left engine nacelle, the left fuselage skin between stations 400 and 440, and the passenger window assembly at seat 14A. All recovered components were secured, tagged, and transported to the NTSB headquarters in Washington, D.C., for detailed examination.

5.2 Engine Examination Findings
Post-flight teardown and inspection of the left LEAP-1B engine revealed an uncontained failure of the number 13 fan blade. The fracture surface exhibited classic high-cycle fatigue characteristics, including a smooth initiation zone, progressive beach marks, and a final fast-fracture region. The crack originated from a subsurface metallurgical inclusion near the dovetail root, approximately 12 millimeters from the blade platform. The fan case was breached at the 9 o'clock position, and secondary damage was observed to the inlet cowl, thrust reverser cascade vanes, and acoustic liner. The right engine remained fully operational with no evidence of foreign object damage (FOD).

5.3 Fuselage and Cabin Window Damage
High-velocity debris penetrated the left fuselage skin at station 420, waterline 110, creating an irregular aperture measuring approximately 14 inches by 18 inches. The impact compromised the outer and middle panes of the window at row 14, seat A. The inner scratch pane remained structurally intact but was displaced inward by approximately 2.5 inches due to the rapid pressure differential. The resulting decompression event caused a cabin altitude increase from 8,000 feet to 14,500 feet within 12 seconds. Emergency oxygen masks deployed automatically from the passenger service units.

5.4 Debris Field Analysis
Recovered debris included fragments of the fractured fan blade, inlet cowl composite panels, fuselage skin sections, and window frame components. The largest recovered piece of the fan blade measured 18.2 inches in length and was located 45 nautical miles from the point of failure. All debris was cataloged using a standardized grid system, photographed under controlled lighting, and subjected to dimensional metrology and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). No evidence of pre-impact corrosion, thermal degradation, or manufacturing defects was identified in the recovered structural components.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Southwest Airlines Co maintained an FAA-approved Operations Specifications manual detailing emergency response protocols for rapid decompression and engine failure. The company's Flight Operations Manual (FOM) required immediate donning of oxygen masks, initiation of an emergency descent to 10,000 feet or minimum safe altitude, and declaration of an emergency with air traffic control. Crew resource management (CRM) training emphasized standardized callouts, checklist execution, and task delegation. The operator's safety management system (SMS) included mandatory reporting of all abnormal events and a structured internal review process.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
The NTSB has investigated multiple uncontained engine failures involving high-bypass turbofan engines in commercial service. Notable precedents include incidents involving CFM56-7B and LEAP-1B powerplants where fan blade fatigue led to similar uncontained events. These investigations resulted in revised inspection intervals, enhanced non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols, and updated service bulletins addressing blade root geometry and material processing. Historical data indicates that uncontained failures represent a statistically rare occurrence, with industry-wide rates remaining below 0.001 per 100,000 flight hours.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The aircraft and engine were certified under 14 CFR Part 25 (Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes) and 14 CFR Part 33 (Airworthiness Standards: Aircraft Engines), respectively. Compliance with 14 CFR 25.365 (Pressurized compartment loads) and 14 CFR 25.841 (Pressurization systems) was verified during type certification. Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88) requirements for fuel tank system fault tolerance were applicable to the airframe, though not directly related to the propulsion system failure. The operator's maintenance program adhered to 14 CFR 121.373 and 14 CFR 121.375 regarding continuous airworthiness, reliability monitoring, and defect reporting.

6.4 Data Recorder Information
The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered intact and downloaded at the NTSB headquarters. The FDR recorded a sudden loss of left engine N1 and EGT parameters at 1943:12 UTC, followed by a rapid cabin altitude increase from 8,000 feet to 14,500 feet within 12 seconds. The CVR captured the crew's immediate recognition of the event, execution of the emergency descent checklist, and coordination with ATC. All data was preserved, time-synchronized, and analyzed in accordance with NTSB protocols. No anomalies were detected in the recording systems or data acquisition parameters.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the Powerplant and Structures Group in support of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the uncontained engine failure and subsequent rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737-700, registration N772SW, operated by Southwest Airlines. The event occurred on April 17, 2018, during cruise flight at 32,500 feet mean sea level (ft MSL).

The scope of this examination encompasses the left engine (CFM International LEAP-1B), recovered fan blade fragments, engine containment ring segments, impacted fuselage skin panels, cabin window assembly components, and associated flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) parameters. The physical examination and metallurgical testing were conducted between May 2 and May 18, 2018, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the CFM International Engine Test Facility in Evendale, Ohio. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, 49 CFR Part 831, and applicable ASTM/SAE material testing standards.

Items examined included:
- Left engine assembly, serial number (S/N) 884219, part number (P/N) 328A1000-000
- Recovered fan blade fragment, S/N 77412, P/N 328A1000-013
- Engine inlet cowl and containment ring segments
- Fuselage skin panels, stations 420 through 480, left side
- Cabin window frame and glazing assembly, left side, row 14
- FDR (Honeywell SSFDR, P/N 980-4700-042) and CVR (L-3 FA2100, P/N 2100-1020-02) data downloads
- Maintenance records, engine shop visit reports, and non-destructive inspection (NDI) logs

All measurements, test results, and data correlations presented herein are factual observations derived from direct examination, laboratory analysis, and recorded parameter decoding. No operational conclusions or probable cause determinations are included in this report.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737-700, equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines. The LEAP-1B engine features a 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan blade design, a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) containment ring, a 10-stage high-pressure compressor, and a dual-channel Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC) system. The engine was type certified under 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart H, with airworthiness compliance demonstrated per 14 CFR Part 33 and Part 25 requirements. The engine's certification basis includes compliance with 14 CFR 33.94 (containment) and 14 CFR 25.783 (fuselage doors, windows, and pressure vessel integrity), which mandate that the airframe structure withstand the effects of an uncontained engine failure without catastrophic loss of cabin pressurization or structural continuity.

The left engine (S/N 884219) was manufactured in 2015 and installed on the subject aircraft in March 2016. At the time of the event, the engine had accumulated 14,250 flight cycles and 28,412 flight hours. The most recent shop visit occurred in November 2017, during which the engine underwent a performance restoration and fan blade inspection per CFM International Service Bulletin LEAP-1B-72-0045. The inspection was performed by Atlas Air under a Part 145 repair station certificate, utilizing eddy current and ultrasonic phased array NDI techniques. Maintenance records indicate compliance with Southwest Airlines' approved maintenance program, which operates under the regulatory framework of Part 135 for specific charter and maintenance tracking provisions.

The LEAP-1B fan blade design incorporates a titanium alloy leading edge protector, a carbon fiber composite airfoil, and a titanium alloy dovetail root. The containment ring is manufactured from forged Ti-6Al-4V, heat-treated to AMS 4928 specifications, with a nominal thickness of 0.185 inches. The engine nacelle and inlet cowl are constructed from aluminum 2024-T3 and carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) honeycomb sandwich panels. The cabin window assembly consists of a three-pane acrylic glazing system (P/N 65-45678-1) with an outer structural pane, a middle pressure pane, and an inner scratch pane, mounted in an aluminum alloy frame per Boeing Document BAC5000.

Operational history indicates the engine operated within normal parameters throughout its service life, with no recorded exceedances of N1, N2, EGT, or vibration limits. The aircraft's pressurization system, controlled by the cabin pressure controller (CPC), maintained a nominal cabin altitude of 6,500 ft at 32,500 ft MSL cruise, corresponding to a differential pressure (ΔP) of approximately 8.2 PSI.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered fan blade fragment (S/N 77412) revealed a complete separation at the airfoil-to-dovetail transition region. The fracture surface was macroscopically clean, exhibiting distinct fatigue progression zones and a final fast-fracture region. The fatigue crack initiated at the trailing edge, approximately 65% span from the root, within a 12 mm × 8 mm area. Beach marks were clearly visible under low-magnification stereomicroscopy (10x–40x), indicating progressive crack growth over an estimated 1,150–1,300 flight cycles. The final fracture zone measured approximately 142 mm², with a characteristic chevron pattern radiating toward the trailing edge, consistent with high-strain-rate tensile overload.

Metallurgical and chemical analysis was performed per ASTM E399 (fracture toughness) and ASTM E1409 (chemical composition via optical emission spectroscopy). The composite airfoil matrix exhibited a carbon fiber volume fraction of 58.2%, with a resin content of 34.1% and void content of 0.7%, all within CFM International specification limits (void content < 1.5%). The titanium alloy leading edge protector and dovetail root were analyzed per AMS 4911. Chemical composition confirmed Ti-6Al-4V with 6.12% Al, 4.08% V, 0.18% Fe, 0.12% O, and balance Ti. Microhardness testing (Vickers, 1 kg load) yielded an average of HV 348 across the dovetail root, consistent with the specified range of HV 330–360. No evidence of foreign object damage (FOD), corrosion, or manufacturing anomalies was identified.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the fatigue initiation site revealed a localized surface anomaly measuring 0.004 inches in depth, consistent with a machining tool mark from the original manufacturing process. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the absence of contaminant elements. Fatigue crack growth rate calculations, utilizing Paris' Law parameters for Ti-6Al-4V (C = 1.2×10⁻¹¹, m = 3.1), indicate that the crack propagated from the initial 0.004-inch flaw to critical length over approximately 1,220 cycles, aligning with the observed beach mark count.

The engine containment ring exhibited localized plastic deformation and a 45 mm × 32 mm breach on the left forward quadrant. The breach location corresponds to the trajectory of the separated fan blade fragment. Tensile testing of recovered containment ring coupons per ASTM E8 yielded an ultimate tensile strength of 138 ksi and yield strength of 128 ksi, meeting AMS 4928 requirements. The deformation pattern indicates the fragment impacted the ring at an estimated velocity of 1,450 ft/s, exceeding the design containment threshold for localized high-energy impact.

Fuselage skin panels (stations 420–480) were examined for impact damage and structural integrity. The left-side aluminum 2024-T3 skin (nominal thickness 0.063 inches) exhibited a 28 mm × 19 mm penetration at station 445, frame 12. The impact crater showed ductile tearing with radial cracking extending 45 mm. The cabin window frame (P/N 65-45678-1) displayed permanent plastic deformation of 3.2 mm inward, with the outer acrylic pane completely fractured. The middle pressure pane remained intact but exhibited stress whitening and microcracking. The inner scratch pane was undamaged. The window retention clips showed shear deformation consistent with rapid pressure differential loading.

Non-destructive testing of adjacent fuselage stringers and frames revealed no secondary cracking or structural compromise beyond the immediate impact zone. The pressurization bulkhead and door seals remained intact, confirming localized failure rather than systemic structural degradation.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters were extracted from the Honeywell SSFDR using the NTSB Data Analysis Laboratory's proprietary decoding software (v4.8.2). The FDR recorded 88 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with vibration and engine control parameters sampled at 4 Hz. Data synchronization with the CVR and QAR (Quick Access Recorder) was achieved using UTC timecode alignment, with a maximum drift of ±0.15 seconds.

The timeline reconstruction is as follows:
- 14:22:14.8 UTC: Aircraft at 32,500 ft MSL, indicated airspeed 284 knots, Mach 0.78. N1 = 88.4%, N2 = 91.2%, EGT = 742°C, fuel flow = 4,820 lb/hr, cabin ΔP = 8.2 PSI, cabin altitude = 6,480 ft.
- 14:22:15.2 UTC: Left engine N1 vibration (VIB) parameter spikes from 0.6 mils to 4.8 mils. FADEC records a transient N1 command increase to 92.1% in response to vibration compensation logic.
- 14:22:15.9 UTC: N1 rapidly increases to 104.2%, exceeding the redline limit of 100.5%. EGT rises to 890°C within 0.7 seconds. Fuel flow drops to 3,150 lb/hr. FADEC initiates automatic fuel trim reduction and commands autothrottle disconnect.
- 14:22:16.4 UTC: Cabin altitude rate parameter indicates +2,840 ft/min. ΔP drops from 8.2 PSI to 0.4 PSI within 1.2 seconds. Outflow valve position transitions from 42% open to 100% open.
- 14:22:17.1 UTC: Left engine N2 decays to 68.4%. EGT peaks at 912°C before declining. VIB parameter exceeds recorder range (>6.0 mils).
- 14:22:18.5 UTC: Crew initiates emergency descent. Pitch attitude changes from +2.1° to -8.4°. Airspeed increases to 312 knots.
- 14:22:22.0 UTC: Cabin altitude stabilizes at 14,200 ft. ΔP = 0.0 PSI. Outflow valve remains fully open.

Comparison with normal operational parameters confirms a rapid, uncontained failure sequence. Under standard cruise conditions, LEAP-1B N1 vibration remains below 0.8 mils, with EGT margin typically 45–55°C below the redline. The observed N1 overspeed and EGT spike are consistent with sudden loss of fan blade aerodynamic loading and subsequent compressor surge. The FADEC response followed programmed logic per CFM International Engine Control Manual (ECM) LEAP-1B-73-001, which commands fuel reduction and vibration monitoring upon detection of N1/N2 mismatch exceeding 3.5%.

CVR audio analysis corroborates the FDR timeline. At 14:22:15.3 UTC, a loud bang is recorded, followed by crew callouts of "engine failure" and "decompression." The cabin altitude warning horn activates at 14:22:16.1 UTC, consistent with the ΔP drop. The crew's emergency descent initiation aligns with standard operating procedures for rapid decompression.

QAR data, downloaded from the aircraft's ACARS system, confirms the FADEC logged a "FAN BLADE SEPARATION" fault code (ECU Code 34-112) at 14:22:15.6 UTC. The code triggers automatic engine shutdown logic, though the crew manually confirmed the shutdown via the engine master switch at 14:22:19.2 UTC.

Data correlation with physical evidence confirms the sequence: fatigue crack propagation led to sudden blade separation, resulting in uncontained release, nacelle breach, and fuselage impact. The rapid ΔP loss matches the observed window frame deformation and skin penetration. No anomalies were detected in the FDR, CVR, or QAR systems that would indicate data corruption or sensor failure.

5. SUMMARY

The examination and analysis of the left LEAP-1B engine (S/N 884219), recovered components, and recorded flight data yielded the following factual findings:

- A fatigue crack initiated at the trailing edge of the No. 13 fan blade (S/N 77412), approximately 65% span from the root, originating from a 0.004-inch surface machining anomaly.
- The crack propagated over an estimated 1,150–1,300 flight cycles, as evidenced by beach mark spacing and Paris' Law fatigue growth calculations.
- Final fracture occurred at 32,500 ft MSL, resulting in complete blade separation and uncontained release.
- The separated fragment impacted the titanium containment ring, causing a 45 mm × 32 mm breach, and subsequently penetrated the left fuselage skin at station 445, frame 12.
- The cabin window assembly (P/N 65-45678-1) sustained inward plastic deformation of 3.2 mm, with the outer acrylic pane fracturing and the middle pressure pane exhibiting stress whitening.
- FDR data recorded a rapid N1 overspeed to 104.2%, EGT spike to 912°C, and cabin ΔP drop from 8.2 PSI to 0.4 PSI within 1.2 seconds, consistent with uncontained failure and rapid decompression.
- Metallurgical analysis confirmed the fan blade composite matrix and titanium alloy components met CFM International and AMS material specifications. No manufacturing defects, corrosion, or FOD were identified.
- The engine's FADEC system responded per programmed logic, logging fault code 34-112 and initiating fuel trim reduction.
- Maintenance records indicate compliance with Southwest Airlines' approved program and Part 135 tracking requirements, with the most recent NDI inspection performed by Atlas Air in November 2017.
- The containment ring and fuselage structure performed within design parameters for localized impact, though the high-energy fragment trajectory exceeded the nominal containment threshold for the specific impact angle.
- All recorded parameters, physical measurements, and material test results are consistent with a fatigue-driven uncontained engine failure sequence.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER JAMES R. HARRIS
Date: May 14, 2018
Time: 10:00 EDT
Location: NTSB headquarters, Washington, D.C.
Interviewer: Thomas Vance, IIC

Q: Mr. Harris, thank you for coming in today. For the record, please state your full name, your current position, and your role aboard the flight in question.

A: James Robert Harris. I’m a First Officer with Southwest Airlines. I was the right-seat pilot on Flight 1380 on April 17th. I was the monitoring pilot, handling the radios, the QRH, and systems management while the captain flew.

Q: Walk me through the flight from departure up to the point of the event. Include approximate times and your observations.

A: Yeah, sure. We pushed back from LaGuardia around... I want to say 09:45 Eastern. Normal taxi, normal takeoff. We climbed out, handed off to Center, and leveled off at flight level three-two-five. So, 32,500 feet. Autopilot was engaged, autothrottles on, everything was green. I was just running through the cruise checklist, talking to dispatch about fuel burn, maybe checking the weather ahead. It was a very routine morning. I think we were about forty minutes out from Philadelphia when it happened. The clock... I remember glancing at it right before. It was 10:43, maybe 10:44.

Q: Describe the event itself. What did you see, hear, and feel in the cockpit?

A: It was... God, it was loud. Like a cannon shot, honestly. The whole airframe just shuddered violently. I felt a sharp, immediate yaw to the left, and the captain’s hands were already on the yoke. The master caution and master warning both lit up. I looked at the EICAS and the left engine parameters just... fell off the scale. N1 dropped to zero, N2 was spooling down, EGT spiked and then plummeted. We had a fire warning, but it was more than that. Almost instantly, the cabin pressure warning came on. You could hear the wind roaring, like a freight train inside the cabin. It was deafening. The oxygen masks deployed everywhere. I remember thinking, *this isn’t just an engine failure.*

Q: What were your immediate actions following the event?

A: We ran the engine failure and fire checklist. Captain had the controls, I was handling the radios and pulling the QRH. We declared an emergency, requested immediate descent. We were trying to get down to ten thousand as fast as we could, but the decompression was so rapid... the masks dropped, the noise was overwhelming. I remember looking back through the cockpit door—it was actually open, we keep it open during cruise—and seeing... seeing a lot of panic. And then I saw the window. Left side, around row fourteen or fifteen. It was just... gone. The frame was torn out, and there was debris everywhere. I called out the checklist items, but honestly, my voice was shaking. I had to take a breath, reset, and keep going.

Q: You mentioned the cabin window. Can you describe what you observed regarding the flight attendants’ response and the passenger situation?

A: Yeah. The lead flight attendant, she was... she was trying to get to that row. But the wind was pulling everything out. I think it was about three or four minutes after the initial bang. We were descending through twenty thousand. The captain was flying manually, fighting the asymmetry. I was on the radio with Philly approach, giving them our position, our intentions. We were diverting to PHL. When we finally leveled off at ten thousand, the captain asked me to check the cabin. I opened the door, and the noise was still there, but manageable. The flight attendants were already on oxygen. They told me there was a passenger... a woman, she was partially out of the window. They were pulling her back in. It was... it was chaotic. They got her back inside, started CPR. I could see the flight attendants were doing everything they could, but... you know, the situation was beyond anything we train for in the sim.

Q: Let’s discuss the aircraft’s structural response. The 737-700 is certified under 14 CFR Part 25 for transport category operations. Did the airframe behave as expected during the rapid decompression?

A: Structurally, yeah, I mean... the fuselage held. The pressure bulkheads didn’t fail, the wings were fine. But the window... that’s a different story. The debris took out the window and the surrounding skin. I know the certification standards for 14 CFR Part 25 require containment and damage tolerance, but this was an uncontained failure. The shrapnel just... it went right through. The flight controls were still responsive, though. We had some vibration, but the hydraulics were fine. The airplane did what it was designed to do, mostly. It’s just that the energy from that fan blade... it exceeded the design envelope for that specific area.

Q: Have you had any training or experience with newer engine types, like the LEAP-1B, that might have influenced your initial assessment or maintenance awareness?

A: Not directly. I mean, we fly the CFM56-7Bs on the -700s. The LEAP-1B is on the MAX series, right? Different fan blade design, different containment ring, different inspection cycles. I’ve read the bulletins, done the computer-based training, but... honestly, in the moment, you don’t think about the engine model. You just react to the parameters. N1 drops, fire warning, yaw, decompression. The checklist is the same. But yeah, I know Southwest is transitioning, and the maintenance protocols for the LEAP-1B are a bit different. This was definitely the older engine, though. I remember looking at the maintenance logs before the flight, everything was current.

Q: I see from your personnel file that you previously flew for a regional operator under 14 CFR part 135. How did that experience compare to this event, and did it influence your emergency response?

A: Oh, yeah. Back in the day, flying turboprops under part 135, we had... well, we had less automation, obviously. But the emergency training was more... hands-on, I guess. You didn’t have the same level of simulator fidelity. When I moved to Southwest, the training was much more rigorous, especially for high-altitude emergencies. But nothing really prepares you for the actual sound of a window blowing out at cruise. The 135 operations were good for building hours, but this... this was a different beast. I think the part 135 experience helped me stay calm under pressure, though. You learn to prioritize: fly the airplane, communicate, run the checklist. That sequence doesn’t change, no matter what you’re flying.

Q: Let’s go back to the timeline. You mentioned the event occurred around 10:43 AM. Can you confirm the sequence of your emergency descent, approach, and landing?

A: Yeah, I think it was 10:43 Eastern. We started the descent immediately. We were down to ten thousand by... maybe 10:48? Five minutes. We were heavy, so we had to manage speed carefully. We declared a Mayday, got vectors for runway 27L at PHL. The captain was doing a great job, but the left engine was basically a dead weight, creating drag. We had to use a lot of right rudder. We landed... I want to say 10:58. It was a firm landing, but we stopped on the runway. Fire trucks were already there. We shut down the right engine, ran the evacuation checklist. The slides deployed, everyone got out. I was the last one off, after checking the cockpit.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add for the record, Mr. Harris?

A: Just... the crew did everything they could. The flight attendants, they were incredible. And the captain, he kept us flying. I know the investigation is going to look at the fan blade, the inspection intervals, all of it. I just hope... I hope the data helps prevent this from happening again. I’ve been to NTSB headquarters before for training, but sitting here now, it’s... it’s heavy. I’m just glad we got the plane down.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Harris. We’ll review the transcript and may follow up with additional questions as the investigation progresses.

A: Yeah, of course. Whatever you need.

MEMORANDUM

DATE: November 14, 2023
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service & Flight Standards Service
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-19-012 THROUGH A-19-018
REFERENCE: NTSB ACCIDENT NUMBER DCA18MA088; DOCKET NO. FAA-2019-0452; AD 2018-10-09

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendations A-19-012 through A-19-018, issued in the aftermath of the in-flight uncontained engine failure and subsequent rapid decompression event involving a Boeing 737-700, registered N772SW, operated by Southwest Airlines Co., on April 17, 2018. The referenced incident occurred during cruise flight at flight level 325 (32,500 feet MSL) and resulted in one passenger fatality and multiple injuries. This document addresses compliance obligations under 14 CFR Part 21, 14 CFR Part 25, 14 CFR part 121, and Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88), as they pertain to engine containment, fuselage penetration resistance, and operator maintenance program oversight. The regulatory framework herein references Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-10-09, Amendment 39-19288, and subsequent type certificate data sheet (TCDS) revisions for the CFM International LEAP-1B engine series, as integrated into the affected airframe configuration.

2. BACKGROUND
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) maintains regulatory authority over the design, production, and continued airworthiness of civil aircraft and associated powerplants under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations. The subject accident prompted an immediate review of the certification basis for high-bypass turbofan engines installed on transport category aircraft, specifically evaluating compliance with 14 CFR 25.903(d) (Engine containment) and 14 CFR 25.783 (Fuselage doors and windows). Historically, the certification of the Boeing 737 Next Generation series, including the -700 variant, was predicated upon compliance with 14 CFR Part 25, Amendment 25-46, which established baseline requirements for structural integrity and emergency evacuation. Subsequent amendments, including Amendment 25-115, introduced enhanced requirements for damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation.

The operator, Southwest Airlines, holds an Air Carrier Certificate under 14 CFR part 121, Subpart L, and is required to maintain an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.368 and 14 CFR 121.373. The powerplant in question, designated under the LEAP-1B type certificate, is subject to ongoing airworthiness directives issued pursuant to 14 CFR Part 39. Prior to the April 2018 event, the FAA had issued multiple ADs addressing fan blade inspection intervals and ultrasonic testing (UT) protocols for similar engine architectures. However, the uncontained failure mode observed in this incident revealed latent vulnerabilities in the fatigue life prediction models utilized during the original type certification process.

Furthermore, Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 mandates fuel tank system review and maintenance program enhancements to mitigate ignition sources. While SFAR 88 primarily addresses fuel system safety, its underlying risk-assessment methodology has been extrapolated to evaluate secondary structural damage pathways resulting from high-energy debris release. The NTSB’s preliminary findings indicated that the failure originated from a fatigue crack in a fan blade, which propagated undetected through multiple inspection cycles, ultimately resulting in casing breach and fuselage penetration. This sequence necessitated a comprehensive regulatory reassessment of inspection intervals, non-destructive testing (NDT) thresholds, and operator compliance verification mechanisms.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A thorough audit of the operator’s maintenance records, engineering directives, and regulatory compliance documentation reveals that Southwest Airlines maintained nominal adherence to the approved CAMP and applicable ADs at the time of the incident. The assigned Principal Inspector (PI) for the certificate holder confirmed that all mandatory service bulletins and airworthiness directives were incorporated into the operator’s maintenance tracking system within the prescribed compliance windows. However, the investigation identified systemic deficiencies in the predictive maintenance algorithms governing high-cycle fatigue components, particularly those subject to variable operational stress profiles.

Under 14 CFR 21.101, the type certificate holder is obligated to report any condition that could adversely affect the airworthiness of the product. The manufacturer’s service difficulty reporting (SDR) data indicated an anomalous increase in fan blade tip rub events, which were not adequately correlated with the fatigue life extension models approved under the original type certification basis. This disconnect highlights a regulatory gap in the continuous airworthiness notification process, specifically regarding the integration of operational data into revised inspection thresholds.

Additionally, compliance with 14 CFR 121.344 requires operators to establish procedures that ensure the continued airworthiness of all aircraft systems. The FAA’s oversight review determined that while the operator’s Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and configuration deviation list (CDL) were properly maintained, the operator’s engineering department lacked a formalized protocol for real-time telemetry analysis of engine vibration parameters. This deficiency, while not a direct violation of existing regulations, represents a latent risk factor that compromises the proactive identification of incipient structural failures.

The regulatory framework governing engine containment, as codified in 14 CFR Part 25, assumes a deterministic failure mode that does not fully account for the synergistic effects of material degradation, environmental exposure, and extended service intervals. The FAA acknowledges that the current certification standards require modernization to incorporate probabilistic risk assessment methodologies, particularly for legacy airframes retrofitted with next-generation powerplants. The oversight actions taken to date include the issuance of emergency AD 2018-10-09, which mandated immediate ultrasonic inspection of all affected fan blades, and the establishment of a joint industry-government working group to revise the engine maintenance review board (EMRB) guidelines.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified regulatory gaps and operational findings, the FAA hereby mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Enhanced Inspection Protocols: All operators of aircraft equipped with the LEAP-1B engine series shall implement revised ultrasonic inspection intervals in accordance with Service Bulletin CFM-ENG-2018-0042, as incorporated by reference in AD 2023-14-08. Compliance shall be achieved within 180 days of the effective date of this directive. Operators must submit a revised maintenance program supplement to the assigned Principal Inspector for approval, demonstrating integration of the updated inspection thresholds into the CAMP.

b. Telemetry and Vibration Monitoring: Pursuant to 14 CFR 121.344 and 14 CFR 121.373, certificate holders shall install and calibrate real-time engine health monitoring (EHM) systems capable of detecting anomalous vibration signatures indicative of fan blade fatigue. Operators shall submit a compliance plan to the Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) within 90 days, with full operational implementation required within 12 months. The FAA will conduct random audits of EHM data logs to verify compliance.

c. Type Certificate Data Sheet Revision: The Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) shall initiate a rulemaking action to amend 14 CFR Part 25, specifically sections 25.903 and 25.783, to incorporate enhanced debris trajectory modeling and fuselage penetration resistance criteria. A notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) shall be published in the Federal Register within 240 days, with a public comment period of 60 days. The final rule shall establish mandatory retrofit requirements for legacy transport category aircraft operating under 14 CFR part 121.

d. Regulatory Oversight Enhancement: The FAA will implement a quarterly compliance review cycle for all Part 121 operators utilizing high-bypass turbofan engines. The PI assigned to each certificate holder shall conduct on-site audits of maintenance tracking systems, SDR reporting accuracy, and engineering directive implementation. Findings shall be documented in the Safety Assurance System (SAS) and reported to the Office of Aviation Safety in Washington, D.C., for centralized risk assessment.

e. MMEL and Emergency Procedure Updates: Operators shall revise their Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) and emergency response protocols to address rapid decompression scenarios resulting from uncontained engine failures. Training curricula for flight crews and maintenance personnel shall be updated to reflect revised emergency descent procedures and cabin pressure management techniques. Compliance shall be verified during the next scheduled operational evaluation, not to exceed 12 months from the date of this memorandum.

The FAA remains committed to the continuous improvement of aviation safety standards and the rigorous enforcement of regulatory compliance. All affected parties shall acknowledge receipt of this directive and submit a preliminary compliance status report to the designated FSDO within 30 days. Failure to adhere to the prescribed timelines may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR Part 13, including certificate suspension or revocation.

Southwest Flight Diverts After Engine Failure Claims Passenger’s Life

Marcus Thorne, The Metropolitan Herald
PHILADELPHIA — A Southwest Airlines Co. passenger jet bound for Texas made a harrowing emergency landing in Philadelphia on Tuesday after a catastrophic engine failure at 32,500 feet killed one passenger and left several others injured. The Boeing 737-700, carrying 143 passengers and five crew members, was forced to descend rapidly after debris from the left engine breached the fuselage and shattered a cabin window.

The incident, which unfolded during the cruise phase of the flight from New York’s LaGuardia Airport to Dallas Love Field, triggered a sudden loss of cabin pressure. Passengers described a deafening bang followed by a violent rush of wind and oxygen masks dropping from the ceiling. One woman was partially pulled through the broken window before fellow travelers and flight attendants managed to pull her back inside. Despite immediate medical intervention, she was pronounced dead after the aircraft touched down at Philadelphia International Airport.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of life and extend our heartfelt condolences to the family and friends of the passenger,” said a Southwest Airlines Co. spokesperson in a statement released Tuesday evening. “Our crew acted swiftly and professionally under extraordinary circumstances, and we are cooperating fully with federal investigators.” The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it is assisting the National Transportation Safety Board, which has dispatched a team to Philadelphia. “The safety of the flying public remains our highest priority,” an FAA representative said. “We are reviewing all available data to understand the sequence of events.”

The aircraft involved is a 17-year-old Boeing 737-700, a workhorse of the commercial aviation industry known for its reliability. The left engine, a CFM International CFM56-7B, experienced what investigators term an “uncontained engine failure”—a rare event where internal components break apart and exit the engine casing, potentially striking the airframe. The resulting rapid decompression, a sudden drop in cabin pressure that can cause hypoxia and physical trauma, forced the pilots to initiate an emergency descent to a lower, breathable altitude.

Aviation safety experts suggest metal fatigue in one of the engine’s fan blades is the most likely culprit, though the official cause remains under investigation. “We’ve seen similar failures in older high-cycle engines where microscopic cracks go undetected during routine inspections,” said Dr. Alan Mercer, a former NTSB investigator and aviation safety consultant. “The industry has learned hard lessons from past tragedies, which is why maintenance protocols and regulatory frameworks like SFAR 88—which originally addressed fuel tank ignition risks—have continuously evolved to mandate stricter inspection intervals and material testing.” Mercer noted that while the 737-700 fleet operates under standard commercial regulations, the broader aviation sector, including cargo and charter operators like Atlas Air, adheres to rigorous maintenance schedules. He added that newer engine designs, such as the LEAP-1B used on the latest 737 MAX series, incorporate advanced composite materials and real-time health monitoring to mitigate similar risks. “Regulatory oversight, whether under 14 CFR Part 135 for commuter operations or Part 121 for major carriers, demands continuous improvement,” Mercer explained. “Every incident like this reinforces the need for predictive maintenance and enhanced non-destructive testing.”

For those aboard the flight, the minutes following the explosion were marked by panic and heroism. “I heard a sound like a cannon, and then the window just blew out,” said passenger David Chen, 42, who was seated three rows behind the breach. “People were screaming, but the flight attendants kept their voices steady. They told us to put our heads down and breathe normally. I’ll never forget the look on the faces of the people who pulled that woman back in.” The family of the deceased passenger, identified by relatives as Jennifer Riordan, a 43-year-old mother of two from Albuquerque, released a brief statement through a family friend. “She was a devoted wife, mother, and nurse who spent her life caring for others,” the statement read. “We are heartbroken and ask for privacy as we grieve.”

Engine failures resulting in fatalities are exceptionally rare in modern commercial aviation. The last comparable incident involving a U.S. carrier occurred in 2016, when a Southwest Airlines flight suffered a similar engine rupture, though that event did not result in a breach of the cabin. The airline has maintained a strong safety record over its five-decade history, operating one of the largest all-Boeing 737 fleets in the world. Industry analysts note that while the 737-700 model has been in service since the late 1990s, its engines undergo mandatory ultrasonic inspections every 30,000 flight cycles. The National Transportation Safety Board has previously recommended enhanced inspection protocols for aging fleets, a push that has gained renewed urgency following Tuesday’s tragedy.

The investigation is now centered at NTSB headquarters in Washington, D.C., where engineers are analyzing the recovered engine components, cockpit voice recorder data, and flight data recorder information. The IIC, a veteran federal investigator leading the probe, confirmed that the team will examine maintenance records, manufacturing history, and pilot response procedures. “We are treating this with the utmost seriousness,” the IIC said during a Tuesday evening press briefing. “Our team is working around the clock to determine exactly what failed, why it failed, and what steps can be taken to prevent a recurrence.” A preliminary report is expected within 30 days, while a final determination could take up to two years. In the meantime, Southwest Airlines Co. has grounded its fleet of 737-700s equipped with the same engine model for expedited inspections, a precautionary measure that has temporarily disrupted hundreds of flights nationwide.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Engineering and Maintenance Safety Division of Southwest Airlines Co (hereinafter referred to as SWA or the Operator) in support of the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the April 17, 2018, in-flight uncontained engine failure. As the operating carrier, our organization has maintained full cooperation with the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration, and the original equipment manufacturer throughout the investigative process. This document outlines our technical position, synthesizes maintenance and operational data, and provides an expert engineering assessment of the contributing factors that led to the catastrophic fan blade separation, subsequent fuselage penetration, and tragic loss of life.

The scope of this submission encompasses three primary areas: (1) a review of the maintenance history, inspection protocols, and compliance frameworks governing the affected engine; (2) a technical evaluation of the metallurgical and structural failure mechanisms, including the limitations of current non-destructive inspection (NDI) methodologies; and (3) an analysis of cabin window retention performance under high-velocity debris impact conditions. Our position is grounded in empirical data, docketed evidence, and established aerospace engineering principles. While we acknowledge the inherent complexity of fatigue-driven failures in high-cycle rotating machinery, this analysis demonstrates that the event was not the result of systemic maintenance deficiencies or regulatory noncompliance, but rather a convergence of material fatigue characteristics, inspection interval limitations, and probabilistic crack propagation that exceeded the detection thresholds of legacy NDI techniques. We submit this analysis to inform the Board’s findings and to support the development of enhanced, data-driven safety standards for commercial aviation.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, the subject Boeing 737-700 was operating at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet when the left engine experienced an uncontained failure. Flight Data Recorder (FDR) parameters, as documented in the NTSB Powerplant Group Chairman’s Report (Docket Item 14-B), indicate a rapid decay in N1 and N2 rotor speeds, accompanied by a sharp increase in engine vibration levels and a subsequent cabin altitude warning. Debris from the failed fan blade assembly penetrated the left fuselage skin, compromised a passenger cabin window, and initiated rapid decompression. Emergency descent procedures were executed, and the aircraft diverted safely to Philadelphia International Airport. Tragically, one passenger sustained fatal injuries due to partial ejection through the compromised window.

The affected engine, a CFM56-7B series turbofan, had accumulated approximately 32,000 flight cycles and 45,000 flight hours at the time of the event. Maintenance records, reviewed and authenticated by our Chief Inspector of Maintenance, confirm that all inspections, borescope examinations, and component replacements were performed in strict accordance with the approved Maintenance Review Board Report (MRBR), manufacturer service bulletins, and Title 14 CFR Part 121 requirements. The most recent fan blade inspection occurred 1,200 cycles prior to the event, utilizing standard eddy current and ultrasonic techniques. No anomalies were documented.

The Lead Investigator assigned to the propulsion group has coordinated closely with our engineering team to review the recovered fan blade fragments, engine casing, and fuselage penetration site. Metallurgical analysis (Docket Item 22-A) confirms that the failure originated in the dovetail region of a single fan blade, where a fatigue crack initiated at a subsurface inclusion and propagated through approximately 60% of the cross-sectional area before final fracture. The crack exhibited classic beach mark morphology consistent with high-cycle fatigue (HCF) under variable amplitude loading.

It is important to contextualize these findings within the broader regulatory and operational framework. Our maintenance program operates under 14 CFR part 121, which mandates rigorous continuing airworthiness management, reliability monitoring, and defect reporting. Additionally, while Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) was originally promulgated to address fuel tank flammability, its underlying risk-assessment methodology and inspection rigor have profoundly influenced our organization’s approach to comprehensive safety management systems (SMS). The principles of proactive hazard identification, layered inspection protocols, and continuous data feedback loops established under SFAR 88 have been adapted across our engineering divisions, including engine health monitoring and cabin integrity programs.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The uncontained failure of the left engine fan blade represents a complex interaction between material science, cyclic loading environments, and inspection technology limitations. Our engineering assessment focuses on three interrelated domains: fatigue crack initiation and propagation, NDI sensitivity and interval optimization, and cabin window structural response to debris impact.

Fatigue Crack Initiation and Propagation
Fractographic examination of the recovered fan blade reveals that crack initiation occurred at a subsurface microstructural anomaly within the titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) dovetail root. This region is subjected to extreme centrifugal and aerodynamic loading, with stress concentrations amplified by the geometric transition between the blade platform and the dovetail. The crack propagated under mixed-mode loading, with low-cycle fatigue (LCF) dominating during takeoff and climb phases, and high-cycle fatigue (HCF) governing cruise and descent operations. The beach mark spacing indicates a gradual propagation rate over approximately 800–1,000 cycles, consistent with the time elapsed since the last scheduled inspection.

The stochastic nature of fatigue crack growth in titanium alloys is well-documented in aerospace literature. While deterministic models can predict average crack propagation rates, localized microstructural variations, residual stresses from manufacturing processes, and operational load spectra introduce significant variability. In this case, the crack remained subsurface for a substantial portion of its life, rendering it undetectable by conventional surface-oriented NDI methods until it breached the outer boundary.

NDI Sensitivity and Inspection Interval Limitations
Our maintenance program employs a combination of fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI), eddy current testing (ECT), and phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) for fan blade evaluation. The most recent inspection, conducted per the approved maintenance planning document, utilized standard ECT probes calibrated to detect surface-breaking cracks exceeding 0.010 inches in length. However, the subsurface nature of the initiating flaw, combined with the complex geometry of the dovetail, limited the effective penetration depth and signal-to-noise ratio of the inspection equipment.

Industry-wide, the aviation sector has recognized that traditional inspection intervals are often based on conservative statistical models rather than real-time component health data. The gap between the last inspection and the final fracture was within the approved cycle limit, but the crack growth rate exceeded the probabilistic threshold assumed during interval development. This highlights a critical limitation in legacy maintenance programs: they are inherently reactive to known failure modes rather than predictive of emerging anomalies.

Comparative analysis with modern engine architectures, such as the LEAP-1B powerplant, demonstrates significant advancements in dovetail stress distribution, surface treatment processes, and integrated health monitoring. The LEAP-1B engine incorporates optimized blade root geometries, advanced shot-peening techniques, and embedded strain gauges that enable continuous load tracking. While retrofitting these technologies into legacy CFM56-7B fleets is not economically or structurally feasible, the inspection methodologies and predictive algorithms developed for the LEAP-1B architecture provide a valuable benchmark for enhancing legacy NDI protocols.

Cabin Window Structural Response
The penetration of the cabin window by high-velocity debris resulted in rapid decompression and the tragic fatality. The affected window assembly, a multi-pane acrylic and polycarbonate laminate, is designed to withstand cabin pressure differentials and minor impact events. However, the kinetic energy of the fan blade fragment, estimated at approximately 1,200 ft-lbs based on FDR-derived rotor speed decay and trajectory modeling, exceeded the design threshold for localized penetration.

Our structural engineering team has reviewed the window retention frame, fastener torque records, and laminate bonding specifications. All components were within manufacturer tolerances and complied with 14 CFR Part 121 airworthiness standards. The failure mode was not indicative of a systemic design flaw, but rather an extreme, low-probability impact scenario that falls outside the original certification envelope. Modern cabin window designs have since incorporated improved retention clips, reinforced outer panes, and enhanced debris deflection geometries, which should be evaluated for retrofit applicability across the legacy fleet.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the comprehensive review of maintenance records, metallurgical evidence, operational data, and engineering analysis, Southwest Airlines Co concludes the following:

First, the uncontained engine failure was caused by a fatigue crack that initiated at a subsurface microstructural anomaly in the fan blade dovetail and propagated under mixed-mode cyclic loading. The crack growth rate, while within the bounds of known titanium alloy behavior, exceeded the detection capability of the inspection methodology employed at the time of the last scheduled examination.

Second, the maintenance program operated in full compliance with 14 CFR part 121, manufacturer service bulletins, and approved inspection intervals. The failure was not attributable to procedural deviations, inadequate training, or deferred maintenance. Rather, it reflects the inherent limitations of probabilistic inspection scheduling when applied to components with complex stress geometries and subsurface crack initiation mechanisms.

Third, the cabin window penetration and subsequent rapid decompression were the result of an extreme debris impact event that exceeded the original design certification parameters. While the window assembly met all regulatory requirements, the incident underscores the need for enhanced retention standards and improved debris deflection capabilities in legacy aircraft configurations.

We respectfully submit that the primary contributing factors were: (1) the stochastic nature of subsurface fatigue crack initiation in titanium fan blades; (2) the sensitivity limitations of conventional NDI techniques for complex dovetail geometries; and (3) the absence of real-time, predictive health monitoring for legacy engine fleets. These factors, while individually manageable, converged to create a low-probability, high-consequence event.

To mitigate future occurrences, we recommend the following safety improvements: (1) adoption of advanced phased-array ultrasonic and thermographic inspection techniques for high-cycle fan blades; (2) reduction of inspection intervals for blades exceeding 25,000 cycles, calibrated to actual crack growth data rather than conservative statistical models; (3) implementation of AI-assisted NDI data analysis to improve defect recognition and reduce human interpretation variability; and (4) evaluation of enhanced cabin window retention and debris deflection standards for retrofit across the 737 Classic and Next Generation fleets.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In the immediate aftermath of the April 17, 2018, event, Southwest Airlines Co initiated a comprehensive corrective action program in coordination with the FAA, the engine manufacturer, and industry safety organizations. The following actions have been completed or are currently in progress:

Fleet-Wide Inspection Campaign: Within 72 hours of the incident, our organization issued a mandatory service directive requiring 100% of the CFM56-7B fleet to undergo enhanced ultrasonic and eddy current inspections of all fan blade dovetails. Over 1,200 engines were inspected, resulting in the identification and replacement of 14 blades exhibiting early-stage crack indications. All findings were reported to the FAA and incorporated into our reliability tracking database.

Maintenance Program Revision: Our engineering division, under the oversight of the Chief Inspector, revised the approved maintenance planning document to incorporate reduced inspection intervals for high-cycle fan blades. The new protocol mandates phased-array ultrasonic testing at 50% of the previous cycle threshold, with mandatory blade removal and laboratory analysis for any indication exceeding 0.005 inches.

Training and Human Factors Enhancement: We have implemented a revised NDI technician certification program that includes advanced defect recognition training, simulation-based scenario evaluation, and mandatory peer-review protocols for critical component inspections. The program aligns with industry best practices and incorporates lessons learned from the metallurgical analysis of the failed blade.

Cabin Window Integrity Program: In coordination with the airframe manufacturer, we have initiated a fleet-wide inspection of all cabin window retention frames, fastener torque values, and laminate bonding conditions. Windows exhibiting wear, micro-fractures, or retention clip degradation have been replaced with upgraded assemblies featuring reinforced outer panes and improved fastener retention geometry.

Looking forward, Southwest Airlines Co proposes the following initiatives to further enhance safety and operational resilience:

Predictive Maintenance Integration: We are developing a machine learning-driven engine health monitoring system that integrates FDR data, vibration analysis, and historical maintenance records to predict component degradation trends. This system will enable condition-based maintenance scheduling, moving beyond fixed-interval inspections toward real-time risk assessment.

Regulatory Collaboration: We will continue to work with the FAA and industry working groups to advocate for updated airworthiness directives that reflect modern NDI capabilities and fatigue modeling advancements. Our organization supports the harmonization of inspection standards across legacy and next-generation fleets, ensuring that safety improvements are scalable and economically viable.

Industry Knowledge Sharing: We have committed to publishing de-identified inspection data and crack propagation models in industry safety forums, including the Aviation Safety Information Analysis and Sharing (ASIAS) program. By contributing to collective industry knowledge, we aim to accelerate the development of standardized predictive maintenance protocols.

The tragic loss of life on April 17, 2018, remains a profound reminder of the responsibilities we bear as aviation professionals. Southwest Airlines Co remains steadfast in its commitment to continuous safety improvement, regulatory compliance, and transparent collaboration with the NTSB, the FAA, and our industry partners. We submit this analysis with the expectation that it will inform evidence-based safety recommendations and contribute to the ongoing advancement of commercial aviation safety standards.

HEADER:
   TO: Fleet Engineering, Maintenance Control, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance Division
   FROM: Director of Airworthiness & Safety Compliance, Engineering & Maintenance
   DATE: 23 April 2018
   SUBJECT: URGENT: Enhanced Inspection Protocols & Containment Verification Following Uncontained Engine Failure Event
   REF: QA-2018-0417, ENG-ALERT-004, WO-737-8892, AMM-REV-42.1

PURPOSE:
This Safety Communication and Quality Alert is issued to mandate immediate inspection, documentation, and procedural updates for all high-bypass turbofan installations across our fleet. The directive establishes revised non-destructive testing (NDT) intervals, containment ring verification steps, and secondary debris path assessments. Compliance is mandatory for all maintenance bases, line stations, and contracted MRO partners.

BACKGROUND:
On 17 April 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operating at 32,500 feet experienced an uncontained failure of the left engine. Post-incident analysis confirms that a fractured fan blade initiated a cascade event, resulting in fuselage penetration, rapid cabin decompression, and one fatality. Preliminary metallurgical reports indicate high-cycle fatigue originating at the dovetail root, compounded by undetected micro-cracking during previous shop visits.

While our primary fleet operates different engine variants, the failure mode directly impacts our maintenance philosophy regarding fan blade retention, containment system integrity, and post-impact structural assessment. Recent data-sharing agreements with Atlas Air (AAI) have highlighted similar fatigue progression patterns in their CFM56 and LEAP-1B powerplants, particularly in high-cycle, short-haul operational profiles. 

Regulatory frameworks governing these systems remain anchored in 14 CFR Part 25 (Federal Aviation Regulations Part 25), specifically Sections 25.903 and 25.904, which mandate engine containment and fire protection standards. Additionally, our ongoing compliance with SFAR 88 (Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88) requires that all fuel tank safety modifications and wiring harness routing be cross-referenced during any post-debris impact inspection. The April 17 event underscores the necessity of integrating these regulatory baselines into our routine heavy maintenance and line check workflows.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, the following technical directives supersede previous inspection intervals and work card procedures:

1. Fan Blade & Retention System Inspection
   - All fan blades (P/N 44A-9921 series and equivalent) must undergo phased-array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) at the dovetail root and leading edge.
   - Eddy current inspection of the fan disk retention grooves is now required at every 1,500 flight cycles, reduced from the previous 3,000-cycle interval.
   - Reference Work Order WO-737-8892, Task 72-21-00-220-801 for updated torque verification and locking tab replacement procedures.

2. Containment Ring & Secondary Structure Verification
   - Inspect the forward fan case containment ring for micro-fractures, delamination, or impact scoring. Use borescope inspection ports 4A through 4D.
   - Any evidence of casing deformation exceeding 0.015 inches requires immediate engine removal and return to the MRO facility for full teardown.
   - Cross-check adjacent fuselage skin panels, window frames, and primary flight control cable routing for secondary debris impact. Document all findings using Form QA-INS-09.

3. LEAP Engine Fleet Integration
   - Although the incident involved a legacy high-bypass design, our LEAP engine installations (LEAP-1B/1A variants) are subject to identical inspection rigor. The composite fan blade architecture and titanium containment ring require specialized NDT protocols outlined in Service Bulletin SB-LEAP-2018-003.
   - Maintenance Control will issue revised task cards for LEAP-1B fan blade retention checks by 27 April 2018.

4. Regulatory & Documentation Alignment
   - All inspection records must explicitly reference compliance with 14 CFR Part 25 airworthiness standards. Failure to document containment verification will result in a Level 2 nonconformance.
   - SFAR 88 compliance audits will be integrated into the post-inspection sign-off process. Verify that all fuel tank ignition source mitigation wiring remains undisturbed and properly routed following any debris impact assessment.
   - Update the Aircraft Maintenance Log (AML) with the following mandatory entry: “ENG-CONT-VERIFIED PER QA-2018-0417. NDT COMPLETED. NO ANOMALIES DETECTED.”

ACTION REQUIRED:
The following actions are mandatory and time-bound:

1. Immediate Fleet Sweep (0–72 Hours)
   - Line Maintenance Supervisors: Ground all aircraft exceeding 1,200 flight cycles since last fan blade inspection. Initiate PAUT and eddy current checks per WO-737-8892.
   - Maintenance Control: Prioritize hangar slots for aircraft with >15,000 total cycles. Coordinate with AAI technical support for LEAP-1B specific NDT equipment calibration.

2. Procedural Updates & Training (7–14 Days)
   - Quality Assurance Division: Distribute revised work cards and inspection checklists to all domestic and international stations.
