   - Training Department: Conduct mandatory 4-hour recurrent training for all Level 3 and Level 4 powerplant technicians. Focus on containment ring assessment, secondary debris path evaluation, and SFAR 88 wiring verification. Completion certificates must be uploaded to the LMS by 07 May 2018.

3. Reporting & Compliance Verification (Ongoing)
   - All inspection results must be submitted via the Engineering Data Portal (EDP) within 24 hours of completion.
   - Quality Assurance will conduct random audits of 15% of completed inspections. Discrepancies will trigger immediate corrective action requests (CARs) and potential suspension of station maintenance authority.
   - Report any findings of fan blade cracking, retention groove wear, or containment ring deformation directly to the Director of Airworthiness via secure channel ENG-ALERT-004.

This directive remains in effect until superseded by manufacturer service bulletins or FAA Airworthiness Directives. Failure to comply constitutes a violation of internal quality management standards and may result in regulatory noncompliance under 14 CFR Part 25 and SFAR 88. Direct all technical inquiries to Fleet Engineering or the Quality Assurance Help Desk.

1. SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700, operated by Atlas Air, experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. Initial information indicates that debris from the left engine penetrated the fuselage and compromised a passenger cabin window, resulting in rapid decompression and one fatality. The aircraft subsequently diverted to a nearby airport, where it landed without further incident.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary data recovered from the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder are currently undergoing initial readout and validation. Early telemetry suggests a sudden loss of thrust and abnormal vibration parameters associated with the left engine prior to the decompression event. Initial witness accounts from flight crew members and surviving passengers describe a loud bang followed by rapid cabin pressure loss, visible debris ingress, and the deployment of oxygen masks. These accounts remain uncorroborated and are subject to further verification through structured interviews and cross-referencing with recorded data. Meteorological data obtained from the National Weather Service and onboard weather radar indicate that the aircraft was operating in clear air conditions with no significant convective activity, turbulence, or precipitation reported along the flight path at the time of the event. Preliminary examination of the airframe, conducted by the Lead Investigator and structural specialists, revealed localized fuselage damage consistent with high-energy debris impact, primarily concentrated around the left wing root and forward cabin section. The compromised window frame exhibited outward deformation, and adjacent structural panels showed evidence of puncture and tearing. Maintenance records provided by Atlas Air, Inc. indicate that the affected powerplant, identified as a CFM LEAP-1B turbofan, had accumulated approximately 14,200 flight hours and 9,800 cycles since new. Initial review of these records suggests compliance with standard maintenance intervals, though a comprehensive audit is pending. All findings documented herein are preliminary, derived from early-stage data collection, and remain subject to revision as additional evidence is secured and analyzed.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
In accordance with established National Transportation Safety Board protocols, the following investigative groups have been formally activated: Operations, Structures, Powerplants, Systems, Human Performance, and Survival Factors. Each group has been assigned a designated chair and is operating under the direct oversight of the designated Lead Investigator. The investigation is being conducted in coordination with the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, and the operator, all of whom have been designated as parties to the investigation under the provisions of 14 CFR Part 121 and applicable NTSB procedural guidelines. The Chief Inspector has authorized the deployment of specialized forensic engineering teams to the aircraft recovery site and has mandated strict chain-of-custody protocols for all recovered components. To date, the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, and several fragmented engine components have been secured and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination. Additional debris fields have been mapped, and preliminary photographic documentation has been completed. Planned examinations include metallurgical analysis of fractured fan blades, non-destructive testing of the recovered engine casing, and a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s maintenance tracking system. The Systems group will conduct a functional evaluation of the cabin pressurization and emergency oxygen deployment mechanisms, while the Human Performance group will initiate preliminary interviews with flight crew and cabin personnel. All investigative activities are being documented in real time, and access to the investigation site remains restricted to authorized personnel only.

4. NEXT STEPS
The immediate focus of the investigation will center on the complete disassembly and forensic evaluation of the LEAP-1B powerplant, with particular attention to the fan disk, containment ring, and associated mounting hardware. The Powerplants group will coordinate with the engine manufacturer to review design specifications, service bulletins, and historical failure modes relevant to this engine family. Concurrently, the Operations group will finalize the reconstruction of the flight profile, integrating radar data, air traffic control communications, and crew statements to establish a precise timeline of events. The LI will convene a preliminary technical review within the next 30 days to assess initial laboratory results and determine whether additional specialized testing, such as computational fluid dynamics modeling or fatigue crack propagation analysis, is warranted. The Office of the Chief Inspector has directed that all party submissions, maintenance logs, and training records be compiled and submitted to the NTSB docket within 45 days of this report’s issuance. A follow-up factual update will be published upon completion of the initial recorder readouts and the preliminary metallurgical assessments, anticipated within 60 to 90 days. All subsequent findings, procedural adjustments, and investigative milestones will be communicated through official NTSB channels. It is emphasized that the information contained in this document represents early-stage observations only, and no determinations regarding operational deficiencies, maintenance practices, or probable cause have been made. The investigation remains active, and all conclusions will be deferred until a comprehensive analysis of all available evidence is complete.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On April 17, 2018, at 15:43:12 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), an uncontained engine failure occurred aboard a Boeing 737-7H4, registration N772SW, during en route cruise flight. The event transpired at approximately 39.8421° N latitude, 75.6103° W longitude, approximately 30 nautical miles (NM) west-northwest of Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Pennsylvania. The aircraft was operating at a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet mean sea level (MSL), corresponding to Flight Level 325 (FL325). The aircraft subsequently initiated an emergency descent and diverted to PHL, landing on Runway 27L at 16:02:45 EDT.

1.2 Aircraft Type, Registration, and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-7H4, serial number 28421, registered to Southwest Airlines (SWA). The operator, Southwest Airlines, is a certificated air carrier conducting scheduled passenger transportation services. The aircraft was configured for 143 passenger seats and operated under a standard commercial air carrier certificate. The flight was designated as a scheduled revenue service from LaGuardia Airport (LGA), New York, to Dallas Love Field (DAL), Texas.

1.3 Nature of the Flight and Regulatory Classification
The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, governing domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. Maintenance support and component overhaul activities for the propulsion system were contracted to an external repair station operating under 14 CFR Part 135 authority, which maintained a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) interface with the primary operator. The flight plan was filed under instrument flight rules (IFR), and the aircraft was equipped with a functioning flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which were recovered and downloaded for analysis.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1234567, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on January 12, 2018, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 11,247 hours, with 8,912 hours accumulated in the Boeing 737 series. The captain completed a line-oriented flight training (LOFT) session on February 14, 2018, and a proficiency check on March 22, 2018, both of which were documented as satisfactory.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The first officer held an ATP certificate, certificate number 2345678, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. A first-class medical certificate was issued on December 5, 2017, with no restrictions. Total flight time was recorded at 7,634 hours, with 3,189 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer completed recurrent simulator training on January 28, 2018, and a line check on March 10, 2018, with all performance metrics meeting operator standards.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crewmembers were within the 90-day recency requirements for takeoffs and landings as mandated by 14 CFR § 121.439. The captain had accumulated 142 flight hours in the preceding 30 days, while the first officer had accumulated 118 flight hours. Training records indicate completion of emergency descent procedures, rapid decompression drills, and engine failure during cruise scenarios during the most recent recurrent training cycle. The Chief Inspector reviewed the crew training documentation and maintenance release logs prior to the flight, verifying compliance with all applicable airworthiness and operational directives. No discrepancies were noted in the crew qualification files or duty/rest logs, which were in accordance with 14 CFR § 121.470 and § 121.471.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Airframe Data
The Boeing 737-7H4 was manufactured in 2000 and delivered to the operator on May 18, 2000. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 58,412 total flight hours and 42,108 total flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a standard avionics suite, including dual flight management computers (FMC), autopilot/flight director systems, and a digital flight data acquisition unit (DFDAU). The pressurization system utilized a dual-pack configuration with automatic cabin altitude control, set to maintain a maximum differential pressure of 8.6 psi.

3.2 Engine and Propulsion Systems
The aircraft was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B high-bypass turbofan engines, serial numbers 88421 (left) and 88422 (right). The left engine, designated as the number 1 powerplant, had accumulated 14,203 total flight hours and 10,887 cycles since new. The engine was equipped with a 24-blade titanium fan assembly, a full-authority digital engine control (FADEC) system, and a dual-channel electronic engine control (EEC) unit. The engine nacelle consisted of an inlet cowl, fan cowl, thrust reverser, and exhaust nozzle, all secured with quick-release fasteners and torque-sealed hardware.

3.3 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft was maintained in accordance with an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check) was completed on November 12, 2017, at 56,890 airframe hours. The left engine underwent a shop visit on August 4, 2017, during which fan blades were inspected using fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) and eddy current testing (ECT). All blades were cleared for service. Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-02-51, requiring enhanced ultrasonic inspection of fan blade dovetails, was scheduled for compliance at the next engine removal. Maintenance records indicate that the engine was released to service by a certificated repair station operating under 14 CFR Part 135, with all work orders signed off by authorized inspectors. The Chief Inspector verified the maintenance release documentation and confirmed that all deferred items were within minimum equipment list (MEL) allowances.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Conditions
At the time of the event, a high-pressure system was centered over the Mid-Atlantic region, resulting in stable atmospheric conditions. No convective activity, turbulence, or significant weather systems were present along the flight path. The jet stream was located approximately 150 NM north of the accident site, with core winds exceeding 120 knots at FL350.

4.2 Terminal and En Route Data
The Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) automated weather observing system (AWOS) recorded the following METAR at 15:53 EDT: KPHL 171953Z 27008KT 10SM FEW045 18/04 A3012 RMK AO2 SLP198 T01830044. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) issued at 14:00 EDT indicated VFR conditions with winds from 260° at 10 knots, visibility 10 statute miles, and scattered clouds at 4,500 feet AGL. Pilot reports (PIREPs) along the route indicated smooth air, with no reports of icing, turbulence, or volcanic ash.

4.3 Atmospheric Parameters at Event Altitude
At 32,500 feet MSL, the standard atmospheric temperature was approximately -45°C, with a pressure altitude of 32,500 feet and a density altitude of 32,610 feet. The true airspeed (TAS) at Mach 0.78 was approximately 465 knots. Wind data from the aircraft's inertial reference system (IRS) indicated a 200-knot wind from 270° true, resulting in a 15-knot tailwind component. No meteorological anomalies were identified that would have contributed to the propulsion system failure.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Recovery
Debris from the left engine was distributed across a 12-NM radius from the event coordinates. Primary fragments, including sections of the fan cowl, inlet lip, and thrust reverser cascade, were recovered from agricultural fields and residential areas. The largest recovered component, a 4.2-foot section of the forward fan cowl, was located 8.3 NM west of the event site. All recovered debris was cataloged, photographed, and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for forensic examination. The aircraft fuselage exhibited a localized breach on the left side, aft of the L2 passenger door, measuring approximately 18 inches in length and 12 inches in width.

5.2 Engine Examination Findings
Examination of the left engine revealed an uncontained failure originating from the number 13 fan blade. The blade exhibited a fatigue fracture surface with distinct beach marks and a crack initiation site located at the leading edge of the dovetail root. The fracture propagated through approximately 65% of the blade cross-section before catastrophic separation occurred. The released blade impacted the fan case containment ring, which failed to retain the fragment. Radial scoring and gouging were observed on the inner fan case liner, consistent with high-energy debris ejection. The FADEC recorded a rapid N1 decay from 92.4% to 18.1% within 1.8 seconds, accompanied by a vibration spike exceeding 4.5 inches per second (IPS). The right engine operated normally throughout the event, with all parameters within green arc limits.

5.3 Fuselage and Cabin Examination
The fuselage breach resulted in rapid decompression, with cabin altitude climbing from 6,500 feet to 28,000 feet in approximately 4.2 seconds. The passenger oxygen system deployed automatically, with masks dropping from the overhead panels. The left-side window frame adjacent to the breach exhibited plastic deformation and stress cracking, with the outer pane completely separated. Interior examination revealed localized damage to seat 14A, including torn upholstery and displaced seat track hardware. The emergency descent was initiated at 15:43:45 EDT, with the aircraft descending to 10,000 feet MSL at a rate of approximately 4,200 feet per minute. The flight crew donned oxygen masks, declared an emergency, and executed the engine failure and rapid decompression checklists. All remaining passengers and crew survived the event, with one fatality attributed to the decompression event.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Procedures
Southwest Airlines maintains a comprehensive safety management system (SMS) that includes hazard reporting, risk assessment, and continuous monitoring of maintenance and operational data. The operator's maintenance control center (MCC) utilizes a computerized maintenance tracking system to schedule inspections, track component life limits, and manage airworthiness directive compliance. Crew resource management (CRM) training emphasizes standardized communication, checklist discipline, and emergency procedure execution. The operator's policy manual requires immediate reporting of any uncontained engine event, followed by a mandatory grounding of the affected aircraft pending engineering evaluation.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents
Historical data indicates that uncontained engine failures in high-bypass turbofan engines have occurred at a rate of approximately 0.00012 per 1,000 flight hours across the commercial fleet. Previous incidents involving fan blade fatigue fractures have prompted multiple airworthiness directives, enhanced inspection protocols, and revised maintenance intervals. The National Transportation Safety Board has investigated several similar events, with findings consistently pointing to high-cycle fatigue, manufacturing anomalies, or inspection limitations as contributing factors. The operator has implemented fleet-wide enhanced ultrasonic inspections and revised engine removal criteria in response to industry-wide safety recommendations.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The aircraft and engine were certified under 14 CFR Part 25 (Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes) and 14 CFR Part 33 (Airworthiness Standards: Aircraft Engines). Engine containment requirements are specified in § 33.94, which mandates that the engine must be designed and constructed to contain high-energy debris resulting from blade failure. Maintenance and inspection procedures are governed by § 121.373 and § 121.375, which require operators to establish and maintain an approved inspection program. Advisory Circular (AC) 33.28-1 provides guidance on engine containment testing and analysis, while AC 120-92 outlines safety management system implementation for air carriers. The Chief Inspector verified that all maintenance actions complied with the operator's approved maintenance program and applicable FAA directives. No deviations from regulatory requirements were identified in the pre-flight maintenance release or operational documentation.

NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD
SPECIALIST’S FACTUAL REPORT
POWERPLANTS AND STRUCTURES GROUP
REPORT NO: DCA18MA088-ENG-001
DATE: June 12, 2018

1. INTRODUCTION

This report documents the technical examination, material analysis, and flight data evaluation conducted by the NTSB Powerplants and Structures Specialist Group in support of the investigation into the in-flight uncontained engine failure involving a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines Co. (SWA), on April 17, 2018. The examination scope encompassed the left engine (CFM International LEAP-1B), recovered engine debris, fuselage penetration damage, cabin window assembly, and associated flight data recorder (FDR), cockpit voice recorder (CVR), and quick access recorder (QAR) parameters.

The physical examination of the powerplant components and airframe debris was conducted between May 2 and May 18, 2018, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and at the CFM International facility in Evendale, Ohio. Flight data decoding and parameter validation were performed at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory using standard ARINC 717/767 frame extraction protocols. All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB investigative procedures, FAA Advisory Circular 33.28-1, and applicable ASTM/AMS material testing standards. The objective of this report is to present factual findings derived from physical, metallurgical, and data analyses. No conclusions regarding probable cause are presented herein.

2. BACKGROUND

The accident aircraft was equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines. The left engine, part number (P/N) 321-456-789, serial number (S/N) 8842109, was installed on the aircraft on November 14, 2016. The LEAP powerplant is a high-bypass ratio, dual-spool turbofan featuring an 18-blade 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan, a titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) fan case, and an Inconel 718 containment ring. The engine is certified under 14 CFR Part 33, with containment requirements addressed in § 33.94. The airframe pressurization boundary, including passenger windows and door structures, is certified to 14 CFR Part 25, specifically referencing Section 25.783 for fuselage door and window structural integrity under differential pressure and impact loading conditions.

Maintenance records indicate the LEAP engine accumulated 18,420 total time since new (TTSN) and 11,205 total cycles since new (TCSN) at the time of the event. The most recent shop visit was performed on August 22, 2017, by Atlas Air, acting as the authorized maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) contractor. During that visit, the engine underwent a C-check, fan blade borescope inspection, and vibration baseline calibration. All work was documented per the CFM International Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) and FAA-approved repair station procedures. Engine health monitoring (EHM) data from the aircraft’s ACARS system showed nominal performance parameters through the 120 flight cycles preceding the event, with no recorded exceedances of N1, N2, exhaust gas temperature (EGT), or oil pressure limits.

The aircraft was operating at a cruise altitude of 32,500 feet MSL, Mach 0.78, with an indicated airspeed of 285 knots, when the uncontained failure occurred. The flight was en route from LaGuardia Airport (KLGA) to Dallas Love Field (KDAL).

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

3.1 Physical Examination of Recovered Components
The left engine was recovered in multiple segments. The fan case exhibited a primary breach measuring 14.2 inches (longitudinal) by 8.7 inches (circumferential) at the 10 o’clock position, approximately 18 inches aft of the fan frame. The breach edges displayed outward plastic deformation consistent with high-energy debris egress. The Inconel 718 containment ring, located radially outward of the fan case, showed localized yielding and circumferential scoring but remained structurally intact. Secondary debris fragments, including a 2.4-pound outboard fan blade segment, were recovered from the fuselage skin and cabin interior.

The fuselage skin at the point of impact (Station 412, Stringer 14) exhibited a 9.8 x 6.3 inch penetration through the 0.040-inch 2024-T3 Alclad aluminum skin. The surrounding structure showed radial tearing and fastener pull-through consistent with high-velocity impact. The adjacent cabin window assembly (P/N 737-41-0012) was completely dislodged from its frame. The polycarbonate inner pane exhibited brittle fracture with radial cracking originating from the outboard edge, while the outer glass pane remained intact but delaminated from the interlayer.

3.2 Nondestructive and Destructive Testing
All recovered metallic components underwent nondestructive testing (NDT) per ASTM E1444 (magnetic particle) and AMS 2644 (liquid penetrant). No additional cracking was identified in the fan disk, fan frame, or containment ring. The primary fan blade fragment was subjected to fractographic analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The fracture surface revealed a fatigue crack initiation site at the trailing edge root fillet, approximately 0.12 inches from the dovetail base. Beach marks and fatigue striations were clearly visible, indicating progressive crack growth over an estimated 1,800 to 2,200 cycles.

Chemical composition analysis of the fan blade root material confirmed compliance with AMS 4928 for Ti-6Al-4V ELI (Extra Low Interstitial). Tensile testing per ASTM E8 yielded a 0.2% offset yield strength of 128 ksi and an ultimate tensile strength of 138 ksi, both within manufacturer specifications. Fracture toughness testing per ASTM E399 determined a plane-strain fracture toughness (K_Ic) of 64.8 ksi√in. Crack growth rate analysis using the Paris law (da/dN = C(ΔK)^m) with C = 1.2x10^-11 and m = 3.1 indicated that the final fracture occurred when the stress intensity factor exceeded the critical threshold during a high-N1 cruise condition.

3.3 Material and Structural Analysis
The 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan blade exhibited matrix cracking and fiber pull-out at the impact interface. Micro-CT scanning revealed no manufacturing voids or delaminations exceeding 0.005 inches in the recovered sections. The fuselage window frame, constructed from 7075-T6 aluminum alloy, showed plastic deformation of 0.38 inches at the upper mounting lug. Fastener torque verification on adjacent window retainers measured 145 ± 5 in-lbs, consistent with Boeing Standard Practices Manual (BSPM) 20-10-01.

The containment ring’s Inconel 718 material was tested for high-temperature creep resistance per AMS 5662. Hardness measurements averaged 38.5 HRC, within the 36–42 HRC specification. No evidence of thermal degradation or oxidation was observed, confirming the debris egress occurred within the first 0.8 seconds of the failure event, prior to significant thermal exposure.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

4.1 Flight Data Recorder Parameters
The FDR was recovered intact and decoded using standard ARINC 717 frame extraction. Data was sampled at 1 Hz for primary engine parameters and 4 Hz for vibration and pressure differentials. The following parameters were analyzed:
- N1 (Fan Speed): 89.4% (pre-event) → 104.2% (T+0.0s) → 0% (T+1.2s)
- N2 (Core Speed): 91.1% → 98.7% → 12.3%
- EGT: 712°C → 985°C (T+0.3s) → 410°C (T+2.1s)
- Engine Vibration (1xN1): 0.18 ips → 4.82 ips (T+0.1s) → 0.00 ips
- Cabin Differential Pressure (ΔP): 8.2 PSI → 2.1 PSI (T+1.8s)
- Altitude: 32,500 ft MSL → 31,800 ft MSL (T+12s)
- Indicated Airspeed: 285 KIAS → 268 KIAS (T+8s)

4.2 Timeline Reconstruction
At 14:22:17.3 UTC, the FDR recorded a sudden 1xN1 vibration spike to 4.82 inches per second, coinciding with a 14.8% N1 overspeed and a 273°C EGT exceedance. The rapid N1 decay to 0% within 1.2 seconds indicates complete aerodynamic and mechanical disruption of the fan stage. Cabin ΔP dropped from 8.2 PSI to 2.1 PSI over 1.8 seconds, consistent with a 9.8-inch fuselage breach at 32,500 ft MSL. The outflow valve commanded to full open at T+0.4s per automatic pressurization logic. The aircraft initiated an emergency descent at T+0.9s, reaching 10,000 ft MSL at 14:28:41 UTC.

4.3 QAR and EHM Trend Analysis
Quick Access Recorder data was cross-referenced with the aircraft’s Engine Condition Monitoring (ECM) system. Over the preceding 120 cycles, a gradual increase in 1xN1 vibration was observed, rising from 0.12 ips to 0.24 ips. This trend remained within the manufacturer’s green band (0.00–0.35 ips) and did not trigger maintenance alerts. No oil pressure fluctuations, fuel flow anomalies, or core temperature deviations were recorded prior to the event. The data aligns with a progressive fatigue crack that reached critical length during a steady-state cruise condition.

4.4 CVR Audio Correlation
The CVR captured a sharp acoustic impulse at 14:22:17.1 UTC, followed by a 3-second period of high-frequency broadband noise consistent with uncontained debris impact and aerodynamic disruption. The master caution and cabin altitude warning activated at T+0.6s and T+1.1s, respectively. Crew callouts confirmed rapid decompression and immediate initiation of emergency descent procedures. Audio spectral analysis of the impact event showed peak energy at 1.2 kHz, correlating with the calculated debris velocity of approximately 1,150 ft/s at the point of fuselage penetration.

5. SUMMARY

The following factual findings are derived from the physical examination, material testing, and flight data analysis:

1. The left LEAP-1B engine (P/N 321-456-789, S/N 8842109) experienced an uncontained failure initiated by fatigue crack propagation in the outboard section of a Ti-6Al-4V ELI fan blade.
2. Fractographic analysis identified a crack initiation site at the trailing edge root fillet, with fatigue striations indicating progressive growth over approximately 1,800–2,200 cycles prior to final fracture.
3. The fan case sustained a 14.2 x 8.7 inch breach at the 10 o’clock position. The Inconel 718 containment ring exhibited localized yielding but remained intact, indicating secondary debris bypassed the primary containment path.
4. A 2.4-pound fan blade fragment penetrated the 0.040-inch 2024-T3 Alclad fuselage skin at Station 412, Stringer 14, creating a 9.8 x 6.3 inch opening.
5. The adjacent cabin window assembly was dislodged. The polycarbonate inner pane exhibited brittle fracture with radial cracking originating from the outboard edge. Structural fasteners and window frame deformation were consistent with high-velocity impact loading.
6. Material testing confirmed all recovered metallic components met applicable AMS and ASTM specifications for chemical composition, tensile strength, and fracture toughness. No manufacturing defects or corrosion were identified in the fan blade root region.
7. FDR data recorded a sudden N1 overspeed to 104.2%, EGT exceedance to 985°C, and 1xN1 vibration spike to 4.82 ips at 14:22:17.3 UTC. Cabin differential pressure decreased from 8.2 PSI to 2.1 PSI within 1.8 seconds.
8. QAR/ECM trend data showed a gradual increase in 1xN1 vibration over 120 cycles, remaining within manufacturer operational limits. No pre-event exceedances or maintenance alerts were recorded.
9. The aircraft was operating at 32,500 ft MSL, Mach 0.78, 285 KIAS at the time of failure. The emergency descent was initiated within 0.9 seconds of the event, consistent with standard operating procedures.
10. The structural response of the fuselage and window assembly to the debris impact was evaluated against 14 CFR § 25.783 certification requirements for pressurization boundary integrity. The observed damage pattern is consistent with localized high-energy penetration rather than systemic structural failure.

All examinations, tests, and data analyses were conducted in accordance with established NTSB investigative protocols, FAA engineering standards, and manufacturer technical documentation. This report contains factual findings only and does not address operational, maintenance, or regulatory factors beyond the scope of the specialist examination.

INTERVIEW OF FIRST OFFICER MARCUS J. THORNE
Date: May 14, 2018
Time: 10:15 AM EDT
Location: NTSB Regional Office, Fort Worth, Texas
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety

Q: Good morning, Mr. Thorne. Thank you for coming in today. This interview is being recorded for the official record of the Southwest Airlines Flight 1380 investigation. You understand the purpose of this interview and that your statements may be used in the investigation, correct?

A: Yes, ma'am. I understand. I’ve read the advisory, and I’m ready to answer whatever I can.

Q: Please state your full name, title, and your role on the flight in question.

A: Marcus James Thorne. I’m a First Officer with Southwest Airlines. I was the right-seat pilot on Flight 1380 on April 17th.

Q: Can you walk me through your pre-flight preparations that morning?

A: Sure. I reported to the crew room at, uh, Philadelphia International around 06:45. Standard stuff. Weather check, NOTAMs, fuel planning. The aircraft was a 737-700, tail number N772SW. We did the walk-around together, Captain Tammie and I. Everything looked normal. No deferred items, no maintenance write-ups that stood out. I remember checking the engine cowlings, the fan blades, the usual visual inspection. Nothing out of the ordinary. We pushed back around 07:10, I think. Maybe 07:12. We were running a bit behind schedule because of a late inbound, but nothing that affected our procedures.

Q: Take me to the cruise phase. What was the flight like before the event?

A: Smooth. Completely uneventful. We climbed out, got our initial clearance, and leveled off at flight level 325. That’s 32,500 feet. We were on autopilot, monitoring the systems, doing the routine cross-checks. The weather was clear, light turbulence maybe, but nothing significant. I was handling the radios, Captain was flying. We were about, I don’t know, twenty minutes out from our top of descent when it happened.

Q: Describe the moment of the event. What did you see, hear, and feel?

A: It was… it was instantaneous. One second everything’s normal, the next there’s this massive bang. Not like a tire blowout or a compressor stall. It was deeper. Louder. Like a cannon going off right outside the left window. The whole airframe shuddered. I felt a violent yaw to the left, and the aircraft immediately started rolling. The autopilot disengaged with the usual chime, but honestly, I barely registered it over the noise. The captain grabbed the yoke, called “my aircraft,” and I immediately took the throttles back on the left engine. I think I pulled it to idle, maybe even cut it off. I’m not entirely sure on the exact sequence because it all happened in, like, two seconds.

Then the decompression hit. You don’t really hear it as much as you feel it. The air just… ripped out of the cabin. It was like a vacuum. The temperature dropped instantly. I could hear the wind roaring, a high-pitched whistle, and then the oxygen masks deployed. I remember seeing the captain’s mask drop, and I pulled mine down, put it on, and established communication. I said “I have the aircraft,” and she said “you have it.” I was flying, she was running the emergency checklist.

Q: You mentioned a window. What did you observe regarding the cabin structure?

A: When I looked over my left shoulder, I could see… I could see daylight where the window should’ve been. The outer pane was gone. The inner pane was cracked, but it was holding, barely. There was debris, insulation, maybe some seat fabric, just whipping around in the slipstream. I could see a passenger in row 14, I think, leaning toward the opening. The flight attendants were already moving back there. I didn’t see the full extent until we were on the ground, but in the moment, it was just… it was chaos. The cabin pressure warning was screaming, the master caution was lit, and we were descending as fast as we could.

Q: What was your descent profile and communication with ATC?

A: We declared an emergency immediately. “Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, Southwest 1380, rapid decompression, descending to one-zero thousand, diverting to Philadelphia.” ATC cleared us instantly. We leveled off at 10,000, then 5,000, and started the approach. The left engine was shut down, we were on the APU, and the aircraft handled… well, it handled like a 737 with an engine out. Heavy, but controllable. We landed on Runway 27L. I’d say the whole thing, from the bang to wheels down, was maybe twelve, thirteen minutes. Roughly 10:43 to 10:56, if I’m remembering the clock right.

Q: After landing, what was your immediate focus?

A: Evacuation. We stopped on the runway, shut down the remaining engine, and the captain made the call to evacuate. I remember the slide deploying, the smell of jet fuel and ozone, the sound of the emergency equipment. We got everyone out. There was… there was one passenger who didn’t make it. The medical responders took over, and we secured the aircraft. I stayed with the captain until the NTSB and FAA teams arrived.

Q: I’d like to shift to some technical and regulatory context. During your training or maintenance briefings, were there discussions regarding engine certification standards or airworthiness directives that might relate to this event?

A: Yeah, we get regular updates. Southwest Airlines has a pretty robust safety management system, and we’re constantly briefed on ADs and service bulletins. I know the engine on this aircraft is a CFM56-7B, not the newer LEAP-1B that’s on the MAX series. The LEAP-1B has a different containment design, different fan blade geometry, but the CFM56s have been around forever. Still, you never get complacent. The certification under 14 CFR Part 25 requires that the engine casing contain debris in the event of a blade failure, but… well, uncontained failures are rare, and when they happen, they’re usually due to fatigue or manufacturing anomalies. We’re trained to expect the worst, but you don’t really expect it to happen to you.

Q: You mentioned Part 25. How does that relate to the fuselage and window design in your understanding?

A: Part 25 covers transport category airworthiness standards. The windows, the fuselage skin, the pressure bulkheads—they’re all designed to withstand a certain pressure differential and impact energy. The outer pane is structural, the inner is just a scratch pane. In this case, the debris clearly penetrated the outer pane and compromised the inner. I’m not an engineer, obviously, but from what I’ve read in the manuals, the certification assumes a certain level of containment. When that fails, the cabin takes the hit. The rapid decompression is exactly what the emergency procedures are built for, but the human factor… that’s the hard part.

Q: Have you ever operated under different regulatory frameworks, and if so, how does that compare to your current operational environment?

A: I did my early flying for a regional charter operator under 14 CFR Part 135. It’s a different world. Part 135 is more flexible, smaller aircraft, different maintenance tracking, different crew duty limits. When I moved to Southwest, we transitioned to Part 121, which is much more rigid, more standardized, more oversight. The training is deeper, the checklists are more comprehensive, and the maintenance programs are heavily regulated. But honestly, the fundamentals don’t change. You still fly the airplane, you still follow the procedures, you still prioritize safety. The regulations just give you the framework to do it consistently.

Q: Regarding maintenance and production oversight, are you familiar with how 14 CFR Part 21 applies to the aircraft and engine components involved?

A: I’m familiar with it in a general sense. Part 21 covers certification procedures for products and parts. It dictates how engines are type-certified, how production is approved, how airworthiness certificates are issued. When a component like a fan blade fails, the investigation always traces back to the manufacturing process, the inspection intervals, the material testing. I know Southwest’s maintenance team follows strict protocols, and the FAA audits them regularly. But again, I’m a pilot, not a metallurgist. I just know that when something like this happens, it’s usually a chain of events. A microscopic crack, a missed inspection, a stress cycle that exceeded the design life. The system is designed to catch it, but sometimes it slips through.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add about the event, your crew coordination, or the aftermath?

A: Just that… the crew resource management worked exactly as it’s supposed to. Captain and I didn’t have to talk much. We knew each other’s roles. She ran the checklist, I flew the airplane, we communicated clearly, and we got everyone on the ground safely. The flight attendants were incredible. They handled the cabin, they managed the passengers, they did everything right under impossible conditions. I don’t know what else to say. It was… it was a long day. I’ve been through simulator training for this exact scenario, but the reality is different. The noise, the pressure drop, the sight of the damage… it stays with you. But I’m grateful we had the training, the procedures, and the aircraft’s design to fall back on.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll review this transcript and may follow up with additional questions as the investigation progresses. Do you have any questions for us?

A: No, ma’am. I appreciate you taking the time. I just hope the findings help prevent this from happening again.

Q: We share that goal. This interview is concluded at 11:02 AM EDT.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY COMPLIANCE AND OVERSIGHT DIVISION
MEMORANDUM

TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector, Airworthiness Directorate
DATE: November 14, 2018
SUBJECT: REGULATORY RESPONSE TO UNCONTAINED ENGINE FAILURE AND RAPID DECOMPRESSION EVENT
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA18MA071; 14 CFR Parts 25, 33, 121; AD 2018-12-05; Docket No. FAA-2018-0452

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This memorandum constitutes the formal regulatory response, compliance assessment, and oversight directive regarding the uncontained engine failure event involving a Boeing 737-700, registration N772SW, operated by Southwest Airlines Co. (SWA), on April 17, 2018. The incident occurred during cruise flight at flight level 325 (32,500 feet MSL), resulting in fuselage penetration, rapid decompression, and one passenger fatality. This document addresses the applicable regulatory framework under 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, and Alterations), 14 CFR Part 33 (Airworthiness Standards: Engines), and 14 CFR Part 25 (Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes). Reference is made to NTSB Safety Recommendation A-18-014, FAA Docket No. FAA-2018-0452, and Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-12-05, issued under 14 CFR 39.13. All compliance actions herein are binding upon the operator, the type certificate holder, and the designated airworthiness representatives.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory oversight of transport category aircraft propulsion systems and cabin pressurization integrity is governed by a multi-tiered certification and operational framework. Under 14 CFR 33.94, engine type certification requires demonstration of containment capability under uncontained failure conditions, including high-energy debris trajectory analysis. Furthermore, 14 CFR 25.783 mandates fuselage structural integrity and window design standards to withstand debris impact and maintain pressurization during rapid decompression events. The operator, Southwest Airlines, maintains an FAA-approved Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP) pursuant to 14 CFR 121.369, which incorporates manufacturer-recommended service bulletins and mandatory AD compliance tracking.

Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration has issued multiple directives addressing high-cycle fatigue in turbofan engine fan blades and containment ring degradation. Prior to the April 2018 event, AD 2016-08-09 required ultrasonic inspection of specific engine fan blade dovetail regions. The LEAP-1B engine, manufactured by CFM International, holds Type Certificate No. E00015EN and is subject to ongoing airworthiness directives under 14 CFR Part 39. The operator’s Minimum Equipment List (MMEL), approved under 14 CFR 121.628, does not authorize dispatch with known structural or propulsion anomalies that compromise containment or pressurization integrity.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) initiated a major investigation under 49 CFR Part 831, with the Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) coordinating field examination, metallurgical analysis, and operational data review. Preliminary findings indicated accelerated low-cycle fatigue (LCF) propagation in a single fan blade, leading to catastrophic separation and subsequent uncontained release of high-energy debris. The debris trajectory intersected the left fuselage skin and a passenger window assembly, exceeding the design threshold for localized impact resistance as defined in 14 CFR 25.365 and 14 CFR 25.783.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive regulatory audit of Southwest Airlines Co. maintenance records, CAMP documentation, and AD compliance logs reveals substantial adherence to prescribed inspection intervals. However, the investigation identified critical gaps in the predictive maintenance paradigm and the regulatory framework governing high-cycle fatigue monitoring. Specifically, the operator’s reliance on time-based inspection thresholds, as mandated by the engine manufacturer’s Maintenance Planning Document (MPD), failed to account for anomalous operational stressors, including frequent short-haul cycles and rapid thermal transients.

The FAA’s oversight actions, conducted under 14 CFR 121.373 and 14 CFR 183.29, included a targeted surveillance audit of the operator’s engineering and maintenance control centers. The audit confirmed that all applicable ADs were incorporated into the operator’s maintenance tracking system within the regulatory compliance window. Nevertheless, the regulatory framework lacks a mandatory requirement for real-time engine health monitoring (EHM) data integration with airworthiness directives, creating a latency between anomaly detection and corrective action.

The Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) noted that the fuselage window assembly, while compliant with 14 CFR 25.783 at the time of type certification, did not incorporate redundant impact-resistant glazing or secondary containment barriers. The regulatory standard permits localized penetration under extreme uncontained failure scenarios, provided that rapid decompression does not result in catastrophic structural failure. However, the fatality resulting from the decompression event underscores a deficiency in the current regulatory threshold for passenger survivability during rapid pressure loss.

Furthermore, the operator’s MMEL and dispatch deviation procedures did not explicitly address the operational limitations associated with degraded engine containment margins. While 14 CFR 121.628 permits dispatch with certain inoperative equipment, the regulatory guidance does not mandate enhanced inspection protocols following high-energy debris events or uncontained failure precursors. This regulatory gap necessitates a revision to the operator’s approved maintenance program and the broader airworthiness directive framework.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to 14 CFR 39.13 and 14 CFR 121.369, the following corrective actions and compliance mandates are hereby established:

a. Mandatory Enhanced Inspection Protocol: Southwest Airlines shall implement an accelerated ultrasonic inspection regime for all LEAP-1B engine fan blades, reducing the inspection interval from 30,000 flight cycles to 15,000 flight cycles. This action shall be incorporated into the operator’s CAMP within 30 calendar days of this memorandum’s issuance, in accordance with AD 2018-12-05, Amendment 39-19342.

b. Real-Time EHM Integration: The operator shall deploy a certified engine health monitoring system capable of transmitting real-time vibration, temperature, and acoustic emission data to the maintenance control center. Compliance with this requirement shall be achieved within 180 days, pursuant to 14 CFR 121.344 and FAA Advisory Circular 120-79A.

c. Fuselage and Window Assembly Modification: The Type Certificate Holder shall develop and submit a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) application for reinforced passenger window assemblies and secondary debris containment barriers. The FAA will expedite review under 14 CFR 21.113 and 14 CFR 25.783. Operators shall incorporate the modification within 24 months of STC issuance.

d. MMEL and Dispatch Procedure Revision: The operator shall revise its FAA-approved MMEL to explicitly prohibit dispatch with any engine exhibiting EHM anomaly flags or exceeding prescribed vibration thresholds. The revised MMEL shall be submitted to the Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) for approval within 60 days, in compliance with 14 CFR 121.628 and FAA Order 8900.1, Volume 3, Chapter 18.

e. Regulatory Oversight and Follow-Up: The FAA’s Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) shall conduct quarterly compliance audits of the operator’s maintenance tracking system, EHM data utilization, and AD incorporation procedures. The Investigator-in-Charge (IIC) shall receive biannual progress reports detailing inspection completion rates, anomaly resolution timelines, and crew training updates related to rapid decompression emergency procedures.

Failure to achieve compliance within the stipulated timelines will result in enforcement action under 14 CFR 13.19 and potential suspension of operating certificates pursuant to 14 CFR 119.5. All corrective actions shall be documented in the FAA’s Safety Assurance System (SAS) and reported to the NTSB Office of Aviation Safety for ongoing investigation closure.

This memorandum constitutes the official regulatory response and shall be retained in the administrative docket for future rulemaking consideration under 14 CFR Part 11.

HEADLINE: Southwest Airlines Jet Makes Emergency Landing After Engine Failure Kills One Passenger

BYLINE: By Marcus Thorne, The National Chronicle
DATELINE: PHILADELPHIA —

A Southwest Airlines passenger jet bound for Texas made a harrowing emergency landing in Philadelphia on Tuesday after a catastrophic engine failure tore through the aircraft’s fuselage, killing one passenger and injuring several others. The Boeing 737-700, carrying 144 passengers and five crew members, was cruising at 32,500 feet when the left engine suffered an uncontained failure, sending high-velocity debris into the cabin and triggering a rapid loss of pressure.

The incident unfolded in seconds. A fractured fan blade from the engine broke apart, piercing the aircraft’s outer shell and shattering a cabin window. The sudden breach caused explosive decompression, violently pulling a passenger partially out of the window before fellow travelers and flight attendants pulled her back inside. Despite immediate medical attention, the woman later died from her injuries. The flight crew executed an emergency descent, diverting to Philadelphia International Airport, where the aircraft landed safely with its left engine severely damaged.

“Our hearts are with the family and friends of the passenger who lost her life today,” said a Southwest Airlines spokesperson in a statement released shortly after the landing. “We are cooperating fully with federal investigators and have grounded the affected aircraft for a thorough examination.” The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatched a team to Philadelphia to lead the probe. “We are treating this as a high-priority investigation,” said NTSB Chairman Robert Sumwalt during a press briefing. “The preliminary evidence points to an uncontained engine failure, and we will leave no stone unturned in determining the root cause.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) echoed the urgency, announcing immediate inspections of similar engines across the commercial fleet.

The aircraft, a 17-year-old Boeing 737-700 operated by the carrier, was en route from New York’s LaGuardia Airport to Dallas Love Field. The jet was powered by CFM International CFM56-7B turbofan engines, a workhorse of the narrow-body aviation industry. While this specific model predates newer engine designs like the LEAP-1B, which powers the latest generation of 737 MAX aircraft, both share similar certification pathways and maintenance protocols. The flight’s crew, highly trained in emergency procedures, managed to stabilize the aircraft despite the extreme aerodynamic and pressurization challenges.

Aviation safety experts suggest metal fatigue likely played a central role in the blade’s failure. “Uncontained engine failures are rare, but when they occur, they’re almost always traced to microscopic cracks that develop over thousands of flight cycles,” said Dr. Marcus Chen, an aerospace engineering professor at Purdue University. “The fan blades undergo immense centrifugal force, and without rigorous non-destructive testing, those cracks can propagate until catastrophic separation occurs.” Investigators will examine maintenance logs, engine manufacturing records, and the recovered debris to pinpoint whether the failure stemmed from a production flaw, maintenance oversight, or operational stress.

Inside the cabin, passengers described a scene of sheer terror followed by remarkable solidarity. “There was a deafening bang, and then the air just vanished,” said passenger David Miller, 42, who was seated three rows behind the damaged window. “Oxygen masks dropped, people were screaming, but the flight attendants were incredibly calm. They kept telling us to breathe and stay seated.” The deceased passenger, identified by family members as Jennifer Riordan, a 43-year-old mother of two from Albuquerque, New Mexico, was remembered as a devoted community volunteer. “She was the kind of person who always put others first,” her brother said in a tearful statement. “We are devastated, but we’re grateful to the passengers and crew who tried to save her.”

Commercial aviation has seen a handful of similar incidents over the decades, prompting sweeping regulatory changes. Following a series of fuel tank explosions in the 1990s, the FAA implemented Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88), a directive designed to mitigate ignition risks in aircraft fuel systems. While unrelated to engine failures, SFAR 88 exemplifies the industry’s iterative approach to safety. Engine certification and manufacturing standards are governed by Part 21 of the Federal Aviation Regulations, which outlines procedures for design approval and production oversight. Meanwhile, 14 CFR Part 25 establishes the rigorous airworthiness standards for transport-category aircraft, including requirements for containing engine debris and protecting the cabin from high-energy fragments. Despite these safeguards, the aviation industry continues to refine inspection techniques, particularly for aging fleets. For context, cargo operator Atlas Air and other commercial carriers have recently faced scrutiny over maintenance scheduling, highlighting the broader industry challenge of balancing operational demands with rigorous safety protocols.

The NTSB has recovered the fractured fan blade and is conducting metallurgical analysis at its laboratory in Washington, D.C. Southwest Airlines has voluntarily suspended flights for 118 aircraft equipped with the same engine model pending ultrasonic inspections. The FAA is expected to issue an emergency airworthiness directive within days, mandating accelerated inspection intervals for all CFM56-7B engines. “We are committed to transparency and will release findings as they become available,” Sumwalt said. “Until then, we urge the public to trust that our regulatory framework is working to ensure the skies remain safe.” As investigators piece together the timeline, the aviation community mourns a tragic loss while reaffirming its dedication to preventing future incidents.

1. INTRODUCTION

Southwest Airlines (SWA) submits this technical analysis to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in support of the investigative hearing regarding the April 17, 2018, uncontained engine failure event. As the operator of the subject Boeing 737-700, Southwest bears responsibility for the execution of its FAA-approved maintenance program, operational procedures, and crew training protocols. This submission outlines the Operator’s technical position, grounded in metallurgical evidence, maintenance records, flight data, and regulatory compliance frameworks. The scope of this document encompasses an engineering assessment of the MCAS engine failure mechanism, an evaluation of inspection methodologies and interval adequacy, an analysis of the rapid decompression event relative to cabin structural design criteria, and a review of the Operator’s adherence to applicable airworthiness and certification standards. Southwest Airlines approaches this investigation with full transparency, recognizing the tragic loss of life and the imperative to advance aviation safety through rigorous, evidence-based analysis. Our position is that the failure originated from a latent material anomaly within the fan blade assembly, which propagated below the detection threshold of industry-standard non-destructive testing (NDT) at the time of the last scheduled inspection. The Operator’s maintenance program, training protocols, and emergency response procedures were executed in strict accordance with approved manuals, manufacturer service bulletins, and federal regulations. This submission will demonstrate that while uncontained failures present inherent engineering challenges, Southwest’s safety management system (SMS) and compliance posture were robust, and that targeted industry-wide improvements in predictive maintenance and debris containment standards will yield the most meaningful safety gains.

On 17 April 2018, a Boeing 737-700 operated by Southwest Airlines experienced an uncontained engine failure during cruise at 32,500 feet. 1. SYNOPSIS
On April 17, 2018, at approximately 15:43 Eastern Daylight Time, a Boeing 737-700, operated by Southwest Airlines, experienced an uncontained engine failure while in cruise flight at an altitude of 32,500 feet. The event resulted in rapid cabin decompression, structural damage to the airframe, and one passenger fatality. The flight crew successfully executed an emergency descent and diverted to a nearby airport, where the aircraft landed without further incident.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information indicates that the left engine experienced a sudden, uncontained failure during the cruise phase of flight. Initial data recovered from the flight data recorder (FDR) suggests a rapid loss of engine parameters consistent with a fan blade separation event, though this remains subject to verification. Crew and passenger accounts, gathered through initial interviews, describe a loud acoustic event followed by significant airframe vibration, the immediate deployment of passenger oxygen masks, and visible damage to the left-side cabin window. The flight crew reported a rapid loss of cabin pressure and initiated an emergency descent in accordance with standard operating procedures.

Meteorological data obtained from the National Weather Service and air traffic control radar indicate that the aircraft was operating in generally benign en route conditions at the time of the occurrence. No significant convective activity, severe turbulence, or icing conditions were reported along the flight path. Preliminary examination of the airframe reveals that debris from the left engine penetrated the fuselage skin and compromised the structural integrity of a passenger window frame. The resulting rapid decompression appears to have caused localized interior damage and contributed to the fatal injury of one occupant. The remainder of the cabin sustained minor damage consistent with sudden pressure differential and emergency equipment deployment.

It is important to note that all findings documented herein are preliminary in nature. The sequence of events, mechanical conditions, and operational factors remain under active review and are subject to revision as additional evidence is collected and analyzed.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to examine the circumstances surrounding this occurrence. The following groups have been formally established and are currently conducting field and laboratory examinations: Powerplants, Structures, Systems, Operations, Human Performance, Survival Factors, and Air Traffic Control. Each group is operating under the direction of an NTSB Investigator-in-Charge and is adhering to established investigative protocols.

Parties to the investigation have been designated in accordance with standard NTSB procedures. Participating entities include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, Southwest Airlines Co. (SWA), the pilots’ union, the flight attendants’ union, and relevant maintenance and training organizations. All parties have been briefed on their roles, responsibilities, and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding investigative materials.

To date, the following evidence has been secured and is undergoing preliminary examination:
- The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and flight data recorder (FDR) have been recovered and transported to the NTSB laboratory for data extraction and validation.
- Recovered engine components, including fan blade fragments, cowling sections, and containment ring debris, have been cataloged and secured for metallurgical and dimensional analysis.
- Maintenance records, engine shop visit documentation, and operational logs for the affected aircraft and its powerplant have been requested and are currently under review.
- Airframe components, including the damaged fuselage panel and compromised window assembly, have been preserved for structural evaluation.

Planned examinations include a comprehensive teardown of the affected engine, detailed fractographic analysis of recovered metallic components, and a review of the aircraft’s compliance with applicable airworthiness directives and maintenance programs. Investigators will also evaluate the operational context, including crew training, emergency response procedures, and adherence to 14 CFR part 121 (Part 121) requirements. Additionally, the investigation will assess the applicability and implementation of Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) fuel tank safety provisions, as well as any relevant maintenance tracking protocols associated with the CFM International LEAP engine. All analytical processes will be conducted with the understanding that initial observations may evolve as testing progresses.

4. NEXT STEPS
The investigative teams will proceed with a structured series of technical evaluations and data reviews over the coming weeks. Priority activities include the complete readout and synchronization of CVR and FDR data, the initiation of engine teardown procedures at the manufacturer’s facility, and the continuation of metallurgical testing on recovered debris. Maintenance and operational records will be cross-referenced with manufacturer service bulletins and regulatory compliance documentation to establish a comprehensive maintenance and operational history.

Interviews with flight crew members, cabin crew, maintenance personnel, and air traffic controllers will continue, with a focus on clarifying the timeline of events, crew resource management, and emergency procedure execution. The Survival Factors group will conduct a detailed analysis of cabin pressure dynamics, oxygen system performance, and occupant injury mechanisms. The Structures group will perform finite element modeling and stress analysis to evaluate the fuselage damage progression and containment effectiveness.

A preliminary report summarizing the factual information gathered to date is anticipated to be released within thirty (30) days of the accident date, in accordance with NTSB policy. Subsequent updates will be issued as significant technical milestones are reached or as new information warrants public disclosure. The investigation will remain open until all technical analyses are complete, all contributing factors are evaluated, and safety recommendations, if warranted, are formulated.

All conclusions, causal determinations, and safety recommendations remain strictly preliminary at this stage. The findings documented in this report are based on early-stage data collection and are subject to change as the investigation advances. The NTSB will continue to coordinate with all participating parties and regulatory agencies to ensure a thorough, objective, and scientifically rigorous examination of the occurrence.
